context_blocks.text: A graph search usually remembers which vertices it has visited. With only logarithmic space, it can store a constant number of vertex names and counters, but cannot keep a separate visited bit for every vertex. The input may be rescanned as often as necessary. The challenge is to organize those repeated scans so that arbitrary directed paths can be detected without retaining a large search frontier.

Nondeterminism gives a simple logarithmic-space procedure: keep the current vertex and a length counter, guess the next edge, and accept if t is reached within n−1 edges. Any reachable target has a simple path within that bound. For a general nondeterministic logspace computation, vertices can instead represent machine configurations. An accepting computation becomes a directed path, explaining why this graph problem captures the whole class NL.

Savitch’s algorithm recursively asks whether a path can pass through a candidate midpoint. It saves space by recomputing subproblems, but a logarithmic recursion depth with logarithmic information per level uses O(log² n) space. Its running time is quasipolynomial. Reducing the storage to a single logarithmic factor would also force polynomial time in the stated machine model.

For undirected graphs, Reingold already achieved the logarithmic target. Edge direction is therefore a substantive part of this card. Likewise, NL=coNL shows that nonreachability has a nondeterministic logspace procedure; it does not remove nondeterminism. Recent connections with random-walk estimation make the landscape richer, while leaving the same deterministic directed question.

cards.title: Sliding-scale PCP conjecture
cards.formal: Do constants a,b,c>0 and q≥1 exist such that 3-SAT has a verifier using at most a log₂(N+2) random bits and q queries to a proof of at most (N+2)^b symbols over an alphabet of size at most (N+2)^b, with perfect completeness and soundness at most (N+2)^(−c)?
cards.definitions: N is the bit length of an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula. A uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier receives the input, a uniform random bit string and oracle access to a fixed proof string. It reads at most q alphabet symbols, each encoded with O(log N) bits, and accepts or rejects. Queries may be adaptive. On a satisfiable formula some proof is always accepted; on an unsatisfiable formula every proof has acceptance probability at most (N+2)^(−c). Polynomial bounds and all constants are universal. No cryptographic soundness assumption or interaction is allowed.

context_blocks.text: The PCP theorem achieves constant error with a constant number of queries. Driving soundness down to an inverse polynomial while retaining a constant number of queries would give substantially stronger verification and constraint-satisfaction gaps.

Dinur, Harsha and Kindler obtain inverse-polynomial error with polyloglogarithmically many queries. Their paper explicitly names the constant-query polynomial-alphabet endpoint as the sliding-scale conjecture in this regime. This is different from asking that a constant-error PCP have linear proof length.

cards.why: A central quantitative PCP barrier controlling the strength of gap amplification and inapproximability.

cards.title: P_R versus NP_R in the Blum–Shub–Smale model
cards.formal: Is P_ℝ=NP_ℝ for the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered field of real numbers?
cards.definitions: Inputs are finite tuples x∈ℝ^n, with input size n. A machine has a finite program and finitely many fixed real constants. It can store and copy real numbers, perform +, −, ×, and division by a nonzero number, and branch on the sign or equality to zero of a stored real, at unit cost per operation; the ordinary BSS input, output and register-shift operations are included. P_ℝ consists of subsets of the disjoint union of the spaces ℝ^n decidable by one such deterministic machine in polynomially many steps as a function of n. NP_ℝ consists of sets for which membership of x is equivalent to existence of a real witness y of length bounded by a polynomial in n that is accepted by one deterministic BSS verifier in polynomially many steps. Machine constants are finite and independent of input length; witnesses may contain arbitrary reals. The target is equality of these classes, not equality in a finite-precision or bit-cost model.

context_blocks.text: The BSS model treats exact field operations and order tests as elementary computation. Its version of nondeterminism allows real witnesses and captures basic real algebraic feasibility problems.

This separation is a foundational question about algebraic computation over a continuum. Classical P versus NP does not by itself answer it: the input representation, cost model and certificates differ.

cards.title: CLS versus FP
cards.formal: Does CLS⊆FP? Equivalently, is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the following Either-Solution problem: given an End-of-Line instance and an independent Localopt instance, return a valid solution of at least one of them?
cards.definitions: Every circuit is an explicitly encoded acyclic Boolean circuit with fan-in-two AND/OR, NOT, constants, listed wires and ordered input/output nodes. An End-of-Line instance consists of S,P:{0,1}^n→{0,1}^n, n≥1, satisfying P(0^n)=0^n and S(0^n)≠0^n. An accepted output is a bit string v∈{0,1}^n with P(S(v))≠v, or with both v≠0^n and S(P(v))≠v. In particular v=0^n is permitted only for the first condition. A Localopt instance consists of T:{0,1}^m→{0,1}^m and V:{0,1}^m→{0,1}^r, with m,r≥1. Treat V’s output as an unsigned binary integer; an accepted local-search output is w with V(T(w))≥V(w). The joint instance contains both independent sets of circuits; n,m,r may differ. A solution is a tag selecting one instance and a string meeting that instance’s condition. On malformed encodings or failure of the two easily checkable End-of-Line conditions, output INVALID; on a valid joint instance INVALID is forbidden. The algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial in the combined encoded length, including all circuit input/output nodes. It receives no advice, randomness or oracle. Total NP search problems are polynomially bounded input-output relations with polynomial-time verifiable outputs and at least one output for each input. A reduction maps an input to an instance and transforms every valid answer back to a valid original answer, using deterministic polynomial time for both maps. PPAD and PLS are the classes reducing to End-of-Line and Localopt respectively. The source proves that the either-solution problem is complete for their intersection and that CLS=PPAD∩PLS. These equalities give the stated equivalent discrete formulation of CLS⊆FP; no new smoothness or numerical promise is introduced.

context_blocks.text: CLS captures total search tasks motivated by continuous local improvement. Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender and Savani proved that it equals PPAD∩PLS, connecting this optimization class to two discrete existence principles.

The equivalent task presented here gives two independent succinct problems and asks for a solution to either one. The known completeness theorem means that an efficient algorithm for this task would solve every problem in CLS. The theorem identifies the class; it does not supply a polynomial-time solution algorithm.

cards.title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer b≥2 and every real x∈[0,1), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?
cards.why: A proof would impose a strong arithmetic restriction on numbers generated at the fastest possible asymptotic output rate. The checked 2024 source also records that the conjecture would rule out linear-time integer multiplication on multitape Turing machines.

progress.text: Linear-time and real-time sequence generation are shown to coincide for multitape machines.
The published revisiting paper proves transcendence restrictions for pushdown and exponential-growth morphic models.
ICALP work proves additional word-based transcendence results while explicitly retaining the full conjecture.
Automata compute digits from specially represented inputs; a June thesis abstract still describes the general conjecture as open.

cards.definitions: Write x=∑_{n≥1}d_n b^(−n), where d_n∈{0,…,b−1}, using the unique expansion that is not eventually all b−1; a terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means x=p/q for integers p,q with q≠0. Algebraic means P(x)=0 for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant C≥1 such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing t_n for the step at which d_n appears, 1≤t_(n+1)−t_n≤C for every n≥1. The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.

context_blocks.title: A steady stream of digits
context_blocks.text: For example, 1/7=0.142857142857… in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, √2−1 is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies x²+2x−1=0. The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

context_blocks.title: The finite description is not the resource bound
context_blocks.text: The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

context_blocks.title: Why sources also say linear time
context_blocks.text: Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

context_blocks.title: What the partial results establish
context_blocks.text: Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The input representation matters
context_blocks.text: The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from b^n supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.

sentences: The question concerns a fixed machine that prints all digits of a real number with bounded delay between outputs.
Every rational number permits this because its expansion is eventually periodic.
The conjecture says that any irrational number generated this quickly must be transcendental.
It quantifies over unrestricted deterministic multitape machines, beyond the restricted automata covered by known partial results.
A proof would connect the arithmetic nature of numbers to a stringent computation bound and rule out linear-time integer multiplication.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant C≥1 such that, for every integer n≥1, the function S_n:{0,1,2}^n→{0,1,2}^n that removes all symbols 2 and appends the same number of 2s on the right, preserving the order of the other symbols, is computed by a Boolean circuit with at most Cn gates in the model below?
cards.definitions: Encode symbols 0,1,2 as 00,01,10 respectively. The circuit has 2n input bits and 2n output bits, with arbitrary fan-out, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and optional Boolean constant gates. Size counts all non-input gates, including constants; wires and output designations cost nothing. Correctness is required only on concatenations of the three valid encodings; output on inputs containing 11 is unrestricted. If i_1<...<i_m are exactly the indices with a_i≠2, the required decoded output is a_(i_1)...a_(i_m) followed by n−m copies of 2. In particular, 0s and 1s retain their relative order. The circuit may depend on n; no uniform construction algorithm, depth bound, monotonicity restriction or indivisible-record model is imposed. The constant C is independent of n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.

importance.reason: A specific circuit-size barrier beyond generic lower-bound statements; stable compaction connects elementary data movement with unrestricted Boolean computation.

cards.title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space simultaneously
cards.formal: Does there exist a computable compiler that takes any deterministic multitape Turing machine M to a reversible multitape machine R such that the following holds? For each M there are constants c_M >= 1 and an integer d_M >= 1 so that, on every input x on which M halts, R halts with the pair (x,M(x)), uses at most c_M S_M(x) tape cells, and takes at most c_M T_M(x)^{d_M} steps. R must not halt on an input on which M does not halt. Here S_M counts total storage including input and output, and T_M is at least the input length, as defined below.
cards.definitions: Machines have a finite state set, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary input symbols and a blank, and a fixed finite number of tapes and heads. Each step reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols, and moves each head by at most one cell. The complete configuration includes state, tapes, and head positions. Reversible means the partial one-step function on configurations is injective. The input x is initially present with delimiters on one tape and all other tapes are blank. M has a designated finite binary output on halting. S_M(x) is the number of cells initially occupied or visited on any tape during that run, with a minimum of 1; input and output cells are included. T_M(x) is max(1,|x|,number of transitions). Apply the same storage convention to R. Its output tapes retain x and M(x), and all auxiliary tapes are blank on termination. The compiler must halt on every finite syntactically valid machine description; its own running time is unrestricted. Simulation here preserves the computed partial function, not every intermediate configuration. The overhead constants may depend on M but not on x.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that such a compiler and bounds exist, or prove that no such compiler can satisfy them for all deterministic machines. Both resource guarantees must hold simultaneously for the same reversible simulation.
cards.why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

importance.reason: A basic simultaneous-resource question about reversible computation, connecting time-space complexity with the informational cost of computation.

context_blocks.text: Saving the input is necessary when the simulated function is many-to-one: reversible configurations cannot merge different initial inputs into one final configuration. Counting input and output storage prevents free external memory from changing the target.

Known general simulations occupy different parts of the time-space tradeoff. Polynomial-time simulations use more than linear space in general; a simulation with O(S) space can take exponential time. The requested conjunction does not follow from either result separately.

The compiler formulation makes the simulation uniform across inputs, while allowing machine-dependent constants. It is the polynomial-time, linear-space version requested here, rather than a demand for nearly linear time.

context_blocks.text: IP = PSPACE alone does not guarantee that producing the proof costs only a polynomial in the original computation time.

Interactive proofs separate the effort of checking a computation from the effort of producing a convincing transcript. The usual class equality allows an honest prover to use enormous resources. cards.title: Formula versus circuit noise thresholds
cards.formal: For p in [0,1/2), let Reliable(p) mean that there exists a constant delta>0 such that for every n>=1 and every Boolean function f:{0,1}^n->{0,1}, some finite circuit C of the kind below satisfies Pr[C(x)=f(x)]>=1/2+delta for every input x. Is Reliable(p) true exactly for p<(3-sqrt(7))/4? In particular, is it false at the boundary as well as above it?
cards.definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input sources x_1,...,x_n, constant sources 0 and 1, gates of fan-in at most two, and one designated output wire. Any Boolean function of a gate's input bits is allowed. Each gate is evaluated once in topological order and independently flips its correct Boolean output with probability exactly p. All outgoing wires from that gate carry the same resulting bit; reuse does not generate fresh independent copies. Inputs, constants, and wires are noiseless. Every computational gate, including the output gate when present, obeys the noise rule; there is no extra noiseless decoder. Fan-out is unrestricted, and different incoming paths may share gates. C may depend on p,n,f but not on x. Its size and construction time are unrestricted. The probability is solely over independent gate failures. Delta may depend on p but is common to all n,f,x. A formula is the restricted case in which computational gates have fan-out at most one, with input variables still allowed to occur repeatedly.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the stated equivalence for the full interval 0<=p<1/2, including p=(3-sqrt(7))/4. A proof or refutation must use the specified independent gate-flip model and a uniform positive correctness advantage across all functions.
cards.why: The problem asks how much unreliable local computation can be tolerated when arbitrary redundancy and reuse are available. It would determine whether sharing intermediate noisy values changes the fundamental threshold already known for formulas.

importance.reason: A sharp reliability boundary for general classical computation, separating the effects of gate errors from circuit size and design effort.

context_blocks.text: The success advantage must be fixed before choosing a function or its number of inputs. Allowing it to shrink with the function would describe a much weaker task. The noisy output itself is read, so the target does not assume an unlimited perfect final computation.

Unger establishes the exact threshold for two-input formulas, extending the earlier NAND-gate result, and conjectures the same threshold for circuits. Shared subcomputations correlate wire values even though the underlying gate failures are independent.

Later work studies asymmetric noise on AND and XOR gates and relates reliability to amplification. Its different gate-specific error assumptions and formula bounds do not settle the common-noise, unrestricted-fan-out proposition here.

progress.text: Unger proves the formula threshold (3-sqrt(7))/4, including impossibility at equality, and states the circuit extension as a conjecture.

cards.title: Closure of d-DNNF under negation
cards.formal: Do a constant c>0 and an integer k>=1 exist such that, for every finite variable set X and every d-DNNF circuit C over X of size s, there is a d-DNNF circuit D over X of size at most c(s+1)^k computing the Boolean complement of C on every assignment X->{0,1}? No algorithm for finding D within that bound is required.
cards.definitions: An NNF circuit is a finite rooted directed acyclic graph whose leaves are constants 0,1 or literals x,not-x for x in X, and whose internal nodes are AND or OR gates. Edges run from a gate to its inputs. The variable set of a subcircuit comprises the variables occurring in its reachable literals. Decomposable means that the input subcircuits of every AND gate have pairwise disjoint variable sets. Deterministic means that no assignment to X makes two different inputs of any OR gate both true. A d-DNNF satisfies both properties. Size is the total number of vertices plus edges; fan-in is arbitrary and part of that size. Evaluation has the usual Boolean meaning. No negation gates above leaves, additional variables, or requirement of compatibility with a common variable decomposition tree is allowed. Constants c,k are independent of X and C. The output D may use any decompositions meeting these conditions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal polynomial size bound, or prove that no constants c,k satisfy it. Algorithmic difficulty of producing a small complement alone does not refute this size-existence statement.
cards.why: Deterministic decomposable circuits represent Boolean solution sets while supporting exact counting. Closure under complement asks whether a compact representation of satisfying assignments necessarily gives a comparably compact representation of nonsatisfying assignments, independently of construction time.

importance.reason: A central representational-closure question in knowledge compilation that separates succinctness from the cost of performing a logical operation.

context_blocks.text: Decomposability prevents conjunctions from sharing variables and determinism prevents disjunctions from sharing satisfying assignments. Negating a circuit syntactically need not preserve both properties.

Structured d-DNNFs additionally respect a variable decomposition tree. The 2024 negative result for that restricted class cannot be transferred automatically to unrestricted d-DNNF, since a complementary circuit here may use other decompositions.

The STACS 2026 discussion retains complementation as an open question. The separate algorithmic question asks for a polynomial-time procedure producing the complement. Such a procedure implies the size bound on this card; the converse is not established. Both targets are retained because an existence theorem would settle a representation barrier without necessarily supplying the algorithmic transformation.
The stronger polynomial-time construction question is retained as TCS-0306. The existence of small complementary circuits does not by itself give an efficient algorithm for constructing them.

references.locator: Problem 2

cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula, as permitted by the source’s SAT convention. To fix a binary representation, encode a literal by a sign bit (0 for xᵢ, 1 for ¬xᵢ), followed by the positive index i in Elias gamma code: ⌊log₂i⌋ zero bits followed by the ordinary binary representation of i. Consecutive triples of literals are clauses, and the formula is their conjunction. Repeated literals and clauses are allowed, the empty conjunction is true, and malformed strings are rejected. SATₙ:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} is 1 exactly for strings encoding satisfiable formulas. The parameter n counts all encoding bits, including signs and indices, rather than the number of distinct variables or clauses. This explicit binary-list convention fixes the source’s otherwise implicit SAT representation. A De Morgan formula is a rooted tree with AND and OR gates of fan-in two. Each leaf is an input bit, its negation, or a Boolean constant. Equivalently, unary NOT gates can be used anywhere and then pushed to the leaves without changing the leaf count. Internal computations cannot be shared between two parents. Its size is the number of leaf occurrences, so repeated uses of the same variable are charged separately. All input strings must be answered exactly. A family is LOGTIME-uniform when one deterministic machine, given binary n and a binary position j, returns the requested bit of the description of its n-input formula or circuit in O(log n) time, on a standard multitape Turing machine; positions outside the description return zero. Descriptions are explicit binary netlists: a header gives the number of nodes and the output node, nodes have consecutive binary identifiers and gate-type records, and a list gives each wire’s source, destination and input port, with negation flags when applicable. Each integer field is self-delimited in binary. Input-node records give their input-bit indices or a constant 0 or 1. The family may choose a consistent numbering but must have one such uniform description algorithm for every n. There is no advice and no randomness. Polynomial-size candidate families have polynomial-length descriptions and O(log n)-bit identifiers; the machine’s description and running-time constant are independent of n. The exponent ε is chosen once, before quantifying over families and their uniformity machines. A family has O(n^(3+ε)) leaves if some constant C bounds its size by Cn^(3+ε) for all sufficiently large n. Constants may depend on the family and ε, but not n. The source writes “requires” such size; the formal statement adopts uniform-class nonmembership, equivalently arbitrarily large failures of each candidate big-O bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that there is a fixed ε>0 for which every correct LOGTIME-uniform De Morgan formula family has, for every C>0 and every N₀, some n≥N₀ with more than Cn^(3+ε) leaves. Alternatively, refute this by proving that for every ε>0 some correct LOGTIME-uniform family has O(n^(3+ε)) leaves. The target is exact worst-case computation of SAT, with the stated basis, uniformity and size measure.

cards.title: Subquadratic deterministic simulation of nondeterministic space
cards.formal: For every space-constructible function s:ℕ→ℕ with s(n)≥⌈log₂(n+2)⌉, is every language in NSPACE(O(s(n))) decidable deterministically in o(s(n)²) space? Equivalently, for each such s and each language L accepted by an O(s(n))-space nondeterministic machine, must there exist one deterministic decider D for L whose maximum workspace g_D(n) on n-bit inputs satisfies lim(n→∞) g_D(n)/s(n)²=0?
cards.why: Would improve the general memory overhead for eliminating nondeterminism beyond a theorem that has stood since 1970. Even a slowly vanishing improvement would sharpen a basic relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic computation, including the logarithmic-space regime.
cards.status_note: Full source question read and standard space conventions made explicit. cards.definitions: Inputs are binary strings of length n. Machines have a finite control, a two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space is the maximum total number of visited work-tape cells; the read-only input itself is not charged. Machines are uniform, with no advice, random bits, oracle or uncharged auxiliary memory. Nondeterministic machines have finitely many possible next moves, accept exactly when some branch accepts, and halt on every branch; the space bound applies to every branch and every input of length n. NSPACE(O(s(n))) denotes languages with such a machine using at most C s(n) cells for some fixed C and all sufficiently large n. A deterministic decider must halt on every input, with no imposed running-time bound. A function s is space-constructible here if a deterministic machine on 1ⁿ can output 1^s(n) using O(s(n)) work cells, with output written on a separate write-only tape. The standard at-least-logarithmic space-constructible regime of Savitch’s theorem supplies the source’s implicit parameter convention. The little-o containment means that the decider and its improvement rate may depend on L and s. It does not require a fixed exponent saving s^(2−ε) or one common improvement rate for all languages.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed containment for every admitted space bound and every nondeterministic language, with deterministic workspace little-o of s(n)². Alternatively, refute it by identifying an admitted s and a language in NSPACE(O(s(n))) for which no deterministic decider has that little-o space bound. A constant-factor saving in s(n)², a simulation of only a special graph family, or a bound that excludes separately supplied catalytic memory does not meet the stated guarantee.

context_blocks.title: What nondeterminism costs in memory
context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic machine can choose among several next moves and accepts if some sequence of choices succeeds. A deterministic simulation must decide the same question without those choices. Savitch’s theorem shows that squaring the workspace is enough, even though the simulation may take much longer.

context_blocks.title: Any vanishing fraction would count
context_blocks.text: If a nondeterministic computation uses about s cells, the target is a deterministic simulation whose memory divided by s² tends to zero. A bound such as s²/log(s+2) would qualify, while 0.01s² would not. These expressions illustrate the meaning of little-o; the question imposes no particular rate of improvement.

context_blocks.title: The logarithmic-space case
context_blocks.text: For s(n) of order log n, the target becomes deterministic o(log² n) space for every language in nondeterministic logarithmic space. This includes directed reachability: given a directed graph and two vertices, decide whether there is a directed path between them. The full card quantifies over all admitted s and does not restrict inputs to a special graph family.

context_blocks.title: Where tree evaluation fits in the history
context_blocks.text: The source was posed after Cook and Mertz’s STOC 2024 improvement for tree evaluation. That problem evaluates a tree of explicitly supplied functions and leaf values, and its stated space bound is O(log N·log log N) in the tree-evaluation input size N. The general nondeterministic-space simulation remains the target of the 2025 question.

context_blocks.title: Conditional progress
context_blocks.text: The 2025 connectivity paper states alternatives linking improvements in reachability and derandomization. Its abstract does not give an unconditional simulation of every nondeterministic-space computation in o(s²) space.

context_blocks.title: Catalytic memory is an additional resource
context_blocks.text: A 2026 directed-reachability preprint trades ordinary workspace against catalytic memory, which begins with arbitrary contents and must be restored. Its abstract does not state the requested improvement in total ordinary workspace.

cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula, as permitted by the source’s SAT convention. To fix a binary representation, encode a literal by a sign bit (0 for xᵢ, 1 for ¬xᵢ), followed by the positive index i in Elias gamma code: ⌊log₂i⌋ zero bits followed by the ordinary binary representation of i. Consecutive triples of literals are clauses, and the formula is their conjunction. Repeated literals and clauses are allowed, the empty conjunction is true, and malformed strings are rejected. SATₙ:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} is 1 exactly for strings encoding satisfiable formulas. The parameter n counts all encoding bits, including signs and indices, rather than the number of distinct variables or clauses. This explicit binary-list convention fixes the source’s otherwise implicit SAT representation. A depth-three majority circuit is an acyclic circuit with at most three majority gates on every input-to-output path. A majority gate with k≥1 incoming wires outputs 1 exactly when at least ⌈k/2⌉ of its inputs are 1. Input bits and constants 0,1 are available, and wires may be negated; NOT gates do not add a majority layer. This is the usual MAJORITY/NOT convention, with negations represented on wires. Wires may repeat the same source, but every occurrence is charged. Size is the total number of wires entering majority gates, including wires from input nodes, constants and other gates; it is not the gate count. Fan-in and fan-out are otherwise unrestricted, and there are no arbitrary real weights. All input strings must be answered exactly. A family is LOGTIME-uniform when one deterministic machine, given binary n and a binary position j, returns the requested bit of the description of its n-input formula or circuit in O(log n) time, on a standard multitape Turing machine; positions outside the description return zero. Descriptions are explicit binary netlists: a header gives the number of nodes and the output node, nodes have consecutive binary identifiers and gate-type records, and a list gives each wire’s source, destination and input port, with negation flags when applicable. Each integer field is self-delimited in binary. Input-node records give their input-bit indices or a constant 0 or 1. The family may choose a consistent numbering but must have one such uniform description algorithm for every n. There is no advice and no randomness. Polynomial-size candidate families have polynomial-length descriptions and O(log n)-bit identifiers; the machine’s description and running-time constant are independent of n. The exponent ε is chosen once, before quantifying over families and their uniformity machines. A family has O(n^(5/2+ε)) wires if some constant C bounds its size by Cn^(5/2+ε) for all sufficiently large n. Constants may depend on the family and ε, but not n. The source writes “requires” such size; the formal statement adopts uniform-class nonmembership, equivalently arbitrarily large failures of each candidate big-O bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that there is a fixed ε>0 for which every correct LOGTIME-uniform depth-three MAJORITY/NOT circuit family has, for every C>0 and every N₀, some n≥N₀ with more than Cn^(5/2+ε) wires. Alternatively, refute this by proving that for every ε>0 some correct LOGTIME-uniform family has O(n^(5/2+ε)) wires. The target is exact worst-case computation of SAT, with the stated basis, uniformity and size measure.

context_blocks.title: A quantitative lower bound for satisfiability
context_blocks.text: The object computing SAT receives the bits of a formula and outputs whether some assignment satisfies it. This card asks whether even a uniformly described depth-three MAJORITY/NOT circuit must exceed the n^5/2 scale by a fixed positive exponent. The circuit or formula that decides SAT is distinct from the 3-CNF formula encoded in its input.

context_blocks.title: What is being counted
context_blocks.text: A single majority gate on n inputs has n incoming wires. A circuit can therefore have few gates and many connections. The source asks for a wire bound above n^(5/2); a statement about gate count alone has a different numerical scale.

context_blocks.title: Uniformity constrains the whole family
context_blocks.text: A separate small circuit for every input length could contain information chosen independently at each length. LOGTIME-uniformity requires one short-running algorithm to describe all those circuits locally. The input to that description algorithm is the input length and a position in the description, not a particular SAT instance.

context_blocks.title: A fixed exponent, with a stated asymptotic convention
context_blocks.text: The question is whether SAT lies outside the uniform size-O(n^(5/2+ε)) class for some fixed ε>0. Thus every correct uniform family must exceed any constant multiple of that bound at arbitrarily large lengths. This uses the standard class-nonmembership interpretation of the source’s lower-bound question; it does not add an almost-everywhere requirement.

context_blocks.title: Dated progress and its scope
context_blocks.text: Kane and Williams prove a wire lower bound of order n^(5/2) divided by a power of log n for an explicit function Bn against a class containing depth-three majority circuits. The 2016 column separately asks for SAT to exceed the 5/2 exponent under LOGTIME-uniformity. A lower bound for Bn cannot simply be relabeled as that stronger uniform SAT bound.

cards.context:
The object computing SAT receives the bits of a formula and outputs whether some assignment satisfies it. This card asks whether even a uniformly described depth-three MAJORITY/NOT circuit must exceed the n^5/2 scale by a fixed positive exponent. The circuit or formula that decides SAT is distinct from the 3-CNF formula encoded in its input.

A single majority gate on n inputs has n incoming wires. A circuit can therefore have few gates and many connections. The source asks for a wire bound above n^(5/2); a statement about gate count alone has a different numerical scale.

A separate small circuit for every input length could contain information chosen independently at each length. LOGTIME-uniformity requires one short-running algorithm to describe all those circuits locally. The input to that description algorithm is the input length and a position in the description, not a particular SAT instance.

The question is whether SAT lies outside the uniform size-O(n^(5/2+ε)) class for some fixed ε>0. Thus every correct uniform family must exceed any constant multiple of that bound at arbitrarily large lengths. This uses the standard class-nonmembership interpretation of the source’s lower-bound question; it does not add an almost-everywhere requirement.

Kane and Williams prove a wire lower bound of order n^(5/2) divided by a power of log n for an explicit function Bn against a class containing depth-three majority circuits. The 2016 column separately asks for SAT to exceed the 5/2 exponent under LOGTIME-uniformity. A lower bound for Bn cannot simply be relabeled as that stronger uniform SAT bound.

cards.title: Polynomial-time weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that solves the following problem? The input consists of an unambiguous DNF $F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j$ over n Boolean variables, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n encoded in binary, and an integer threshold t encoded in binary. Decide whether there exists $a\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that $F(a)=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t$. Each T_j is an explicitly listed conjunction of literals. Unambiguous means that no assignment satisfies two distinct terms simultaneously.
cards.definitions: A literal is either x_i or its negation. A term is true exactly when all its literals are true; the DNF is true when at least one term is true. Contradictory terms can be discarded. For the remaining terms, unambiguity is equivalent to every pair containing opposite literals on some variable, so this promise is itself checkable in polynomial time. Weights are exact integers, with no rounding. The running time must depend polynomially on their bit lengths rather than on their numerical sum. The threshold uses at least, not exactly; a strict-threshold formulation is equivalent by shifting the integer threshold by one. The output is a yes/no answer. A tautology has no falsifying assignment and always gives no, regardless of the threshold.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all such inputs, or prove that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-hardness proof would provide a negative answer conditional on P differing from NP; its assumption must be stated. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a method only for unweighted assignments, or hardness after changing the comparison to exact equality does not settle the specified question.
cards.why: The problem separates easy counting from optimization on the complement of a simple disjoint representation. It tests whether unambiguity retains its algorithmic value when a compactly encoded additive objective is introduced, and it bears on the power of knowledge-compilation representations under negation.

importance.reason: A focused but structural tractability question connecting unambiguous representations, binary-weight optimization, and complementation. It has a clear gap between polynomial unweighted methods and an unresolved weighted case.

progress.text: Monet formulates the binary-weight optimization problem and records NP membership of its decision version, polynomial-time weighted satisfaction, and a pseudopolynomial dynamic program for falsification.
The Dagstuhl seminar on database representation and provenance presents this exact question by linking to Monet’s formulation. The catalogue’s separate TCS-0485 record comes from that link.

Amarilli’s maintained list still asks for a polynomial-time weighted-falsifiability algorithm and discusses its connection to complementation of d-DNNFs. Monet’s original question has no posted answer at this check.

context_blocks.text: Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint. This is useful for counting: after fixing the literals of one consistent term, every remaining variable is free, and the term’s satisfying assignments can be counted directly. Summing across terms gives the total without any inclusion-exclusion correction. Subtracting that count from 2^n decides whether a falsifying assignment exists at all.

The weighted version asks where the complement lies relative to an additive score. Knowing how many points lie outside the DNF does not reveal whether even one of them has a large score. For example, take F=(x AND y) OR ((NOT x) AND z), whose two terms are incompatible. With weights 8, 3, and 5, the assignment (1,0,1) falsifies F and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has larger score 16 but satisfies F, so unconstrained maximization does not answer the question.

There is an important asymmetry between maximizing over satisfying and falsifying assignments. To maximize over satisfying assignments, optimize each term separately by setting every unrestricted positive-weight variable to one, then take the best result. To falsify the DNF, every term must fail at once, and choices made to destroy one term can interact with all the others.

Dynamic programming over achievable scores gives a pseudopolynomial algorithm; it becomes polynomial when weights are unary. The missing guarantee is polynomial dependence on binary descriptions of potentially large weights. Amarilli also explains a connection to complementing compiled Boolean representations: efficient complementation into a representation supporting weighted maximization would give an algorithm, while suitable hardness would obstruct that route.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant C such that, for every n≥2, every integer word length w≥⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every list x₁,…,xₙ∈{0,…,2ʷ−1}, the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most Cn?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
cards.why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

importance.reason: A foundational algorithmic primitive whose optimal complexity tests the computational power of the word RAM and would affect many tasks built on ordering integer keys.

progress.text: Han–Thorup achieve O(n√log log n) expected time and linear space for arbitrary word-sized integer keys.
Han’s journal paper gives deterministic O(n log log n) time and linear space, following STOC 2002.

context_blocks.text: Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles w=O(log n). Divide each key into digits of about log₂n bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size O(n). There are O(1+w/log n) passes, giving O(n(1+w/log n)) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If w=(log n)^{3/2}, however, that same argument takes about √log n passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for w=Ω((log n)² log log n), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’s O(n√log log n), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic O(n log log n) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.

cards.title: Sorting X + Y
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer n≥2 and every X=(x₁,…,xₙ), Y=(y₁,…,yₙ)∈ℝⁿ, A outputs a permutation ((i₁,j₁),…,(i_{n²},j_{n²})) of [n]×[n] satisfying x_{i_r}+y_{j_r}≤x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}} for 1≤r<n², in at most Cn² unit-cost operations?
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.
cards.status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The 2017/2018 decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.

cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All n² index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of b=d⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for some fixed integer d≥3 chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ᵇ, quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by O(n log n) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the O(n²) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/n² ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.

context_blocks.text: The input is small compared with the output. For X=(0,3) and Y=(1,4), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are n² output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for n² unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix M_ij=x_i+y_j increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as M_ij+M_kl=M_il+M_kj. The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all n² sums takes O(n² log n) time. Writing the required output already takes Ω(n²) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that O(n²) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining O(n² log n) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained O(n log² n) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of X+Y. The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.

cards.title: Hypergraph cut sparsifiers with O(n/ε²) hyperedges
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C>0 such that, for every integer n≥2, every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph H on V=[n], and every real ε∈(0,1/2), there is a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph H′ on the same V with at most Cn/ε² hyperedges and (1−ε)cut_H(S)≤cut_H′(S)≤(1+ε)cut_H(S) for every S⊆V simultaneously?
cards.why: Tests whether preserving all cuts of a multiway interaction system requires any more hyperedges than the graph sparsification upper bound. It separates the number of retained interactions from their incidence storage and from the cost of computing them.
cards.status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No Cn/ε² existence theorem or matching refutation was located. The old quadratic upper bound has been superseded by O(n log n/ε²). The original source permits an arbitrary weighted hypergraph on the same vertices; this card preserves that scope. Later near-optimal storage statements do not remove the logarithmic edge-count gap.

cards.definitions: A hypergraph H=(V,E,w) has E⊆{e⊆V:|e|≥2} and weights w:E→ℝ_{≥0}. Its cut value is cut_H(S)=Σ_{e∈E: e∩S≠∅ and e∩(V\S)≠∅}w(e): a crossing hyperedge contributes its weight once, independently of how many of its vertices lie on either side. Zero-weight edges may be discarded; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. Empty or singleton hyperedges never cross a cut and are omitted without loss. H′=(V,E′,w′) follows the same conventions, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights. The output edge set E′ need not be a subset of E, following the original problem statement; new vertices are not permitted. Size means |E′|, not Σ_{e∈E′}|e|, weight-encoding length or total storage bits. C is independent of n, ε, edge count, rank and all weights. The empty edge set is allowed, and a zero input cut must remain exactly zero. This is a finite-object existence question: no construction algorithm, running-time or probability guarantee is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence statement with one constant C, or prove that the minimum required number of hyperedges times ε²/n is unbounded over the permitted inputs and accuracies. For a negative answer, the lower bound must allow arbitrary nonnegative hyperedges on the original vertex set. A growing logarithmic factor or a counterexample only to a particular sampling method does not resolve the target.

context_blocks.text: A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge {1,2,3,4} of weight one contributes one to both the partition {1}|{2,3,4} and the partition {1,2}|{3,4}. Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit O(n/ε²)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using O(n log n/ε²) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.
The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the Cn/ε² hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

cards.context:
A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge {1,2,3,4} of weight one contributes one to both the partition {1}|{2,3,4} and the partition {1,2}|{3,4}. Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit O(n/ε²)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using O(n log n/ε²) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.

The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the Cn/ε² hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

benchmark_focus.reason: A universal cut-preserving reduction of hypergraphs to few weighted hyperedges is a broad compression target supporting many downstream algorithms. Its focus is the size of a combinatorial sparsifier, with no query-interface guarantee.

cards.title: Near-linear-time approximation of reachability diameter
cards.formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least 2/3 in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving D(G)=0 on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
cards.why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
cards.definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.

progress.text: Theorem 9 gives an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in near-linear time. Theorem 7 gives additive error $k$ in $O(nm/k)$ time; these guarantees leave the constant-factor near-linear target unresolved.

Corollary 5 conditionally excludes better-than-two approximation below the Boolean-matrix-multiplication exponent; its combinatorial version excludes truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms under combinatorial BMM. These results do not exclude every constant approximation.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Open Problem 1 at ESA 2026; the near-linear constant-factor target is a focused part of that broader question.

context_blocks.text: A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.
The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.

cards.title: Set-system sparsifiers of size proportional to chain length
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C>0 such that for every integer m≥1, every family S⊆2^{[m]}, every weight vector w∈ℝ≥0^m and every 0<ε<1, there is a reweighting w̃∈ℝ≥0^m with at most C·CL(S)/ε² nonzero coordinates and satisfying (1−ε)∑_{i∈A}wᵢ≤∑_{i∈A}w̃ᵢ≤(1+ε)∑_{i∈A}wᵢ simultaneously for every A∈S?
cards.why: Would give a sharp structural bound for simultaneous multiplicative compression of arbitrary weighted set families. It asks whether chain length and squared inverse accuracy fully account for the necessary support, without logarithmic losses.

references.title: Multiplicative Error Set System Sparsification: A Simpler Proof via Chain Length Contraction
references.authors: Brakensiek, Joshua; Guruswami, Venkatesan; Putterman, Aaron
references.locator: Conjecture 23; PDF page 13

cards.definitions: Here [m]={1,…,m}, and S is any finite collection of subsets, including possibly the empty collection. The support of w̃ is {i:w̃ᵢ>0}; coordinates outside it are dropped, while retained coordinates may receive arbitrary nonnegative real weights. No normalization such as ∑wᵢ=1 is imposed. Following the source’s witness definition, a chain of length ℓ consists of distinct coordinates a₁,…,a_ℓ and distinct sets A₁,…,A_ℓ∈S with aᵢ∈Aᵢ for every i and aⱼ∉Aᵢ whenever i<j. CL(S) is the maximum possible ℓ, allowing ℓ=0. Equivalently, take the union-closure U(S)={⋃T:T⊆S}, including the empty union; CL(S) is the largest number of strict inclusions in an ascending chain starting from ∅ in U(S). Thus CL(S)=0 when S is empty or contains only ∅. It is not merely the largest chain in the original family. A (1±ε) sparsifier is a reweighting satisfying the simultaneous inequalities in the statement. Sets of original weight zero must retain weight exactly zero. All data and weights are quantified mathematically; the question places no running-time, oracle-access, randomness or bit-complexity requirement on finding w̃. The same C must work independently of m, S, w and ε. The source allows ε>0; values ε≥1 admit the zero reweighting, so restricting the nontrivial question to 0<ε<1 preserves it.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence bound with one absolute constant C, or refute it by showing that for every C there are a family, weights and an accuracy parameter for which every multiplicative sparsifier needs more than C·CL(S)/ε² coordinates. Bounds with an additional unbounded logarithmic factor do not meet the conjecture; an efficient construction is not required.

context_blocks.title: Preserve all set weights with fewer coordinates
context_blocks.text: A coordinate can represent an edge, a constraint or a position of a codeword. A sparsifier removes coordinates and compensates by reweighting those it keeps. The same reweighting must preserve every specified set’s weight, including small-weight sets, which makes multiplicative error stronger than a global additive-error allowance.

context_blocks.title: One set can be represented by one weighted coordinate
context_blocks.text: If S contains only the whole nonempty universe, its chain length is one. Placing the entire total weight on any one coordinate preserves that sole set weight exactly. A large universe alone therefore does not force a large sparsifier.

context_blocks.title: Union-closure sees constraints absent from direct containment
context_blocks.text: If S consists of all m singleton sets, the original sets are pairwise incomparable. Their unions nevertheless form a chain of m strict inclusions, so CL(S)=m. With unit original weights and ε<1, every singleton must retain positive weight; all m coordinates are necessary. This explains why the conjecture uses chain length in the union-closure.

context_blocks.title: The current upper bound still has logarithmic overhead
context_blocks.text: The paper gives support O(CL(S)·log²(CL(S)/ε)·(log log(CL(S)/ε))²/ε²), with the usual constant-size adjustments to logarithms near one. This already removes dependence on the universe size from the overhead. Conjecture 23 asks whether all remaining logarithmic factors can be removed.

context_blocks.title: Existence and computation remain separate
context_blocks.text: The source notes that its main existence bound is not efficiently implementable in full generality. The conjecture itself only asks whether a small reweighting exists. Proving such a bound for every set family would already sharpen broad cut, code and constraint sparsification principles.

references.authors: Abrishami, Tara; Chudnovsky, Maria; Pilipczuk, Marcin; Rzążewski, Paweł
references.locator: Conjecture 10; PDF page 10

cards.definitions: The input is a finite undirected simple graph G=(V,E), with n=|V|, and integer weights w:V→N. An independent set I⊆V contains no adjacent pair, and its weight is Σ_{v∈I}w(v), with the empty set having weight zero. S_{t,t,t} is the tree formed by three paths of t edges sharing one common endpoint and otherwise having disjoint vertices; it has 3t+1 vertices and one degree-three center. An induced copy requires exactly the edges of that tree among its selected vertices. K_r is the complete graph on r vertices, so excluding it means every clique has size at most r−1. The algorithm is promised both exclusions. For each fixed t,r its running time must be at most n^{c(t,r)} times a constant depending on t,r, with arithmetic and comparisons on weights counted at unit cost as in the source. No bounded maximum degree, excluded biclique, or supplied graph decomposition is assumed. This is polynomial time for each fixed t,r, not necessarily a fixed-parameter bound f(t,r)n^C with universal C.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an exact polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed t,r, or refute the universal algorithmic assertion, for example by an appropriate conditional hardness result for one fixed pair. Approximation or an algorithm requiring an additional bounded-degree or biclique exclusion promise does not establish the conjecture.

references.authors: Otachi, Yota; Suzuki, Akira; Tamura, Yuma

cards.definitions: G=(V,E) is a finite undirected simple graph with n=|V|. For A⊆V, the cut graph G[A,V∖A] keeps exactly those edges with one endpoint in each side; edges internal to either side are discarded. An induced matching in this bipartite graph is a set of vertex-disjoint edges whose endpoints induce exactly those matching edges. Let mim_G(A) be its maximum size. A branch decomposition (T,L) consists of a tree T whose internal nodes have degree three and a bijection L from V to the leaves of T. Deleting a tree edge splits its leaves and hence V into A and V∖A. The decomposition width is the maximum mim_G(A) over its tree-edge cuts. The graph’s mim-width is the minimum over all such decompositions. The target is a decomposition of width ≤1, including width zero for edgeless graphs; empty and one-vertex graphs have the trivial width-zero convention. Runtime is polynomial in the ordinary explicit graph input size. No decomposition or bounded-width promise is supplied. The tree need not be a caterpillar: restricting it to one would instead ask about linear mim-width.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm that returns a valid width-at-most-one decomposition on every yes-instance and rejects every no-instance in polynomial time, or establish an obstruction to this guarantee. Algorithms using a supplied decomposition, recognizing only a subclass, or deciding width at most two do not settle the question.

cards.definitions: The input is a directed graph G=(V,E), with V=[n], n≥2, no loops or parallel arcs, and distinguished s≠t. Both opposite arcs between two vertices are allowed. The graph is unweighted; every arc has length one. A simple s-to-t path is a sequence v₀=s,v₁,…,v_ℓ=t of pairwise distinct vertices with (v_{j−1},v_j)∈E for 1≤j≤ℓ, and its length is ℓ. If t is reachable from s, dist_G(s,t) is the minimum length of such a path. If t is unreachable, the instance is a no-instance. The input lists all vertices and arcs using binary vertex labels; N is the full encoding length. Polynomial time means one deterministic multitape Turing machine that decides every instance in at most C(N+1)^a steps for absolute constants C,a. NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions; in particular, a hardness proof can give a map from Boolean satisfiability instances to these graph instances that preserves yes/no answers. The decision problem is in NP: an at-most-n-vertex path is a polynomial-size certificate, and reachability distance and the path conditions can be checked in polynomial time. No planarity, acyclicity, connectivity or uniqueness of shortest paths is promised.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine the problem’s complexity in the stated unrestricted directed, unweighted model. A deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm establishes tractability; a polynomial-time many-one reduction from SAT establishes NP-completeness, since membership in NP is known. The latter excludes a polynomial-time algorithm under P≠NP. The question does not assume a P/NP-complete dichotomy in advance; any different established classification must explain the remaining boundary. Bounds only for planar graphs, or hardness when k is variable, do not classify the fixed k=1 problem.
