context_blocks.text: Homotopy type theory treats identity as mathematical data that can itself have nontrivial identities. This makes it a natural setting for spaces and higher structures, but it changes what it means to give a diagram. In set-level mathematics, equations between composites can be recorded once and used without further information. For general types, chosen identifications can have multiple distinct witnesses, and comparisons between those witnesses may matter in the next dimension.

A semisimplicial type begins with a type A₀ of vertices. For every ordered pair of vertices, A₁ gives a type of edges. For every triangle boundary—three vertices and three specified edges—A₂ gives a type of fillers. At dimension three, a filler is indexed by four vertices, six edges and four triangular fillers sharing their appropriate faces. Nothing forces a filler to exist, and the type of fillers may itself have arbitrarily rich homotopy.

The finite telescope description records shared boundaries through dependent types. A triangle’s three edges are already assigned the required endpoints; one does not choose unrelated edges and then append a collection of endpoint equations. The same idea works at each externally fixed dimension. The difficulty is making the whole construction into one function that accepts an internal natural number, rather than a growing list of separately written definitions.

This is why the card distinguishes its externally specified D_j from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for D_100 and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary n:ℕ. The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this card asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over U₀ preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.

cards.title: Scott-continuous lambda models with theory λβ
cards.formal: Does there exist a pointed directed-complete partial order D and Scott-continuous maps F:D→[D→D] and L:[D→D]→D with F∘L=id such that, for every pair of finite untyped lambda terms M,N, equality of their interpretations for every environment in D holds if and only if M and N are beta-convertible?
cards.why: A foundational completeness question for denotational semantics: does the mathematical structure used to describe approximation and recursion inevitably identify programs beyond beta-conversion, or can it preserve every distinction made by that computation rule?
cards.status_note: The exact question is explicit in Honsell’s primary statement. A search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of its λβ alternative. The inspected 2025–2026 filter-model papers study unsolvables and other equational theories. Proofs were not independently verified.

cards.definitions: Terms are generated by variables from a countably infinite set, application MN and abstraction λx.M, modulo renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility is the least equivalence relation closed under application and abstraction containing (λx.M)N=M[N/x], with capture-avoiding substitution. A directed set is nonempty and every two of its elements have an upper bound in the set. D is a set with a partial order, a least element, and a supremum for every directed subset. Scott-continuous means monotone and preserving directed suprema. [D→D] consists of all Scott-continuous functions, ordered pointwise. An environment ρ assigns an element of D to each variable. Interpret x as ρ(x), MN as F(⟦M⟧ρ)(⟦N⟧ρ), and λx.M as L(d↦⟦M⟧(ρ[x:=d])). The desired condition is ∀M,N: (∀ρ, ⟦M⟧ρ=⟦N⟧ρ) ⇔ M=βN. Models need not be countable, algebraic, effectively presented or extensional; in particular L∘F=id is not required. These are set-based directed-complete orders and all their continuous maps, without a restriction to graph models.

context_blocks.text: The untyped lambda calculus describes functions using variables, application and abstraction. Beta-reduction substitutes an argument into a function body. A denotational model assigns mathematical meanings to terms and makes every beta-conversion valid. The question asks whether continuity can coexist with complete precision: no two terms should become equal in the model unless beta-conversion already equates them.

In domain semantics, an order represents increasing information and a directed supremum combines compatible approximations. Scott continuity requires functions to preserve these suprema. The map L represents each continuous self-map by an element of D, and F turns an element back into its associated self-map. The equation F∘L=id ensures that interpreting function application recovers the represented function. This makes beta-reduction sound.

Representability is a semantic condition. The element representing a continuous function need not be denoted by any finite lambda term. Requiring every continuous function to have a finite program would change the question. The model need not have computable elements, a computable ordering or a computable interpretation algorithm.

Extensional equality makes an additional identification. If x is not free in f, eta-conversion equates λx.f x with f, although these terms need not be beta-convertible. Imposing L∘F=id would validate this extra equality. This card therefore requires only the retraction in the other direction and keeps the beta-eta version as a separate target.

Quotienting syntax by beta-conversion gives a term model with exactly the desired equality. It does not automatically provide a pointed dcpo representing all continuous self-maps. The issue is whether the exact syntactic theory can be realized in this particular semantic setting.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra prove that the effective models defined in their paper cannot have theory exactly λβ or λβη. They also prove non-enumerability of the order theory, which records inequalities between denotations. Equational theory records equalities instead. A theorem restricted to effective models, or to order rather than equality, cannot be generalized silently to arbitrary dcpos.

Divergent terms reveal another source of extra equations. A term is unsolvable when no finite reduction exposes a head normal form: an outer variable applied to arguments after any leading abstractions. A sensible model equates all unsolvable closed terms. This is stronger than beta-conversion, which distinguishes some of them. cards.formal: For every pure type system (S,A,R) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?

cards.definitions: S is a set of sorts, A⊆S×S is a set of axioms, and R⊆S×S×S is a set of product rules. Terms are finite expressions t ::= x | s | t u | λx:B.t | Πx:B.C, with s∈S and variables from a countably infinite set, modulo renaming bound variables. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. Typing is the least relation Γ⊢t:B generated by the following rules. Axiom: ∅⊢s:t when (s,t)∈A. Start: Γ,x:B⊢x:B when Γ⊢B:s and x is fresh. Weakening: Γ,x:C⊢t:B when Γ⊢t:B, Γ⊢C:s and x is fresh. Product: Γ⊢Πx:B.C:s₃ when Γ⊢B:s₁, Γ,x:B⊢C:s₂ and (s₁,s₂,s₃)∈R. Abstraction: Γ⊢λx:B.t:Πx:B.C when Γ,x:B⊢t:C and Γ⊢Πx:B.C:s for a sort s. Application: Γ⊢t u:C[u/x] when Γ⊢t:Πx:B.C and Γ⊢u:B. Conversion: Γ⊢t:C when Γ⊢t:B, Γ⊢C:s and B=βC. All substitutions avoid capture. A beta step contracts (λx:B.t)u to t[u/x] at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. =β is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of those steps. A term is typable if Γ⊢t:B for some finite Γ,B. Weak normalization means that each typable term has some finite beta-reduction sequence ending in a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means that no typable term starts an infinite beta-reduction sequence. Both predicates quantify over open as well as closed terms and over all their reduction choices. The sets S,A,R need not be finite, decidable or functional.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.

context_blocks.text: A term can contain several reducible applications, so computation involves choices. Weak normalization says that some sequence reaches a normal form. Strong normalization says that every sequence of beta-reductions terminates. The conjecture asks whether these two system-wide properties coincide for all pure type systems, a common framework for typed lambda calculi.

The distinction is real for untyped terms. Let Ω=(λz.zz)(λz.zz). The term (λx.y)Ω reduces to y in one step if the outer application is chosen, but it can also reduce Ω forever. Thus it is weakly but not strongly normalizing. This only illustrates the distinction: a counterexample to the conjecture needs a pure type system whose entire collection of typable terms is weakly normalizing.

A pure type system specifies which sorts classify other sorts and which dependent function types may be formed, through its sets A and R. The common typing rules generate the resulting calculus. Familiar simply typed, polymorphic and dependent systems fit the framework, but the conjecture also covers unusual specifications, beyond established proof languages.

The global hypothesis concerns every typable term. Confluence cannot replace it: confluence says that two finite reductions can be joined, making normal forms unique when they exist. It does not prevent an infinite path from coexisting with a terminating path. The untyped example already separates these ideas.

Reduction here includes type annotations and components of dependent products. Termination of an implementation’s selected evaluation strategy therefore differs from strong normalization of the calculus. Results after erasing annotations, or for closed programs only, have a different scope from the property of every annotated typable term in every context.

Sørensen’s 1997 work proves the implication for specified classes of typed calculi. Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend it to a class of non-dependent pure type systems in 2001. Their structural hypotheses are substantive: the theorem does not claim to cover every non-dependent specification, let alone every dependent one. The TLCA list records these as partial results.

Mull’s TYPES 2022 paper, published in 2023, enlarges the known class using a translation preserving typability and infinite reduction paths while removing certain sorts and rules. The theorem includes some systems with dependent rules that earlier results did not cover. The author explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture; the translation’s structural hypotheses cannot be omitted.

A universal implication would connect the existence of normal forms with complete freedom of reduction order throughout this family of type theories. A counterexample would identify a system in which every term can finish, yet some legal choices continue forever. Either outcome would sharpen normalization arguments in proof checking and the metatheory of dependent types.

cards.title: Parity games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants K,c>0 such that, on every finite parity game G and designated vertex s, A decides whether Even has a winning strategy from s in at most K(L+1)^c steps, where L is the explicit binary encoding length of (G,s)?
cards.definitions: G consists of a nonempty vertex set V={1,…,n}, a directed edge set E⊆V×V with at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition V=V_Even⊔V_Odd, and a priority function p:V→N. Self-loops are allowed. The input explicitly lists all vertices, edges, owner bits and priorities, with integers in binary and delimiters; s∈V is included. A play is an infinite sequence v_0v_1… with v_0=s and (v_i,v_(i+1))∈E. At a vertex owned by a player that player chooses the next vertex. A strategy maps every finite valid play ending at a vertex owned by that player to a legal successor. Even wins a play if the minimum priority occurring infinitely often is even; Odd wins otherwise. A winning strategy for Even makes every play consistent with it winning for Even, irrespective of Odd’s choices. The algorithm must answer YES exactly when such a strategy exists. Strategies are not part of the input. The number and magnitude of priorities are unrestricted input data; the running-time exponent may not depend on them. The task has perfect information, alternating vertex ownership and no probabilistic transitions.

context_blocks.text: Parity games describe infinite behavior using a finite graph and a priority condition. The question is not how to simulate an infinite play; it is how to decide whether one player can force the eventual recurrence pattern of priorities to favor it. This decision problem underlies central constructions in logical verification and synthesis.

Positional determinacy says that a winning player can choose moves using only the current vertex. Thus finite strategies suffice even though the winning condition concerns an infinite play. Their existence does not by itself give a polynomial-time algorithm for finding or choosing the winning strategy. The problem lies in both NP and coNP, and more precisely in UP and coUP.

Calude and coauthors established a quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017. Czerwiński and coauthors proved quasipolynomial lower bounds for separating automata used by a broad collection of such algorithms. That lower bound concerns the specified approach, not arbitrary algorithms for parity games.

A November 2025 preprint by Rick van der Heijden claims a polynomial-time algorithm for the full problem. This review located and inspected the claim but did not independently verify its proof or find an authoritative resolution of its correctness. It must be visible on the card rather than omitted from a statement that the problem is confirmed open.

Suilen and Pérez’s April 2026 paper still describes polynomial-time parity-game solving as a longstanding open question while reducing parity games to a robust-MDP threshold problem. This later usage is evidence about the literature, not a proof that the earlier claim is false. The card therefore carries an explicitly unverified current status while completing the mathematical formulation and preserving its historical identifier.

cards.title: Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every input k≥1, c_0,…,c_(k−1)∈Z and u_0,…,u_(k−1)∈Z, and correctly decides whether the sequence defined by u_(t+k)=∑_(j=0)^(k−1)c_j u_(t+j) for all t≥0 has u_t=0 for some integer t≥0?
cards.definitions: All integers, including k, are given in binary with signs and delimiters; the input explicitly lists exactly k coefficients and k initial values. These data uniquely define the infinite integer sequence. The order k is unrestricted and is part of the input, not a fixed parameter. Coefficients may vanish, the supplied recurrence need not be of minimal order, and no simplicity, non-degeneracy or nonzero-leading-product promise is imposed. The search includes the given initial terms and all subsequent nonnegative indices. There is no supplied upper bound on t. The required output is YES exactly when a zero occurs and NO otherwise; only termination and correctness are demanded, without a time or space bound. This is the discrete recurrence problem over integers, not the continuous-time Skolem problem or the question whether every term is nonnegative.

context_blocks.text: A short recurrence determines infinitely many exact integer values. Testing any particular term is effective, but deciding that no term will ever be zero requires a terminating procedure for a global property. Even this elementary linear evolution leaves an unresolved boundary between arithmetic structure and algorithmic decision.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem constrains zero sets to a finite union of arithmetic progressions together with a finite exceptional set. That qualitative description is not, by itself, an algorithm that determines all exceptional zeros from the input. The distinction explains why a structural theorem about the sequence does not automatically settle the decision question.

Bilu and coauthors study simple recurrences and relate termination of their proposed procedure to transcendence conjectures. The arbitrary integer recurrence in this card also allows repeated characteristic roots and other cases outside the simple setting. Conditional termination for a subclass therefore has a different scope from an unconditional decision algorithm for the full input domain.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell improve the complexity of low-order and bounded-index versions. Their July 2026 revision places the unrestricted order-at-most-four problem in coRP. A bounded index range is additional input, and an order bound of four excludes general recurrences; neither restriction answers the unrestricted decision problem.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 paper obtains general decidability conditionally on a strengthened Cramér-type conjecture. Its unconditional density results for possible large zeros do not guarantee a decision for each individual recurrence. The new review preserves TCS-5773 and its original 2022 source rather than creating a second general Skolem entry.

cards.title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in the total input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a finite directed graph G=(V,E), a partition V=V_Max⊔V_Min, integer edge weights w:E→Z, and a start vertex s, determine whether Max has a strategy σ such that every strategy τ of Min produces a play s=v_0,v_1,… satisfying liminf_{T→∞}(1/T) sum_{t=0}^{T−1} w(v_t,v_{t+1})≥0.
cards.definitions: The graph, its ownership partition, its start vertex and all weights are represented explicitly; weights use signed binary. Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge, so plays are infinite. The owner of the current vertex chooses the next edge with full knowledge of the finite history. Strategies are arbitrary deterministic functions of this history. There are no chance vertices, simultaneous moves, hidden observations or multiple payoff coordinates. Max seeks a nonnegative lower limit of average accumulated weight; equality zero is winning. No bound is imposed on intermediate losses or on the size W=max(1,max_e |w(e)|). The running-time requirement concerns ordinary bit operations, so a polynomial dependence on W is not sufficient. Zero threshold loses no generality: a binary rational threshold a/b with b>0 can be absorbed by replacing w(e) with b w(e)−a, with polynomial growth of the encoding.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that this exact winner-decision language is in P, or prove that it is outside P. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a smoothed or average-case guarantee, or a lower bound for one strategy-improvement rule does not settle the unrestricted worst-case question. Strongly polynomial time would suffice but is a stronger requirement than this card asks for.
cards.why: A foundational complexity question for long-run adversarial optimization. It connects finite graph games, quantitative verification, resource reasoning and tropical algebra, with short optimal strategies but no known polynomial-time method to find the winner on arbitrary binary-weighted inputs.

importance.reason: A canonical NP∩coNP problem central to quantitative synthesis and long-run control; resolving the binary-weight complexity gap would have consequences across several equivalent algebraic and game formulations.

progress.text: Zwick and Paterson give pseudopolynomial algorithms, establish the complexity framework, and reduce mean-payoff games to simple stochastic games.
Brim, Chaloupka, Doyen, Gentilini and Raskin obtain O(nmW) arithmetic-operation bounds for threshold decision and winning-strategy synthesis via energy games.
Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann derive tight bounds for value iteration using universal graphs, a restricted algorithmic framework.

Loff and Skomra publish smoothed polynomial guarantees for games on ergodic graphs with independently perturbed rewards. The published theorem includes the ergodicity restriction omitted from the earlier arXiv abstract.
Maat’s preprint gives direct connections between strategy improvement and simplex variants under nondegeneracy assumptions, without a general polynomial iteration bound.
Adenwalla and coauthors give connections to graph-class chromatic boundedness and explicitly retain the general polynomial-time question in §3.7.2.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The July 2026 primary source explicitly states that polynomial-time solution with binary weights remains open. The card fixes a single deterministic mean-payoff objective with a nonnegative liminf threshold. Pseudopolynomial, ergodic smoothed-analysis and framework-specific results do not resolve arbitrary worst-case inputs.

context_blocks.text: Mean payoff measures sustainable long-run performance. Edge weights can represent net resource gains, rewards or the negative of costs; an adversary controls some of the transitions. A finite initial loss disappears from the limiting average, while a repeatedly traversed cycle continues to matter. For example, eventually repeating weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one, regardless of any fixed initial prefix. This distinguishes the objective from requiring the accumulated sum to remain nonnegative at every step.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players, so a player can make the same choice whenever a vertex is revisited. With both choices fixed, the resulting path eventually repeats a cycle, and its value is the cycle’s average weight. This yields compact certificates and NP∩coNP membership. It does not make the search easy: the number of positional strategy combinations can be exponential. Zwick and Paterson gave the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games.

The size of a weight and the size of its representation differ sharply. A weight 2^b takes only b+1 binary digits. An algorithm using O(nmW) arithmetic operations, where n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges, can therefore take exponential time in the input length. Brim and coauthors obtain such a pseudopolynomial bound for the threshold problem through energy-game progress measures. The result is powerful for small weights, but it leaves the dependence needed for this question unresolved.

Universal graphs provide a way to organize and compare value-iteration algorithms. Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish tight bounds within that framework, including improved dependence on the largest weight for a fixed number of vertices. Such a matching lower bound identifies a limitation of the framework being analyzed; it does not rule out an unrelated polynomial-time algorithm for mean-payoff games.

Smoothed analysis gives a different kind of progress. Loff and Skomra’s ICALP 2024 theorem obtains polynomial running time with high probability after sufficiently random independent perturbations of rewards, on ergodic game graphs. Here ergodicity is stronger than ordinary strong connectivity: for every reward assignment, the game value is independent of the start vertex. The theorem helps explain efficiency on perturbed inputs while retaining both a graph restriction and distributional assumptions. It does not decide the present worst-case complexity question.

There are also increasingly direct links to linear optimization. Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies many strategy-improvement variants with instances of the simplex algorithm under nondegeneracy assumptions. This gives a structural bridge between algorithms and their lower-bound constructions. A correspondence between local improvement methods, however, is not a proof that their number of iterations is polynomial.

A July 2026 preprint by Adenwalla and coauthors connects tropical inequality systems and mean-payoff games with deciding chromatic boundedness for certain classes of graphs defined by equality patterns. Its reverse encoding uses a specified succinct representation. This creates another setting in which a solver would be useful. The paper explicitly leaves polynomial-time mean-payoff solving open, and its graph-class reduction should not be mistaken for a polynomial algorithm for games.

cards.title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which, on every first-order sentence φ in the language {0,1,+,−,×,<,exp}, halts and correctly decides whether φ is true in (R,0,1,+,−,×,<,x↦e^x)?
cards.definitions: Sentences have finite syntax and no free variables. Terms are formed from variables, 0,1, the unary symbols − and exp, and binary + and ×; atomic formulas are equalities or strict inequalities of terms. Formulas use Boolean connectives and first-order quantifiers, all ranging over R. Equality has its usual logical interpretation. Inputs are finite parenthesized strings over a fixed finite alphabet, with variable indices written in binary; any fixed effectively interconvertible syntax encoding gives the same decidability question. No arbitrary real constants or oracles for real numbers are allowed. The symbol exp denotes the standard real exponential function on all of R, not a restricted function or an unspecified solution in another structure. There is no time or space bound beyond termination. A positive resolution must be unconditional, rather than assuming an unresolved transcendence conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
cards.why: Locate a fundamental decidability boundary beyond polynomial real arithmetic, where exact reasoning interacts with transcendence.

importance.reason: A longstanding central question of real model theory with direct relevance to symbolic reasoning about exponential expressions. The explicit 2026 conditional result confirms continuing specialist interest without settling the unconditional target.

progress.text: Macintyre–Wilkie obtain conditional decidability from Schanuel’s conjecture, as recalled by the 2026 primary source.
Berarducci–Gallinaro v2 retains the Schanuel assumption for the full real exponential theory.

references.locator: Revised 23 June 2026; abstract and introduction distinguish full conditional and restricted unconditional statements

cards.status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. The June 2026 revision remains conditional for the full theory, and no unconditional decision procedure or undecidability result was found.
cards.review_note: Preserves the unrestricted real-exponential-theory question. The finite signature and effective syntax specify the input; no resource bound or extra real parameters are silently added.

statement_review.reason: The statement and definitions specify the target, domains, quantifiers and relevant computational model; this is an editorial formulation review, not a formal verification.

selection_provenance.approval_basis: User requested approximately five additions from GPT and five from Claude after the proposal audits.

context_blocks.text: First-order arithmetic over the real numbers can describe polynomial equalities, inequalities and quantifier alternation. Adding the exponential function permits expressions involving growth and decay that are unavailable in the polynomial language. The target is exact truth of every sentence, including cases in which a numerical approximation alone cannot distinguish equality from a very small nonzero quantity.

The syntax is finite even though the quantified domain is infinite. An algorithm receives a formula such as an existential statement about real solutions; it does not receive an arbitrary real constant as an infinitely long input. Fixing the standard exponential function and excluding such parameters prevents representation choices from changing the decision problem.

Macintyre and Wilkie proved decidability under Schanuel’s conjecture. Berarducci and Gallinaro’s 2026 paper obtains an axiomatization under the same assumption and recovers that conditional decidability result. Its unconditional result for a related restricted exponential setting does not settle the unrestricted theory on this card.

This question is not the task of efficiently evaluating e^x to a specified error. Exact logical decision also includes formulas with arbitrary quantifier patterns and exact equalities. Conversely, the card imposes no polynomial running-time demand. An unconditional terminating algorithm of any complexity would answer it affirmatively.

The catalogue already contains individual questions about linear recurrences and linear dynamical systems. TCS-6265 concerns safety exactly at a specific robustness threshold, not the full elementary theory of the real exponential field. The new card supplies a broader, distinct boundary for algorithmic reasoning with real analytic operations.

cards.title: Continuous Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, given any dimension d≥1, rational matrix A∈Q^{d×d}, and rational column vectors b,c∈Q^d, always halts and correctly decides whether cᵀexp(tA)b=0 for some real t≥0?
cards.definitions: Every input rational is represented exactly by a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. The dimension is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. The matrix exponential is exp(tA)=Σ_{j=0}^∞ t^j A^j/j!, and x(t)=exp(tA)b is the unique real solution of x′(t)=Ax(t), x(0)=b. The target is the hyperplane {x:cᵀx=0}; c=0 is allowed and gives an immediate yes instance. Time ranges over all finite nonnegative real numbers, not just rational or integer times. Equality is exact. A zero at t=0 counts, as does a trajectory that is identically in the hyperplane. If the scalar function approaches zero only in the limit t→∞, the answer is no unless it also has a finite zero. No promise of diagonalizability, simple eigenvalues, bounded dimension, stability, spectral separation, transverse intersection, or robust distance from the hyperplane is supplied. The requested algorithm is an ordinary finite-input decision procedure without real-number or number-theoretic oracles; no complexity upper bound is prescribed. This card retains the rational-data version; some cited work treats the more general real-algebraic-data version.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an unconditional always-halting decision algorithm for every rational input, or prove that no such Turing algorithm exists. A conditional procedure assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a solver for a fixed low dimension, a procedure that may run forever on some inputs, or a certified answer only under a nonzero distance promise is partial progress. An undecidability theorem allowing more general coefficients or nonlinear differential equations must be reduced to this rational linear model to refute the proposition.
cards.why: A minimal exact reachability question for continuous linear systems whose decidability remains unresolved, linking algorithmic verification to real analysis, transcendence and effective number theory.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary for verification of linear differential systems, with a precisely finite rational input and an unrestricted exact reachability target.

progress.text: Bell and coauthors establish the continuous Skolem framework, equivalent formulations and decidable special cases.
Chonev–Ouaknine–Worrell obtain conditional bounded decidability and reductions for restricted frequency patterns.
Their recurrent-reachability work decides infinitely many zeros at differential order at most seven and supplies effective last-zero bounds in that regime.
Platzer–Qian explain why exact closed-target reachability is not covered by their completeness results for open properties.
The Skolem/Positivity survey records continuous analogues and their distinct analytic obstacles.

cards.status_note: No unconditional decision procedure or undecidability proof for this rational linear model was found through 11 September 2026. Bounded conditional results, low-order recurrence algorithms, approximate/robust verification and nonlinear-system hardness do not settle the unbounded exact question.

context_blocks.text: Linear differential equations have explicit matrix-exponential solutions, yet an explicit formula does not automatically decide whether a trajectory hits an exact target. The scalar output cᵀx(t) may combine growth, decay, polynomial factors and oscillations. The matrix and vectors are finite rational data, while the possible hitting time is an unrestricted real number. This makes the question a basic test of what exact verification can decide even for linear continuous dynamics.

Numerical proximity is insufficient. The one-dimensional system x′=−x, x(0)=1 has output e^{−t}, which becomes arbitrarily small but never reaches zero. Conversely, a zero need not be accompanied by a sign change: the polynomial (t−1)² touches zero and returns to positive values. Such a polynomial is itself an output of a rational nilpotent linear system. A grid search or a sign-change detector can therefore miss the distinction required by the card.

Simple degenerate cases can be removed exactly. The initial-time condition is cᵀb=0. By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, the scalar function is identically zero precisely when cᵀA^j b=0 for j=0,…,d−1. These are finite rational calculations. Outside that case, analyticity ensures only finitely many zeros in each bounded interval, but neither a uniform numerical precision nor a final time beyond all zeros follows from that finiteness statement.

Spectral decomposition writes the output as a sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials, with conjugate terms combining into real sine and cosine expressions. The imaginary parts of eigenvalues give oscillation frequencies. Repeated eigenvalues can introduce polynomial factors. Competing terms can nearly cancel at very large times, so a proof that the long-term behaviour is simple enough to inspect is a substantive part of an unbounded decision procedure.

Chonev, Ouaknine and Worrell prove decidability of the bounded Continuous Skolem problem assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. That conjecture gives a transcendence-degree lower bound for complex numbers linearly independent over the rationals together with their exponentials. Their algorithm uses it to handle possible tangential zeros. The result does not supply an unconditional bounded-time procedure, and a bounded-time procedure alone does not supply a stopping criterion for checking all t≥0.

The same paper reduces certain unbounded spectral cases to the bounded problem, including the case with at most one rationally independent frequency. A separate recurrent-reachability result decides whether a solution of differential order at most seven has infinitely many zeros and gives an effective last-zero bound when it has only finitely many. Combined with the conditional bounded solver, this yields conditional decisions in that low-order regime. Infinite recurrence and existence of even one zero are nevertheless different questions.

The broader algebraic-coefficient formulations reveal a connection with effective Diophantine approximation: handling multiple independent oscillations can entail computing quantities measuring unusually good rational approximations to algebraic numbers. Those implications are evidence of the mathematical obstacles, not undecidability proofs. Their precise dimension thresholds belong to the coefficient model of the cited theorem; this card does not automatically transfer them to the rational-matrix representation fixed above.

Platzer and Qian’s 2025 completeness theorem for compact initial-value problems concerns specified open safety and liveness properties. Its discussion explicitly identifies exact hyperplane reachability as an obstacle to replacing those topological conditions by arbitrary closed targets. A proof system that certifies entry into an open neighbourhood need not decide whether the trajectory touches its central hyperplane. This distinction matters when interpreting advances in numerical verification as progress on exact decision questions.

The July 2026 survey by Bacik and coauthors places the continuous problem alongside discrete recurrence questions, while emphasizing differences in technique. Sampling only integer times gives a sequence but changes the question: for example, a rational rotation system can have output cos t and reach zero at π/2. The card asks whether any real hitting time exists, so discrete-time zero testing cannot simply replace the continuous analysis.

cards.title: Decidability of multiplicative-exponential linear logic
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite propositional MELL sequent Γ in the calculus below, halts and answers yes exactly when ⊢Γ has a finite derivation? There is no promised bound on formula size or exponential nesting and no requested time bound beyond termination on every input.
cards.why: MELL combines resource-sensitive composition with controlled reuse. Its decision problem connects automated proof search to branching counter systems and tests a fundamental boundary of algorithmic reasoning about resources.

progress.text: Straßburger identifies gaps in the earlier proposed MELL decision procedure and distinguishes it from the decidable logic with unrestricted contraction.
Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove decidability of reachability for two-dimensional branching VASS; their introduction still leaves general dimension open.
Bizière, Leroux and Sutre state a general decidability result and its MELL consequence. Theorem 3.3 supplies the claimed separation property. The proof is not independently verified in this review.

cards.definitions: Use atoms p_i and their distinct dual literals p_i^⊥ for integers i≥0. Formulas are finite syntax trees generated by A ::= p_i | p_i^⊥ | 1 | ⊥ | (A⊗A) | (A⅋A) | !A | ?A. A sequent Γ is a finite multiset of formulas; commas denote multiset union, retaining multiplicity. The following rules, read from premises to conclusion, define derivations. Identity has no premises and concludes ⊢p_i,p_i^⊥. The unit rule has no premises and concludes ⊢1. Tensor takes ⊢Γ,A and ⊢Δ,B to ⊢Γ,Δ,A⊗B. Par takes ⊢Γ,A,B to ⊢Γ,A⅋B. The other unit rule takes ⊢Γ to ⊢Γ,⊥. Dereliction takes ⊢Γ,A to ⊢Γ,?A. Weakening takes ⊢Γ to ⊢Γ,?A. Contraction takes ⊢Γ,?A,?A to ⊢Γ,?A. Promotion takes ⊢?Γ,A to ⊢?Γ,!A, where every formula in ?Γ has outermost symbol ?. Contexts may be empty, and all displayed formula and context choices are arbitrary subject to these conditions. A derivation is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are the two nullary rules and whose internal nodes are instances of the other rules. There are no further rules; exchange is implicit in multisets. This is the cut-free presentation of classical commutative MELL, whose usual cut rule is admissible. Inputs explicitly list formula trees with constructor delimiters and binary atom indices; malformed strings are rejected. Formulas contain neither additives nor quantifiers, and there is just one pair of exponential modalities ! and ?.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the provable sequents of this calculus form a decidable language, or prove that no algorithm can decide that language. A procedure that terminates only on provable sequents does not establish decidability.

context_blocks.text: Linear logic treats assumptions as resources whose occurrences matter. An ordinary assumption cannot automatically be copied or discarded. For example, the resource-reading of p→p⊗p asks for two copies from one and is unavailable in general; marking the input !p permits reuse. MELL keeps multiplicative composition together with these reuse modalities.

The rules make each proposed finite proof checkable. That does not by itself make provability decidable: searching through larger proofs will eventually find a proof when one exists, but need not terminate when none exists. The question asks for a single procedure that also gives a terminating negative answer.

The restrictions on contraction and promotion are part of the problem. Allowing unrestricted contraction gives a different logic, and adding additive connectives or several interacting subexponential modalities changes the decidability boundary. A published 2015 decidability argument was challenged in Straßburger’s 2019 paper, which identifies gaps and separates MELL from its decidable relevant variant.

Branching vector addition systems describe trees of computations with nonnegative integer resources. Their general reachability problem is inter-reducible with MELL provability. The 2025 result in the original reference establishes decidability for two-dimensional systems, so its dimension restriction cannot be omitted.

Status update: the July 2026 preprint claims decidability of general branching vector addition systems and explicitly states that MELL provability follows. This reaches the full decision question, unlike the earlier low-dimensional result. This card records the claim with uncertain status because its proof has not been independently verified here.

cards.title: Unconditional decidability of exact time-bounded CTMDP reachability
cards.formal: Is there an unconditional algorithm that, for every finite rational-rate CTMDP with a designated absorbing state good, rational deadline T>0 and rational threshold vector r, decides whether sup_π Pr_s^π[reach good by T]>r_s for every non-target state s, with timed positional policies as defined below?
cards.definitions: The input lists a finite state set S={1,…,n}∪{good}, n≥1; a nonempty finite action set A_s for each state; nonnegative rational rates q(s,a,t) for t≠s; T∈Q_{>0}; and r∈([0,1]∩Q)^n. Integers and rational numerators/positive denominators are binary encoded. All rates out of good are zero, and the diagonal generator entry is q(s,a,s)=−Σ_{t≠s}q(s,a,t). A decision vector d chooses one action d(s)∈A_s at each state. A policy is a Lebesgue-measurable map π:[0,T]→∏_s A_s: at elapsed time u in state s the instantaneous generator row is q(s,π(u)(s),·). Actions may change while the process remains in the same state, not only at jumps. Policies are deterministic and may depend on time and current state, with no computability restriction. For a fixed policy and initial state s, its probability law is the finite-state inhomogeneous Markov jump law with this bounded measurable generator. Equivalently its row distribution ρ_s(u) is the unique absolutely continuous solution of ρ_s(0)=e_s and ρ_s′(u)=ρ_s(u)Q^{π(u)} for almost every u. Bounded rates ensure nonexplosion. Since good is absorbing, the probability of reaching it at some time in [0,T] equals ρ_s(T)_good. The supremum is taken over all such policies separately for each initial state. This defines the value without an attainment assumption; the source also proves existence of an optimal piecewise-constant timed positional policy. The decision uses strict > in every coordinate, so equality to any threshold requires NO. The algorithm is a deterministic Turing machine that halts with the correct YES/NO result on every valid encoding; there is no requested complexity bound and no number-theoretic oracle or unproved premise. Invalid encodings may be rejected.

context_blocks.text: A continuous-time decision process combines random event times with choices that can vary with elapsed time. The question concerns exact comparison of the best probability of reaching a target before a deadline.

Majumdar, Salamati and Soudjani define the strict vector-threshold question and prove its decidability assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. Their result does not give an unconditional decision procedure, and numerical approximation alone does not decide equality at the threshold.

cards.why: Settle a foundational exact-verification question for continuous-time controlled stochastic systems.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a terminating exact decision procedure with an unconditional proof for the specified strict vector-threshold predicate, or prove this language undecidable. Additive approximations, a procedure that may fail to halt at equality, or a theorem conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture do not settle it.

cards.title: Shortest runs in 3-D VASS
cards.formal: Is there no single-exponential bound on shortest runs in binary-encoded three-dimensional vector addition systems with states? Precisely, is it true that for every integer k≥1, every real C>0 and every N₀≥1, there is a reachable instance I of encoding length N≥N₀ whose shortest source-to-target run has more than 2^(C N^k) transitions?
cards.why: Isolates how much witness complexity three unbounded counters can force. Resolving the single-exponential threshold would clarify the gap between low-dimensional reachability and the much more expensive behavior possible when the number of counters grows.
cards.status_note: Original question and the 2025 explicit binary formulation checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The July 2026 preprint improves the upper bound but does not resolve whether single-exponential shortest runs always suffice. No resolution of that threshold was located; proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Czerwiński asks for a three-counter shortest-run lower bound beyond the exponential scale; the upper-bound discussion is historical.
The ICALP paper obtains a triple-exponential shortest-run upper bound and 2-EXPSPACE membership. Section 7 retains the question whether single-exponential runs suffice for binary 3-VASS.

Chen and coauthors state a doubly-exponential shortest-run upper bound and EXPSPACE membership in a new preprint. This review checked the model and theorem statements, not the full proof; the result does not supply the requested super-single-exponential lower bound.

cards.definitions: A three-dimensional vector addition system with states (3-VASS) is a finite set Q of control states and a finite transition set T⊆Q×ℤ³×Q. A configuration is (q,u) with q∈Q and u∈ℕ³, where ℕ includes zero. A transition (q,a,q′) sends (q,u) to (q′,u+a) only when every coordinate of u+a is nonnegative. There are no zero tests or counter bounds. A reachability instance I consists of Q,T and two configurations s,t. It is reachable if some finite sequence of enabled transitions sends s to t. Its shortest-run length ℓ(I) is the minimum number of transitions in such a sequence; the empty run is allowed, and ℓ(I)=0 when s=t. Unreachable instances are excluded from the quantified claim. N is the bit length of an explicit description: states are numbered, the transition list and the source and target are given explicitly, and all integer coordinates are written in signed binary (nonnegative binary for configurations), with delimiters and state indices included. Usual explicit binary-list encodings differ by polynomial factors, which do not affect existence of a 2^(N^O(1)) bound. The dimension is always exactly three, while the number of states, transitions and counter magnitudes may grow. No finite-reachability-set promise or effective construction of the hard instances is required. The single-exponential convention and binary encoding follow the explicit later formulation in Section 7 of the 2025 source.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed unboundedness beyond every 2^(C N^k), or refute it by proving that there are fixed C>0 and integer k≥1 for which every reachable binary 3-VASS instance I has ℓ(I)≤2^(C |I|^k), after adjusting C to include the finitely many small sizes. A long run alone is insufficient: the lower bound concerns the shortest run between the chosen configurations. Neither a lower bound with a growing number of counters nor the mere existence of many reachable configurations establishes this target.

context_blocks.title: Three counters, infinitely many configurations
context_blocks.text: The control graph is finite, but each counter may become arbitrarily large. A transition can consume tokens from one counter and produce tokens in another, provided it never makes a counter negative. Reachability asks whether a target configuration can be obtained from a given start through legal transitions.

context_blocks.title: Why the binary encoding matters
context_blocks.text: Consider one state and the single transition (−1,+1,0), from counters (2^r,0,0) to (0,2^r,0). Every successful run has exactly 2^r steps, although the instance uses only O(r) bits. This gives exponential length in the input description. The question asks whether shortest runs can exceed every bound 2^(N^k), with fixed k, rather than merely whether exponential runs occur.

context_blocks.title: Shortest paths control witness size
context_blocks.text: A reachable target may have many very long runs leading to it. Only the minimum length is relevant here. A single-exponential shortest-run upper bound would allow the binary reachability problem to be decided in polynomial space, as the 2025 source explains. A lower bound on the number or largest size of reachable configurations is a different assertion.

context_blocks.title: The known upper bound has changed
context_blocks.text: The 2019 question mentioned a tower-type upper bound. The ICALP 2025 work gives a triple-exponential bound on shortest runs, and the July 2026 preprint states an improvement to a doubly-exponential bound. These upper bounds do not establish that any shortest run actually needs more than single-exponential length.

references.title: One-Clock Synthesis Problems
references.authors: Lasota, Sławomir; Lehaut, Mathieu; Parreaux, Julie; Piórkowski, Radosław
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 19; PDF page 19

cards.definitions: In round i≥1, Timer chooses a_i∈T and a nonnegative rational delay τ_i; after observing this move, Monitor chooses b_i∈M. Put t_i=∑_{j≤i}τ_j. The resulting infinite timed word is ((a_i,b_i),t_i)_{i≥1}. Timestamps may be equal or bounded above: no non-Zeno requirement is imposed. A has finitely many locations, sets of initial and accepting locations, one clock x initially zero, and finitely many transitions (ℓ,(a,b),g,Y,ℓ′), where g is a finite conjunction of x⋈c tests with ⋈∈{<,≤,=,≥,>} and c a nonnegative integer, and Y either resets x to zero or leaves it unchanged. In the ordinary model, delay τ adds τ to the clock before checking g and applying the optional reset. In the 1-resetting extension, the value checked is frac(x+τ), its fractional part; that value is retained unless the transition resets it. A word belongs to L(A) iff some run visits accepting locations infinitely often. Neither player controls this accepting-run existential quantifier. The designated owner wins exactly words in L(A), and the other player wins its complement. A Timer strategy maps finite Monitor histories to the next pair (a,τ); a Monitor strategy maps nonempty histories of Timer’s letters and timestamps to the next b. Each player can reconstruct its own past moves from its strategy. A strategy wins if every opposing response sequence yields a winning word. Determinacy requires the existence of one such strategy; a finite-state controller or synthesis algorithm is an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that at least one player has a winning unrestricted strategy in every game for both specified clock variants, or give a game in one of these variants in which neither player has a winning strategy. Undecidability of deciding the winner, or failure of finite-memory strategies, is not a nondeterminacy example.

context_blocks.title: One player controls time; both choose letters
context_blocks.text: Timer announces a letter and how much time has elapsed. Monitor sees that information before answering. The automaton evaluates their combined infinite timed word. This is a perfect-information turn-based game, rather than a game in which both players simultaneously choose delays.

context_blocks.title: Every play has a winner, but that is not determinacy
context_blocks.text: For any completed play, membership in L(A) decides the winner. Determinacy asks for a stronger statement: before the opponent’s future choices are known, can one player choose a rule that wins against all of them?

context_blocks.title: A simple determined example
context_blocks.text: Let both alphabets be {0,1}, let Monitor own the language of words in which a_i=b_i in every round, and let A ignore its clock. Monitor wins by replying with the observed a_i. General nondeterministic timed winning languages need not have such an immediate response rule.

context_blocks.title: The paper settles synthesis questions, not this existence question
context_blocks.text: The source proves undecidability across its synthesis variants, already with one clock, and studies when a finite controller suffices. It explicitly leaves determinacy unresolved. An undecidable winner problem can still have a winner for every individual game.

context_blocks.title: The clock conventions are part of the question
context_blocks.text: Replacing rational delays by arbitrary real choices, forbidding convergent time sequences, restricting strategies to controllers, or assigning control of nondeterministic runs to a player changes the game. The 1-resetting extension also has its own transition semantics and is included explicitly.

cards.title: Truth-table reconstruction of intuitionistic connectives
cards.formal: For every n≥1 and every propositional formula F(p₁,…,pₙ) built from ∧, ∨, → and ¬, suppose that each disjunction subformula P∨Q has both P and Q free of → and ¬, each implication subformula P→Q has P free of → and ¬, and each negation subformula ¬P has P free of → and ¬. Let c_F be a fresh n-ary connective with the constructive truth-table natural-deduction rules below, derived from the classical Boolean truth table of F. Must c_F(A₁,…,Aₙ) and F(A₁,…,Aₙ) be interderivable in intuitionistic logic with those rules, for every substitution of formulas A₁,…,Aₙ? The syntactic restriction is checked on the template F before substitution.
cards.why: Would give a syntactic guarantee that automatic proof-rule generation preserves a defined connective’s intuitionistic meaning, clarifying the expressive limits of truth-table natural deduction.

references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 26; PDF page 26

cards.definitions: Formulas are finite syntax trees over propositional variables and the listed connectives; repeated variables are allowed. The restriction “free of → and ¬” means that only variables, ∧ and ∨ occur in that subformula. The Boolean truth table t_F:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} evaluates ∧ as conjunction, ∨ as disjunction, → as material implication and ¬ as complement. For a substitution A=(A₁,…,Aₙ), write Φ=c_F(A). Derivations are finite intuitionistic natural-deduction derivations with the usual assumption, conjunction, disjunction, implication and negation rules, including falsity elimination; ¬B has its usual intuitionistic meaning B→⊥. Add the following rule schemata, with Γ a finite context and D any formula. For each row r with t_F(r)=0, from Γ⊢Φ, all premises Γ⊢Aᵢ with rᵢ=1, and all premises Γ,Aⱼ⊢D with rⱼ=0, infer Γ⊢D, discharging the indicated extra assumptions. For each row r with t_F(r)=1, from all Γ⊢Aᵢ with rᵢ=1 and all Γ,Aⱼ⊢Φ with rⱼ=0, infer Γ⊢Φ, again discharging the indicated assumptions. An empty family of premises contributes no requirement. Rule instances may use arbitrary formulas in the extended language; no excluded-middle or classical introduction rule is added. Interderivable means that both Φ⊢F(A) and F(A)⊢Φ have such derivations. This is an exact syntactic equivalence claim with no computational-resource or probability bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove both derivability directions for every qualifying formula template and every substitution, or refute the universal statement with a qualifying template for which at least one direction is not derivable in the specified calculus. A mismatch for a template violating the syntactic condition is not a counterexample; classical equivalence alone is insufficient.

cards.title: Decidability of approximate synthesis with arbitrary rational discounting
cards.formal: Is approximate synthesis decidable for deterministic discounted-sum specifications over finite words, with an arbitrary rational discount factor 0<λ<1? Given a finite deterministic weighted automaton defining S, a rational tolerance ν and a comparison symbol ⋖∈{<,≤}, decide whether there exists a deterministic finite-state transducer T such that dom(T)=dom(S) and, for every input word u in this domain, S(u⊗T(u)) is finite and bestVal_S(u)−S(u⊗T(u)) ⋖ ν. Here bestVal_S(u)=max{S(u⊗v): v has length |u| and S(u⊗v)>−∞}. One algorithm must halt and answer correctly on every such finite input, including both comparison modes; its input includes λ. The source settles the subclass λ=1/k for integers k≥2 and leaves general rational λ open.
cards.why: Would determine whether near-optimal terminating reactive behavior can be synthesized when future rewards are discounted by any rational factor, extending beyond arithmetic restrictions on the discount and beyond exact-optimum synthesis.
cards.status_note: Read the deterministic finite-word model, partial domain, transducer convention, regret condition and exact discount indexing in the conference and full versions. Checked later discounted-sum determinization/comparison work and focused synthesis searches through 12 September 2026. No result settling the general rational-discount question was found; searches are not exhaustive and theorem proofs were not independently audited.

progress.text: The source establishes the reciprocal-integer-discount subclass and leaves approximate synthesis for general rational discounting open.

cards.definitions: Let I and O be finite nonempty, disjoint input and output alphabets. For u=a₁…a_n∈I* and v=b₁…b_n∈O*, their convolution here is the alternating word u⊗v=a₁b₁…a_nb_n, of length 2n. A deterministic weighted automaton consists of finitely many states, one initial state, a partial transition function on I∪O, a set of accepting states and one integer weight on each transition. If the unique run on u⊗v exists and ends in an accepting state, and its transition weights are z₁,…,z_{2n}, then S(u⊗v)=Σ_{j=1}^{2n}λʲz_j. Otherwise S(u⊗v)=−∞. An accepting empty run has value zero. Discounting is per individual input or output transition, begins with λ¹, and has no multiplying normalization factor 1−λ. The domain dom(S) consists of the input words admitting at least one finite-valued output word. The maximum defining bestVal is attained because there are finitely many length-|u| output words. T has finite states, an initial state, a total deterministic transition map (state,input symbol)↦(output symbol,next state), and accepting states. It outputs exactly one symbol immediately after each input symbol, with no lookahead or end-of-word output; T(u) is defined precisely when the run ends in an accepting state. Its acceptance domain must equal dom(S), even though its internal run can produce symbols on other inputs. The number of transducer states is not bounded in advance. Thus a single finite-state policy must work for all word lengths and all input continuations, while the offline comparison bestVal may use the entire word. All transitions, alphabets, weights, λ and ν have finite explicit encodings; integers are binary and rationals have binary numerators and positive denominators. No computation-time bound, error probability or approximation of the decision answer is permitted. The tolerance is an additive difference in discounted value, not a ratio or per-symbol average.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a total decision algorithm for existence of a finite-state realizer satisfying the exact domain and additive regret condition, or prove this decision problem undecidable. Report which comparison modes are covered. Deciding only fixed-threshold synthesis S(u⊗T(u))≥c, only zero regret, only reciprocal-integer discounting, or only a prescribed finite horizon does not decide the stated general problem. A procedure that finds a realizer on yes instances but may run forever on no instances is not a decider.

context_blocks.title: Online outputs are compared with hindsight
context_blocks.text: For each completed input word, the specification assigns values to admissible output words. Approximate synthesis asks for one finite-state online transducer whose value stays within a given additive tolerance of the best output chosen with full knowledge of that word.

context_blocks.title: Partial domains are part of correctness
context_blocks.text: Some input words have no admissible output. The synthesized transducer must recognize exactly the specification’s input domain and meet the quantitative requirement on every word in it. The domain need not be prefix closed, so accepted finite executions cannot be replaced by a requirement on all prefixes indiscriminately.

context_blocks.title: The already solved tasks are different
context_blocks.text: The source proves decidability for fixed-threshold and best-value discounted-sum synthesis. cards.title: P versus NC
cards.formal: Is P=NC, where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
cards.definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For L∈NC there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family (Cₙ)ₙ≥0 such that Cₙ decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most C(n+2)ᶜ gates, and has depth at most C(log₂(n+2))ᵏ. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic O(log(n+2))-space transducer given 1ⁿ must output the description of Cₙ; its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish P≠NC.
cards.why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.

importance.reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.

progress.text: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization.
Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations.
Raz and McKenzie prove monotone NC≠monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits.

Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size 2^{n^{Ω(1)}}, improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.

context_blocks.text: Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm visits the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. The question is whether the Boolean function described by an arbitrary such circuit always has an efficiently constructible, much shallower evaluation circuit. Depth of the supplied circuit and depth of an algorithm that evaluates it are different quantities.

For example, a long chain that successively ANDs input bits can be replaced by a balanced tree of AND gates with logarithmic depth. Thus a long chain in the input is not by itself a lower bound on the time needed to evaluate it. Circuit Value allows arbitrary sharing and combinations of gate types, rather than promising this particular associative form.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals NC¹.

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. The separation measures the cost of forbidding negation. It supplies progress in circuit lower bounds while leaving the general uniform parallel-computation question untouched.

cards.title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
cards.formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most Cn(log(n+2))^a bits of memory and C(log(n+2))^b passes, with success probability at least 2/3 for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set [n], n≥2, with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous O(n logᵃ(n+2))-bit space and O(logᵇ(n+2))-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least 2/3 on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.
cards.why: Determine whether global directed reachability can be recovered from repeated sequential scans with only nearly linear memory, a central unresolved graph-streaming tradeoff.

importance.reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.

progress.text: Guruswami–Onak establish multipass superlinear space lower bounds for directed reachability decision; these imply Ω(log n/log log n) passes in semi-streaming space.
Jambulapati–Liu–Sidford develop nearly linear-work, approximately square-root-depth parallel reachability and its sparse shortcut construction.
Chen and coauthors prove almost-quadratic space is necessary for o(√log n) passes, strengthening the few-pass space tradeoff.
Assadi and coauthors state and explain the n^{1/2+o(1)}-pass semi-streaming implementation, including path recovery, in Proposition 4.
Assadi’s survey records the gap and explains the transition from search lower bounds to reachability-decision lower bounds.
The revised streaming-monotonicity paper retains the square-root reachability benchmark and reduces faster approximation to faster reachability.

context_blocks.text: Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most n−1 scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and n^{1/2+o(1)} depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting n^{1/2+o(1)}-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

A reachability-preserving shortcut is an extra arc (u,v) added only when the original graph already contains a directed path from u to v. Such arcs can reduce the number of edges in a path without changing which vertices are reachable. The cited streaming upper bound constructs and uses a sparse collection within its memory budget; its pass guarantee is part of that implementation, not a consequence of the existence of shortcuts alone.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires Ω(log n/log log n) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that o(√log n) passes require n^{2−o(1)} space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the Ω(log n/log log n) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies n^{1/2+o(1)} as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.
