cards.title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
cards.why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
cards.definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.

progress.text: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette.
Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence.

The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The target is deterministic and uniform in both degree and graph size; fast randomized coloring is not a resolution.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.

cards.title: Near-linear-palette LOCAL coloring in O(log* n) rounds
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants K,C and one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that, for every simple n-vertex graph and supplied maximum-degree bound $\Delta\ge2$, outputs a proper coloring with at most $\lceil K\Delta^{1.001}\rceil$ colors in at most $C(1+\log^*n)$ rounds? Vertices know n and Delta and have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. Neither K nor C may depend on Delta or n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the uniform algorithm and constants, or prove that no such constants and algorithm exist. A log-star n bound with a degree-dependent hidden constant does not settle this proposition.
cards.why: I include this because it separates the cost of symmetry breaking from the number of colors used to absorb local conflicts. A solution would clarify whether the quadratic palette in a foundational distributed primitive reflects an intrinsic limitation or merely the current method of reducing identifiers to colors.
cards.definitions: Proper means that every input edge has differently colored endpoints. Colors are integers from one shared palette. The identifier bound has a fixed polynomial range in n. Log-star uses base two. The target is deterministic worst-case elapsed rounds over graphs and valid identifier assignments. Delta is not treated as a fixed constant outside the asymptotic bound.

progress.text: Linial’s color reduction gives an $O(\Delta^2)$-coloring in $O(\log^*n)$ rounds. Symmetry-breaking lower bounds also show that the graph-size dependence cannot in general become o(log-star n) when degree is fixed.
Maus and Tonoyan revisit the local color-reduction method and extend it to list and conflict constraints. Their result does not establish the near-linear palette at the requested uniform round bound.
Suomela explicitly lists the Delta-to-the-1.001 palette target within O(log-star n) deterministic rounds.

Because the graph family ranges over every degree, hiding a large degree-dependent factor in the running time would erase the intended tradeoff.

For example, fixing degree first and then saying that an algorithm takes a constant number of rounds is insufficient: that constant might grow as the degree squared. The question instead requires one numerical multiplier on log-star n that works as both graph size and degree grow. This is why all the constants are quantified explicitly.

Classical color reduction reaches a quadratic-degree palette in iterated-logarithmic time. The source lists reducing the palette below that quadratic scale, and in particular to degree raised to 1.001, as unresolved. The card focuses on that one concrete target; optimal Delta+1 coloring with a larger degree-dependent round budget is a separate question.

cards.definitions: There are n=3t+1 parties with pairwise authenticated channels and a designated sender holding a message m of ℓ bits. Honest-to-honest messages are eventually delivered, with no upper bound on delay; Byzantine parties may deviate arbitrarily. Validity requires every honest party eventually to deliver m when the sender is honest. Agreement requires all honest deliveries to have the same value. Integrity allows each honest party at most one delivery, and totality requires that if one honest party delivers, all honest parties eventually do so. A Byzantine sender may cause no delivery. Let C_A(n,ℓ) be the worst-case total number of bits sent by honest parties in one execution of protocol A, over admissible inputs, faults and delivery schedules. Faulty-party transmissions are not charged. For a faulty sender, the source measures the effective message length by the largest payload fragment an honest party sends under the protocol’s declared encoding. The large-message overhead is L_A(n)=limsup_{ℓ→∞} C_A(n,ℓ)/(nℓ). This uses the upper limit to include protocols without a limiting coefficient; it agrees with the source’s limit whenever that limit exists. The proposed bound is liminf_{t→∞}L_A(3t+1)≥3/2; equivalently, no constant improvement below 3/2 is possible uniformly for all sufficiently large n and sufficiently long messages. The source permits collision-resistant hashing and, for signature-based protocols, signature setup, counting their transmitted bits through a security parameter κ. The payload comparison discards lower-order terms in ℓ, such as O(κn²log n), and uses the source’s cryptographic correctness convention. There is no bound of three on the number of rounds and no restriction that the sender’s first-round total be o(nℓ).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal 3/2 lower bound in the stated unrestricted asynchronous model, or give a correct protocol with a strictly smaller asymptotic worst-case payload coefficient. An upper bound of 3/2 or a lower bound only for three-round, weakly balanced protocols does not resolve this question.

context_blocks.title: Two restrictions remain in the known lower bound

context_blocks.title: Failure-free behavior is not the objective

cards.definitions: The communication network is a finite undirected simple graph G=(V,E), |V|=n≥2. Every edge has a supplied direction, known to its endpoints; no acyclicity is promised. A vertex’s outdegree is its number of outgoing edges, and every vertex has outdegree at most the supplied bound β. Its indegree and total degree may be arbitrarily large. A proper coloring assigns each vertex a label from one common palette so that endpoints of every edge have different labels, regardless of the edge direction. Vertices execute the same deterministic algorithm in synchronous rounds, have unique identifiers of O(log n) bits, know their incident ports and edge directions, and may know n and β. Each round allows a separate message of unbounded size to each neighbor in either direction and unrestricted finite local computation. Cost is worst-case round count over graphs, orientations and identifiers. No precomputed coloring or graph decomposition is supplied. The function f may grow arbitrarily fast with β, but cannot depend on n, total degree or the orientation’s path lengths. Both the exponent improvement ε and the coefficient of log* n must be uniform over β and n. Here log* n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach a value at most one. Edgeless graphs, including the β=0 case, can be assigned one color separately.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the uniform deterministic algorithm with the stated palette and additive round bound, or establish that no such ε, constants, computable f and algorithm exist. A palette reduction by only logarithmic factors, a runtime depending on total degree, or a multiplicative log n term does not establish this claim.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm, with fixed polynomials p and q, that solves every rational linear program $\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}$, where A has m rows and n columns, using at most p(m+n) elementary arithmetic, comparison, and data-transfer operations, while every intermediate rational number has binary encoding length at most q(N)? Here N is the total input bit length. Solving means returning an exact optimal rational solution if one exists, or correctly reporting infeasibility or an objective unbounded below.
cards.definitions: A is in Q^(m by n), b in Q^m, and c in Q^n, with m,n>=1. All coefficients are supplied explicitly as binary signed numerators and positive denominators. No full-rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, coefficient-size, or conditioning promise is made. Elementary scalar operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero quantity, comparisons, and transfers of stored values. The program is fixed and finite; no oracle, advice, randomization, floor operation, or uncharged access to binary digits is allowed. Rational encoding length means the bit length of a numerator-denominator representation. The polynomial p is independent of N and of every coefficient magnitude; q may depend on N. Consequently the algorithm must also admit a polynomial-time bit implementation. The output is a solution vector, not a required optimal basis. Infeasible means that the feasible set is empty; unbounded means it is nonempty and the infimum of c^T x is minus infinity. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This isolates whether the combinatorial dimensions of a linear program suffice to control its arithmetic complexity. A resolution would clarify the relation between numerical precision, polyhedral structure, and the complexity of one of optimization’s basic models.

importance.reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.

progress.text: The ellipsoid method and early interior-point algorithms establish polynomial-time solvability in the total input bit length. They do not provide a general strongly polynomial operation bound.

Tardos gives an algorithm whose arithmetic count is independent of the right-hand side and objective magnitudes, with remaining dependence on the constraint matrix. Small integer entries in that matrix give important strongly polynomial special cases.

Allamigeon, Gaubert, and Vandame construct LP families forcing exponentially many iterations for the self-concordant-barrier path-following methods covered by their theorem. This restricts a route to solving the problem; it is not an unrestricted LP lower bound.

Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver, and Végh solve minimum-cost generalized flow and LPs with at most two nonzeros per row or column in strongly polynomial time. Their analysis also controls intermediate bit lengths.

Dadush, Ma, Natura, and Végh improve interior-point bounds in terms of straight-line complexity and give strongly polynomial trust-region subroutines. Straight-line complexity can itself be large, so these are not dimension-only bounds for arbitrary LPs.

Version 10 of Awoniyi’s preprint claims at most 2(m+n) complementary-pivot iterations for general LP. This review has not validated the termination/correctness argument and complete bit-complexity guarantee, and found no independent primary confirmation. The claim is not promoted to an established resolution.

This card records it without treating it as established: correctness, the iteration bound, and the full strongly polynomial guarantee have not been independently validated in this review. context_blocks.text: Linear programming is already solvable in polynomial time when input length includes the bits used to write its coefficients. The unresolved issue is whether the number of arithmetic decisions can depend only on the number of constraints and variables. Very large capacities, costs, or denominators may require long arithmetic operands, but the question asks whether they must also force more arithmetic steps.

Both requirements in the definition are essential. Bounding the number of steps while allowing intermediate integers with exponentially many bits could hide enormous computation inside single arithmetic operations. Bounding only total bit time gives ordinary polynomial-time linear programming, which is already known. The strongly polynomial target combines a dimension-only operation count with controlled numerical representation.

Combinatorial optimization supplies positive examples. Tardos’s method removes dependence on the magnitudes of the right-hand side and objective, and yields strongly polynomial bounds for suitable small-coefficient constraint matrices. More recently, a strongly polynomial algorithm was obtained when each row, or each column, has at most two nonzero entries. These cases show that large numerical data alone need not force many arithmetic steps.

For unrestricted matrices, an algorithm may need a different way to navigate the feasible region. Long central paths can defeat broad classes of path-following methods, even though other approaches remain possible. A separate status issue is a 2025 preprint, revised in July 2026, claiming a general solution. Its claim is recorded below, but this review has not established its correctness or found independent validation.

sentences: Linear programming optimizes a linear objective subject to linear equality and nonnegativity constraints.
The question asks whether every rational instance can be solved using a number of arithmetic operations polynomial only in its numbers of variables and constraints.
Intermediate numbers must also have encoding lengths bounded polynomially in the full input length.
Existing polynomial-time guarantees may depend on how many bits describe the coefficients, which is the dependence this target seeks to remove.
A solution must handle exact optima, infeasibility, and unbounded objectives within the same strongly polynomial framework.

cards.context:
Linear programming is already solvable in polynomial time when input length includes the bits used to write its coefficients. The unresolved issue is whether the number of arithmetic decisions can depend only on the number of constraints and variables. Very large capacities, costs, or denominators may require long arithmetic operands, but the question asks whether they must also force more arithmetic steps.

Both requirements in the definition are essential. Bounding the number of steps while allowing intermediate integers with exponentially many bits could hide enormous computation inside single arithmetic operations. Bounding only total bit time gives ordinary polynomial-time linear programming, which is already known. The strongly polynomial target combines a dimension-only operation count with controlled numerical representation.

Combinatorial optimization supplies positive examples. Tardos’s method removes dependence on the magnitudes of the right-hand side and objective, and yields strongly polynomial bounds for suitable small-coefficient constraint matrices. More recently, a strongly polynomial algorithm was obtained when each row, or each column, has at most two nonzero entries. These cases show that large numerical data alone need not force many arithmetic steps.

For unrestricted matrices, an algorithm may need a different way to navigate the feasible region. Long central paths can defeat broad classes of path-following methods, even though other approaches remain possible. A separate status issue is a 2025 preprint, revised in July 2026, claiming a general solution. Its claim is recorded below, but this review has not established its correctness or found independent validation.

benchmark_focus.reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.

cards.title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the following language in P in the ordinary Turing model: all lists of symmetric rational matrices A_0,A_1,…,A_m∈Q^{n×n} for which there exists a real vector x∈R^m satisfying A_0+sum_{i=1}^m x_i A_i⪰0? Both m and n are unbounded parts of the input, and the algorithm must decide exact nonemptiness in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
cards.definitions: Every matrix entry is an explicitly supplied rational number, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; all matrices have the same size n≥1. A symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite, written M⪰0, when zᵀMz≥0 for every real vector z, equivalently when all eigenvalues are nonnegative. The unknown x ranges over all real vectors, not just rational vectors. Singular feasible matrices count as YES. There is no strict-feasibility, boundedness, conditioning, rank, or distance-to-infeasibility promise, and no radius or accuracy parameter is supplied. The output is one bit specifying whether any feasible x exists; an explicit feasible point is not required. An affine subspace given by rational linear equations can be parametrized by rational Gaussian elimination, so this is also the rational-affine-subspace intersection formulation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic boundary between numerical convex optimization and exact efficient computation. Resolving it would clarify what semidefinite programming can guarantee without hidden regularity or witness-size assumptions, with consequences for optimization relaxations, algebraic certificates and verification.

importance.reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The primary literature retains general exact SDP feasibility as an open polynomial-time problem. Ramana’s dual does not establish NP∩coNP membership in the Turing model, and recent convex-polynomial optimization results address a different constraint family. This card permits real witnesses, singular feasible points, weak infeasibility and unbounded feasible regions.

context_blocks.text: Semidefinite constraints replace scalar nonnegativity by nonnegativity of a quadratic form in every direction. They include linear inequalities as the diagonal-matrix special case and support powerful relaxations in combinatorial optimization. Approximation algorithms are well developed, but their guarantees require attention to input geometry and numerical precision. De Klerk and Vallentin establish polynomial bit complexity for a short-step interior-point method under appropriate assumptions; their theorem is about controlled approximation, not arbitrary exact feasibility.

The unrestricted problem is decidable. Introduce a real n×n matrix Y and impose A_0+sum_i x_i A_i=YYᵀ. These are finitely many polynomial equations of degree at most two, and a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when such a factor exists. General real-algebraic decision procedures therefore apply. Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop more specialized symbolic algorithms, including treatment of degenerate feasible sets. None of this supplies polynomial time when both input dimensions vary.

Exact feasibility can differ even from arbitrarily close approximation. The matrix M(t) with rows (0,1) and (1,t) has determinant −1, so it is never positive semidefinite. Yet as t tends to positive infinity, its negative eigenvalue (t−√(t²+4))/2 tends to zero. Thus these infeasible matrices approach the positive semidefinite cone arbitrarily closely. A numerical tolerance alone cannot distinguish this situation from a singular feasible matrix.

Rational input also need not admit a rational witness. Consider a block diagonal matrix with blocks [[x,2],[2,2x]] and [[2,x],[x,1]]. The first block is positive semidefinite exactly when x≥√2, and the second when |x|≤√2. The whole matrix is therefore feasible exactly at x=√2. All coefficient matrices are rational, but searching only rational substitutions would miss the solution. This example explains why the domain of the unknowns is part of the formal question.

Even rational feasible points can be enormous. Conditions x_1≥2 and [[x_{i+1},x_i],[x_i,1]]⪰0 force x_{i+1}≥x_i², hence x_k≥2^{2^{k−1}}. A block diagonal LMI encodes the chain compactly, while writing its final coordinate in ordinary binary needs exponentially many digits in k. Pataki and Touzov analyze how such growth arises beyond isolated examples, including connections to singularity degree. Large explicit witnesses obstruct a naive search algorithm; they do not prove that deciding existence is hard.

Ramana’s exact dual provides an alternative feasibility system of polynomial description size without regularity assumptions. In the Turing model, it implies that semidefinite feasibility belongs to NP if and only if it belongs to coNP. It does not establish either membership individually. The corresponding NP∩coNP theorem over exact real-number machines belongs to a different computational model. This distinction prevents a common overstatement of what SDP duality proves about bit complexity.
Pataki’s October 2025 work gives a new derivation and a fuller description of the feasible set of Ramana’s dual using facial reduction.

A separate STOC 2026 result by Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer obtains small approximate solutions for minimizing convex polynomials over polyhedra. That result concerns polynomial objectives with linear constraints; the authors explicitly contrast it with the large-solution obstacle for semidefinite programs. It does not settle general exact semidefinite feasibility.

cards.title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions: A clutter C on a finite ground set E is a family of subsets of E, no one properly containing another. In the original instance all members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover T⊆E meets every member, and τ(C) is the smallest cover size. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members, with maximum size ν(C). Deleting e removes e from the ground set and discards all members containing e. Contracting e removes it from the ground set and from every member, and retains only inclusion-minimal resulting members. A minor results from any sequence of these operations. The packing property means τ(C′)=ν(C′) for every minor C′. For the empty family both values are zero; for a minor containing the empty set both are defined as +∞, with the empty member permitted arbitrarily many times in a packing. For w∈ℤ_{≥0}^E, let τ_w(C)=min{Σ_{e∈T}w_e:T covers C}. Let ν_w(C) be the maximum of Σ_{F∈C}y_F over nonnegative integers y_F satisfying Σ_{F∋e}y_F≤w_e for every e∈E. Thus a weighted packing may use a member repeatedly, subject to capacities w. The max-flow min-cut property is τ_w(C)=ν_w(C) for every such w. The original nonempty-member assumption makes these weighted optima finite.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the packing property implies τ_w=ν_w for every finite clutter and every nonnegative integer weight vector, or give a finite clutter and weight vector with the packing property and τ_w>ν_w. A counterexample must verify equality for all minors, not merely for the original unweighted clutter. Finite searches, proofs for a proper subclass, or fractional optimality alone do not resolve the universal statement.

context_blocks.text: Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

If A is the member-by-element incidence matrix, the associated linear programs are min wᵀx subject to Ax≥1 and x≥0, and max 1ᵀy subject to Aᵀy≤w and y≥0. Equality of the two integer optima forces their values to agree with the fractional optimum by weak and strong duality. This is the standard MFMC integrality requirement.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

cards.why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.

importance.reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal: For every fixed integer c≥1, does there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm A_c with the following guarantee? Given n≥2, a nonsingular rational n×n matrix A with m nonzero entries, a nonzero rational vector b, and an integer 1≤p≤c·ceil(log_2 n), output a rational vector x̂ such that ||Ax̂−b||_2≤2^(−p)||b||_2 with probability at least 2/3. Each numerator and positive denominator of A and b has at most c·ceil(log_2 n) binary digits, and the spectral condition number κ_2(A) is promised at most n^c. The worst-case running time must be O_c(m log^(d_c)n) for some constant d_c independent of the input.
cards.definitions: The input lists the row index, column index and rational value of each nonzero coefficient, without duplicate positions, together with the n entries of b; hence n≤m≤n². The Euclidean norm is ||v||_2=(Σ_i v_i²)^(1/2), and κ_2(A)=σ_max(A)/σ_min(A), the ratio of its largest and smallest singular values. Nonsingularity makes the denominator positive. A may be nonsymmetric, indefinite and unrelated to a graph Laplacian. The algorithm need only meet its guarantee on promised inputs; it is not asked to certify the condition-number promise. Computation uses a word RAM with Θ(log n)-bit words, conventional arithmetic, comparison, bit operations and memory access; all operations on longer numbers, preprocessing, random-bit generation and writing the output are charged. No operation on an arbitrary real number has unit cost. Converting word operations to bit operations changes only polylogarithmic factors. Constants and the fixed program may depend on c, but neither nonuniform advice depending on n nor a supplied inverse or preconditioner is allowed. Here ε=2^(−p); this is the polynomial-condition, inverse-polynomial-accuracy regime of the near-input-size target. The output is the full list of n rational coordinates, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; every output bit is charged. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.

importance.reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.

Nie strengthens matrix anti-concentration and improves the block Krylov solver. The November 2021 preprint, revised in December, appears at STOC 2022.
Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang publish a sparsity-preserving reduction from general equations to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes.

The Simons workshop report is revised to reflect status through 20 August, retaining questions about extending scalable solvers and understanding finite-precision iterative methods. It does not give a universal nearly linear algorithm.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. This is an editorial, fully specified near-linear target in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime, not a named positive conjecture. The faster-than-matrix-multiplication problem has already been solved. The August 2026 report discusses broader scalable solvers but does not claim this universal guarantee; the simplicial-Laplacian reduction is not a general running-time lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Solving Ax=b is a basic operation inside scientific simulation, optimization and data analysis. A sparse input can be read and multiplied by a vector without scanning all n² matrix positions. The question is whether solving one system can always be comparably inexpensive, up to powers of logarithms. Peng and Vempala frame the general complexity problem around exploiting sparsity while also controlling numerical precision, rather than treating arithmetic on exact real numbers as free.

The target fixes a residual norm because different meanings of approximate solution can conceal different costs. If x*=A^(-1)b, the elementary inequality ||x̂−x*||_2/||x*||_2≤κ_2(A)·||Ax̂−b||_2/||b||_2 relates residual error to forward error. Thus a tiny residual need not mean an equally tiny solution error. For instance, A=diag(1,δ), b=(1,δ) and x̂=(1,0) have residual δ while the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The condition promise and requested accuracy make this dependence explicit.

Nearly linear solvers already exist for major structured families. Spielman and Teng establish such algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant systems using preconditioning and graph structure. Their guarantee is naturally expressed in the matrix energy norm. For positive-definite systems, norm comparisons relate this guarantee to residual accuracy, with conditioning affecting the required tolerance. An arbitrary sparse matrix lacks the diagonal-dominance structure that supports this machinery.

Peng and Vempala’s SODA 2021 result breaks the matrix-multiplication barrier for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. They implement a randomized block Krylov approach using structured factorizations and a numerical-stability analysis. This is why merely asking for a sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication would be an obsolete open question. The stronger near-input-size target remains far beyond that theorem.

Nie improves the required anti-concentration bounds for random Krylov matrices. His STOC 2022 result yields a bound of Õ(m^((ω−2)/(ω−1))n²) in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. For m=Õ(n), this becomes Õ(n^((3ω−4)/(ω−1))). The paper’s numerical exponent 2.2716 uses the matrix-multiplication bound available at that time; it is not a claim about today’s best numerical value of ω. Either expression remains far above linear for very sparse inputs.

The distinction between a sparse matrix and a structurally easy sparse matrix is sharpened by Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang. They reduce general linear equations with polynomially bounded integer coefficients and conditioning to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes while preserving sparsity up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, extending graph-Laplacian techniques to those higher-dimensional Laplacians would already have general consequences. This is a completeness reduction, not an unconditional proof that a near-linear solver cannot exist.

The Simons workshop report, revised in August 2026, calls for broader classes of scalably solvable systems and studies the finite-precision behavior of iterative methods. Its benchmark questions are more focused than a universal worst-case solver, and its discussion of preconditioning makes clear that constructing a useful preconditioner is itself part of the computational task. The present card is an explicit editorial formulation of the general complexity target; it is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report.

The output requirement also matters. An explicit n-vector is compatible with nearly linear time because a nonsingular n×n input has at least n nonzeros. Returning only access to a vector, a few observables, or a quantum state encoding its normalized coordinates changes the task. Conversely, demanding an exact rational solution could introduce much larger output encodings; the specified numerical approximation avoids building that extra requirement into the question.

sentences: A sparse linear system stores only the nonzero entries of its coefficient matrix, making matrix-vector multiplication relatively cheap.
The question asks whether solving every well-conditioned rational system approximately can take nearly linear time in that sparse input size.
The saved formulation bounds coefficient lengths, conditioning, and requested residual accuracy to avoid hiding excessive numerical costs.
It seeks an explicit solution vector with high enough success probability from a randomized classical algorithm.
Such a result would extend the efficiency of structured Laplacian solvers to general sparse matrices, where sparsity alone currently provides much less algorithmic structure.

cards.context:
Solving Ax=b is a basic operation inside scientific simulation, optimization and data analysis. A sparse input can be read and multiplied by a vector without scanning all n² matrix positions. The question is whether solving one system can always be comparably inexpensive, up to powers of logarithms. Peng and Vempala frame the general complexity problem around exploiting sparsity while also controlling numerical precision, rather than treating arithmetic on exact real numbers as free.

The target fixes a residual norm because different meanings of approximate solution can conceal different costs. If x*=A^(-1)b, the elementary inequality ||x̂−x*||_2/||x*||_2≤κ_2(A)·||Ax̂−b||_2/||b||_2 relates residual error to forward error. Thus a tiny residual need not mean an equally tiny solution error. For instance, A=diag(1,δ), b=(1,δ) and x̂=(1,0) have residual δ while the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The condition promise and requested accuracy make this dependence explicit.

Nearly linear solvers already exist for major structured families. Spielman and Teng establish such algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant systems using preconditioning and graph structure. Their guarantee is naturally expressed in the matrix energy norm. For positive-definite systems, norm comparisons relate this guarantee to residual accuracy, with conditioning affecting the required tolerance. An arbitrary sparse matrix lacks the diagonal-dominance structure that supports this machinery.

Peng and Vempala’s SODA 2021 result breaks the matrix-multiplication barrier for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. They implement a randomized block Krylov approach using structured factorizations and a numerical-stability analysis. This is why merely asking for a sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication would be an obsolete open question. The stronger near-input-size target remains far beyond that theorem.

Nie improves the required anti-concentration bounds for random Krylov matrices. His STOC 2022 result yields a bound of Õ(m^((ω−2)/(ω−1))n²) in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. For m=Õ(n), this becomes Õ(n^((3ω−4)/(ω−1))). The paper’s numerical exponent 2.2716 uses the matrix-multiplication bound available at that time; it is not a claim about today’s best numerical value of ω. Either expression remains far above linear for very sparse inputs.

The distinction between a sparse matrix and a structurally easy sparse matrix is sharpened by Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang. They reduce general linear equations with polynomially bounded integer coefficients and conditioning to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes while preserving sparsity up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, extending graph-Laplacian techniques to those higher-dimensional Laplacians would already have general consequences. This is a completeness reduction, not an unconditional proof that a near-linear solver cannot exist.

The Simons workshop report, revised in August 2026, calls for broader classes of scalably solvable systems and studies the finite-precision behavior of iterative methods. Its benchmark questions are more focused than a universal worst-case solver, and its discussion of preconditioning makes clear that constructing a useful preconditioner is itself part of the computational task. The present card is an explicit editorial formulation of the general complexity target; it is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report.

The output requirement also matters. An explicit n-vector is compatible with nearly linear time because a nonsingular n×n input has at least n nonzeros. Returning only access to a vector, a few observables, or a quantum state encoding its normalized coordinates changes the task. Conversely, demanding an exact rational solution could introduce much larger output encodings; the specified numerical approximation avoids building that extra requirement into the question.

benchmark_focus.reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.

cards.title: Smale’s seventh problem
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C,K>0, an integer k≥1 and a deterministic real-number algorithm A in the model below such that, for every integer N≥2, A(N) outputs N distinct points x₁,…,x_N on S² in at most KN^k operations and E_N(x₁,…,x_N)≤E_N*+C ln N?
cards.why: Connects the complexity of constructing global near-minimizers with discrete potential theory and the conditioning of polynomial-root problems. Its logarithmic total-energy tolerance is much sharper than leading-order equidistribution.

cards.definitions: S²={x∈ℝ³: x₁²+x₂²+x₃²=1}. The energy is E_N(x₁,…,x_N)=Σ_{i≠j}−ln‖x_i−x_j‖₂, counting ordered pairs; collisions have energy +∞. E_N* is the infimum over all N-tuples on S². ln is the natural logarithm and ‖·‖₂ is Euclidean distance. The algorithm is one finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants, independent of N. It has exact real registers and a finite-control tape machine with register copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, and branching on the sign of a register. Tape movements and each scalar arithmetic, comparison or copy operation have unit cost. Input is the integer N as an exact real value; output is a list of 3N real coordinates. Any finite tape/register storage used by the program is charged through its operations. There is no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, random sample or minimization oracle. Polynomial time is in N, not in log N. The inequality is a mathematical condition on the output; the algorithm need not evaluate the energy. This specifies the real-number computation convention in Smale’s problem; coordinates need not be rational and no bit-cost bound is asserted.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants C,K,k, fixed independently of N, with the stated running time and total-energy guarantee for every integer N≥2. A negative answer proves that no such program and constants exist. Failure of one construction, a lower bound for a restricted method, or energy estimates for finitely many cardinalities do not establish the negation.

context_blocks.text: Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance C ln N is an additive error in the total energy. It is small compared with its known expansion E_N*=(1/2−ln 2)N²−(N/2)ln N+aN+o(N), where a is a universal constant. Matching only the leading N² term, or even allowing a linear error, leaves far more uncertainty than the target permits. Uniform-looking points and good numerical values for finitely many N do not establish this error bound.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an O(√N ln N) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least 1−exp(−N ln N). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the √N scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

cards.title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic primal-simplex pivot algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every rational linear program max{cᵀx: Ax=b, x≥0} with A of full row rank, a finite optimum, and any supplied feasible basis B_0, the algorithm reaches a basis whose reduced costs are all nonpositive using at most p(L) bit operations in total? Here L is the binary input length of A,b,c and B_0, and every basis change must be a legal improving simplex pivot as defined below.
cards.definitions: A has m rows and n columns with 1≤m≤n; all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicit binary integers. A basis B is a set of m columns with invertible A_B. Its basic solution is x_B=A_B^{-1}b and x_j=0 for j∉B, and feasibility means x_B≥0. An entering column j∉B must have reduced cost r_j=c_j−c_BᵀA_B^{-1}A_j>0. Put a=A_B^{-1}A_j. Choose a leaving basic index i attaining θ=min_{k∈B:a_k>0}x_k/a_k, and replace i by j in the basis. The finite-optimum promise ensures that this minimum exists for an improving column. Ties may be resolved by the rule; θ=0 is an allowed degenerate pivot and counts toward the bound. The rule may inspect the whole input and maintain history, with all preprocessing, pivot selection, exact arithmetic, helper computations and memory operations charged to p(L). It must follow these basis exchanges on the supplied LP from B_0: it may not jump to another feasible basis or replace the feasible region by an extended formulation. The required terminal condition r_j≤0 for all j∉B certifies optimality. This is the supplied-feasible-basis optimization version; phase-I feasibility construction is not part of this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a rule and prove its total polynomial bit complexity for every promised input and initial feasible basis, or prove that no such rule exists. Merely bounding the number of pivots while leaving their selection computationally unbounded is insufficient. A lower bound for a prescribed family of rules, or for nonlinear objectives, does not establish the negative answer for all rules here.
cards.why: A fundamental question about whether local, improving basis exchanges can support efficient global optimization. It would explain a central practical algorithm and sharpen the relationship between polyhedral geometry, degeneracy and algorithmic access to an optimum.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem about one of the most important optimization algorithms; the existence and efficient discovery of short improving basis paths remain unresolved even though LP itself is polynomial-time solvable.

progress.text: Spielman and Teng establish polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm; this is a distributional guarantee rather than worst-case polynomial bit complexity.
Disser and Mosis give an unconditional active-set lower bound using a nonlinear polynomial objective on a hypercube; the linear-objective question remains open.
Bach, Disser, Huiberts and Mosis strengthen the all-rules active-set lower bound to convex quadratic maximization. The latest preprint version is dated 22 October 2025.
Disser, Loho, Maat and Mosis publish superpolynomial lower bounds for specified ranking-based classes, with explicit information and memory restrictions.

Kukharenko and Sanità publish an antistalling rule bounding consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by n−m−1, given an improving feasible direction. It leaves the global pivot count open.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The STACS 2026 and March 2026 primary publications retain the general polynomial simplex question as open. This card fixes deterministic total bit complexity for legal improving primal-simplex pivots from any supplied feasible basis on a finite-optimum rational LP. Strongly polynomial algorithms, nonlinear active-set bounds and distributional performance are distinct formulations.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming already has algorithms with polynomial bit complexity, including ellipsoid and interior-point methods. The unresolved question is whether the same guarantee can be achieved while moving through bases by the simplex method. A pivot rule determines which improving direction to expose next and how to break ties. The STACS 2026 paper on ranking-based rules states that the general question remains open.

There are two obstacles to a polynomial guarantee. First, a short route to an optimal basis must exist under the permitted improving moves. Second, the rule must discover such a route efficiently. Knowing the optimum from another computation does not authorize skipping the route: every intervening basis exchange is still required. Likewise, a short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short path along improving edges.

The bit-complexity requirement is deliberately weaker than strongly polynomial simplex. It permits the running time to depend polynomially on the number of bits in coefficients. A strongly polynomial rule would instead bound its arithmetic work polynomially in m and n, together with appropriate bounds on the sizes of numbers used. Therefore this card does not assert that a positive answer alone settles Smale’s strongly polynomial LP problem or a diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy means several bases can describe the same vertex. A legal pivot with θ=0 changes the basis without improving the objective value, so an algorithm can stall even if the geometric route is short. Kukharenko and Sanità’s March 2026 paper bounds a block of consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by n−m−1, given an improving feasible direction. Such a direction can be obtained using an LP solver. This controls local stalling, but does not bound how many different nonoptimal vertices the method must visit.

Positive average-case results are also substantial. Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm under random perturbations of the input. Smoothed analysis studies the expected behavior around an arbitrary instance as a function of perturbation size. It helps explain good practical performance, but does not give a deterministic worst-case guarantee on every exact rational instance.

The 2026 ranking-based lower bounds exclude broader families than a single greedy rule. One result covers index-ranking rules with a specified limit on their memory states; another covers memoryless rules using rankings by index, reduced cost and objective improvement. Full access to numerical data and unrestricted polynomially bounded history are allowed in this card, so those lower bounds do not cover every candidate.

A striking neighboring result does exclude every pivot rule for the active-set method with a nonlinear objective. Disser and Mosis first use higher-degree polynomial objectives on the hypercube. Bach and coauthors then obtain the phenomenon for maximizing a convex quadratic function, published at SODA 2026. The direction of optimization matters: this is convex maximization. Their construction does not have a linear objective, and the authors explicitly distinguish it from a general simplex lower bound.

cards.title: Komlós conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal real constant C>0 such that, for all integers m,n≥1 and every real matrix A∈ℝ^{m×n} with ∑_{i=1}^m A_{ij}²≤1 for each column j, there is a vector x∈{−1,1}^n satisfying max_{1≤i≤m}|∑_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j|≤C?
cards.definitions: All matrices are finite. Columns may have arbitrary real entries, including negative entries. The sign vector may depend on the entire matrix; C may not depend on the dimensions or entries. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic or input-encoding requirement.

context_blocks.text: Discrepancy measures how accurately a fractional choice can be replaced by signs while controlling many linear constraints simultaneously. Komlós asks whether normalizing every column in Euclidean norm suffices to bound every coordinate of the signed sum by an absolute constant.

The 2025 improvement gives a polylogarithmic bound smaller than the classical square-root-logarithmic bound, but does not reach a constant. Komlós implies the Beck–Fiala conjecture after scaling an incidence matrix; the converse is not known. Both are retained as established landmarks with different hypotheses, rather than as unrelated questions.

cards.why: A defining vector-balancing conjecture with consequences for rounding, approximation and the geometry of linear constraints.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

Both are retained as established landmarks with different hypotheses, rather than as unrelated questions.

cards.title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given n≥1, a rational P-matrix M∈Q^(n×n) and q∈Q^n, outputs rational vectors z,w≥0 satisfying w=Mz+q and zᵀw=0?
cards.definitions: A principal submatrix M[S,S] uses the same nonempty index set S⊆{1,…,n} for rows and columns. M is a P-matrix when det M[S,S]>0 for every such S. All matrix and vector entries are explicitly listed as binary signed numerators and positive denominators; N denotes their total bit length including dimensions and separators. The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine whose running time, including output, is at most one polynomial p(N) independent of n and the entries. It must terminate within that bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs, but its output is required to satisfy the equations only when M is a P-matrix. No P-matrix recognition or certificate is supplied or required. Inequalities are coordinatewise, and zᵀw=Σ_i z_i w_i. There is no symmetry, positive-definiteness, sparsity, nondegeneracy or coefficient-size promise beyond rational encoding and the P-matrix condition. A numerical approximation alone is not an output solution.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

importance.reason: A longstanding general optimization question with a strong total-search interpretation and continuing work on both structural and algorithmic restrictions. It asks for ordinary polynomial bit complexity, distinct from strong polynomiality of LP and exact SDP feasibility.

context_blocks.text: Complementarity combines linear constraints with a discrete choice: in each coordinate, at least one of z_i and w_i must vanish. For example, when M is the identity, a negative entry of q is compensated by a positive z entry, while a positive q entry remains in w. For a general matrix the coordinates interact, so the zero pattern cannot be chosen independently.

The P-matrix condition guarantees exactly one solution for every right-hand side q. This removes failure of existence and ambiguity of the answer, yet does not supply a polynomial-time method to find that answer. The distinction is a central example of total search: a mathematical existence theorem can be much easier to state than a fast algorithmic realization.

Exact rational output is meaningful in the bit model. Once a complementary zero pattern is fixed, the remaining coordinates satisfy a nonsingular rational linear system on a principal submatrix. Determinant bounds give polynomial bit length for the solution. Thus the question does not hide an unavoidable exponentially long output.

Several matrix subclasses admit polynomial algorithms. Results for tridiagonal and Hessenberg P-matrices demonstrate how additional structure can make the problem tractable. Such restrictions are absent from this card. Likewise, a polynomial iteration count involving a condition-dependent parameter does not give a polynomial bound in the full input length without a bound on that parameter.

The current target concerns solving rational LCP instances, not recognizing the P-matrix promise and not solving every abstract orientation problem. It complements the existing cards for linear programming and exact semidefinite feasibility.

cards.title: Beck–Fiala conjecture
cards.formal: Is there a universal C>0 such that, for all integers m,n,t≥1 and every A∈{0,1}^{m×n} having at most t ones in each column, some x∈{−1,1}^n satisfies max_i |∑_j A_{ij}x_j|≤C√t?
cards.definitions: The matrix is the incidence matrix of a finite set system: its columns are elements and its rows are sets. Thus each element belongs to at most t sets. Empty sets and unused elements are allowed. The bound is independent of the number of elements and sets. The question asks for existence of a signing, without an algorithmic time requirement.

context_blocks.text: Bounded element frequency is a basic sparsity assumption in rounding problems. The conjecture asks whether its discrepancy cost is proportional to the square root of the frequency even when the system is arbitrarily large.

Recent results prove this scale for substantial ranges of t relative to the size of the system. The full statement includes all frequencies and remains stronger than those range-restricted results. The separate Komlós conjecture implies this statement by rescaling each incidence column.

cards.why: A central discrepancy conjecture governing how local incidence restrictions control global rounding error.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.formal: Do constants C,c>0 and a deterministic algorithm exist that decide whether Ax≤b has an integer solution x∈ℤ^n in at most 2^(Cn)(L+1)^c bit operations, for every rational matrix A and vector b?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. context_blocks.text: Integer programming is polynomial-time solvable in every fixed dimension, but the dependence on dimension determines how far that tractability extends. cards.title: Superpolynomial semidefinite extension complexity of perfect matching
cards.formal: For every C,c>0, does some even n≥2 satisfy xc_SDP(P_n)>Cn^c, where P_n is the perfect-matching polytope of K_n?
cards.definitions: P_n⊆ℝ^(n choose 2) is the convex hull of the zero-one incidence vectors of all perfect matchings of the complete graph on n labeled vertices. A size-r semidefinite lift is an affine subspace L of the real symmetric r×r matrices and an affine map π into ℝ^(n choose 2) such that P_n=π(L∩S_+^r), where S_+^r consists of positive semidefinite matrices. xc_SDP is the smallest such integer r. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers and need not be efficiently generated. The representation is exact; approximate relaxations and linear lifts are different notions.

context_blocks.text: Perfect matching can be optimized in polynomial time, yet exact linear descriptions in higher-dimensional spaces can require exponentially many inequalities. The question asks whether positive semidefinite constraints also suffer a superpolynomial representation barrier.

A linear extension-complexity lower bound is not a semidefinite one. Allowing an arbitrary affine slice of a positive semidefinite cone makes the model substantially stronger. A lower bound here would separate efficient optimization from compact exact SDP representation for a canonical tractable polytope.

cards.title: Woodall’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite weakly connected loopless directed multigraph D that is not strongly connected, let τ(D) be the minimum size of a directed cut. Must D contain τ(D) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins?
cards.definitions: A directed multigraph has a finite vertex set V and a finite set A of individually distinguished arcs; parallel arcs are allowed and loops are excluded. Weak connectivity means connectivity after forgetting arc directions. Strong connectivity means that every ordered pair of vertices is joined by a directed path. For ∅≠U⊊V, let δ⁺(U) be the arcs with tail in U and head outside U, and δ⁻(U) the arcs entering U. A directed cut, or dicut, is δ⁺(U) with δ⁻(U)=∅. Under the stated graph assumptions the family of dicuts is nonempty and each dicut has positive size, so τ(D)=min{|δ⁺(U)|:∅≠U⊊V, δ⁻(U)=∅} is a finite positive integer. A dijoin is a subset J⊆A meeting every dicut. Pairwise arc-disjoint means Jᵢ∩Jⱼ=∅ for i≠j. Every arc has unit capacity; no zero-capacity arcs or other weights are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of τ(D) pairwise disjoint dijoins for every stated D, or give a finite D satisfying the assumptions and prove that its maximum packing is smaller than τ(D). Since each dijoin must meet a smallest dicut, τ(D) is always an upper bound. An approximation by a constant fraction of τ, a fractional packing, or a theorem confined to a proper graph subclass is partial progress.

context_blocks.text: A dijoin selects arcs that collectively intercept every one-way boundary of a digraph. Packing dijoins asks how many separate selections can provide this complete coverage without sharing an arc. The smallest one-way boundary is an immediate bottleneck. Woodall’s conjecture says that this visible bottleneck is the only obstruction.

Schrijver lists this exact min–max equality as Survey Question 34. The adjacent Question 33 asks for a polynomial-time algorithm finding a maximum packing. The equality is the structural target here; no efficient construction is demanded as part of a positive answer.

The absence of weights matters. The stronger Edmonds–Giles statement permits arcs of capacity zero as well as one and is false. Deleting a zero-capacity arc can change which sets are dicuts, so it cannot generally turn a weighted counterexample into an unweighted one. The current formulation avoids that false strengthening.

Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi prove that at least ⌊τ/6⌋ disjoint dijoins can be constructed in polynomial time. Their argument connects dijoin packing to nowhere-zero flows in the underlying undirected graph. This supplies a constant-factor guarantee while retaining the exact Woodall equality as open.

Weakly disconnected graphs have a zero-size cut and give a trivial zero-packing case. Strongly connected graphs have no dicuts, making the empty set a vacuous dijoin. Restricting the statement to the nontrivial case fixes the meaning of the minimum and maximum without changing the substantive conjecture.

This belongs to combinatorial optimization through the relation between packing and covering, integrality and constructive approximation. It is distinct from a minimum-cost dijoin problem or from maximum directed cut: those optimize different objects, even though some of the vocabulary overlaps.

cards.title: Log-squared query complexity for fixed-dimensional Tarski
cards.formal: Let Q(n,k) be the minimum worst-case number of adaptive deterministic value queries needed to find any fixed point of an unknown monotone function $f:[n]^k\to[n]^k$, where [n]={1,...,n} and monotonicity is with respect to coordinatewise order. A query at x reveals the entire vector f(x). Is it true that for every integer k>=1 there is a constant C_k such that $Q(n,k)\le C_k(1+\log_2 n)^2$ for every n>=2? Arbitrary finite computation between queries is allowed. Constants may depend on k but not on n or f. This asks for an exponent independent of the fixed dimension, not a polynomial bound on C_k.
cards.definitions: For x,y in the grid, x<=y means x_i<=y_i for every coordinate i. The oracle is promised to satisfy x<=y implies f(x)<=f(y). A valid output is any x with f(x)=x; no minimum or maximum fixed point is required. An adaptive query procedure can choose each query using all earlier queries and answers, and must terminate correctly for every promised oracle. Equivalently, Q(n,k) is the minimum depth of a finite deterministic oracle decision tree whose leaves output valid fixed points for every monotone function consistent with that leaf. Neither a circuit description nor the table of f is part of the input. Query cost is one per returned vector, and places no restriction on the bit complexity of choosing the next query. The finite product grid is a complete lattice, so a fixed point always exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the bound for every fixed k, or show that there is a fixed k for which Q(n,k)/(1+log_2 n)^2 is unbounded as n grows. A growing factor depending only on k is permitted. A bound whose logarithmic exponent grows with k does not answer yes. A lower bound obtained only by letting k grow with n does not answer no unless it implies failure at some fixed k.
cards.why: This probes the information cost of finding a guaranteed fixed point under monotonicity, a basic organizing principle in algorithms, semantics, and equilibrium computation. The same sharp bound in dimensions two, three, and four makes the dependence on dimension a substantive structural mystery rather than just a loose analysis of one algorithm.

importance.reason: A broad oracle-complexity question about monotone fixed points, with a surprising low-dimensional pattern and connections to equilibrium search. It distinguishes intrinsic information requirements from implementation time.

progress.text: Etessami, Papadimitriou, Rubinstein, and Yannakakis prove an Omega(log^2 n) lower bound already in two dimensions, including for randomized algorithms; the 2022 seminar records this starting point.
Fearnley, Pálvölgyi, and Savani give an O(log^2 n)-query algorithm in three dimensions, matching the two-dimensional lower bound.
Brânzei, Phillips, and Recker prove randomized query lower bound Omega(k log^2 n / log k) for n,k>=2. For fixed k this remains quadratic in log n, so it does not rule out the card’s target.

Chen, Li, and Yannakakis obtain O(log^2 n) queries in four dimensions and improve the exponent in every fixed dimension. Section 9 proposes the possibility of a generic dimension-dependent constant times log^2 n.

context_blocks.text: Starting at the bottom of the grid and repeatedly applying f gives a nondecreasing chain until a fixed point is reached. This directly proves existence constructively, but the chain can contain a number of steps proportional to n times the dimension. Since the coordinates need only log n bits to describe, dependence on n can be exponentially larger than dependence on the coordinate description length.

One-dimensional search can exploit order by repeatedly discarding a large interval. In a product order, two points can be incomparable: one coordinate is larger and another smaller. The oracle’s monotonicity then does not directly compare their images. The question asks whether these multidimensional interactions must eventually increase the power of log n, or whether they can be absorbed into a dimension-dependent constant.

The first surprise was that dimensions two and three both have Theta(log^2 n) query complexity. Chen, Li, and Yannakakis extend this equality to dimension four in their March 2026 preprint. Their more general upper bound is O(log^(ceil((k-1)/3)+1) n) for fixed k. The concluding discussion explicitly raises a bound of the form f(k) log^2 n, which is the target on this card.

Query complexity and computational efficiency must be separated here. The 2026 algorithm uses expensive intermediate search and counting; its authors leave a time-efficient implementation open. Even a positive answer to this card would only limit how much oracle information is needed. Obtaining a polynomial-time algorithm when both k and log n are input parameters would require additional control of the constants and the work between queries.

cards.title: Constant-factor entrywise ℓ₁ rank-k approximation with variable k
cards.formal: Do a uniform randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm A and an absolute constant C≥1 exist such that, for every rational matrix M∈Q^(m×n) and input integer 0≤k≤min(m,n), A returns rational factors U∈Q^(m×k), V∈Q^(k×n) with ∥M−UV∥₁≤C·OPT_k(M) with probability at least 2/3, where OPT_k(M)=min_{rank(B)≤k, B real}∥M−B∥₁?
cards.definitions: m,n≥1; dimensions, k and each signed rational numerator and positive denominator are explicitly encoded in binary. The input length L counts the whole dense matrix description. ∥W∥₁=Σ_ij|W_ij| is the entrywise norm; rank is matrix rank over R. The optimum is over all real m×n matrices of rank at most k and is attained, since a minimizing sequence can be confined to a bounded closed sublevel set. The output consists of binary rational entries of U and V; for k=0 their product denotes the zero matrix. There is a single polynomial P such that A halts within P(L) Turing-machine steps on every input and every random tape, including the time to write its factors. Therefore the factors have polynomial total encoded length; no unit-cost exact real arithmetic or implicit algebraic-number oracle is available. The approximation factor C and polynomial exponent are independent of m,n,k and entry magnitudes. The probability is over independent fair algorithm coins for each fixed input. Only the displayed multiplicative error is allowed. In particular, when rank(M)≤k and OPT_k(M)=0, success requires exact equality UV=M. cards.definitions: Let M∈Z^{d×n} have columns ω_i, and let P=conv{ω_1,…,ω_n}={Σ_i a_iω_i: a_i≥0, Σ_i a_i=1}. The promise 0∈int(P) uses interior in R^d, not relative interior in a smaller affine space. A Gaussian rational v_i has the form a_i+b_i√(−1), with a_i,b_i∈Q; v_i≠0 ensures q_i=|v_i|²=a_i²+b_i²>0. The logarithm and exponential in f are the real natural logarithm and exponential. Under the promise, f is strictly convex, attains its minimum, and has exactly one minimizer x*∈R^d. Integers and rational numerators/denominators are encoded in binary. If B and b are the respective total encoding lengths of M and v, the target bit complexity is poly(d,n,B,b,p), including the rational output. Precision is supplied as an integer p and the running time is polynomial in its numerical value. This standard dyadic-accuracy convention spells out the source’s log(1/ε) dependence for ε=2^{−p}; a general binary rational accuracy request also incurs the cost of reading that request. No bound on a Hessian condition number or on the numerical magnitudes of the integer weights is an additional promise.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an algorithm with the stated bit-complexity and Euclidean error guarantee on every promised input, or establish an obstruction to this guarantee. A small value of f(x)−min f, a small gradient, or convergence without the polynomial dependence on coefficient bit lengths and requested precision does not suffice.

cards.definitions: An MDP is M=(S,A,P,R,γ), where S and A are finite nonempty explicitly listed sets, P(s,a,s′)≥0 is rational and Σ_{s′∈S}P(s,a,s′)=1 for each s,a, R:S×A→Q is a rational reward function, and γ is a rational discount factor with 0<γ≤1. Tables for transitions and rewards are explicit, and rationals are encoded as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. All actions in A are available in every state, as in the source model. H is a nonnegative integer in binary, so its numerical value may be exponential in its encoding length. A policy σ assigns a probability distribution over actions to every observed finite history of states and actions. Starting at s₀, sample aₜ from the policy after observing the history and then sample sₜ₊₁ from P(sₜ,aₜ,·). The payoff is Σ_{t=0}^{H−1}γᵗR(sₜ,aₜ); it is zero when H=0. Expectation is over transition randomness and any policy randomization. The policy is existentially quantified and is not an exponentially long table supplied as part of the input. Finite-horizon fully observed MDPs have an optimal deterministic Markov policy, depending on the current state and the time step; this does not assert a stationary policy. Let V_H(s₀) be the maximum of that expectation over policies. The answer is yes exactly when V_H(s₀)≥θ, including equality. There is no approximation tolerance or separation promise around θ. If N is the total input encoding length, complexity refers to a uniform Turing-machine decision algorithm and its worst-case bit cost as a function of N. Arithmetic on exponentially long rational numbers is not a unit-cost operation. EXPTIME denotes the union of deterministic time classes 2^{N^c} over fixed constants c. A classification by completeness requires both a membership algorithm and hardness under uniform polynomial-time many-one reductions for this exact threshold language.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify the threshold problem’s decision-complexity class with a matching upper bound and hardness classification under polynomial-time many-one reductions. The existing exponential-time upper bound alone does not finish the task. A lower bound for recognizing an optimal first action, computing an entire optimal policy, or outputting the exact value is not automatically a lower bound for deciding comparison with one explicitly encoded threshold.
