cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every n,s≥1, every Boolean function f representable by a DNF with at most s terms on n variables, every distribution D on {0,1}ⁿ, and all accuracy and confidence parameters ε,δ∈(0,1), PAC learns f from independent D-distributed labelled examples in time polynomial in n,s,1/ε and log(1/δ)? The output may be any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis; membership queries are not allowed.
cards.definitions: A literal is a variable x_i or its negation. A term is a conjunction of literals, and a disjunctive normal form (DNF) is an OR of terms. Terms may have arbitrary width up to n after simplification. The size parameter s bounds the number of terms; counting literal occurrences instead changes polynomial bounds by at most a factor n. The target DNF is unknown: the learner is supplied only n, the upper bound s, and learning parameters. For an exact encoding, supply integers t,b≥2 and set ε=1/t and δ=2^(−b). One fixed probabilistic Turing machine must use at most p(n,s,t,b) steps for one fixed polynomial p, on every sequence of sample and random outcomes. Each example-oracle request supplies a fresh pair (x,f(x)) with x drawn independently from the same arbitrary unknown D; the learner cannot select x. Receiving and reading the n-bit sample counts toward the time bound. Samples are noiseless and realizable by the promised target. The output is an explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit h on n input bits, not necessarily a DNF. With probability at least 1−δ over the examples and internal randomness, Pr_{x drawn from D}[h(x)≠f(x)]≤ε. Writing and evaluating this circuit have polynomial cost. Reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence suffice for the usual general parameters by rounding toward stronger guarantees. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

context_blocks.text: A DNF represents a union of rule-defined regions: an example is accepted when it satisfies at least one conjunction of feature conditions. The task is to infer accurate predictions from observations, without being given those rules. Feldman’s introduction identifies the general distribution-free question before studying more structured input distributions; that introductory question is the source of this catalogue record.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to using polynomially many examples. There are at most 3ⁿ simplified conjunctions, since each variable is absent, positive or negative. Padding a DNF with empty slots bounds the number of candidate formulas by (3ⁿ+1)^s. The finite-class union bound therefore gives O((ns+log(1/δ))/ε) samples sufficient for every consistent DNF in this class to generalize. Exhaustively finding such a DNF may still take enormous time. The question asks whether that computational search can be avoided, even by outputting a different representation.

The distinction between a constant and a growing number of terms is essential. The classical n^{O(s)} algorithm is polynomial for each fixed s, but does not provide a single polynomial in n and s. Servedio’s 2025 survey records the longstanding goal and the subexponential distribution-free upper bound 2^{Õ(n^{1/3} log s)}. For polynomially many terms and fixed learning accuracy, this still leaves a substantial gap to polynomial time.

A distribution-free learner must handle probability concentrated on any subset of the Boolean cube. An argument that a long conjunction rarely holds under independent uniform coordinates need not survive such a distribution. Feldman’s Fourier-based work uses uniform or product structure and, in some settings, additional query access. Its positive results should not be read as a solution from arbitrary-distribution random examples alone.

Allowing hypotheses outside the target class is substantive. A hardness proof for producing another DNF can leave open an efficient learner that outputs a Boolean circuit or a polynomial threshold function. Daniely and Shalev-Shwartz obtain hardness that also covers improper learning, under their assumption about refuting random K-SAT. The assumption is part of that theorem, so it supplies evidence against efficient learning without deciding the unconditional question posed here.

Daniely and Vardi later derive hardness for DNF with a growing number of terms from an assumption about local pseudorandom generators. This gives a second precise route connecting the computational difficulty of learning compact rules to average-case complexity. Neither theorem should be abbreviated to an unconditional assertion that DNF cannot be learned.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering paper obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning under a uniform training distribution in a framework permitting abstention under distribution shift. Those distribution, output and runtime guarantees differ from the present target. This recent result was included in the status check and does not supply the required polynomial-time distribution-free learner.

A positive resolution would also give the learner sought in TCS-6543: every k-junta can be written as a DNF with at most 2^k terms, and the uniform distribution is one allowed choice of D. This implication goes from general DNF learning to junta learning; learning juntas alone does not supply an algorithm for general DNF targets. The two cards retain distinct targets. The mislabelled legacy record TCS-0023 is consolidated with the junta card because its actual cited problem concerns growing junta support.

cards.why: Determine whether compact Boolean rules that need only polynomially many observations can also be learned with polynomial computation, without assumptions on the input distribution. A positive result would cover decision trees and uniform-example juntas; a negative result would identify a fundamental computational barrier in realizable learning even when the output representation is unrestricted.

cards.title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized learner which, for all n,s≥1 and rational ε∈(0,1), learns every size-at-most-s Boolean decision tree on n variables from uniform random labeled examples in time poly(n,s,1/ε), with error at most ε and success probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: A decision tree has internal nodes querying one input coordinate, two outgoing edges labeled zero and one, and leaves labeled zero or one. Size counts all nodes. Samples are independent uniform x∈{0,1}^n labeled by the unknown target f. The learner receives n,s,ε and may draw samples but cannot request labels at chosen inputs. It outputs a Boolean circuit h of polynomial size, with Pr_{x uniform}[h(x)≠f(x)]≤ε on at least two thirds of runs. All sampling, computation, circuit writing and evaluation costs use classical bit operations; the total worst-case learning time has one polynomial bound.

context_blocks.text: Decision trees are an elementary representation for Boolean classification. Uniform data removes distributional pathologies but still leaves open whether random examples suffice for fully polynomial learning.

Kalai and Teng contrast the unresolved uniform-distribution problem with their positive result for most perturbed product distributions. Chosen-input queries can provide information unavailable from examples alone. The existing proper-learning card allows membership queries and requires a tree output. This target permits improper output but removes that query access.

cards.title: Distribution-free improper learning of two unrestricted halfspaces
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized learner that, for every distribution on {0,1}^n and every target equal to the intersection of two integer-weight halfspaces, outputs an efficiently evaluable hypothesis of error at most ε with probability at least 2/3 in time polynomial in n, a supplied target-length bound B and 1/ε?
cards.definitions: A halfspace is h(x)=1 exactly when Σ_i w_i x_i≥θ, with w_i,θ∈Z in signed binary; equality is positive. The target f is the conjunction of two such predicates. Its description length is the bit length of a list of both weight vectors and thresholds, using self-delimiting binary integers. The learner receives n and B in unary and a rational ε with 0<ε<1/2 in binary. It is promised that f has at least one such description of length at most B, but receives neither that description nor its weights. An example oracle returns independent pairs (x,f(x)) with x sampled from an arbitrary fixed distribution D on {0,1}^n. The learner receives only these labeled examples and its own independent fair coins. Each oracle call costs at least n+1 steps to receive its bits; all further work is charged in Turing-machine bit steps. Membership queries, advice and descriptions or probability evaluations of D are absent. There must be a fixed polynomial P such that on every random tape the running time, and hence sample count and output length, are bounded by P(n+B+⌈1/ε⌉+len(ε)). Output a deterministic Boolean circuit H:{0,1}^n→{0,1} in the explicit AND/OR/NOT basis. The success condition is Pr_examples,coins[Pr_x∼D[H(x)≠f(x)]≤ε]≥2/3, uniformly over n,B,ε,D and every promised f. Circuit evaluation costs polynomial time in its output encoding. The hypothesis need not be an intersection of halfspaces. Encoding an arbitrary deterministic polynomial-time evaluator by its Boolean circuit preserves this unrestricted efficient-output convention.

context_blocks.text: A single halfspace is efficiently learnable, but combining only two thresholds introduces a longstanding computational obstacle. Allowing an arbitrary output representation avoids the known hardness of proper learning.

The existing TCS-6544 explicitly assumes a positive margin and polynomial dependence on its reciprocal. This candidate instead concerns unrestricted integer-weight thresholds on the Boolean cube. The distinction affects the running time and cannot be hidden behind their similar titles.

cards.title: Statistical-query complexity of sparse halfspaces
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants C≥2 and a,b>0 such that, for every n≥2 and 1≤r≤n, SQ-DIM(Hn,r, 1/[C(r log₂ n)^a])≤C n^b, where Hn,r is the class of r-sparse halfspaces on {0,1}ⁿ and SQ-DIM is the distribution-worst-case correlation parameter defined below?
cards.why: Clarifies whether a statistical-query learner can exploit sparsity while tolerating coarse, sample-efficient estimates. The problem isolates an informational obstruction from the cost of reading many irrelevant coordinates, without assuming a favorable data distribution.
cards.status_note: Source Problem 3 and its definitions checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. No resolution of this worst-distribution, inverse-poly(r log n) parameter question was located. Results for noisy, Gaussian, smoothed or ordinary sample-access learning do not automatically settle it. No exhaustive literature or proof audit is claimed.

cards.definitions: A member of Hn,r is a function h:{0,1}ⁿ→{−1,+1} of the form h(x)=+1 if ∑j wⱼxⱼ≥θ and h(x)=−1 otherwise, where w∈ℝⁿ has at most r nonzero coordinates and θ∈ℝ. Different weight representations of the same function define one member. For any probability distribution D on the finite cube and 0<γ<1, SQ-DIM(Hn,r,D,γ) is the largest integer d for which there are d distinct functions h₁,…,hd in Hn,r satisfying |∑x D(x)hᵢ(x)hⱼ(x)|≤γ whenever i≠j. Then SQ-DIM(Hn,r,γ) is the maximum of this integer over all D, without any uniformity, product-distribution or margin promise. These maxima exist because the Boolean function class is finite and each feasible correlation condition is a closed constraint on the finite probability simplex. The constants C,a,b must work simultaneously for all n,r and all distributions. This is exactly the polynomial-versus-superpolynomial parameter question in source Problem 3, with its O(1) exponents made explicit. It asks for an upper bound on this dimension, not polynomial time to enumerate the functions or evaluate real weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound for some fixed C,a,b, or prove its negation: for every choice of such constants there are n,r and a distribution supporting a family larger than Cn^b with pairwise absolute correlations at most 1/[C(r log₂ n)^a]. The target is this source-defined parameter statement, not a guarantee restricted to one distribution or to halfspaces with large margin.

context_blocks.title: Learning with many irrelevant coordinates
context_blocks.text: A sparse halfspace uses at most r of n coordinates, even though the learner does not know which ones matter. For example, a rule depending only on x₇ is one-sparse regardless of how many other features are supplied. Attribute efficiency asks whether learning can benefit from this sparsity without requiring labeled information proportional to every coordinate.

context_blocks.title: What a statistical query reveals
context_blocks.text: An SQ learner asks for an approximate expectation of a bounded function φ(x,h(x))∈[−1,1]. A tolerance τ allows any answer within τ of the true expectation. Smaller tolerance requires more precise information. The source relates inverse-polynomial tolerance in r log n to attribute-efficient use of labeled examples.

context_blocks.title: Why nearly uncorrelated functions appear
context_blocks.text: Under the uniform distribution, the one-sparse rules 2x₁−1 and 2x₂−1 have correlation zero: they agree as often as they disagree. SQ-DIM asks how many candidate halfspaces can be almost uncorrelated at once under the same distribution. It then takes the worst distribution, which need not be uniform.

context_blocks.title: The two polynomial requirements differ
context_blocks.text: The allowed correlation scale is inverse-polynomial in r log n, while the required bound on the number of nearly uncorrelated functions is polynomial in n. Replacing the latter with a polynomial in r log n would ask for a stronger statement. Allowing inverse-polynomial tolerance in n instead would change the intended attribute-efficiency regime.

context_blocks.title: What the source result establishes
context_blocks.text: The source gives bounds connecting this correlation parameter to weak SQ learning. Its discussion of converting weak learning to high accuracy additionally allows unlabeled samples. The exact Problem 3 dimension question keeps those access models distinct.

cards.title: Local regularization for multiclass learning
cards.formal: Does every realizably PAC-learnable multiclass hypothesis class H admit a fixed local regularizer ψ:H×X→ℝ≥0 such that every learner induced by ψ, under the pointwise minimum-score rule below, PAC learns H? This is the existence part of the source question; optimal sample complexity is a separate refinement.
cards.why: Tests whether a fixed preference over hypotheses at each prediction point is a general principle for multiclass learning. A negative answer would identify a limit of regularization even when improper prediction is allowed; a positive answer would give a common template for all learnable multiclass classes.
cards.status_note: As of 11 September 2026, two checked preprints claim a negative resolution. Their theorem statements and local-regularization/PAC definitions match the main target, but the full impossibility proofs were not independently audited and no accepted publication was verified. Retained as uncertain rather than certified open or resolved.

cards.definitions: Let X be an instance space, Y a label space that may be infinite, and H⊆Y^X a nonempty class of predictors h:X→Y. A distribution D on labeled examples X×Y is realizable by H if some h*∈H satisfies PrD[h*(x)≠y]=0. The risk of a predictor g is LD(g)=PrD[g(x)≠y]. A learner A maps a finite labeled sample S to a predictor A(S), which need not belong to H. It PAC learns H if, for every ε,δ∈(0,1), there is mA(ε,δ)<∞ such that for every H-realizable D and every m≥mA(ε,δ), a sample S of m independent draws from D satisfies Pr[LD(A(S))>ε]≤δ. Probability spaces, predictors and learners are understood with measurable error events, so these probabilities are defined. There is no running-time requirement. For a nonempty realizable sample S, the version space H[S] consists of all h∈H agreeing with every labeled example in S. A local regularizer assigns each pair (h,x) a nonnegative real score ψ(h,x), fixed before observing S. It is admissible only if a minimum score on H[S] is attained at every test point x and the induced prediction rules are well-defined; an empty argmin cannot make the claim vacuously true. A learner is induced by ψ when A(S)(x) belongs to {h(x): h∈argmin g∈H[S] ψ(g,x)} for every such S,x. On empty or unrealizable samples its behavior is unrestricted. The quantifier “every induced learner” includes every valid tie-breaking rule; its sample bound may depend on that learner. The regularizer can depend on H and x, but not on S, its size, its unlabeled points, D, ε or δ.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every realizably PAC-learnable H has such an admissible regularizer, or give a PAC-learnable class H and prove that every admissible local regularizer induces at least one learner that is not PAC consistent in the stated distribution-independent sense. A favorable tie-breaking rule alone is insufficient. Neither a transductive separation nor failure of proper learning alone settles this PAC question.

context_blocks.title: A different preference at each test point
context_blocks.text: A regularizer expresses which hypotheses the learning rule prefers. Local regularization lets that preference depend on the new point being classified. After training, only hypotheses that fit the sample remain eligible, and the rule predicts using a least-scored eligible hypothesis at that point.

context_blocks.title: Why the prediction can be outside the class
context_blocks.text: One hypothesis might be preferred in one region of X and another in a different region. The resulting predictor can combine their labels without being a single hypothesis from H. This flexibility matters because some multiclass problems are learnable only by allowing such improper output.

context_blocks.title: Ties carry a real quantifier
context_blocks.text: The source asks the regularizer to succeed for every induced tie-breaking learner. If all scores are zero, the rule imposes no preference among sample-consistent hypotheses. Selecting one specially chosen successful learner from those ties would not show that the regularizer itself learns the class. Likewise, score minima must exist for the prediction rule to be meaningful.

context_blocks.title: Sample-dependent regularization is a different model
context_blocks.text: The source reports a general positive result when a local regularizer may first use the unlabeled training points. Here the score function is fixed independently of the sample. The question tests whether that extra sample information is necessary for a general multiclass learning rule.

context_blocks.title: Two 2026 claims of a negative resolution
context_blocks.text: Hou’s July preprint claims a countable learnable class beyond all local regularizers. The August preprint by Asilis and coauthors independently claims a PAC counterexample under the same worst-case tie convention and acknowledges Hou’s work. The checked statements match the main question, but their full lower-bound proofs have not been independently verified in this review. The card therefore records a claimed negative resolution with uncertain status.

references.title: Limitations of Membership Queries in Testable Learning
references.locator: Conjecture 6; PDF page 5

cards.definitions: A concept class C_n is a nonempty set of functions X_n→{0,1}, with a fixed common input and hypothesis representation in both models. Data consist of independent examples (x,f*(x)), where x follows an unknown distribution P on X_n and f*:X_n→{0,1} is an arbitrary fixed labeling function, not necessarily in C_n. A membership query chooses any x∈X_n and receives f*(x); repeated queries have the same label. For h∈C_n, define err_P(h)=Pr_{x∼P}[h(x)≠f*(x)] and opt=inf_{g∈C_n}err_P(g). Given accuracy ε and failure probability δ, a testable learner returns h∈C_n or the rejection symbol ⊥. Soundness holds for every P and f*: Pr[h≠⊥ and err_P(h)>opt+ε]≤δ. Completeness holds whenever P=D_n: Pr[h=⊥]≤δ. Probabilities are over samples and the learner’s randomness. This explicitly uses the usual joint bad-output event for the source’s informal “if it outputs” guarantee, not conditioning on a potentially extremely rare acceptance event. The sample-only learner has no membership oracle and satisfies the same two guarantees. Running time includes sample/query processing and writing the hypothesis; encodings and any given target-distribution description are unchanged. Polynomial overhead is understood in the standard parameterized sense, accounting for input size, 1/ε and log(1/δ) as well as the query learner’s time. The agnostic coefficient on opt is exactly one; an unspecified constant multiple is the different semi-agnostic model.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication by constructing sample-only testable learners with polynomially related resource bounds and the same agnostic guarantee, or exhibit a class/distribution family with a superpolynomial separation between the two testable-learning access models. Reducing query-based testable learning merely to ordinary sample-based agnostic learning is insufficient, because ordinary learning lacks soundness outside the target distribution.

context_blocks.title: The learner may refuse an unsupported prediction

context_blocks.title: Chosen queries can probe rare inputs
context_blocks.text: If the data distribution rarely samples a certain input, ordinary examples may never reveal its label. Membership queries allow the learner to inspect it directly. context_blocks.title: Agnostic does not mean the labels change on repeated queries

context_blocks.title: The known reduction stops at ordinary learning

cards.definitions: The ambient dimension d and number k of hidden ReLU units are positive integers supplied as bounds to the learner; 0<ε<1 is the desired accuracy. The activation ReLU(z)=max{0,z} has no bias or threshold shift here. The hidden unit vectors v_i and output coefficients w_i are unknown. Positivity concerns the output coefficients w_i, not the coordinates of v_i. The learner receives fresh i.i.d. samples from the stated distribution, not queries at chosen inputs. Its output H:R^d→R succeeds when (E_{X∼N(0,I_d)}[(H(X)−F(X))²])^{1/2}≤ε. The probability of at least 9/10 is over both samples and learner randomness; the error expectation uses a fresh Gaussian input. A single polynomial must bound sample count, running time, output-description size and evaluation cost as d,k,1/ε vary; k is not fixed. As in the source, examples have real coordinates and complexity is the arithmetic/sample complexity of the learning model, not an asserted finite-bit bound for exact Gaussian observations. H need not itself have k ReLU units. There is no separation, rank, conditioning or identifiability assumption on the v_i. Zero coefficients simply allow fewer than k active units.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a learner satisfying the simultaneous polynomial dependence on d,k,1/ε for all normalized nonnegative-weight targets, or establish a valid hardness obstruction to that guarantee in the same sample-access model. A result only for fixed k, well-separated parameters, proper learning, or a restricted query algorithm does not resolve the full question.

cards.definitions: Let X be an instance set, Y a label set and ∅≠H⊆Y^X a known hypothesis class. On round t an adversary presents x_t∈X, the learner chooses a probability distribution p_t on Y, and the adversary then reveals y_t∈Y. The learner suffers loss 1−p_t(y_t), the probability of a wrong randomized prediction. It observes the actual label, not just whether its prediction was correct. Its regret is Σ_{t=1}^T(1−p_t(y_t))−min_{h∈H}Σ_{t=1}^T1[h(x_t)≠y_t]. Let R_T(H) be the infimum over learner strategies of the supremum of this regret over adversarial plays; the adversary may observe p_t before choosing y_t. This distribution-valued convention already accounts for prediction randomness. There is no computational-efficiency restriction on a strategy, and it may know T. A depth-d Littlestone tree is a complete binary tree with an instance x∈X at each internal node and two distinct labels from Y on its two outgoing edges. It is shattered by H if every root-to-leaf path has some h∈H whose labels on the encountered instances equal all the path’s edge labels. The Littlestone dimension L(H) is the greatest shattered depth, or infinity if depths are unbounded. The question asks R_T(H)≤C√(L(H)T) with one numerical C valid for all H,X,Y and T≥L(H)≥1. If L(H)=0 all hypotheses agree pointwise and zero regret is attainable; for T<d a bound must be capped at T, so the displayed two-sided asymptotic target is stated only for T≥d.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal label-independent O(√(dT)) upper bound, or give classes and horizons with unbounded ratio R_T(H)/√(dT). Removing a factor depending on T while retaining a factor depending on |Y| does not give the requested universal bound.

cards.definitions: Arithmetic in 𝔽₂={0,1} uses addition and multiplication modulo two; ⟨a,x⟩=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿaᵢxᵢ mod 2. First choose x uniformly from {0,1}^n and hold it fixed. Independently for each t, choose a_t uniformly from {0,1}^n and a noise bit Z_t with Pr[Z_t=1]=1/2−ε; observe (a_t,b_t) with b_t=⟨a_t,x⟩+Z_t mod 2. Noise bits, query vectors and internal learner coins are mutually independent. The learner outputs one estimate x̂; success means x̂=x, and its probability averages over x, all observations and internal coins. The learner sees each sample once in order, cannot choose a_t or revisit discarded observations, and has no computational-time restriction. Formally use a branching program with T+1 layers and width at most 2^S, one start vertex and one outgoing edge for each possible sample at each nonterminal vertex, all going to the next layer. Leaves, possibly in earlier layers, are labelled by estimates in {0,1}^n. Randomized learners may use fresh coins to choose state updates; retained coins are part of the state. Equivalently, the lower bound may be checked on deterministic nonuniform programs, since a random tape can be fixed to achieve at least the average success under this fixed input distribution without increasing width or length. The program may depend on n and ε; its transition description, current layer and input sample are not charged as stored data. Memory counts persistent state bits, S=⌈log₂(width)⌉, and T is the maximum number of consumed samples, not its expectation. No hypothesis is made about the hardness of LPN in unrestricted computation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal bounded-error memory/sample tradeoff with constants uniform in ε, or refute that asymptotic claim by showing that no such constants can work. A bound Ω(n²/ε), a result only for constant ε, or a lower bound in a restricted statistical-query model does not settle the proposed dependence on noise.

context_blocks.title: Noise reduces the information in each equation
context_blocks.text: Without noise, every observation is a correct linear relation about the hidden vector. Here the relation is only slightly more likely to be right than wrong when ε is small. The question asks whether this forces a quadratic loss in the storage threshold as the bias tends to zero.

references.title: Optimal Collusion-Free Teaching
references.authors: David Kirkpatrick, Hans U. Simon, Sandra Zilles
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 12; PDF page 12

cards.definitions: A concept C∈C is a subset of the finite instance set X, identified with its indicator function 1_C:X→{0,1}. A labeled sample is an unordered subset of X×{0,1}. It is consistent with C if each (x,y) in it has y=1_C(x). A teaching map T assigns a sample T(C) consistent with C to every concept C in the class. It is non-clashing if, for every distinct C,D∈C, T(C) is not consistent with D or T(D) is not consistent with C. Equivalently, some point appearing in either teaching set has different labels under C and D. The condition is pairwise: T(C) need not by itself distinguish C from every other concept. A positive example has label 1 and a negative example has label 0; both count as one example. The size of T is max_{C∈C}|T(C)|, and NCTD(C) is the minimum of that size over all non-clashing teaching maps. The minimum exists because X and C are finite and giving all labels is a valid map. No sample order, extra message or additional side information is part of this definition. A subset S⊆X is shattered by C when {C∩S:C∈C}=2ˢ. The VC dimension VC(C) is the maximum cardinality of a shattered set. For a singleton concept class it is zero, and the empty teaching set works. The statement quantifies over all finite X and nonempty C, including that case; it concerns existence of a map, without an efficiency or encoding-size requirement on constructing it. The positive-only parameter NCTD⁺ restricts T(C) to samples with label 1 and can be larger. It is not the parameter in this conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the exact inequality for every finite concept class by establishing existence of a valid map of maximum size at most its VC dimension, or give a finite concept class and a proof that every non-clashing teaching map has larger maximum size. A quadratic bound or even a larger-constant linear bound is insufficient. A separation for positive-only maps, another teaching model, or an algorithmic hardness result for finding maps does not refute this existence statement.

cards.title: Uniform convergence under Dobrushin dependence
cards.formal: For every a∈[0,1), does there exist a finite constant C_a such that the following holds uniformly? Let m≥1, let H be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions on a measurable instance space X with finite VC dimension d, and let P_m be a joint law of S=(Z₁,…,Z_m), Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)∈X×{0,1}, whose marginals all equal D and whose total-variation Dobrushin coefficient is at most a. For every δ∈(0,1), require Pr_{S∼P_m}[sup_{h∈H}|L_S(h)−L_D(h)|>C_a√((d+log(2/δ))/m)]≤δ. Here L_S and L_D are zero-one losses and the conditional-kernel and measurability conventions below are part of the model. This card reads the source’s proposed extension quantitatively, using the iid-order finite-VC rate stated in equation (18) of its full version; it is not merely a claim that some unspecified convergence rate exists.
cards.why: Would determine whether the standard weak-influence condition suffices for the uniform statistical guarantees that make finite VC dimension useful, beyond the already-known existence of a successful learner.

references.authors: Yuval Dagan, Constantinos Daskalakis, Nishanth Dikkala, Siddhartha Jayanti

cards.definitions: Write Z=X×{0,1}. For each i, take a probability kernel κ_i(·|z_{−i}) that is a version of the conditional law of Z_i given all other coordinates under P_m. These kernels are defined on the entire product Z^{m−1}, including configurations of zero marginal probability. For i≠j define c_{ij}=sup{TV(κ_i(·|u),κ_i(·|v)):u,v∈Z^{m−1}, u and v agree except possibly in coordinate j}, where TV(μ,ν)=sup_{B measurable}|μ(B)−ν(B)|. In a finite space this is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences. The admissibility promise is existence of such conditional-kernel versions with max_i Σ_{j≠i}c_{ij}≤a. Thus the influence of coordinate j on coordinate i is bounded, and the sum is over influences entering i; it is not a column-sum or a Markov-chain mixing-time condition. Specifying versions on null configurations prevents undefined conditioning from deciding the promise. Kernels satisfying this global bound and a measurable random supremum in the displayed event are assumed; these are the explicit regularity conventions for the source’s conditional-distribution notation. No independence, graph degree, spatial dimension, stationarity or exchangeability beyond identical marginals is assumed. For h:X→{0,1}, L_S(h)=m⁻¹Σ_i 1{h(X_i)≠Y_i}, and L_D(h)=E_{(X,Y)∼D}1{h(X)≠Y}. A finite F⊆X is shattered if every binary labeling of F is the restriction of a member of H. VC(H) is the largest size of a shattered set, or infinity if these sizes are unbounded. The hypothesis d<∞ includes d=0. The constant C_a may depend on the fixed upper bound a and may diverge as a approaches one, but must be independent of m,d,δ,X,H,D and P_m. The law P_m may be different for each m; no consistency of an infinite process is required. The logarithm is natural. This is a statistical inequality, with no algorithmic running-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of such a constant for every fixed a<1, uniformly over all the displayed models and parameters, or refute this quantified rate. A negative answer must defeat every proposed constant for some fixed a<1; a family with its coefficient tending to one does not by itself suffice. Proving generalization only for a particular learner, a bound depending on the cardinality of H, a slower rate, or a result needing stronger log-influence assumptions does not establish the displayed extension.

The question allows its constant to depend on a<1. It asks whether the usual sample-size dependence survives throughout that regime, without specifying an optimal blow-up as a approaches the boundary.

cards.title: Proper unlabeled compression of ample classes
cards.formal: Does every nonempty ample concept class C⊆{0,1}ᵁ on a finite domain U admit a proper unlabeled sample compression scheme of size at most d=VC(C)? Precisely, do there exist maps κ:RS(C)→{A⊆U:|A|≤d} and ρ:{A⊆U:|A|≤d}→C such that, for every realizable labeled partial sample s, κ(s)⊆dom(s) and ρ(κ(s)) agrees with every label in s? cards.definitions: A concept c∈C is a function c:U→{0,1}. A set A⊆U is shattered by C if {c|_A:c∈C}={0,1}ᴬ. It is strongly shattered if some b:U∖A→{0,1} has the property that, for every a:A→{0,1}, the combined labeling a∪b belongs to C. Thus strong shattering requires a full cube of concepts with identical labels outside A. The class is ample when every shattered set is strongly shattered; ample classes are also called lopsided or shattering-extremal. Its VC dimension d is the maximum size of a shattered set. A labeled partial sample is a function s:A→{0,1} on some A⊆U, equivalently a set of pairs (x,s(x)) with distinct x. It is realizable if s=c|_A for some c∈C; RS(C) contains every such sample, including the empty sample. The compressor κ sees the entire labeled sample and may use its labels to choose a subset κ(s) of its domain, of size at most d. It sends only that subset. The reconstructor ρ receives no labels, ordering, multiplicities, sample size, omitted sample points or auxiliary bits; U,C,κ and ρ are fixed and shared beforehand. It returns a total concept belonging to C, which must agree with the original entire sample, including omitted labels. This is the proper convention explicitly used in the full source. Requiring ρ on all subsets of size at most d is equivalent to defining it only on Im(κ), because C is nonempty and unused inputs can be assigned any fixed concept. The existence of κ,ρ is quantified separately for each finite C; no running-time bound for constructing or evaluating them, distributional assumption or probability of error is part of the statement. For d=0 a nonempty class has a single concept and the empty compressed set suffices. A maximum class of dimension d has cardinality Σ_{j=0}^d binomial(|U|,j); every maximum class is ample, but the converse need not hold.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the two maps with the stated d-point bound for every finite nonempty ample class, or give an ample class with a proof that no such pair of maps exists. A scheme retaining labels, returning a hypothesis outside C, storing extra information, or exceeding d points does not meet the target. A scheme that handles only full concepts rather than every realizable partial sample is also insufficient. Failure of a proposed corner-peeling construction alone does not refute existence of a compression scheme.

cards.title: Quasipolynomial AC⁰ self-learning
cards.formal: Does AC⁰ admit uniform quasipolynomial-size AC⁰ self-learners? More precisely, for every fixed integers d,k≥1 and fixed rational constants ε,δ∈(0,1/100], do there exist constants D,a≥1 and a uniform family of randomized multi-output oracle AC⁰ circuits Lₙ, of depth at most D and total size at most Q(n)=2^{a⌈log₂(n+2)⌉^a}, such that for every n≥1 and every Boolean function f on n bits with an AC⁰ circuit of depth at most d and at most n^k gates, Lₙ with membership-query oracle f outputs an effective description of a depth-at-most-D AC⁰ hypothesis h of size at most Q(n), with Pr[Pr_{x uniform in {0,1}ⁿ}[h(x)≠f(x)]≤ε]≥1−δ? The outer probability is over the learner’s independent fair random input bits. This is the fixed-constant learning-parameter reading of the source’s self-learning question.
cards.why: Tests whether learning a shallow Boolean computation intrinsically needs stronger gates or greater depth than evaluating it. The restriction links learning complexity with the circuit complexity of approximate minimization and with derandomization, beyond the usual sequential running-time measure.

cards.definitions:
An AC⁰ circuit is a finite Boolean directed acyclic circuit with unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants 0 and 1, and input bits. Depth is the greatest number of gates on a directed input-to-output path. Circuit descriptions may be nonuniform for the target function: the guarantee covers every eligible f at each length, not merely one uniformly generated target family. Neither majority/threshold gates nor parity gates are added to the basis.

For the learner, an oracle gate has n ordered Boolean inputs y₁,…,yₙ and returns the bit f(y₁,…,yₙ). Each oracle gate counts as one gate in the depth; its query wires count in the size. Query bits may depend on answers at earlier gates, but the total circuit depth remains bounded by D. The learner is a circuit with multiple output bits and at most Q(n) independent fair random input bits; there is no further source of information about f. Size here bounds gates, wires, input terminals and output terminals together. The number of random bits and all circuit topology are fixed before f is supplied. No unrestricted computation is allowed between queries. The accuracy distribution is uniform on the target’s entire n-bit domain, independently of the learner’s coins. This is not distribution-free PAC learning and does not require a fixed output or fixed queries on most random tapes.

An effective output is an explicit layered description of a Boolean AC⁰ circuit on n bits. One concrete convention uses D ordered layers of padded gate slots, a gate-type field for each slot, Boolean adjacency masks to earlier layers or input terminals, and an output-selector mask. NOT slots have exactly one predecessor; all edges go to later layers. Unused slots are constants. The format has polynomial length in the number of slots, and evaluating a valid encoded circuit on an input is possible by an AC⁰ circuit of depth O(D) and polynomial size in the encoding length. Both the description length and hypothesis gates/wires are bounded by Q(n); invalid descriptions count as failures. Enlarging a and D absorbs the polynomial overhead of this explicit encoding and standard layering. The output h has no f-oracle gates. A constant-depth circuit with only one additional top threshold gate would not meet the stated hypothesis class.

Uniformity means that, for the fixed d,k,ε,δ, one deterministic Turing algorithm given 1ⁿ generates the entire description of Lₙ in time polynomial in Q(n). The algorithm, its polynomial exponent, D and a may depend on those four fixed parameters, but not on n or f. There is no advice depending on f and no claim of polynomial-time generation in n. The source explicitly leaves general ε,δ dependence informal and often fixes sufficiently small constants; the statement adopts that constant-parameter interpretation. It does not demand a single learner whose complexity is polynomial in 1/ε and log(1/δ), nor learner or hypothesis depth equal to target depth. All bounds apply to every n; constant padding can handle small lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies the uniform oracle-circuit families and proves all depth, size, encoding and probability guarantees for every fixed d,k,ε,δ in the specified ranges and every eligible target. A negative answer disproves this universal existence claim, for example for some fixed parameter choice against all permitted learner depths and quasipolynomial size exponents. Quasipolynomial sequential running time, unrestricted hypothesis circuits, or a threshold-augmented hypothesis class alone do not meet the target.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme with negligible correctness error and security against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversaries? General constructions and security proofs may use the code of the one-way function; they need not be black-box.
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that every uniform classical PPT inverter I has negligible probability, for x uniform in {0,1}ⁿ, of outputting z∈{0,1}ⁿ with f(z)=f(x) on input (1ⁿ,f(x)). A function ν(n) is negligible if for every d>0 it is eventually at most n^{−d}. The scheme comprises uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Enc, Dec. Gen(1ⁿ) randomly outputs public and secret bit strings (pk,sk); Enc(1ⁿ,pk,b) randomly encrypts a bit b; Dec(1ⁿ,sk,c) deterministically outputs a bit or failure. For each b, the probability over honest generation and encryption that decryption is wrong is negligible. Security means that for every uniform classical PPT adversary A, in the experiment (pk,sk)←Gen(1ⁿ), b←{0,1}, c←Enc(1ⁿ,pk,b), the advantage |Pr[A(1ⁿ,pk,c)=b]−1/2| is negligible. The adversary knows all algorithms and can encrypt arbitrary chosen bits itself with fresh randomness. This bit-message formulation extends to polynomially long messages by independent bit encryption and a hybrid argument. All runtime bounds are worst-case polynomial in the security parameter and appropriate input lengths. There is no shared secret before key generation, trusted setup, random oracle, quantum state, or auxiliary hardness assumption. Security is eventually negligible at all sufficiently large parameters, not merely infinitely often.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is the main unresolved boundary between the assumptions needed for private-key and public-key cryptography. It asks whether generic computational one-wayness already contains the structure needed to establish encrypted communication without a pre-shared secret.

importance.reason: A central minimal-assumption question in cryptographic foundations, separating the known reach of generic one-wayness from public-key communication.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Rudich establish the fundamental oracle and black-box barriers to obtaining key agreement from one-way permutations; this also constrains public-key encryption constructions.
Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove pseudorandom generators can be constructed from any OWF, establishing the generic route underlying private-key cryptography.
Barak and Mahmoody prove the quadratic-query attack on random-oracle key agreement. The result sharpens the oracle-model limitation without excluding arbitrary non-black-box constructions.
MIT’s foundations lecture explicitly presents PKE from OWFs as a major open question and distinguishes it from the established black-box separations.

Chatterjee, Mu, and Vasudevan construct PKE from planted MinRank hardness on random instances. The 2025 preprint appears at EUROCRYPT 2026; it adds a concrete foundation, not a reduction from an arbitrary OWF.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the supplied MIT lecture. Research through 10 September 2026 found no standard-model implication from arbitrary OWFs alone or refutation of that general implication. The formulation fixes uniform classical adversaries and allows non-black-box constructions; oracle barriers and stronger concrete assumptions are kept separate.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function creates an asymmetry between evaluating a map and finding a preimage of a random image. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: anyone holding the public information can produce ciphertexts, yet a receiver possessing related secret information can recover their messages. The question is whether this additional structure is implicit in every possible source of one-wayness.

One-way functions already suffice for pseudorandom generators and, through the standard chain of constructions, private-key encryption. There the honest parties initially share a secret. Public-key encryption removes that initial shared secret, so the existence of symmetric cryptography is not already a construction of the desired public-key primitive.

The classical obstacle is the Impagliazzo–Rudich black-box separation. Roughly, an idealized one-way-function oracle can supply private-key cryptographic hardness without enabling the necessary key agreement. A construction allowed to inspect and reason about a concrete function’s program lies outside the oracle interface, which is why the general implication remains open despite this barrier.

Public-key encryption would give a two-message key-agreement protocol: send a public key, then send an encryption of a freshly chosen shared secret. Barak and Mahmoody show a quadratic-query attack on key agreement built from a random oracle, matching the limited query advantage of Merkle puzzles. The theorem counts oracle queries and allows extensive other computation; it is not an unconditional attack on every standard-model encryption scheme.

New constructions continue to broaden the available assumptions. Chatterjee, Mu, and Vasudevan base public-key encryption on a planted MinRank problem over random instances, equivalently a rank-metric decoding assumption, rather than hiding a specially structured efficiently decodable code. This is progress in the choice of concrete hardness assumptions. It still assumes that specific problem is hard, a property not supplied merely by the existence of some arbitrary OWF.

cards.title: One-way functions from P ≠ NP
cards.formal: Does P≠NP imply that there exists a deterministic polynomial-time computable function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every constant c>0, all sufficiently large n satisfy $\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}[\,|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\,]\le n^{-c}$, where $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$?
cards.definitions: Uₙ is the uniform distribution on n-bit strings. The function f is computed by one deterministic Turing machine in worst-case polynomial time; in particular its output length is polynomially bounded in n. The inverter receives n in unary and the output f(x), uses independent unbiased random bits, and runs in worst-case polynomial time in the length of its input on every random tape. Its output may be an n-bit candidate or failure. Finding any n-bit preimage counts as success, not only recovering the original x. The probability includes both the choice of x and the inverter’s coins. Formally, for every fixed inverter I and real c>0 there exists N(I,c) such that the inequality holds for every n≥N(I,c). This is eventual negligible inversion probability, not security only at infinitely many lengths. Algorithms have no oracle, nonuniform advice, trapdoor, or quantum computation. The premise P≠NP concerns ordinary uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision versus polynomial-time verification. The task is an existence implication and does not require a black-box construction or a particular proof method.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A positive answer would base fundamental cryptographic hardness on the best-known general conjecture about efficient computation. A negative answer would demonstrate that efficient verification and worst-case intractability can coexist without this basic form of usable secrecy. The problem identifies the gap between computational difficulty and adversarial security.

importance.reason: A foundational question about the weakest assumptions supporting cryptography, linking NP hardness, average-case complexity, inversion, and pseudorandomness.

progress.text: The theory of computational cryptography develops reductions from one-way functions. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby establish equivalence between existence of one-way functions and pseudorandom generators.
Bogdanov and Trevisan give a nonadaptive oracle-reduction barrier to basing average-case NP hardness or one-way security on NP-complete worst-case hardness, unless PH collapses.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.9 explicitly asks whether P≠NP implies one-way functions, and separately asks about stronger average-case premises and trapdoor conclusions. This card fixes the basic one-way-function implication.

Liu and Pass strengthen characterizations using boundary hardness of randomized time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity. Their ordinary deterministic K^t consequence assumes exponential circuit hardness for derandomization; it does not derive one-way functions from P≠NP alone.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the original source. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no derivation of eventually secure classical one-way functions from P≠NP alone was located. The security quantifiers are stronger than an infinitely-often one-wayness target.

context_blocks.text: If P=NP, an inverter can search for a preimage one bit at a time. At each step, it asks whether the current prefix can be extended to an n-bit string mapping to the given output. That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply P≠NP. The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely P≠NP.

sentences: The statement P ≠ NP guarantees that some efficiently verifiable problems cannot be solved efficiently on every input.
Cryptographic one-way functions require a stronger kind of difficulty: efficient attackers must fail to invert outputs generated from random inputs.
This project asks whether worst-case hardness alone forces that average-case cryptographic hardness to exist.
A function that is hard only on an extremely rare set would not provide the required security.
Resolving the implication would clarify whether the most familiar complexity assumption already contains the foundations of computational cryptography.

cards.context:
If P=NP, an inverter can search for a preimage one bit at a time. At each step, it asks whether the current prefix can be extended to an n-bit string mapping to the given output. That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply P≠NP. The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely P≠NP.

benchmark_focus.reason: A foundational question about the weakest assumptions supporting cryptography, linking NP hardness, average-case complexity, inversion, and pseudorandomness.

cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
cards.definitions: Fix q(n) to be the least prime at least n^4 for every integer n≥2. Let χ_n be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to exp(−πe²/n²). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial m(n), the ensembles (A,A s+e mod q) and (A,u) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in Z_q^(m×n), s is uniform in Z_q^n, the m coordinates of e are independent χ_n samples, and u is independent uniform in Z_q^m. Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than n^(−c) eventually for every constant c>0. No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in λ+|C| that outputs a Boolean circuit O(1^λ,C) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible μ_p such that for every |C|≤p(λ), with probability at least 1−μ_p(λ) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences C_0,λ and C_1,λ with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Asks whether a single basic noisy-linear-equation assumption supports general program obfuscation. Resolving the implication would clarify the strength of LWE and the assumption cost of a broad family of cryptographic constructions that currently use iO as a separate resource.

importance.reason: A central assumption-minimization problem for general obfuscation, with consequences throughout cryptography and a crucial distinction between ordinary LWE and strengthened LWE-based assumptions.

progress.text: Barak and coauthors establish impossibility for general virtual-black-box obfuscation while introducing weaker obfuscation notions, including the indistinguishability target.
Regev develops LWE, lattice-hardness connections and public-key encryption; these results supply the standard noisy-equation foundation, rather than general obfuscation.
Jain, Lin, and Sahai construct general iO from four well-founded assumptions with the quantitative security specified in their theorem. The JACM publication does not reduce the list to LWE.
Their follow-up removes LWE, obtaining iO from LPN over prime fields, DLIN, and local PRGs under subexponential security. It explicitly leaves minimal assumption sets open.

Brakerski and coauthors obtain iO from circular-security properties of LWE-based encryption, including randomness-leakage resilience. They also repair a limitation in a previous exponentially-efficient-obfuscation transformation.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No construction from the plain polynomial-hard decisional-LWE assumption fixed here was identified. Existing multi-assumption and circular-security constructions do not settle it. Polynomial hardness, polynomial modulus/noise ratio, classical adversaries, arbitrary circuits and no auxiliary leakage are explicit choices that make the broad LWE-alone question unambiguous.

context_blocks.text: Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of exactly the same function. After obfuscation, an efficient observer should not tell which implementation was used. Equality of size prevents a trivial distinction from the amount of code supplied; padding can put implementations under a common size bound. This definition does not say that every secret written into an arbitrary program is hidden. A secret that the function itself reveals through its outputs remains visible.

That distinction is necessary. Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement, which would make code reveal no more than oracle access to its function. Their impossibility theorem does not rule out indistinguishability obfuscation. The weaker comparison between equivalent implementations has therefore become a central target, rather than an informal promise to make arbitrary software unreadable.

LWE supplies a particularly concrete potential foundation. Its samples are linear equations modulo a public integer, perturbed by small independent errors. Exact equations would reveal the secret by linear algebra; the errors obstruct that approach. Regev introduced reductions connecting LWE to worst-case lattice problems and used it to build public-key encryption. This card fixes a particular ordinary decisional-LWE ensemble so that the noise distribution, modulus, number of samples, and adversarial resources cannot vary silently.

Jain, Lin, and Sahai established general-circuit iO from a combination of four assumptions: LWE, LPN over large fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and a bilinear-group assumption. Their theorem uses stronger quantitative security than mere polynomial hardness. Its Journal of the ACM version appeared in February 2026, following the STOC 2021 work. That publication is an important foundation for iO, but is not a 2026 construction from plain LWE alone.

A follow-up by the same authors removes LWE from that combination, leaving the other three assumptions. Eliminating LWE from a sufficient set is logically different from eliminating all the other assumptions while retaining LWE. The follow-up explicitly poses the possibility that LWE alone might suffice, without claiming a resolution.

Brakerski, Döttling, Garg, and Malavolta give another route using LWE-based encryption with circular randomness-leakage resilience. The construction uses that stronger assumption. Its security experiment exposes structured information related to keys and encryption randomness, whereas ordinary LWE supplies only the noisy linear samples defined above. Calling the construction LWE-based therefore does not remove the extra security hypothesis.

A solution would unify the assumptions behind many uses of obfuscation with an established lattice-learning problem. The specific target here is deliberately demanding: ordinary polynomial security and a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio. Even a construction from plain LWE with stronger quantitative hardness would be substantial progress, but the security loss would still need attention before it established this exact implication. The question concerns mathematical feasibility; it does not impose practical code size or execution speed.

cards.title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional LWE, with the parameter convention below, imply a classical compact fully homomorphic encryption scheme whose keys are generated without an evaluation-depth bound, secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries without any additional circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption?
cards.definitions: Fix the following ordinary LWE assumption: for every fixed integer c≥3 and polynomial sample count M(d), let q(d) be the least prime at least d^c, let s be uniform in Z_q^d, let A be uniform in Z_q^{M(d)×d}, and let the coordinates of e be independent integers with probability proportional to exp(−πz²/(4d)), reduced modulo q. The ensembles (A,As+e mod q) and (A,u), for independent uniform u∈Z_q^{M(d)}, are computationally indistinguishable against nonuniform classical circuits of size polynomial in d. Thus the error distribution is the discrete Gaussian D_{Z,2√d}; only ordinary independently generated LWE samples are assumed hard. The FHE scheme has uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms Gen(1^λ)→(pk,evk,sk), Enc(pk,b), Eval(evk,C,c₁,…,c_t), and Dec(sk,c), with bit plaintexts and Boolean circuits over AND, OR and NOT. Gen takes no circuit-size or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial P such that keys, fresh bit ciphertexts, evaluated one-bit ciphertexts and the time to decrypt a valid output are bounded by P(λ), independently of C and t. Evaluation is polynomial-time in λ and its total input length. For every polynomial p, uniformly over all circuits C of size and input count at most p(λ) and all input bits b₁,…,b_t, decrypting Eval on independent encryptions of these bits equals C(b₁,…,b_t), except with negligible probability over generation, encryption and evaluation. Ordinary decryption is correct with negligible error. Given both pk and evk, every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary has negligible advantage in distinguishing an encryption of 0 from one of 1. Negligible means smaller than λ^{-a} eventually for every a>0. No subsequent secret-key assistance, ideal oracle, external trusted setup, superpolynomial adversary-hardness assumption, functional-encryption assumption or obfuscation assumption is allowed. This fixes a polynomial-modulus version of “standard LWE”; it does not assume any encryptions of secrets or correlated hints are secure.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether ordinary LWE alone supports compact encrypted computation at arbitrary polynomial depth with one fixed key set.

importance.reason: A central foundational gap in fully homomorphic encryption, separating established leveled LWE constructions from reusable fixed-depth-independent keys and their extra security assumptions.

progress.text: Brakerski–Vaikuntanathan establish leveled FHE from ordinary LWE; the journal abstract explicitly separates the additional weak circular-security assumption for removing levels.
Brakerski’s quantum-FHE paper records a classical bootstrappable GSW-style scheme with polynomial modulus, citing Brakerski–Vaikuntanathan; this does not eliminate the separate key-cycle issue.
Micciancio’s slides pose the ordinary-LWE circular-security question and distinguish FHE from full composability.
Bitansky–Solomon bootstrap via functional encryption under polynomial hardness assumptions; extra primitives remain, and nonuniform security needs an additional complexity assumption.
Wang–Huang–Tang remove CRS and circularity assumptions in a dynamic multi-key construction whose formal setup still takes L.
Liu and coauthors’ quantum proposal retains L+1 key layers and a quantum evaluator, outside the target model.

cards.status_note: No classical unleveled compact FHE construction from the specified ordinary LWE assumption alone was found through 11 September 2026. Functional-encryption constructions use additional assumptions. The inspected February and April 2026 no-circularity proposals retain explicit level bounds; the latter also uses quantum evaluation. This card fixes polynomial-modulus LWE, nonuniform classical security and fresh-input FHE correctness.

context_blocks.text: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on encrypted data and return an encrypted answer. Compactness makes this substantive: the client should decrypt a short answer, rather than receive the original ciphertexts together with the whole circuit and perform the computation itself. Here all four algorithms are classical, and the ciphertext for one output bit remains bounded by a fixed polynomial in the security parameter.

The order of choices is the heart of the problem. In a leveled scheme, the user first chooses a maximum depth L and generates keys suitable for that level. This can support every circuit up to L without revealing the data. The present question asks for one key-generation algorithm that receives only the security parameter and supports every polynomial-depth circuit later supplied to the evaluator. Choosing L=λ¹⁰ during setup still leaves deeper polynomial computations outside the guarantee.

Lattice ciphertexts generally include small errors that hide the plaintext. Homomorphic operations transform the desired message and these errors together. Once the error exceeds the decryption tolerance, the output may no longer decode correctly. Gentry’s bootstrapping idea refreshes a ciphertext by homomorphically evaluating a decryption circuit, with the secret key itself provided in encrypted form. Micciancio’s teaching slides explain both this noise issue and the associated circular-security question.

A chain of independent keys avoids the immediate circularity. Encrypt the secret key at level i under the public key at level i+1, then use the next level to refresh the current ciphertext. The usual hybrid proof can replace those encryptions in reverse order because the chain has an endpoint. But the public material grows with the number of refreshes planned in advance. Closing the chain into a cycle reuses a bounded collection of keys and changes the security argument.

Brakerski and Vaikuntanathan’s construction makes the distinction explicit in its journal abstract: ordinary LWE gives leveled FHE, while removing the depth restriction uses an additional weak circular-security assumption. Later bootstrapping work supports polynomial-modulus parameters and polynomial lattice approximation factors. Improvements in error growth and efficiency do not themselves justify exposing the secret-key encryptions needed to reuse the keys.

The requested proof need not avoid bootstrapping, or even avoid encrypted keys. It must justify the actual public evaluation information using ordinary LWE alone. Conversely, it is not enough to prove that some artificially designed CPA-secure encryption scheme becomes insecure when encrypting its own key. Such a counterexample refutes an automatic upgrade for every scheme; it does not rule out designing a particular FHE scheme with a valid ordinary-LWE proof.

Bitansky and Solomon obtain FHE without circular-security assumptions using functional encryption, under polynomial hardness assumptions. This is a significant positive result for a broader assumption set. In their ITCS 2023 construction, the available functional-encryption instantiation uses assumptions including LPN, bilinear SXDH and shallow pseudorandom generators, in addition to the LWE-based homomorphic component. The basic theorem protects against uniform adversaries; their nonuniform extension requires an additional worst-case complexity assumption. Neither version establishes LWE alone under the convention here.

Recent claims also require checking the formal setup. Wang, Huang and Tang’s February 2026 dynamic multi-key scheme advertises avoiding a common reference string and circular security. Definition 2.2 nevertheless gives Setup the depth parameter L, and the construction chooses its dimension and modulus using L. Its stated compactness also permits dependence on L. This is a leveled guarantee, even though the number of participating keys can change dynamically.

Liu and coauthors’ April 2026 quantum homomorphic proposal also advertises classical LWE and no circular-security assumption. Its Section 3.4 uses L+1 independent key layers; a later discussion explicitly preallocates L evaluation gadgets. It therefore retains a level bound, and its evaluator performs quantum operations. These scope differences already prevent it from settling the classical, depth-independent target; this review does not validate its separate efficiency or quantum-security claims.

There is a further definitional distinction between evaluating one arbitrary circuit on fresh ciphertexts and repeatedly evaluating new circuits on the resulting ciphertexts. Micciancio’s slides show that correctness for the first task does not automatically imply correctness for the second. This card asks for the usual fresh-input FHE guarantee. Establishing full composability would be an additional accomplishment, rather than an implicit condition that makes the target harder.

A solution would remove a central gap between the clean assumption used to prove the security of leveled lattice encryption and the extra assumption used to reuse a fixed key set indefinitely over polynomial computations. It would clarify the foundation of FHE independently of practical parameter optimization, and could improve the assumptions of constructions that use unrestricted encrypted computation as a component.

cards.title: Sub-square-root share-size exponents in perfect secret sharing
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants K>0 and 0<c<1/2 such that, for every n≥1 and every monotone access structure Γ on [n] with ∅∉Γ and [n]∈Γ, there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with max_i log₂|S_i|≤K·2^(cn), where S_i is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?
cards.why: A worst-case storage benchmark for information-theoretic access control, separating the power of general secret sharing from linear schemes. The newly reported bound directly addresses its strict exponential threshold.
cards.status_note: Direct positive resolution claimed by Nir, ECCC TR26-146, August 2026, Theorem 1.5. Checked 11 September 2026; statement and model alignment were checked, but the proof was not independently verified. Do not treat this as an unqualified open problem.

progress.text: Applebaum–Nir give a general upper exponent log₂(3/2)≈0.585.
The Dagstuhl seminar poses the strict c<1/2 target; the printed historical exponent differs from the cited construction.
Nir states a matching nonlinear upper bound with exponent 0.496 in Theorem 1.5.

cards.definitions: [n]={1,…,n}. An access structure Γ⊆2^[n] is monotone when A∈Γ and A⊆B⊆[n] imply B∈Γ. A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on {0,1} and shares X_i∈S_i, where each S_i is a finite nonempty set. For each A∈Γ there is a deterministic map r_A:∏_{i∈A}S_i→{0,1} such that r_A((X_i)_{i∈A})=B with probability one. For each A∉Γ, the conditional distributions of (X_i)_{i∈A} given B=0 and B=1 are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding log₂|S_i| up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish universal K>0 and 0<c<1/2 with the stated guarantee for every n and every monotone access structure, or prove that no such constants exist. A refutation must rule out all permitted schemes, including nonlinear ones. An upper bound with exponent exactly 1/2 or a lower bound confined to linear schemes does not resolve the target.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size 2^{0.496n+o(n)}. Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and 1/2 absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs log₂ M, even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is 1.5^{n+o(n)}, equivalently 2^{0.58496…n+o(n)}. This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy c<1/2.
