An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be N/2, which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
cards.formal: Is GI∈BQP? Equivalently, does a uniform quantum algorithm decide, on every pair of finite simple graphs on n vertices given by their adjacency matrices, whether they are isomorphic, with error probability at most 1/3 and worst-case total running time n^{O(1)}?
cards.definitions: A graph is finite, undirected, loopless and has no parallel edges. For equally sized vertex sets [n]={1,…,n}, an isomorphism from G to H is a bijection π:[n]→[n] satisfying {u,v}∈E(G) if and only if {π(u),π(v)}∈E(H) for every u≠v. The input consists of the two explicitly written binary adjacency matrices; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately and empty graphs are handled trivially. There are no promises of rigidity, bounded degree, typicality, or a particular input distribution. BQP means a polynomial-time uniform family of quantum circuits over a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T, acting on computational-basis encodings of the classical input and initialized ancillas, with a measured output bit. There must be fixed constants C,c such that all gates, measurements and classical control can be implemented within C(n+2)ᶜ total elementary operations. The algorithm accepts each isomorphic pair with probability at least 2/3 and each nonisomorphic pair with probability at most 1/3. It receives no nonuniform advice, witness, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle or uncounted memory-preparation service. The target is the decision problem for an ordinary vertex permutation; it is not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove membership by giving a correct uniform quantum algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial total cost, or prove GI∉BQP. A classical polynomial-time algorithm would also answer yes. A separation for a specified Fourier-sampling or sieve model is not a negative answer for unrestricted BQP; an invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic pairs is not a complete positive answer.
cards.why: A canonical test of whether quantum computation can efficiently recognize equivalence of explicit combinatorial structures, beyond the algebraic problems already handled by standard period finding.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm for ordinary graph isomorphism, or proof of GI∉BQP, was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 correlation tests, state-isomorphism classifications and NPA hierarchy results do not settle this question.

context_blocks.text: Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound exp((log n)^{O(1)}). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

One tempting quantum approach uses the action of permutations on graphs. The state that is a uniform superposition over all distinct labeled copies of G would be identical for isomorphic graphs and orthogonal for nonisomorphic ones. If such states could always be prepared efficiently, an overlap test would help. The state-preparation step is the difficulty: preparing a superposition of pairs |π⟩|πG⟩ is easy, but coherently removing the permutation register does not follow from that construction. Simply discarding the register gives a mixed state, not the desired pure superposition.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to Ω(n log n) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to GI∈BQP would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

This illustrates why a photonic sampling procedure is not automatically a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all graphs. One must account for how many samples or correlations are required to distinguish a worst-case pair, how accurately they must be estimated, and the classical work used to interpret them. Efficiently generating individual samples does not by itself establish a uniform bound for the complete decision task.

May 2026 work by Gheorghiu, Jacobs, Mehraban and Motamedi studies isomorphism of quantum states under group actions. They show, among other results, that a Clifford-group state problem is at least as hard as ordinary graph isomorphism, while a Pauli-group variant is BQP-complete. The direction and the group matter: the BQP algorithm for the Pauli problem is not thereby an algorithm for the GI-hard Clifford problem.

A further naming distinction appears in the 2026 paper on the NPA hierarchy by Kar, Roberson, Seppelt and Zeman. It studies a quantum isomorphism relation and its noncommutative semidefinite relaxations, with polynomial-time algorithms at each fixed level. Those statements concern a different relation on graphs and fixed relaxations; they do not establish a quantum algorithm deciding whether an ordinary vertex bijection exists.

A positive answer would enlarge the collection of important exact structure problems known to admit efficient quantum algorithms, unless a classical polynomial algorithm arrived at the same time. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so GI∉BQP would in particular imply P≠NP. The question is fundamental on both sides, independently of any particular physical implementation.

cards.title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
cards.formal: For every entangled finite-dimensional bipartite state ρ, do finitely many copies ρ^⊗k and local filters suffice to produce correlations violating a Bell inequality, without an auxiliary entangled state?
cards.definitions: A state is a positive semidefinite trace-one operator on H_A⊗H_B. It is entangled when it is not a convex combination of product states. Local filters are trace-nonincreasing completely positive maps F_A,F_B applied to the respective k-fold systems before measurement questions are selected; the joint success probability must be positive. Normalize the successful filtered state. Each party then chooses a local measurement from a finite set of positive-operator-valued measurements. The resulting conditional distribution p(a,b|x,y) is Bell-nonlocal when it has no representation Σ_λ q_λ p_A(a|x,λ)p_B(b|y,λ), with nonnegative q_λ summing to one. Such a representation is precisely a local hidden-variable model for finite questions and answers. Local ancillary states and shared randomness are allowed, but no additional shared entangled state is supplied.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement and observable Bell nonlocality are related but distinct resources. This question asks whether repeated access to the same entanglement always reveals nonlocal behavior after local preprocessing.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove an activation result using a suitable auxiliary state. That resource is stronger than additional copies of the given state and is expressly excluded here. Direct one-copy Bell tests also do not settle the finite-copy filtered target.

cards.why: Determine whether every bipartite entangled state has an intrinsic finite-copy nonlocal manifestation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

references.authors: John Bostanci; Andrew Huang; Vinod Vaikuntanathan
references.locator: Introduction

cards.review_note: The statement and listed results were individually checked against the cited sources. New proofs were not independently verified. The assessment of importance is editorial.

context_blocks.text: Advice is not a witness chosen for an individual input. It is one nonuniform information resource shared by an entire input-length class.

For a fixed input length, the advice must support all inputs of that length. It cannot be tailored after seeing the particular instance. This makes it different from a witness, which is chosen to establish a claim about one input. A fresh copy of the same quantum advice state can be supplied for each computation.

The possible advantage is not that a measurement reveals an arbitrary amount of classical information from a few qubits. Instead, the algorithm might use the input to choose which computation to perform with the advice. The open question is whether polynomial-length classical advice can always support an equally effective computation for every input.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove that polynomial classical advice suffices for every language decidable with polynomial quantum advice, or prove a separation of the two unrelativized advice classes.

references.locator: Definitions 1.1–1.2; Theorems 1.5, 1.7; Question 1.9

cards.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.

context_blocks.text: A quantum proof can be much larger than the portion a verifier actually inspects. An interactive oracle proof lets a prover supply such messages over several rounds, with the verifier charged for the qubits it touches. Communication volume and access complexity are therefore different resources.

The strong model requires the verifier to hand each received quantum message back in full and forbids sending an additional quantum message of its own. It still has private workspace. Returning a message does not mean undoing the measurement or channel applied to the queried qubits; the resulting state can be returned.

For example, a protocol might inspect only two qubits from an enormous register. That has constant query complexity but still transmits the enormous register. Conversely, allowing the verifier to retain part of a received message changes the protocol model even if the amount of communication is small.

The existing constructions meet different combinations of the desired bounds: general qIOPs have polynomial communication, while the strong construction has exponential communication. The question asks for polynomial communication in the strong model itself. The constant-round requirement and constant total query budget must hold together.

cards.definitions: In each round the prover supplies a quantum register W. The verifier chooses queried positions through a measurement and applies a quantum channel only to those qubits and its private register; query cost counts accessed message qubits, summed over rounds. It returns the entire W register, may send additional classical information, and sends no additional quantum register. It can retain its own private workspace, but cannot retain any part of a prover-message register. The parties have no initial shared entanglement. Total prover-message length counts the full incoming registers, not only queried qubits. This restates the strong model of Definitions 5.1–5.2 and 5.13–5.15.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol for every QMA promise problem, or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no protocol meeting all these bounds. Polynomial communication in the weaker general qIOP model does not suffice.

importance.reason: Tests how far succinct interactive verification can extend to quantum proofs with explicit communication restrictions; affects a broad proof-system design space.

cards.context:
A quantum proof can be much larger than the portion a verifier actually inspects. An interactive oracle proof lets a prover supply such messages over several rounds, with the verifier charged for the qubits it touches. Communication volume and access complexity are therefore different resources.

The strong model requires the verifier to hand each received quantum message back in full and forbids sending an additional quantum message of its own. It still has private workspace. Returning a message does not mean undoing the measurement or channel applied to the queried qubits; the resulting state can be returned.

For example, a protocol might inspect only two qubits from an enormous register. That has constant query complexity but still transmits the enormous register. Conversely, allowing the verifier to retain part of a received message changes the protocol model even if the amount of communication is small.

The existing constructions meet different combinations of the desired bounds: general qIOPs have polynomial communication, while the strong construction has exponential communication. The question asks for polynomial communication in the strong model itself. The constant-round requirement and constant total query budget must hold together.

cards.definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function A:{0,1}*→{0,1}; it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of {0,1}*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns A(z). Quantum access uses the unitary |z,b⟩↦|z,b⊕A(z)⟩, extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. BQP^A consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least 2/3, and on every no input with probability at most 1/3. One standard machine convention uses Hadamard H=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], T=diag(1,e^(iπ/4)) and CNOT |a,b⟩↦|a,a⊕b⟩ gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An IP^A protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least 2/3 on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most 1/3 on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in IP^A. Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and language L with the stated separation, ruling out every polynomial-time classical interactive proof for L relative to A. Alternatively, prove BQP^A⊆IP^A for every classical Boolean oracle A. A lower bound for a fixed round limit does not by itself exclude all polynomial-round protocols.

context_blocks.title: Can a classical verifier trust a quantum computation?
context_blocks.text: A quantum computer might efficiently decide a language while a classical computer cannot directly reproduce its calculation. An interactive proof lets the verifier ask questions and test the answers. This card asks whether even an all-powerful helper can always make the quantum answer classically checkable when both sides must use a supplied oracle through its query interface.

context_blocks.title: The same function, different query access
context_blocks.text: The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for L={x:A(x)=1}, the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

context_blocks.title: Two distinct single-prover questions
context_blocks.text: For every oracle, IP_BQP^A⊆BQP^A and IP_BQP^A⊆IP^A by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from IP_BQP. The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

context_blocks.title: Unbounded cheating is part of the guarantee
context_blocks.text: The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

context_blocks.title: What the 2026 multiple-prover result changes
context_blocks.text: Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state BQP^A⊆MIP^A for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.

cards.context:
A proof of a quantum answer is useful for verification by a classical computer only if the honest quantum device can actually provide it. An interactive proof with an unrestricted prover does not guarantee this. This card asks whether some oracle world separates efficient quantum computation from verification with an efficient quantum honest prover.

The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for L={x:A(x)=1}, the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

For every oracle, IP_BQP^A⊆BQP^A and IP_BQP^A⊆IP^A by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from IP_BQP. The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state BQP^A⊆MIP^A for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.

cards.definitions: For bits s,x₁,…,xₙ∈{0,1}, FANOUTₙ|s,x₁,…,xₙ⟩=|s,s⊕x₁,…,s⊕xₙ⟩, extended linearly to all states; ⊕ is addition modulo two. A permitted circuit acts on n+1+a(n) qubits for some finite a(n)≥0. Its gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitary matrices over ℂ and generalized Toffoli gates: for any k≥1 distinct controls and a distinct target, |z₁,…,z_k,t⟩ maps to |z₁,…,z_k,t⊕(z₁⋯z_k)⟩. Each layer contains gates on disjoint sets of qubits, and depth is the number of layers. Gates may connect any qubits; fanout gates, measurements, postselection and classical feed-forward are not additional primitives. Exact implementation means that for some global phase e^(iφₙ), independent of the input state ψ, Cₙ(|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩^⊗a(n))=e^(iφₙ)(FANOUTₙ|ψ⟩)⊗|0⟩^⊗a(n) for every unit vector ψ in (ℂ²)^⊗(n+1). The ancillas must return to zero, as in the source’s implementation definition. Gate count, ancilla count and gate arities may grow arbitrarily with n but must be finite at each n. The family is nonuniform: there is no required circuit-generation algorithm or finite gate alphabet. The one depth bound d must work for all n. QAC0 usually adds a polynomial-size bound; this question explicitly drops it.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an exact clean-ancilla implementation with a depth bound independent of n, or prove that no such bound exists even when size, ancilla count and Toffoli arity are unrestricted. An approximation with arbitrarily small nonzero error, a lower bound only for polynomial-size circuits, or a bound for one fixed small depth does not settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: Fanout is a coherent controlled operation
context_blocks.text: On a basis input, the control flips every target when it is one and leaves them unchanged when it is zero. The same circuit must act correctly on superpositions, including inputs entangled with other systems. Agreement only on measured classical outputs would be weaker.

context_blocks.title: This operation does not clone an arbitrary quantum state
context_blocks.text: For example, applying two-target fanout to |+⟩|00⟩ yields (|000⟩+|111⟩)/√2. It does not yield three independent copies of |+⟩. The target is therefore compatible with the distinction between coherent basis fanout and cloning.

context_blocks.title: Only depth is restricted
context_blocks.text: A Toffoli gate may inspect many controls in one layer, but a qubit cannot participate in several gates in that same layer. The question permits enormous circuits and arbitrarily many zero-initialized ancillas. A negative answer would therefore be a structural limitation of constant depth, beyond ordinary polynomial-size lower bounds.

cards.definitions: Write n=|x|. QMA consists of promise problems whose YES instances have polynomial-qubit quantum witnesses accepted by a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with probability at least 2/3, while every witness on a NO instance is accepted with probability at most 1/3. In the requested game, a classical verifier samples correlated questions, sends one to each of r noncommunicating provers, receives one classical answer from each, and decides acceptance in polynomial time. The provers may share entanglement prepared before the questions arrive. For each L, r and an exponent a are fixed independently of n, and every individual message has at most O((log(n+2))^a) bits. Honest efficiency includes a uniform quantum polynomial-time setup algorithm which, given x and polynomially many copies of a polynomial-qubit state ψ_x, prepares the shared state, followed by uniform quantum polynomial-time local response algorithms. The state ψ_x is an existential witness depending on x, not a supplied circuit for preparing it. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary local quantum strategies with arbitrary finite-dimensional shared entanglement; only communication after separation is forbidden. There is no promise on inputs outside L_yes∪L_no. The fixed gap can be amplified by a constant number of repetitions without changing the polylogarithmic communication scale. The question imposes no logarithmic bound on the verifier’s total random bits and no additional cryptographic assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated protocol for every QMA promise problem, proving both witness-assisted honest efficiency and soundness against unrestricted entangled provers; or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no such protocol. A protocol with polynomial-length answers, or one whose honest entanglement cannot be prepared efficiently from a polynomial witness, does not meet this target.

cards.definitions: R(σ) permutes the tensor factors labelled by X: R(σ)|a⟩=|a∘σ⁻¹⟩ for a∈{0,1}^X. A finite abstract group acting on X is represented by its image in Sym(X); only this action matters. Circuit wires are W=X⊔Y, with X active and Y workspace. Allowed gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitaries and unbounded-fan-in reversible threshold/equality gates. For S⊆W, target h∉S and integer t≥0, a threshold gate flips bit a_h exactly when ∑_{s∈S}a_s≥t; an equality gate flips it exactly when this sum equals t, leaving all other bits unchanged and extending linearly to quantum states. Layers are sets of pairwise commuting gates; gates within a layer may share wires. A wire permutation acts on a gate by relabelling its target and controls while preserving the one-qubit matrix or threshold value. The circuit is Γ-symmetric if, for each σ∈Γ, some permutation π of W restricts to σ on X and maps each layer to itself as a set of labelled gates. The extensions π need not be selected as a group homomorphism. This is a syntactic circuit condition, stronger than merely requiring its resulting unitary to commute with Γ. Implementation is exact on the full active Hilbert space, with clean workspace, no intermediate measurements or postselection, and no uniformity or finite-angle-encoding restriction on the arbitrary one-qubit gates. An overall input-independent phase can be absorbed into an allowed one-qubit phase gate.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove exact implementability for every finite permutation action and every commuting unitary, or exhibit an action and a commuting unitary that no finite circuit in this model implements. A lower bound only on polynomial-size circuits does not refute universality. Implementing only the invariant-state subspace does not implement an arbitrary unitary on the whole space.

context_blocks.title: Symmetry must be visible throughout the circuit
context_blocks.text: Suppose Γ swaps two active wires. Applying the same one-qubit gate to both wires in a common layer respects that swap. Applying different gates to the two wires generally does not. More elaborate circuits may use extra wires, but every active-wire symmetry must still extend to a relabelling that preserves every layer.

cards.title: Tight quantum query lower bounds for uniformity testing
cards.formal: Does testing whether an unknown distribution p on [d] is exactly uniform or has total variation distance greater than ε from uniform require Ω(min{d^{1/3}/ε^{4/3}, √d/ε}) quantum queries to a synthesizer for p, with success probability at least 0.99 on every promised input? references.authors: Canonne, Clément L.; Kothari, Robin; O'Donnell, Ryan
references.locator: Conjecture 2; PDF page 3

cards.definitions: Write [d]={1,…,d}, u_d(i)=1/d and d_TV(p,u_d)=(1/2)Σ_i|p_i−1/d|. The algorithm receives d and ε and oracle access to a unitary U_p satisfying U_p|0^k⟩=Σ_i√p_i|i⟩|ψ_i⟩, where each garbage state |ψ_i⟩ is normalized. The extension of U_p away from |0^k⟩ and its garbage states are arbitrary; the tester must work for every valid oracle satisfying the promise. A query is one application of U_p, U_p† or controlled-U_p; intervening quantum operations, ancillas and measurements are unrestricted and do not count toward query complexity. The code is used as a black box: the tester does not get a classical description to inspect for free. Let Q(d,ε) be the minimum worst-case number of such queries among testers whose probability of the correct yes/no output is at least 0.99 for every oracle with p=u_d or d_TV(p,u_d)>ε, taking the worst case over allowed oracle-register sizes. No guarantee is required in the intermediate gap. The conjecture asks for an absolute c>0 with Q(d,ε)≥c min{d^{1/3}ε^{-4/3},d^{1/2}ε^{-1}} throughout the stated parameter range, up to conventional finite asymptotic exceptions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform two-parameter lower bound in this oracle model, or refute it by a tester with a smaller worst-case asymptotic query complexity in a valid parameter regime. Lower bounds for classical samples, one particular algorithm, constant ε only, or a restricted family of quantum testers do not establish the full claim.

context_blocks.title: Running a sampler backwards is extra information
context_blocks.text: Ordinary sample access reveals only independent outcomes. Coherent access to a sampler and its inverse permits interference between executions. This can reduce the number of calls needed to detect a departure from uniformity; a classical sample lower bound therefore does not automatically apply.

context_blocks.title: The upper bound has two regimes
context_blocks.text: The paper establishes O(min{d^{1/3}/ε^{4/3},√d/ε}) queries. The terms cross at ε=d^{-1/2}: the first governs larger errors and the second smaller errors. The question asks whether any quantum tester can improve this full dependence.

context_blocks.title: Separate lower bounds leave a gap
context_blocks.text: The source recalls Ω(d^{1/3}) queries for constant ε and Ω(1/ε) already on a two-element domain. Knowing both separately does not yield their conjectured joint dependence. For example, at ε=d^{-1/2} the target is Ω(d).

context_blocks.title: A stronger variant fixes a special oracle structure
context_blocks.text: For a string x∈[d]^m, the standard oracle maps |j,z⟩ to |j,z⊕x_j⟩ and defines p_i=|{j:x_j=i}|/m. The authors also conjecture the same lower bound even with this structure available, in the worst case over m and x. This is a stronger claim than the arbitrary-synthesizer target selected here; fixed small m can cap the cost through reading the entire string.

cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair (L_yes,L_no) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings, with no required answer outside their union. Membership in StoqMA(a,b) means there is a deterministic polynomial-time procedure which, given x of length n, produces a verification circuit V_x on m(n)+r(n)+s(n) qubits, all counts polynomially bounded in n. Its initial state is |w⟩⊗|0⟩^{⊗r}⊗|+⟩^{⊗s}, where |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and the m-qubit witness has norm one. The circuit uses only classical reversible gates: NOT flips a bit, CNOT flips its target if its control is one, and Toffoli flips its target if both controls are one. These gates act linearly on computational-basis states. There are no intermediate measurements or arbitrary quantum gates. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the {|+⟩,|−⟩} basis, with |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2, and outcome + means acceptance. Its acceptance probability is the squared norm after projection onto |+⟩ on that qubit. If x∈L_yes, some witness with real nonnegative computational-basis amplitudes must be accepted with probability at least a(n). If x∈L_no, every normalized witness, including arbitrary complex amplitudes, must be accepted with probability at most b(n). The source proves that a maximizing witness can be chosen nonnegative. Efficient threshold computability is understood in the standard precision sense: their values can be approximated within 2^{−t} in time polynomial in n+t. The inverse-polynomial gap permits this conventional representation. Class containment quantifies over promise problems and asserts existence of new uniform verifiers; it does not demand a blackbox compiler acting on an arbitrary verifier description. Polynomial bounds of the new verifier may depend on the original verifier, q and ℓ. Soundness approaches 1/2 from above, not zero; the requested improvement is relative to the stoquastic acceptance baseline.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the containment for every admissible a,b and ℓ, or refute this universally quantified amplification statement. A positive answer must achieve both exponentially small completeness error and exponentially small excess soundness above 1/2 while retaining the allowed gates, initial ancillas and final measurement. Soundness-only repetition, perfect-completeness special cases, extra destructive-interference gates, or additional unentangled provers do not establish the claim.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume ZF+DC+AD. Do both assertions hold? (I) Every Turing-invariant function f:2^ω→2^ω is either constant in Turing degree on a cone or satisfies x≤_T f(x) on a cone. (II) Cone-wise Turing reducibility prewellorders all such functions that are above the identity on a cone, and the pointwise jump f′ has rank exactly rank(f)+1 in this prewellorder.
cards.definitions: A real x∈2^ω is an infinite binary sequence, identified with a subset of the natural numbers. Write x≤_T y if an oracle Turing machine with oracle y computes x, and x≡_T y for mutual reducibility. A function f is Turing-invariant when x≡_T y implies f(x)≡_T f(y). A cone above a real a is {x:a≤_T x}. Being constant on a cone means ∃a,b ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≡_T b; the output sequences need not be literally equal. Define f≤_M g by ∃a ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≤_T g(x), and f≡_M g by mutual ≤_M. Let F be the set of all Turing-invariant f for which id≤_M f, where id(x)=x. The prewellorder assertion says that ≤_M is total on F and its quotient by ≡_M is well-ordered. The rank of f is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly preceding [f]. The jump of a real y is y′={e: the e-th oracle program with oracle y halts on input e}; f′(x)=f(x)′. ZF is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. DC is dependent choice: every serial binary relation on a nonempty set admits an infinite successive chain. AD says every infinite game in which two players alternately choose natural numbers, with an arbitrary specified set of winning sequences, is determined. Functions are not assumed computable, Borel, order-preserving, or uniformly Turing-invariant. Cone bases may depend on the functions being compared.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in Walsh’s March 2026 survey; checked through 10 September 2026. The saved draft’s already-settled regressive subcase has been replaced by the full quantified Part I, together with Part II. context_blocks.text: The Turing degrees form a complicated partial order, with many incomparable and specially constructed degrees. Yet operations arising naturally by relativizing mathematical definitions often produce a much more organized hierarchy. Martin’s conjecture attempts to make that phenomenon precise through invariance under Turing equivalence and comparison on cones, rather than through an undefined requirement that a construction be “natural.”

The two parts have different jobs. Part I rules out a function that remains nonconstant on every cone but never uniformly reaches the input degree on any cone. Part II concerns functions already above the identity. It asserts comparability and well-foundedness of their cone-equivalence classes, and says that taking an oracle halting problem moves exactly one level up, leaving no intervening class.

Cone-wise comparison ignores behaviour below a fixed computational base. This is meaningful under determinacy: every Turing-invariant set either contains a cone or is disjoint from one, giving Martin’s zero-one measure on degree-invariant sets. Thus “almost everywhere” in the literature means on a cone, not outside a null set for ordinary Lebesgue measure on binary sequences.

Restricting to functions below the identity gives a strictly narrower case with a known theorem: Slaman and Steel show that a Turing-invariant function satisfying f(x)≤_T x on a cone must be constant there or equivalent to the identity on a smaller cone. The unresolved Part I quantifies over all invariant functions, including ones not initially comparable with the identity.

Uniform invariance is another substantial restriction. It requires a single map that turns indices witnessing x≡_T y into indices witnessing f(x)≡_T f(y), independently of the actual reals. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the conjecture for this subclass. Merely preserving equivalence classes, as the question requires, does not supply that uniform map.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and more generally for measure-preserving invariant functions. Here measure-preserving means that for every fixed degree a there is a cone on which f(x) computes a. Their theorem supplies major new cases.
The March 2026 survey by Walsh still presents the full conjecture as open and keeps the Borel restriction on the earlier Part II result for order-preserving functions.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
cards.definitions: Work in Cantor space 2^N, with coordinates numbered 0,1,… and fair-coin product measure μ. For a finite binary string σ, the cylinder [σ]={X:σ is a prefix of X} has measure 2^{−|σ|}. A Martin-Löf test is a sequence (U_k)_{k≥1} of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs (k,σ), with U_k equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and μ(U_k)≤2^{−k}. A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test X∉⋂_k U_k. A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier q∈[0,2], before seeing X(j). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After X(j) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by 2−q if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. q=1 allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.

cards.status_note: The revised 2025 primary paper and its journal version explicitly retain KLR=MLR as a major open problem. Its finite-family/open-set obstruction is not a separating infinite sequence. No later resolution found through 11 September 2026. The formulation fixes fair-coin measure, fresh adaptive coordinates, rational fair bets, partial computability and unbounded-capital success.

context_blocks.text: These are two ways to say that an individual infinite sequence behaves randomly. Martin-Löf tests describe effectively recognizable events of arbitrarily small probability, and a sequence is nonrandom if one test catches it at every level. The betting definition instead asks whether an algorithm can turn knowledge of selected bits into unbounded profit. It measures mathematical unpredictability of a whole sequence, rather than a statistical confidence score assigned to a finite data sample.

The betting order is adaptive. A strategy may inspect a faraway coordinate before deciding which earlier, still unseen coordinate to bet on. It may also read a coordinate with a zero wager to gather information. It cannot bet on a bit already revealed, since that would permit guaranteed profit even from a fair-coin sequence. Its choice of the next position must be computed using only the information it has actually observed.

The known implication from Martin-Löf randomness follows from the fairness of the bets. For a fixed strategy starting with capital one, the set of sequences on which capital ever reaches a threshold R has measure at most 1/R. Reaching a threshold is witnessed after finitely many completed actions and can be effectively enumerated. Taking increasing thresholds produces a Martin-Löf test covering the sequences on which this strategy succeeds. The unresolved direction would convert every effective failure of randomness into success of some permitted gambler.

Choosing the query order in advance is insufficient. Kastermans and Lempp show that randomness against computable injective query orders is weaker than Martin-Löf randomness; they also establish the separation for computable permutation orders. The full Kolmogorov–Loveland definition permits choices that depend on observed bit values. Consequently their separating sequences do not establish the separation requested here.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan prove that Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequences have arbitrarily dense subsequences that are Martin-Löf random. A key splitting result says that when a computable set of coordinates and its complement are both infinite, at least one of the two resulting subsequences is Martin-Löf random. This places the notion close to Martin-Löf randomness, but the randomness of a subsequence does not by itself imply randomness of the original interleaving.

Generalized betting games use a different query model. Generalized betting games may split a current set of possible sequences into computably described pieces, instead of querying exactly one fresh bit. Petrović’s 2021 paper gives a pair of strategies in a generalized half-betting model that together succeed on every non-Martin-Löf-random sequence. The greater freedom of the query is part of that theorem, so it does not directly give two Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies.

Petrović’s 2025 result identifies a limitation of a method used for those more flexible games. Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies do not admit the same finite-family guarantee of uniformly forcing large capital on every sequence in a sufficiently small effective open set. The paper constructs small open sets containing sequences on which the relevant capital bounds are not exceeded. This is a barrier to that style of quantitative coverage argument.

The remaining quantifier matters: finding a suitable sequence inside each of arbitrarily small open sets need not produce one sequence lying in every level of a single Martin-Löf test. Likewise, excluding one fixed finite family of gamblers does not exclude a strategy chosen separately for each nonrandom sequence. The 2025 paper explicitly keeps the equivalence question open.

A positive answer would show that the ability to choose unseen coordinates adaptively compensates for the restrictions of an ordinary computable betting procedure. A negative answer would exhibit effective statistical nonrandomness that escapes every such procedure. Either outcome would resolve a basic mismatch between two precise definitions of randomness and sharpen our understanding of what information an adaptive algorithm can extract from an infinite object.

cards.title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
cards.formal: Is every order automorphism of the partial order (Dₜ,≤ₜ) of all Turing degrees the identity? Equivalently, does every bijection π:Dₜ→Dₜ satisfying a≤ₜb if and only if π(a)≤ₜπ(b), for all a,b∈Dₜ, also satisfy π(a)=a for every a∈Dₜ?
cards.definitions: For sets A,B⊆ℕ, A≤ₜB means that an oracle Turing machine with membership-query access to B halts on every natural-number input and decides membership in A. There is no time or space bound. A≡ₜB means A≤ₜB and B≤ₜA. The Turing degree [A] is the equivalence class of A under ≡ₜ, and Dₜ is the quotient of all subsets of ℕ by this equivalence. The relation [A]≤ₜ[B] is independent of the chosen representatives and is a partial order. An automorphism is any set-theoretic bijection of Dₜ preserving and reflecting this order. It is not assumed computable, definable, continuous, measure-preserving or induced by one operation on representatives. The domain includes all degrees, not only degrees of computably enumerable sets or degrees below a fixed bound. The question is interpreted for the actual degree structure in ordinary set theory, for example ZFC.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every such bijection fixes every degree, or prove the existence of one order automorphism and one degree that it moves. An automorphism of a proper substructure, a non-surjective order embedding, or a permutation of subsets that fails to descend to degrees is not a counterexample. Rigidity of one cone or of a restricted class of induced automorphisms is only a partial positive result. An independence result should specify the axiomatic base and would settle provability relative to that base rather than assert either mathematical answer.
cards.why: A central structural question about relative computability: whether the ordering of computational power has any nontrivial global symmetry. It tests how much mathematical information is recoverable from reducibility alone.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of degree theory, closely tied to the intrinsic definability of computational structure and constrained by deep but incomplete rigidity theorems.

cards.status_note: Literature search checked through 10 September 2026. The checked primary sources explicitly retain general rigidity as open; no later verified resolution was located. The last substantive result documented here is the 2018 journal article, not a claimed 2026 advance. The historical Cooper announcement is distinguished from an independently verified solution.

context_blocks.text: Turing degrees classify decision problems by what can be computed from an oracle for them. Different encodings that compute one another become one point, and the order records comparative computational power. The rigidity question asks whether this order has any genuine symmetry: could all degrees be consistently relabeled, changing at least one degree while preserving every reducibility comparison? A positive answer would make the entire relative-computability structure intrinsically asymmetric.

Elementary examples illustrate what is already forced. The degree 0 of computable sets is the unique least element and therefore cannot move. The join of [A] and [B] is represented by A⊕B, which stores A on even positions and B on odd positions; because it is the least upper bound, every order automorphism preserves joins as well. These observations do not identify arbitrary degrees, whose patterns of predecessors and successors are far more complicated.

The Turing jump sends [A] to the degree of the halting problem for machines equipped with oracle A. Shore and Slaman prove that this operation is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Consequently every automorphism commutes with the jump, and fixes 0′, 0″ and all finite iterates starting from 0. This is a major restriction, but commuting with an operation does not by itself force a map to fix every argument.

Slaman and Woodin prove that every automorphism fixes every degree above 0″. Their analysis also shows that the automorphism group is at most countable, despite the continuum-sized underlying degree structure. The unresolved region is the complement of that upper cone. It includes degrees incomparable with 0″, not just degrees strictly below it. Thus describing the remaining question as only the interval below 0″ would omit part of the problem.

One possible way to construct an automorphism would be to permute the natural-number coordinates of every oracle set. Kjos-Hanssen rules this out: if one permutation of ℕ induces an order automorphism on all Turing degrees, the induced automorphism is trivial, and the permutation itself must be computable. His result also treats homeomorphisms of Cantor space preserving all Bernoulli product measures. The full question imposes none of these representation or measure restrictions.

Rigidity must also be distinguished from defining every single degree by a first-order formula without parameters. There are only countably many such formulas but uncountably many degrees, so the latter is impossible. A rigid infinite structure can contain elements that are not individually definable: absence of global symmetries is weaker than having a separate finite logical description of each element.

The historical literature includes an announced nontrivial automorphism by Cooper in 1999. Slaman’s survey explicitly reports that its construction had not been independently verified and continues to treat rigidity as open. Kjos-Hanssen’s later journal article likewise states the general question as open. These cards follow the established partial-result literature; an old announcement alone is not treated as a resolution.

This is a foundational computability question rather than an efficient-algorithm problem. Its significance is whether relative computability already determines its own global structure, or whether the degree order admits hidden symmetries that are invisible to all reducibility comparisons.

The join of [A] and [B] is represented by A⊕B, which stores A on even positions and B on odd positions; because it is the least upper bound, every order automorphism preserves joins as well. These observations do not identify arbitrary degrees, whose patterns of predecessors and successors are far more complicated.

The Turing jump sends [A] to the degree of the halting problem for machines equipped with oracle A. Shore and Slaman prove that this operation is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Consequently every automorphism commutes with the jump, and fixes 0′, 0″ and all finite iterates starting from 0. This is a major restriction, but commuting with an operation does not by itself force a map to fix every argument.

Slaman and Woodin prove that every automorphism fixes every degree above 0″. Their analysis also shows that the automorphism group is at most countable, despite the continuum-sized underlying degree structure. The unresolved region is the complement of that upper cone. It includes degrees incomparable with 0″, not just degrees strictly below it. Thus describing the remaining question as only the interval below 0″ would omit part of the problem.

One possible way to construct an automorphism would be to permute the natural-number coordinates of every oracle set. Kjos-Hanssen rules this out: if one permutation of ℕ induces an order automorphism on all Turing degrees, the induced automorphism is trivial, and the permutation itself must be computable. His result also treats homeomorphisms of Cantor space preserving all Bernoulli product measures. The full question imposes none of these representation or measure restrictions.

Rigidity must also be distinguished from defining every single degree by a first-order formula without parameters. There are only countably many such formulas but uncountably many degrees, so the latter is impossible. A rigid infinite structure can contain elements that are not individually definable: absence of global symmetries is weaker than having a separate finite logical description of each element.

The historical literature includes an announced nontrivial automorphism by Cooper in 1999. Slaman’s survey explicitly reports that its construction had not been independently verified and continues to treat rigidity as open. Kjos-Hanssen’s later journal article likewise states the general question as open. These cards follow the established partial-result literature; an old announcement alone is not treated as a resolution.

This is a foundational computability question rather than an efficient-algorithm problem. Its significance is whether relative computability already determines its own global structure, or whether the degree order admits hidden symmetries that are invisible to all reducibility comparisons.

cards.title: Busy Beaver BB(6)
cards.formal: Determine the exact value of $BB(6)=S(6)$ by specifying a machine $M_*\in\mathcal{M}_6$ that halts on the blank tape and proving that $T(M)\le T(M_*)$ for every $M\in\mathcal{M}_6$ that halts on the blank tape. Here $\mathcal{M}_6$ is the class of deterministic Turing machines with six nonhalting states, two tape symbols and one initially all-zero, bi-infinite tape, as defined below, and $T(M)$ counts transitions up to and including the first entry into the separate halting state. The answer is then $BB(6)=T(M_*)$; the witness runtime is an exact description of the value.
cards.definitions: The states are A, B, C, D, E, F and a separate halting state Z; Z is not one of the six states being counted. Tape cells are indexed by the integers and contain 0 or 1. Initially every cell contains 0, the head is at cell 0, and the state is A. For each nonhalting state and scanned symbol, the transition table specifies a symbol to write, a move by exactly one cell left or right, and a next state. Execution stops on entering Z, including that final write-and-move transition in T(M). Unreachable states are allowed. The finite set of these transition tables is $\mathcal{M}_6$. Here BB is the runtime (maximum-shift) function S, not the function $\Sigma$ that maximizes the number of 1s left on the tape. In the progress note, $2\uparrow\uparrow k$ is a tower of k twos, and $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 1=2$, $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)$. For a halting machine M, T(M) is the least positive integer t at which the execution enters Z. The answer convention never applies T to a nonhalting machine: halting of the proposed witness is a required part of its certificate. Its explicitly specified transition table together with that certificate defines a terminating step-counting computation and hence a unique exact integer, even when evaluating that computation is impractical.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the complete twelve-entry transition table of a particular machine M_* in the stated class. Provide Lean-checked proofs that (1) M_* halts from the specified blank-tape initial configuration, and (2) every machine M in this class that halts from that initial configuration executes at most T(M_*) transitions. Together these certify BB(6)=T(M_*) exactly. The runtime of this proved-halting concrete machine is an accepted finite description of the integer; a simple closed form, decimal expansion, separately evaluated integer literal or full execution trace is not required. Specifying a machine without proving its halting and universal maximality, restating the defining maximum over all machines, or giving only an approximate or one-sided bound does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: This is a defining concrete problem in computability: identify the longest finite computation possible in a fixed, exceptionally small universal machine formalism. A proof would advance the boundary of complete mathematical understanding of small programs and test methods for nontermination proofs, recurrence analysis, and formal verification. The significance lies in establishing the exact boundary, not merely constructing a machine with an enormous runtime.

context_blocks.text: Fixing the number of states leaves finitely many machines, so a maximum halting time exists. Nevertheless, enumerating their transition tables does not tell us when to stop waiting for the machines that never halt. The Busy Beaver function packages that obstruction into a sequence of finite integers. Noncomputability of the whole sequence does not prevent individual values from being established.

The five-state case provides a concrete precedent: the bbchallenge collaboration proved S(5)=47,176,870 with the Coq proof assistant. Its proof combines a complete enumeration after symmetry reductions with methods that certify halting or nonhalting. The paper makes precise how a finite search can be accompanied by a universal proof.

Six states introduce obstacles beyond running a larger search. The Antihydra machine has a halting question expressed through an integer recurrence whose parity behavior is still unresolved. A probabilistic heuristic about that behavior is not a proof that the machine runs forever. An exact Busy Beaver bound would also decide its halting behavior in principle, even if the required finite computation were physically infeasible.

The target is the exact six-state runtime maximum. A concrete machine with proved halting and universal maximality specifies that integer through its runtime, without a simple closed form or decimal expansion. Runtime and final tape output are different extremal quantities, and machine conventions matter. Existing catalogue questions about Busy Beaver growth, logical thresholds, or population protocols therefore remain separate problems.

cards.title: Reversal of Hindman’s theorem to the ω-jump
cards.formal: Over RCA₀, does Hindman’s finite-sums theorem imply ACA₀⁺? Equivalently, does RCA₀+HT prove that every set X has an ω-th Turing jump?
cards.definitions: Work in classical two-sorted second-order arithmetic, with number variables and variables for sets of natural numbers. RCA₀ has the usual elementary arithmetic axioms, Σ⁰₁ induction and Δ⁰₁ comprehension, allowing set parameters. HT is the assertion that for every integer k≥1 and every coloring c of the positive integers into {0,…,k−1}, there exist an infinite set H of positive integers and a color i such that c(Σ_{h∈F}h)=i for every nonempty finite subset F of H. Terms in a sum are distinct; there is no fixed upper bound on their number and no additional sparsity requirement on H. For a set X, its Turing jump X′ is {e: the e-th oracle Turing machine with oracle X halts on input e}, using one fixed effective enumeration. The ω-jump existence axiom says ∀X∃Y [Y₀=X and ∀j(Y_{j+1}=Y_j′)], where Y_j={e:⟨j,e⟩∈Y} and ⟨·,·⟩ is a fixed primitive recursive pairing. ACA₀⁺ is RCA₀ plus that axiom. The question is formal provability of this implication over the stated base, not truth of Hindman’s theorem in ordinary set theory and not a single-instance computability claim.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the ω-jump existence axiom in RCA₀+HT, or prove nonimplication by constructing a model of RCA₀+HT in which some set has no coded ω-jump. A standard-natural-number model is sufficient for a separation but is not required. A lower bound of ACA₀ alone, an upper bound of ACA₀⁺, or a theorem about only bounded-length sums does not decide this implication. A negative answer need not show that HT is equivalent to ACA₀; an intermediate strength would also refute the implication.
cards.why: A longstanding gap in the computational and axiomatic strength of a central infinite combinatorial theorem, with a precise target at the ω-th Turing jump.

importance.reason: A landmark reverse-mathematical calibration problem connecting finite-sums combinatorics, oracle computation and the hierarchy of set-existence axioms.

progress.text: Blass–Hirst–Simpson establish ACA₀⁺⇒HT⇒ACA₀ over RCA₀, leaving the reversal in this card open.

context_blocks.text: Hindman’s theorem says that a finite coloring contains an infinite set whose entire collection of finite sums has one color. This is much more than finding an infinite monochromatic subset: the same color must work for single elements, pairs, triples and every larger finite selection. For parity coloring, the positive even numbers give an immediate example. The theorem must also handle colorings with no such simple arithmetic description.

The combinatorial statement is a theorem, not the unresolved claim on this card. Reverse mathematics asks which set-existence axioms are needed to prove it. One works over a deliberately weak base theory and compares stronger principles by implication. The inherited paper records the classical bounds ACA₀⁺⇒HT⇒ACA₀ and identifies closing this gap as a major open problem. This card asks specifically whether the upper implication reverses.

ACA₀ allows arithmetic comprehension; equivalently over the base theory, every set has its Turing jump. An individual jump supplies answers to halting questions relative to the given set. Repeating that operation a fixed finite number of times yields increasingly strong information. The ω-jump places every finite iterate into the sections of one set. Being able to discuss each fixed finite stage is not the same as having this whole sequence available as a single object.

The distinction is visible in the model consisting of the standard natural numbers together with all arithmetical sets. It is closed under the ordinary Turing jump, since jumping an arithmetical set still yields an arithmetical set. It does not contain the join of all finite jumps of the empty set. Thus ACA₀⁺ demands more set existence than ACA₀. Whether Hindman’s theorem already forces that additional existence is the precise issue here.

The computability bounds show why ordinary computable colorings already matter. The account by Csima and coauthors recalls a computable coloring for which every finite-sums solution computes the halting set, and an upper bound placing a solution in the (ω+1)-st jump of the coloring. These are bounds on information in solutions. Neither identifies the exact reverse-mathematical strength, and noncomputability alone falls far short of an ω-jump reversal.

Restricted sum lengths have provided substantial progress without closing the full gap. Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski prove that the version requiring monochromatic singletons and pairs already implies ACA₀; four colors suffice without an additional sparsity condition. Their results for sums of exactly n≥3 terms use an apartness condition on the binary supports of the chosen integers. These carefully specified variants should not be merged with unrestricted HT.

Even replacing “at most two” by “exactly two” changes the logical picture. Csima and coauthors construct a computable two-color instance of the exactly-two version with no Σ⁰₂ solution and prove a lower bound through diagonally noncomputable functions relative to the halting set. Yet exactly-two sums follow from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, placing that principle strictly below full HT over the base. This is a useful warning that small wording changes can alter the problem.

There is a separate combinatorial principle known to capture the desired upper level exactly. Carlucci–Zdanowski prove that Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large finite sets is equivalent to ACA₀⁺. A finite set F is exactly large when |F|=min(F)+1, so its dimension varies with its elements. This yields a potential comparison target: an implication from HT to this precisely defined Ramsey principle would suffice. Its equivalence does not itself supply that missing implication.

Recent results in the neighboring theory of variable words require the same care. Liu–Patey’s June 2026 preprint, revised in July, gives low₂ solutions to the Ordered Variable Word theorem for colorings of ordinary words and proves each fixed-dimensional unordered Carlson–Simpson lemma in ACA₀. The paper distinguishes these principles from ordered higher-dimensional counterparts and still describes ACA₀⁺ as the weakest known system proving HT. Its new upper bounds should not be transferred to Hindman’s theorem.

Le Houérou–Patey’s July 2026 preprint obtains a conservation result for a one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle with two colors. It controls which arithmetical consequences that particular principle adds to a weak theory. This is a different assertion from constructing the ω-jump out of unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity. Together the recent papers sharpen nearby boundaries without answering the implication stated here.

A positive answer would make a concrete additive-combinatorial theorem a characterization of closure under all finite Turing jumps at once. A negative answer would show that known proofs use more set existence than the theorem itself entails. Either outcome would clarify the information content of an infinite combinatorial search principle, which is the reason for its place in the computability part of this catalogue.

cards.title: Universality of Turing equivalence
cards.formal: For every countable Borel equivalence relation E on a standard Borel space X, does there exist a Borel function f:X→2^ℕ such that x E y if and only if f(x)≡_T f(y), for all x,y∈X?
cards.definitions: The space 2^ℕ consists of all infinite binary sequences, identified with subsets of ℕ. For a,b∈2^ℕ, a≤_T b means that some oracle Turing machine with oracle b computes every bit of a and halts on every input coordinate; a≡_T b means both a≤_T b and b≤_T a. There is no time or space restriction on these computations. A standard Borel space is a set with the Borel σ-algebra of some Polish topology. The relation E must be a Borel subset of X×X and each equivalence class must be at most countable; X itself may be uncountable. The function f is Borel measurable: inverse images of Borel sets are Borel. It need not be computable, continuous, injective on points, or uniform on indices witnessing equivalence. It must preserve both equivalence and inequivalence on every input pair, not merely almost everywhere for a chosen measure. The quantifiers ask for a separate Borel reduction for each E, without requiring an algorithm that takes a code for E and outputs f. This is the ordinary ZFC formulation of Borel universality.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that Turing equivalence is universal by producing the requisite Borel reductions, or prove it is not by identifying one countable Borel relation that does not reduce to it. Equivalently, settle whether E_∞≤_B≡_T for a fixed standard universal countable Borel relation E_∞. A negative theorem conditional on a form of Martin’s conjecture must be labeled conditional. Failure of reductions with an additional uniformity or computability requirement is not a negative solution to the unrestricted Borel question.
cards.why: A central bridge between computability and descriptive set theory, asking whether equality of computational power can encode every countable Borel classification problem.

context_blocks.text: Two infinite binary sequences have the same Turing degree when each can compute the other. This partitions all possible oracles by their computational power. The universality question asks how complicated that partition is as a classification problem: can every countable Borel pattern of equivalence be represented exactly by equality of Turing degrees? The objects being classified are infinite sequences, not finite machine descriptions.

There are countably many oracle programs. Consequently, for a fixed oracle b, only countably many sequences can be computed from b, and its Turing-equivalence class is countable. The relation is Borel because a claim that an oracle program computes a given sequence can be written using countably many conditions about finite computations. Thus Turing equivalence itself belongs to the class of relations compared on this card.

A Borel reduction is a structured assignment of invariants. If f reduces E to Turing equivalence, the Turing degree of f(x) is a complete invariant for the E-class of x: equivalent objects receive the same degree, and inequivalent objects receive different degrees. Distinct representatives of one E-class may receive different binary sequences, provided those sequences have the same degree. Injectivity on equivalence classes is essential; injectivity on individual points is not.

It suffices to study a single standard benchmark E_∞. One realization is the orbit relation for the shift action of the free group F₂ on {0,1}^{F₂}: two labelings x,y are equivalent when y(h)=x(g⁻¹h) for some group element g and every h∈F₂. This countable Borel relation is universal. A reduction of that one relation to Turing equivalence would therefore answer the full universally quantified question.

The inherited Caicedo–Löwe survey records the question as Question 6 in its discussion of Martin’s conjecture. It traces the universality problem to Kechris and distinguishes it from nearby statements about arithmetic equivalence and uniform coding. The source is a 2019 preprint; the later published chapter updates the year in its title. The card retains the exact inherited version and locator.

There are strong positive results for neighboring relations. Slaman and Steel proved that arithmetic equivalence is universal; Marks, Slaman and Steel provide a published proof and discussion. Arithmetic equivalence allows each sequence to be computed from some finite Turing jump of the other, with the finite jump levels depending on the pair. That extra allowance changes which sequences become equivalent.

In the other direction, Marks proved universality of polynomial-time Turing equivalence, as well as polynomial-time many-one equivalence. These compare arbitrary languages over finite strings by resource-bounded oracle reductions. The theorem concerns the entire space of languages, not only decidable languages or languages inside a familiar complexity class. It establishes universality for a finer relation than unrestricted Turing equivalence.

Finer and coarser relations do not give an automatic transfer here. A coding that keeps two outputs inequivalent under polynomial-time reductions may still make them equivalent under unrestricted oracle computation. Once that happens, the reverse implication required of a Borel reduction fails. Preserving the encoding under all additional computations is the missing task; simply reusing the polynomial-time result does not complete it.

There is also a structural obstruction to familiar coding approaches. With Turing equivalence generated in its usual way by oracle-program reductions, it is not uniformly universal. Roughly, uniformity would require indices for computations between encoded outputs to be chosen solely from the indices witnessing the original equivalence, independently of the particular objects. Marks develops this distinction and shows why the choice of generating maps must be specified.

The present problem permits arbitrary Borel reductions, so that uniform obstruction is not the desired nonuniversality theorem. Whether ordinary universality must entail appropriate stronger uniformity properties is itself part of the surrounding theory. A proof that rules out one common coding pattern therefore reveals a methodological barrier without exhausting all Borel encodings.

Martin’s conjecture supplies a competing prediction. Its Borel form implies that Turing equivalence is not universal; in particular, it obstructs reducing two disjoint copies of Turing equivalence into one copy. Conversely, a universality proof would contradict that prediction. The point is a genuine conditional connection between two major structural questions, not an unconditional settlement in either direction.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision investigates an older question about writing Turing equivalence as an increasing union whose stages omit certain uniformly computable infinite sequences. A positive answer would imply nonuniform invariant functions and universality of ordinary many-one equivalence. Their consequences remain conditional on that decomposition question, and concern distinctions among degree relations that must not be collapsed into a proof of Turing universality.

Settling the card would tell us whether mutual computability provides a universal language for countable Borel classification, or has a structural limitation absent from some nearby degree notions. Either outcome would matter beyond computability: it would constrain the ways orbit equivalence relations, invariants and definable encodings can interact. The answer criterion is a precise existence theorem for reductions, with no algorithmic-efficiency requirement hidden inside the word “Borel.”
