cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The exact symmetric-maximizer conjecture is false, but the universal O(d√n) influence bound remains open in the checked primary literature, including the April 2026 revisions on rational degree and Boolean surface area.

context_blocks.text: The quantitative target is the maximum influence as a function of dimension and degree. The following history concerns the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture and the separately disproved exact-extremizer claim.

A polynomial threshold function first evaluates a low-degree real polynomial and then keeps only its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority votes and weighted voting rules. Quadratic threshold functions can also include pairwise interactions between inputs. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic simplicity forces the function to change its output relatively rarely along the edges of the Boolean cube.

Total influence counts those changes in an averaged way. If D is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then I(f)=2D/2^n. The maximum possible influence of an arbitrary Boolean function is n, achieved by parity. A degree-d bound of C d√n would sharply restrict the boundary when d is small compared with √n; once d≥√n, the elementary bound I(f)≤n already suffices with C=1.

Majority shows why a square root is unavoidable. For odd n, flipping a coordinate changes majority exactly when the other n−1 coordinates split evenly, giving I(MAJ_n)=n·binom(n−1,(n−1)/2)/2^(n−1), asymptotic to √(2n/π). Thus even degree one permits influence growing with dimension. The target is not a constant influence bound for every fixed-degree function.

There is a natural higher-degree candidate: place d parallel threshold hyperplanes between consecutive central Hamming layers, then take the sign of the product of their linear equations. The sign alternates at those layers. When the layers lie near the center, their boundaries together have order d√n. Gotsman and Linial proposed the much stronger assertion that this symmetric construction maximizes influence exactly.

Chapman disproved that exact assertion for most parameter pairs, including quadratic examples in every odd dimension at least five. The paper carefully separates its exact conjecture from Conjecture 1.2, the asymptotic statement discussed here, and leaves the latter open. Its SODA publication was in 2018; the arXiv copy was uploaded in 2021. Neither date turns the disproved exact formulation into a refutation of the remaining asymptotic question.

Products of d linear threshold signs satisfy the desired order by a simple union bound: if the product changes across an edge, at least one factor changes. Summing the factors’ influence bounds gives O(d√n). But a general degree-d polynomial need not factor into d linear forms, and its sign need not admit such a representation. This identifies one tempting argument and the missing structural fact it would need.

Kane proved the near-optimal dimensional estimate I(f)≤√n·(log n)^{O(d log d)}·2^{O(d² log d)} for d≥2. For each fixed d, this is √n times a polylogarithmic factor, establishing the correct exponent of n. The extra logarithms can still grow without bound, while the dependence on d is much larger than linear. Removing these losses is exactly what the displayed conjecture demands.

The proof program uses random restrictions and comparisons between Boolean and Gaussian polynomial behavior. Anti-concentration helps ensure that a small perturbation rarely carries the polynomial through zero. Such transfers must deal with coordinates of high influence and with the discrete cube’s concentrated mass. The continuous analogue is informative, but it is not a direct proof for arbitrary Boolean threshold polynomials.

For quadratic functions there are useful structural subcases. Kim, Maldonado and Wellens analyze the graph whose edges indicate nonzero quadratic coefficients and establish asymptotic estimates under restrictions such as low fractional chromatic number or few edges. This connects the influence question to the interaction graph, while leaving general dense quadratic interactions outside those special guarantees.

A 2026 paper by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a polylogarithmic bound, for fixed degree, on Boolean surface area BSA(f)=E[√s_f(x)]. The April 27 revision strengthens its original subpolynomial estimate. This is significant new control of boundary geometry, but BSA is a different moment from I(f)=E[s_f(x)]. A bound on the expectation of the square root does not directly bound the expectation by its square.

Indeed, pointwise s_f(x)≤√n·√s_f(x) yields only I(f)≤√n·BSA(f). Substituting the new polylogarithmic surface-area bound still leaves a factor depending on log n, with degree-dependent constants. This calculation explains why that recent theorem is compatible with the influence conjecture remaining open, without diminishing its improvement for the different boundary measure.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision on rational degree also restates the influence conjecture and proposes a weaker version using nondeterministic degree. Their theorem resolves a separate polynomial relation between rational and ordinary degree, rather than this threshold-degree inequality. These connections help explain the conjecture’s importance for the relationships among Boolean complexity measures, in addition to its learning and circuit applications.

cards.formal: For every integer n≥2 and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on [n] to {0,1} that is invariant under every permutation of [n] and monotone under adding edges, is D(f)=n(n−1)/2, where D(f) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
cards.why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.

cards.definitions: Write [n]={1,…,n} and U_n={{i,j}:1≤i<j≤n}; a graph is an arbitrary edge set E⊆U_n, with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means E⊆F implies f(E)≤f(F). Invariance means f(π(E))=f(E) for every permutation π of [n], where π(E)={{π(i),π(j)}:{i,j}∈E}. A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in U_n and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output f(E) for every E⊆U_n. The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and D(f) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives D(f)≤|U_n|.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove D(f)=|U_n| for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most |U_n|−1. A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair {1,2} is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning n=p^k for a prime p and an integer k≥1. Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.

The exact claim is known for prime-power vertex counts, while results about quantum queries, infinite graphs and broader topological symmetry must be distinguished from the full finite deterministic question.

cards.title: Polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For a total Boolean function $F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}$, let $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)$ be public-coin randomized communication complexity and $Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F)$ quantum communication complexity with unlimited shared entanglement. Is there a universal polynomial $p$ such that $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)\le p(Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F))$ for every total $F$?
cards.why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

progress.text: For $F=f\circ\mathrm{AND}_2$, the source proves $D^{cc}(F)=O((Q^{cc,*}(F))^7\log^2 n)$. The polylogarithmic factor and the restriction to AND-composed functions prevent this from settling the general question.

cards.review_note: The statement and listed results were individually checked against the cited sources. New proofs were not independently verified. The assessment of importance is editorial.

context_blocks.text: Partial functions can exhibit exponential quantum savings. Requiring correctness on every input pair may fundamentally restrict that advantage.

Alice receives x and Bob receives y. They need to compute a function of both inputs while exchanging as little information as possible. The classical protocol may use randomness, and the quantum protocol may begin with shared entanglement. The cost being compared is the communication, not the complexity of their local computation.

Totality means every pair of legal individual inputs must receive a correct answer, including pairs that a promise problem would exclude. A universal polynomial simulation would limit quantum communication savings across all such functions. A bound for a special composition, or one with an additional dependence on the input length, does not automatically supply that universal relation.

cards.answer_criterion: Establish one polynomial bound valid for every finite total Boolean communication problem, or prove that no universal polynomial bound holds. Promise problems and restricted subclasses do not suffice.
cards.definitions: X and Y are arbitrary finite sets. Cost is the worst-case total number of communicated bits or qubits, and error at most 1/3 is required on every input pair. Public random bits and prior entanglement, respectively, are not charged as communication.

importance.reason: A general classical-versus-quantum comparison across all total communication problems, with a sharp distinction from promise-problem separations.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real ε∈(0,1), does there exist an integer k≥3 such that no deterministic algorithm decides k-SAT on n variables and input length L in time $O(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}L^c)$ for any fixed constant c? Here k is fixed independently of n and L. This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH).
cards.definitions: A k-SAT input is an explicitly encoded conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most k literals xᵢ or ¬xᵢ. Variables are relabeled consecutively and n counts the distinct variables actually present; L counts the full binary formula encoding, including literal indices and delimiters. The decision is exact satisfiability, with no promise about clause density, the number of satisfying assignments, or how the formula was generated. Empty clauses make the input unsatisfiable, and the empty conjunction is satisfiable. Running time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine time. For a fixed k, the algorithm, polynomial exponent, and hidden constant may depend on k and ε, but not on the individual formula. Define sₖ=inf{α≥0 : k-SAT has an O(2^{αn}Lᶜ)-time deterministic algorithm for some constant c}. SETH equivalently asserts limₖ→∞sₖ=1; monotonicity follows because k-SAT is a restriction of (k+1)-SAT. Polynomial factors are retained explicitly so reading the input is allowed even when clauses are repeated. No advice, oracle, random bits, or quantum computation is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

importance.reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi study the optimal exponential rates for k-SAT and their growth with clause width, using critical clauses and sparsification.
SETH-based reductions extend to numerous problems in polynomial time. Vassilevska Williams surveys the reductions, hypotheses, and resulting equivalence and hardness questions.
The parameterized-algorithms textbook gives explicit deterministic definitions of ETH and SETH and separately discusses their randomized analogues.

Jiang and Cai report randomized O*(1.307031578ⁿ) time for general 3-SAT and O*(1.306969598ⁿ) for Unique-3-SAT by refining the analysis of PPSZ. These are preprint bounds for fixed width, not a constant saving valid for every k.

cards.status_note: The cited primary sources state SETH as an open hypothesis. Research through 10 September 2026 found no deterministic all-width constant-saving refutation or unrestricted proof. Bounds for a fixed width, random instances, restricted solvers, or unique satisfiability are not recorded as resolutions.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive search tries all 2ⁿ assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially 2ⁿ time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A 2^{0.9n}-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds 2^{(1−1/k)n} would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond P≠NP, which by itself allows intermediate running times such as 2^{√n}.

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Recent work continues to sharpen small-width algorithms. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports a slightly improved randomized PPSZ bound for general 3-SAT, distinguished from its better bound under a unique-solution promise. sentences: The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis concerns exact satisfiability of Boolean formulas with bounded clause width.
It asserts that no fixed positive saving over exhaustive search's exponent works for every fixed width.
Faster algorithms for small widths remain compatible with the hypothesis because their savings may vanish as width grows.
The statement underlies precise conditional running-time barriers for many polynomial-time problems.
The saved review fixes deterministic algorithms and emphasizes that neither a randomized improvement for 3-SAT nor ordinary P≠NP settles these stronger all-width quantifiers.

cards.context:
Exhaustive search tries all 2ⁿ assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially 2ⁿ time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A 2^{0.9n}-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds 2^{(1−1/k)n} would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond P≠NP, which by itself allows intermediate running times such as 2^{√n}.

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Recent work continues to sharpen small-width algorithms. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports a slightly improved randomized PPSZ bound for general 3-SAT, distinguished from its better bound under a unique-solution promise. Both the fixed width and use of randomness keep this improvement outside the deterministic, all-width saving required to refute the present statement.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every n-vertex directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, outputs all exact shortest-path distances in $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ worst-case time with probability at least 2/3? Use a comparison-addition real RAM: adding, subtracting, and comparing stored real values costs O(1), and standard arithmetic and bit operations on O(log n)-bit index words cost O(1). Unreachable distances must be reported as infinity. Arbitrary real-number encodings or unit-cost floor operations are unavailable.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: I include this because exact distances are a basic graph primitive, and this particular exponent question organizes many conditional lower bounds. A resolution would identify either a common algorithmic improvement across equivalent problems or a precise limitation of what those reductions can accomplish.
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its adjacency matrix, with a special symbol for absent edges. Output contains one distance for every ordered pair, including zero self-distances. Negative-cycle detection outside the promise is not required. Space and preprocessing are included in the algorithm’s ordinary running time. The probability guarantee applies to the complete output matrix on each fixed input. This is a classical sequential model; quantum and parallel work/depth bounds are separate targets.

progress.text: Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish truly subcubic equivalences between APSP and several path, matrix, and weighted-triangle tasks.
Williams gives a randomized real-RAM algorithm with time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$, demonstrating a substantial subpolynomial saving while leaving a fixed exponent improvement unresolved.

Akmal and Fischer solve the node-weighted zero-triangle problem in matrix-multiplication time; their introduction explicitly distinguishes it from the edge-weighted variant governed by the APSP hypothesis.

context_blocks.text: Single-source shortest paths produce one row of a distance matrix. All-pairs shortest paths ask for every row, including the effects of intermediate vertices shared by many shortest routes. Running a source algorithm repeatedly is useful, but does not explain how much computation those rows can share.

For example, a path from u to v can be much cheaper than their direct edge even when it visits many intermediate vertices. Restricting attention to one-hop or two-hop routes changes the problem. Negative edges are allowed here, but negative cycles are excluded so that every reachable distance has a finite optimum.

Matrix formulations expose the shared work: combining two path segments uses a minimum over sums, rather than the ordinary sum of products of ring multiplication. Fast algorithms for ordinary matrix multiplication therefore do not automatically give the required bound for arbitrary weighted distances. Subcubic equivalences connect the problem to several other path and matrix tasks.

The distinction between subcubic and truly subcubic is quantitative. Dividing cubic time by a very large subpolynomial factor still leaves an exponent tending to three. The target asks for a fixed positive exponent saving. The 2026 progress on node-weighted triangles does not settle the edge-weighted problem underlying this hypothesis.

cards.title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is it true that for every ε∈(0,1) there is a fixed integer c≥1 for which no uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm decides bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors on two lists of n vectors in {0,1}^d, with d=⌈c log₂ n⌉, in worst-case time O(n^{2−ε}) and with error probability at most 1/3 on every input?
cards.definitions: Here n≥2 and the two input lists A and B each have length n; repeated vectors are allowed. The answer is YES exactly when some a∈A and b∈B satisfy Σ_{j=1}^d a_j b_j=0 as an integer sum, equivalently their supports are disjoint. This is not an inner product over the field with two elements. Inputs are explicitly supplied as packed binary vectors. Computation uses a uniform classical RAM with words of Θ(log(n+d)) bits, ordinary constant-time word arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, comparisons, memory access and generation of a random word. Each program uses a fixed word-length constant; arbitrary-precision unit-cost operations, nonuniform advice and free preprocessing tables are excluded. Reading, preprocessing and all subsequent computation count in the time bound. For fixed ε and c, hidden time constants and the program may depend on these parameters, but not on n. There is no promise on vector weights, overlap or input distribution. Randomness is internal to the algorithm; correctness must hold for every pair of lists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated lower-bound proposition, or refute it by exhibiting one fixed ε>0 such that for every fixed integer c≥1 an algorithm A_c meets the n^{2−ε} time and error bounds. This quantifier order matters: the algorithms and constants may depend on c, but the exponent saving ε must work for every c. Giving a different positive saving ε_c that tends to zero with c, shaving logarithmic factors from quadratic time, or proving lower bounds only for restricted circuit models does not settle the proposition.
cards.why: A basic disjointness problem anchors a large part of fine-grained complexity. Settling its uniform exponent barrier would reshape conditional lower bounds for strings, geometry and data structures.

importance.reason: One of the principal hypotheses organizing polynomial-time lower bounds across multiple algorithmic areas, with an elementary explicit task and precise dimension dependence.

cards.status_note: The July 2026 primary literature explicitly states the unrestricted OV conjecture as open while proving restricted-model variants. Low-dimensional and average-case improvements do not negate its quantifier order. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Each vector can be viewed as a subset of a universe of d coordinates. The task is to find a disjoint pair across two collections. Although checking one pair is easy, there are n² possible pairs. For logarithmic dimension, packed coordinates make a single check take only a constant number of machine operations when c is fixed. The hypothesis asks whether there is an unavoidable exponent arbitrarily close to two as that fixed dimension constant grows.

The dependence on c is the main subtlety. There are already truly subquadratic algorithms for each fixed c, with a saving that can deteriorate as c increases. The polynomial-method algorithm of Abboud, Williams and Yu runs in time n^{2−1/O(log c)} in the relevant large-c regime. This is consistent with the hypothesis: selecting a sufficiently large c can make that known saving smaller than any proposed universal ε. The source is SODA 2015; some later bibliographies mistakenly label it 2014.

Very small dimension permits another strategy: enumerate possible coordinate patterns and aggregate the input instead of considering all pairs separately. The 2026 low-dimensional algorithms achieve a randomized bound of Õ(1.25^d n), with a further reported O(1.16^d n) bound obtained through computer-aided parameter evaluation. These improve the useful range of the pattern-based approach, but their exponential dependence on d becomes a power of n when d=c log₂ n.

For example, substituting c=2 into 1.25^d n gives, up to constant and logarithmic factors, n^{1+2 log₂ 1.25}, whose exponent is about 1.644. Increasing c increases this exponent. Thus an impressive subquadratic algorithm for one small logarithmic dimension does not supply one exponent saving for all logarithmic dimensions. This numerical example illustrates the quantifiers; it is not an additional algorithmic theorem.

The hypothesis is useful because disjointness can encode compatibility between partial solutions. In the standard split-and-list SAT reduction, each half-assignment produces a vector marking clauses it fails to satisfy. Two half-assignments extend to a satisfying assignment exactly when their vectors are disjoint. Sparsification controls the number of clause coordinates. For the randomized version stated here, the corresponding randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a conditional justification; a deterministic-only SAT assumption must not silently be used to exclude randomized solvers.

Reductions then transfer the conjectured time barrier to problems that look quite different. Rohatgi’s Earth Mover Distance paper, the inherited source for this record, develops one such geometric application. The significance of OV is its role as a common intermediate problem: a new algorithm can overturn a collection of conditional barriers, while an unconditional proof would establish a strong lower bound for a concrete problem already known to be in polynomial time.

Restricted-model lower bounds provide evidence without establishing that unrestricted conclusion. Choudhury and coauthors prove near-quadratic monotone-circuit lower bounds for the negation of OV at logarithmic dimension. This negated predicate says every cross-pair intersects and is monotone in the input bits. Their July 2026 paper also strengthens formula and branching-program bounds. General RAM programs can use operations and intermediate representations beyond those restrictions, so these theorems do not prove the hypothesis as formulated here.

Distributional improvements are a separate frontier. Alman, Andoni and Zhang obtain faster algorithms when vector coordinates are independently sampled with a specified Bernoulli bias, including difficult parameter ranges. Such a result can explain why random instances are easier while leaving adversarial instances unresolved. The card deliberately requires correctness and the stated running time on every input rather than only on a random input distribution.

cards.title: Algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis
cards.formal: Let τ(k) be the infimum of worst-case time exponents of randomized algorithms deciding k-Clique, as specified below, and let ω be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over C. Is liminf_{k→∞} τ(k)/k=ω/3?
cards.definitions: For each fixed integer k≥3, the input is the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph on n≥k labeled vertices; accept iff some k distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. A uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input, and its time bound must hold for every random tape. Set τ(k)=inf{a≥0: such an algorithm runs in O(n^a) time as n→∞}. The program and hidden constants may depend on k, but not on n. Words have C_k⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for some fixed constant C_k; arithmetic modulo the word range, division with remainder, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and indirect memory access cost one step, and a fresh random word costs one step. Initial memory apart from the input is zero; preprocessing counts; there is no nonuniform advice, giant-word operation or free oracle. For ω, let M(N) be the smallest number of binary +,−,× gates in a circuit over C that computes all entries of the product of two formal N×N matrices. Arbitrary complex constants and sharing are allowed, but division and branching are not. Define ω=inf{a:M(N)=O(N^a)}. This fixes the characteristic-zero arithmetic convention, separately from the bit-based graph algorithm. The question concerns the coefficient of k in the exponent; it does not fix k proportional to n or treat the latest published numerical upper bound on ω as its exact value.
cards.answer_criterion: The matrix-multiplication reduction gives the upper asymptotic benchmark ω/3. An affirmative answer therefore proves that, for every δ>0, there is K such that τ(k)≥(ω/3−δ)k for every fixed k≥K. A negative answer proves a strict saving in this coefficient, for example via algorithms with τ(k)≤(ω/3−δ)k for arbitrarily large k and one δ>0. Saving logarithmic time factors or an additive o(k) in the exponent does not refute this leading-exponent formulation.
cards.why: A basic quantitative hardness hypothesis for graph patterns and many reductions in fine-grained complexity, precisely testing whether the matrix-multiplication exponent gives the optimal leading coefficient.

references.authors: Emilien Dupont; Marvin Eisenberger; Borislav Kozlovskii; Abbas Mehrabian; Francisco J. R. Ruiz; Abigail See; Renfei Zhou; Josh Alman; Virginia Vassilevska Williams; Matej Balog

cards.status_note: Open in the stated unrestricted randomized leading-exponent form, following the inherited hypothesis and later primary sources checked through 11 September 2026. The liminf and machine conventions make the asymptotic claim explicit. Logarithmic speedups, matrix-exponent improvements and conditional lower bounds do not settle it.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, clique detection is already a polynomial-time problem: one can inspect every k-element subset. The issue is which polynomial is necessary. An exponent near k and an exponent near 0.79k differ dramatically as the fixed pattern size increases. This is why ordinary NP-hardness, which allows k to vary with the input, leaves the main quantitative question unanswered.

The arithmetic reduction groups the vertices of a candidate clique into three parts. For k=3r, create auxiliary vertices representing r-cliques and join two auxiliary vertices when their represented sets are disjoint and their union is a clique. A triangle in this auxiliary graph represents a 3r-clique in the original graph. There are O(n^r) auxiliary vertices, so matrix-based triangle detection gives the familiar leading time exponent ωk/3.

When k is not divisible by three, the groups have unequal sizes. Rectangular matrix multiplication gives more refined bounds for individual k; padding to the next multiple of three already changes the exponent by only a constant. Because this card asks for the leading coefficient as k grows, those residue-class effects do not alter the target. They would matter in a card asking for the exact exponent at a particular small k.

The inherited source states the hypothesis in the n^{ωk/3−o(k)} form and allows both randomized and deterministic algorithms. The explicit liminf formulation records the order of limits: first study n→∞ for each fixed k, then ask about large k. The model definitions make time, error and machine operations explicit. This avoids relying on an informal distinction between which graph algorithms count as combinatorial.

The word algebraic names the benchmark supplied by matrix multiplication. It does not restrict the algorithms against which the conjecture asserts hardness. A refuting algorithm could use arithmetic, combinatorial structure, randomization, or a combination. Likewise, ω is an unknown mathematical constant defined by the best possible arithmetic circuits, rather than a decimal frozen at the date of an old reduction.

A better upper bound on ω immediately improves the matrix-based clique algorithm without disproving this hypothesis. Conversely, an algorithm whose exponent beats an old numerical estimate may still be slower than the conjectured benchmark using the true ω. The distinction becomes especially relevant after small improvements in matrix multiplication: Dupont and coauthors’ August 2026 note reports ω<2.371177, improving the preceding 2.371339 bound. Its numerical certificate has not been replayed for this catalogue.

Abboud–Fischer–Shechter improve the algorithms usually called combinatorial by logarithmic factors. At fixed k, their displayed detection bound is n^k(log n)^{−(k+1)}(log log n)^{k+3}. Such progress is useful, but the logarithmic factor changes an exponent by o(1) as n grows and does not establish a new leading coefficient below ω/3. Their separate hypergraph and listing results have different outputs or incidence structures.

The hypothesis supports lower bounds for tasks that do not look like clique detection. Das–Lincoln–Lynch–Munro use clique reductions for dynamic Boolean-formula evaluation and counting. A faster data structure with the relevant preprocessing and update guarantees could therefore force faster clique algorithms. This explains the inclusion of an apparently indirect dynamic-data-structure paper as the inherited reference: its computational-hypothesis section states this exact leading-exponent assumption.

Recent work strengthens the network of reductions rather than proving the hypothesis. Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß show that suitable regularity restrictions on partite graphs and hypergraphs preserve the relevant detection exponent, with parameter-dependent factors. This helps transfer conditional hardness to Boolean constraint optimization. Their result cannot be read as an unconditional lower bound for all word-RAM algorithms.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redzic’s January 2026 coverage and partial-domination results similarly give algorithms and matching bounds conditional on clique and hyperclique hypotheses. The 3-uniform hyperclique assumption concerns triples as constraints and has a different exhaustive-search benchmark; it is not the graph hypothesis in this card. Keeping the two separate prevents a strong conditional statement for one problem from being mistaken for a resolution of the other.

The fundamental question is whether all-pairs algebra can capture the optimal leading cost of enforcing every pairwise adjacency in a growing fixed pattern. An affirmative answer would justify a widely used quantitative barrier. A negative answer would identify a way to exploit the clique decision task beyond the matrix-multiplication benchmark, potentially changing many currently conditional optimality claims.

For each fixed k, clique detection is already a polynomial-time problem: one can inspect every k-element subset. The issue is which polynomial is necessary. An exponent near k and an exponent near 0.79k differ dramatically as the fixed pattern size increases. This is why ordinary NP-hardness, which allows k to vary with the input, leaves the main quantitative question unanswered.

The arithmetic reduction groups the vertices of a candidate clique into three parts. For k=3r, create auxiliary vertices representing r-cliques and join two auxiliary vertices when their represented sets are disjoint and their union is a clique. A triangle in this auxiliary graph represents a 3r-clique in the original graph. There are O(n^r) auxiliary vertices, so matrix-based triangle detection gives the familiar leading time exponent ωk/3.

When k is not divisible by three, the groups have unequal sizes. Rectangular matrix multiplication gives more refined bounds for individual k; padding to the next multiple of three already changes the exponent by only a constant. Because this card asks for the leading coefficient as k grows, those residue-class effects do not alter the target. They would matter in a card asking for the exact exponent at a particular small k.

The inherited source states the hypothesis in the n^{ωk/3−o(k)} form and allows both randomized and deterministic algorithms. The explicit liminf formulation records the order of limits: first study n→∞ for each fixed k, then ask about large k. The model definitions make time, error and machine operations explicit. This avoids relying on an informal distinction between which graph algorithms count as combinatorial.

The word algebraic names the benchmark supplied by matrix multiplication. It does not restrict the algorithms against which the conjecture asserts hardness. A refuting algorithm could use arithmetic, combinatorial structure, randomization, or a combination. Likewise, ω is an unknown mathematical constant defined by the best possible arithmetic circuits, rather than a decimal frozen at the date of an old reduction.

A better upper bound on ω immediately improves the matrix-based clique algorithm without disproving this hypothesis. Conversely, an algorithm whose exponent beats an old numerical estimate may still be slower than the conjectured benchmark using the true ω. The distinction becomes especially relevant after small improvements in matrix multiplication: Dupont and coauthors’ August 2026 note reports ω<2.371177, improving the preceding 2.371339 bound. Its numerical certificate has not been replayed for this catalogue.

Abboud–Fischer–Shechter improve the algorithms usually called combinatorial by logarithmic factors. At fixed k, their displayed detection bound is n^k(log n)^{−(k+1)}(log log n)^{k+3}. Such progress is useful, but the logarithmic factor changes an exponent by o(1) as n grows and does not establish a new leading coefficient below ω/3. Their separate hypergraph and listing results have different outputs or incidence structures.

The hypothesis supports lower bounds for tasks that do not look like clique detection. Das–Lincoln–Lynch–Munro use clique reductions for dynamic Boolean-formula evaluation and counting. A faster data structure with the relevant preprocessing and update guarantees could therefore force faster clique algorithms. This explains the inclusion of an apparently indirect dynamic-data-structure paper as the inherited reference: its computational-hypothesis section states this exact leading-exponent assumption.

Recent work strengthens the network of reductions rather than proving the hypothesis. Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß show that suitable regularity restrictions on partite graphs and hypergraphs preserve the relevant detection exponent, with parameter-dependent factors. This helps transfer conditional hardness to Boolean constraint optimization. Their result cannot be read as an unconditional lower bound for all word-RAM algorithms.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redzic’s January 2026 coverage and partial-domination results similarly give algorithms and matching bounds conditional on clique and hyperclique hypotheses. The 3-uniform hyperclique assumption concerns triples as constraints and has a different exhaustive-search benchmark; it is not the graph hypothesis in this card. Keeping the two separate prevents a strong conditional statement for one problem from being mistaken for a resolution of the other.

The fundamental question is whether all-pairs algebra can capture the optimal leading cost of enforcing every pairwise adjacency in a growing fixed pattern. An affirmative answer would justify a widely used quantitative barrier. A negative answer would identify a way to exploit the clique decision task beyond the matrix-multiplication benchmark, potentially changing many currently conditional optimality claims.

cards.title: Hyperclique Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of integers h≥3 and k>h and every constant ε>0, is there no classical randomized O(n^(k−ε))-time algorithm deciding whether an n-vertex h-uniform hypergraph contains a k-clique, with error at most 1/3 on each input?
cards.definitions: The input hypergraph H=([n],E) is simple and unweighted, with E a subset of the h-element subsets of [n]. It is given by a dense table containing one Boolean membership entry for each h-element subset, in a fixed computable order. A k-clique is a set S⊆[n] of k distinct vertices such that every h-element subset of S belongs to E. The task outputs one yes/no bit and requires neither counting nor listing cliques. Fix the classical word-RAM with O(log(n+2))-bit words, constant-time arithmetic, bitwise operations and random access on words; the word-length constant and runtime constants may depend on the fixed h,k,ε. Random bits are allowed, but quantum operations, nonuniform advice and precomputed input-dependent tables are not. All processing of the input and construction of auxiliary data are charged. The excluded algorithm must run in O(n^(k−ε)) steps on every execution and answer correctly with probability at least 2/3 for every input. The quantifiers concern each fixed pair h,k separately, not only a limit as k tends to infinity. The card explicitly uses the bounded-error randomized version of the classical hypothesis.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated exclusion of all such algorithms, or refute it by giving one fixed pair h≥3,k>h, one fixed ε>0 and a correct algorithm with the required worst-case time and per-input success probability. A conditional confirmation must name the stronger assumption. A logarithmic-factor speedup, an algorithm for a sparse or promised subclass, or a circuit-size bound in a restricted algebraic model is not a resolution of the full claim.
cards.why: A principal fine-grained hypothesis for higher-order combinatorial interactions, supporting conditional lower bounds beyond ordinary graph clique and shortest paths.

importance.reason: A foundational unresolved exponent question with consequences for Max-CSP optimization, algebraic identity checking and sparse graph/hypergraph algorithms.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No classical bounded-error algorithm with a fixed positive exponent saving for a covered h,k pair was found in the checked sources. The 2025 regularization and 2026 reductions use or relate the hypothesis; they do not prove it unconditionally.

context_blocks.text: A graph records pairwise compatibility. An h-uniform hypergraph records compatibility of h vertices at a time. For h=3 and k=4, a positive instance contains four vertices whose four triples are all hyperedges. Knowing that every pair participates in some hyperedge is insufficient: the compatible triples must be exactly those supported on the same four vertices. This is the smallest parameter pair covered by the hypothesis.

For fixed h and k, exhaustive search takes O(n^k) time: enumerate all k-element vertex sets and check the fixed number of required hyperedges. The problem is therefore already polynomial-time for every individual card parameter pair. The conjecture asks whether that polynomial exponent can be reduced by a positive constant. Ordinary NP-hardness when k varies would not establish such a fine-grained statement.

The graph case h=2 behaves differently. Matrix multiplication gives algorithms beating the direct k-tuple search for many clique sizes. Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams explain why the corresponding higher-order operation for hypergraphs is a separate obstacle and formulate hyperclique-based lower bounds. This distinction is the reason the present hypothesis starts at h=3, instead of extending a graph-clique bound mechanically to all uniformities.

Their connections to satisfiability concern optimization problems such as Max-h-SAT: find an assignment satisfying as many clauses as possible. A suitable hyperclique speedup would also improve exhaustive-search algorithms for these problems. This must be distinguished from deciding whether every clause of a fixed-width SAT instance is simultaneously satisfiable, for which exponential improvements are already known. The Max-h-SAT hypothesis is an additional assumption, not an unconditional proof.

The fixed exponent saving is essential. A running time n^k divided by any fixed power of log n would not contradict the card. Nor would an improvement available only when k grows with n. Conversely, an O(n^3.99) algorithm for 4-cliques in 3-uniform hypergraphs would be enough to refute the universally quantified statement, without resolving every other h,k pair.

The dense encoding prevents an implicit promise about sparsity. Its size is Θ(n^h) table entries, which is below the exhaustive-search exponent because k>h. Any refuting exponent saving can be reduced to a smaller positive saving so that reading this table still fits the claimed time. Thus routine conversions between explicit dense representations do not provide an artificial refutation.

The inherited paper works with k-partite hypergraphs. This is essentially equivalent for fixed k: make k copies of the vertex set and place an edge between copies in distinct parts whenever their distinct original vertices form an input hyperedge. Selecting one vertex from each part then tests the original clique condition. The vertex blowup depends only on k, preserving a positive polynomial exponent saving.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß go further in their ICALP 2025 regularization theorem. They transfer algorithms between general k-partite hypergraphs and a strongly regular class in which each transversal (h−1)-tuple has the same number of extensions to a hyperedge. Controlling these overlapping incidences without introducing false cliques is the substantive part of the construction. The result shows that this regularity promise does not remove the conjectured difficulty.

The same work uses regularization to classify optimization of Boolean CSPs over assignments with exactly k nonzero variables. The degree of the constraint functions separates easy linear cases, graph-clique cases and higher-degree cases with exhaustive-search lower bounds under a 3-uniform hyperclique assumption. This supplies a reason to study the hypothesis beyond the clique problem itself.

Dudek and coauthors’ STOC 2026 work gives another connection: a refutation for the 3-uniform, 4-clique case would yield a truly subquadratic algorithm for detecting four-term arithmetic progressions in an integer universe. Their paper studies verification of algebraic identities and uses this relationship for conditional lower bounds. It supplies a new consequence or conditional foundation, rather than establishing the hyperclique lower bound outright.

Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß’s ICALP 2026 paper studies when sparsity helps for small independent sets in hypergraphs and Boolean CSPs. Its algorithms have separate vertex-count and edge-count terms, with matching bounds under clique hypotheses. Improved running time on sparse forbidden-hyperedge inputs is compatible with the dense worst-case statement here; taking a complement can turn a sparse instance into a dense one.

The hypothesis expresses a possible computational divide between pairwise and higher-order interactions. Its value is that precise reductions turn it into concrete runtime barriers for other tasks. The proper status is a conjectural foundation for those barriers. Repeated applications and increasingly robust reductions strengthen its usefulness, while a proof or one genuine exponent-saving algorithm would be a qualitatively different result.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic exact edit distance
cards.formal: For the binary alphabet Σ={0,1}, do there exist a constant ε∈(0,1], a constant C>0 and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm A such that, for every n≥1 and every pair x,y∈Σ^n, A outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance ED(x,y) in at most C(n+1)^(2−ε) operations?
cards.why: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.

progress.text: Backurs–Indyk prove a SETH-based obstruction to truly subquadratic exact edit distance; the 2017 full revision also records subsequent developments.

cards.definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. ED(x,y) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has w=ceil(4 log₂(n+2)) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo 2^w, integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving ε cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case O(n^(2−ε)) bound for some fixed ε>0 in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: Edits can shift an entire alignment
context_blocks.text: The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

context_blocks.title: What the quadratic barrier means
context_blocks.text: The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes O(n²) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as n²/log n is smaller than n² but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for n^(2−ε) with one ε>0 that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

context_blocks.title: A precise conditional obstacle
context_blocks.text: The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every δ>0 there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in O(2^((1−δ)N) poly(L)) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Why recent approximation is different
context_blocks.text: Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized (1+η)-approximation for each fixed η>0, with running time n²/2^(log^Ω(1) n). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on η cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

context_blocks.title: Scope of the benchmark
context_blocks.text: The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.

cards.title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
cards.why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
cards.definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.

progress.text: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak formulate OMv and derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems, including reachability and variants of connectivity.
Larsen and Williams give randomized online multiplication in total time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$. This improves the algorithmic baseline without refuting the conjecture.

Hu and Polak show fine-grained equivalences between Boolean OMv and several online non-Boolean products, including min-max, dominance, and equality. These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.

context_blocks.text: If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.

cards.title: ETH versus Gap-ETH
cards.formal: Does the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis imply the deterministic Gap Exponential Time Hypothesis for sparse 3-CNF formulas?
cards.definitions: For a 3-CNF formula F with n variables, let val(F) be the maximum fraction of clauses simultaneously satisfiable. The ETH convention here asserts that there is c>0 for which no deterministic algorithm decides satisfiability of all 3-CNF formulas in time O(2^(cn) poly(L)), where L is the binary encoding length. Gap-ETH asserts that there exist constants B≥1, δ∈(0,1) and c′>0 for which no deterministic algorithm in time O(2^(c′n) poly(L)) distinguishes val(F)=1 from val(F)≤1−δ on formulas with at most Bn clauses. Its inputs are promised to satisfy one of those two alternatives. Empty formulas are satisfiable. All constants are fixed independently of F; randomized versions are not asserted.

context_blocks.text: ETH concerns exact satisfiability, while Gap-ETH postulates comparable exponential hardness even when unsatisfiable inputs violate a fixed fraction of clauses. Their equivalence would unify many exact and approximation lower-bound assumptions.

Bitansky and coauthors distinguish ETH from the stronger gap hypothesis while obtaining exponential hardness for particular approximation tasks. Hardness for those tasks does not imply a gap-preserving sparse 3-CNF statement. This implication is distinct from asking whether either hypothesis is true.

cards.title: Linear-size Circuit-SAT below exhaustive search
cards.formal: For every fixed integer c≥1, do ε_c>0 and a deterministic algorithm exist deciding satisfiability of every Boolean circuit with n inputs and at most cn gates in time O((2−ε_c)^n·n^{O(1)})?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. Circuits are finite acyclic directed graphs with input bits and one output, binary AND and OR gates and unary NOT gates; gates have unrestricted fan-out. Size counts non-input gates. The input lists every gate and predecessor index. Satisfiability means that some assignment to the n input bits makes the output one. The algorithm and the constants in its polynomial factor may depend on c, but ε_c must be positive and independent of n. There is no depth restriction.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive assignment search works in roughly 2^n time regardless of circuit structure. Linear-size circuits restrict the amount of computation performed on each assignment while retaining arbitrary depth and sharing.

Obtaining a fixed exponential saving for every fixed size density would establish a general algorithmic benefit of that restriction. The question is part of the algorithms-to-lower-bounds landscape described by Wigderson. Algorithms for bounded-depth or threshold-restricted circuits do not settle the stated general model.

cards.definitions: The input to MC(ψ) is an explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph G with a partition V=X₁⊔⋯⊔X_k⊔Y. Every part is listed, may be empty, and edges join different parts. The fixed sentence is ψ=(∃x₁∈X₁)⋯(∃x_k∈X_k)(∀y∈Y)φ(x₁,…,x_k,y), where φ is a Boolean formula whose atoms are E(u,v) for distinct variable names u,v among x₁,…,x_k,y. E is symmetric adjacency; equality, extra relations and quantifier alternation inside φ are absent. A universal quantifier over empty Y is true and an existential quantifier over an empty X_i is false. The formula and k are fixed outside the input. Let m=1+|V|+|E|, counting vertex/part-membership records as well as edges; this makes the sparse input-size convention explicit and includes the cost of listed isolated vertices. To define hardness, set every atom E(x_i,x_j) to false in φ and replace E(x_i,y)=E(y,x_i) by z_i. The resulting Boolean function f:{0,1}ᵏ→{0,1} determines H(ψ). For a nonconstant f, H(f) is the largest t∈{0,…,k} such that, for every I⊆[k] of size k−t, there exists an assignment a∈{0,1}ᴵ for which the restricted function on the remaining t variables has exactly one falsifying assignment. Put H(f)=0 if f is constant, and H(ψ)=H(f). Thus the free coordinates must work for every choice of their set, but the pinned values may depend on that set. An h-uniform hypergraph has a finite vertex set and a set of unordered h-element hyperedges. An r-clique is a set of r distinct vertices every h-element subset of which is a hyperedge. The premise uses N, the number of hypergraph vertices, and an explicit adjacency table or list with polynomial-time conversion for fixed h. Use deterministic random-access machines with O(log L)-bit words for input-size parameter L, unit-cost arithmetic, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and indirect access on a constant number of words; arbitrarily long integers do not have unit cost. In the premise L may be taken as N for fixed h,r; in the conclusion it is m. Input encodings use vertex numbers and explicit edges and parts. Machines are uniform in input size, with no length-dependent advice; a different fixed machine and multiplicative constant may be used for each fixed r or ψ. The same δ works for all r in the premise. ε_ψ and its constants may depend on h,ψ and the assumed speedup, but not on m. This common-δ reading retains the premise’s displayed exponent saving rather than replacing it by a single fast clique size.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication for every fixed h≥3, with a positive exponent saving for every fixed graph sentence of that hardness, or rigorously refute the implication. The known reverse-direction hardness result, an example of one easy sentence, or a speedup for only some sentences does not establish the universal conclusion. A theorem for optimizing the number of satisfying universal-variable choices under a different hardness parameter does not by itself answer the decision target.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal: Does P=BPP? Precisely, for every language L for which a randomized Turing machine R runs in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, and satisfies $\Pr[R(x)=1_L(x)]\ge2/3$ for every binary string x, does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine deciding L correctly on every x? The polynomial time bound of the deterministic machine may depend on R.
cards.definitions: Input length is n=|x|. A polynomial-time bound means C(n+1)^k steps for fixed constants C,k, independent of x and of the random bits. R uses independent unbiased random bits, at most one fresh bit per computation step, and outputs a single bit. Its error may be on either yes or no inputs, but is bounded separately on each input. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decision languages and BPP of languages meeting the randomized guarantee above. These are total decision problems, with no excluded promise inputs. No advice, oracle, quantum operations, or input distribution is allowed. The requested deterministic simulation may use a different algorithm; it need not reproduce R's random choices, preserve its precise exponent, or be generated by an effective compiler from R.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This determines whether random bits add power to efficient total decision computation. It is a central organizing question for pseudorandom generators, explicit constructions, and the connection between circuit lower bounds and algorithm design.

importance.reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.

progress.text: Adleman establishes BPP⊆P/poly. Suitable fixed random advice exists for each input length, but uniform polynomial-time computation of that advice is not supplied.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove P=BPP if there is a Boolean function computable in time 2^(O(n)) that requires circuits of size 2^(c n), for some c>0 and all sufficiently large n. The circuit-hardness assumption remains essential to this theorem.

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh, and Zuckerman improve conditional pseudorandomness parameters for algorithms satisfying an insensitivity property of their correct and incorrect random tapes. This concerns finer generators for a specified algorithm class, not unconditional removal of randomness from all BPP computations.

Version 9 of a preprint by Tianrong Lin claims the opposite conclusion P≠BPP, along with stronger separations. This review has not verified that construction or located independent primary validation. The claimed separation is recorded without treating it as established.

context_blocks.text: Randomized decision algorithms may use randomness to avoid exceptional choices or to test a property through a small sample. Their guarantee is pointwise: even the worst input must receive the correct answer with high probability. Repeating an algorithm reduces its error but leaves it randomized. The question asks whether every such use of randomness can ultimately be replaced by a deterministic polynomial computation.

Exhaustive majority evaluation over all random tapes has a time cost exponential in their length. That is correct, but takes exponential time when the tape has polynomial length. A suitable pseudorandom generator would reduce the search to a polynomial-size set of tapes, constructed efficiently. The hard part is ensuring that this small set fools the computation on every input.

A nonuniform version of this idea already works: after error amplification, an averaging argument supplies one polynomial-length advice string that works for every input of a given length. This proves BPP is contained in P/poly. The string can depend on the input length without an efficient procedure to find it, which is exactly why that inclusion does not answer the uniform question.

Strong circuit hardness provides a conditional route to full derandomization. Impagliazzo and Wigderson show that an exponentially circuit-hard function computable in exponential time suffices. The condition is substantially more specific than merely P≠NP. Current work also studies the amount of slowdown and the structure of the randomized algorithm, producing finer conditional results without an unconditional equality proof.

This card concerns computing one correct decision bit. Sampling a distribution, producing one of many valid witnesses, or deciding only inputs with a promise leads to related but different formulations. Keeping these tasks separate prevents a derandomization theorem for one setting from being silently substituted for another.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants C,D and a uniform family of generators G_{n,w,p}:{0,1}^s→{0,1}^n, for all integers n,w≥2 and p≥1, with s≤C(log_2 n+log_2 w+p), such that |Pr_{u uniform in {0,1}^s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]−Pr_{z uniform in {0,1}^n}[B(z)=1]|≤2^(−p) for every length-n, width-at-most-w ordered read-once branching program B? Require a single deterministic algorithm that, given n,w,p,u and an output position i, computes G_{n,w,p}(u)_i using at most D(log_2 n+log_2 w+p) work bits and time (nw·2^p)^D.
cards.definitions: An ordered read-once branching program has layers V_0,…,V_n, each containing at most w states, a designated initial state in V_0, and an accepting subset of V_n. For each layer i−1, each state has one outgoing edge labeled 0 and one labeled 1 to V_i. On input z, the program follows the edge labeled z_i at step i and accepts exactly when the final state is accepting. Different edges may merge; neither regularity nor permutation transitions are required. The order is the fixed order z_1,…,z_n. Programs may be arbitrary nonuniform objects, but the generator cannot inspect their descriptions. The parameters and seed are read-only inputs to the generator algorithm, and the output bit is written separately; all work space, counters and intermediate storage are counted. Seed length is a computable function of the parameters within the stated resources. Uniform seeds induce an ordinary probability distribution, without signed or externally assigned weights. Set ε=2^(−p); this dyadic formulation gives the usual O(log(nw/ε)) target for arbitrary positive error by rounding down to a smaller dyadic tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: An optimal generator would remove randomness from logarithmic-space computation and identify how little entropy suffices to fool every small-memory streaming computation. The question joins explicit constructions, space complexity and the gap between real distributions and useful signed approximations.

importance.reason: A central constructive route to L=BPL, with optimal nonconstructive seed length known and a persistent gap for uniform space-efficient generators despite advances in restricted and weighted models.

Hoza obtains weighted generators with additive log(1/ε) dependence and notes deterministic simulation in space O(S^(3/2)/sqrt(log S)); this is not a logarithmic-seed ordinary PRG.
Cheng and Hoza show that suitable logspace hitting sets imply L=BPL and analyze stronger reductions toward ordinary PRGs; the journal version appears on 20 September 2022.
Cheng and Wu publish improved weighted PRGs via weighted pseudorandom reductions.

Cohen, Doron and Goldgraber give an improved INW analysis for permutation programs. Arbitrary ordered programs remain outside its structural promise.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. ECCC TR26-064 revision 3 explicitly retains the optimal general PRG target and the log-squared barrier. Its new generator is weighted; the July TR26-123 result is restricted to permutation programs. This card requires one ordinary, program-independent distribution family and optimal seed length as well as optimal work space.

context_blocks.text: The program processes a long stream while remembering only its current state. Width w corresponds to about log_2 w bits of memory; length n is the number of random bits it can inspect. A pseudorandom generator replaces that long random stream with the deterministic expansion of a much shorter genuinely random seed. The requirement is simultaneous: the same generated distribution must fool every permitted program, even though their transition tables may be entirely different.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to the seed-length target. After padding to w states, the number of programs is at most w·2^w·w^(2nw). Choose a list of independent uniform n-bit strings and use a uniformly chosen list position as the seed. A concentration bound and union bound show that a list of O(ε^(−2)(nw log w+w)) strings suffices to approximate every acceptance probability. Indexing that list takes O(log n+log w+log(1/ε)) bits. The argument does not tell us how to generate its entries in the tiny workspace required here.

The computational payoff is direct. Fix an input to a bounded-error logarithmic-space randomized machine and view its evolution on random bits as a polynomial-length, polynomial-width branching program. A logarithmic seed permits enumeration of all seeds, regeneration of individual pseudorandom bits and counting accepting runs within logarithmic space. With constant error small enough to preserve the acceptance gap, this would prove L=BPL. The card asks for a uniform generator, which is a particular strong route to that complexity-class equality.

Nisan’s construction gives seed length O(log n·log(nw/ε)). For polynomial width and constant error this is O(log²n), so reaching the target would remove an entire logarithmic factor. The difficulty is generating a universally useful sample space in little space, rather than merely showing that some sample space exists. Even considerable improvements for simpler transition structures need not survive arbitrary merging of states.

Weighted pseudorandom generators relax the distribution requirement. They approximate acceptance by a weighted sum of program evaluations, with weights that may be negative. Hoza’s RANDOM 2021 construction attains seed length O(log²n+log(1/ε)) for width-n, length-n programs, improving the dependence on small error. Such weighted estimates can support deterministic simulation, but negative mass cannot be sampled as an ordinary probability distribution over the generated strings.

Cheng and Wu’s SODA 2026 work improves weighted generators across width and error regimes. Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction and the dependence on the input alphabet. It still constructs a weighted object. Its discussion credits Cheng and Hoza’s earlier reduction showing that sufficiently good ordinary-generator dependence on alphabet size and error would break the log-squared barrier. That implication does not turn the newly constructed weighted generator into an ordinary one.

The role of hitting sets provides another useful distinction. A hitting set ensures that an accepting string is included when the accepting fraction is sufficiently large; it does not directly approximate that fraction. Cheng and Hoza prove that sufficiently strong logspace hitting sets nevertheless imply two-sided logspace derandomization through a more involved reduction. Their results explain why a derandomization theorem need not arrive packaged as the universal probability distribution requested here.

Cohen, Doron and Goldgraber’s July 2026 paper gives an ordinary generator for permutation programs with seed O((log w+log(1/ε))log n), by a new analysis of the INW generator. In this subclass each symbol acts bijectively on the states between layers. The result has optimal logarithmic dependence on length when width and error are fixed, but the permutation promise excludes the arbitrary state merging allowed in this card.
