cards.definitions: A finite loopless multigraph consists of finite sets V and E and a map ∂ assigning to each edge e∈E a two-element subset ∂e⊆V. Distinct edges may have the same endpoints and are still distinct objects. Two distinct edges are adjacent if their endpoint sets intersect. A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to any two adjacent edges. For an integer k≥0 let [k]={1,…,k}, with [0] empty; χ′(G), the chromatic index, is the least k admitting a proper map E→[k]. A list assignment is a function e↦L(e) where each L(e) is a finite subset of the positive integers, used only as distinct color names. Lists may differ, overlap arbitrarily and have an arbitrarily large finite union. The list chromatic index χ′_ℓ(G) is the least k≥0 such that every assignment with |L(e)|≥k admits a proper edge coloring from those lists. Both indices are zero when E is empty and are at most |E| otherwise; hence these minima exist. Requiring lists of exactly k colors is equivalent, since larger lists can be restricted to k colors. Any finite collection of abstract colors can be renamed by distinct positive integers without changing feasibility. Isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and arbitrary parallel-edge multiplicities are allowed. The maximum degree Δ counts edges incident with a vertex, including parallel copies separately, and is zero for an empty vertex set. The target concerns existence, with no required algorithm, running time or bound on color-name bit lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal list-colorability assertion, or refute it. A finite counterexample can specify a multigraph with ordinary chromatic index k and lists of k colors on every edge, together with a proof that no proper coloring from those lists exists. Equality only up to a vanishing relative error, a result for a restricted graph class, or successful coloring of selected list assignments does not resolve the universal claim.

context_blocks.text: Think of an edge as a job requiring its two endpoint resources at the same time, and a color as a time slot. Jobs sharing a resource must use different slots. Ordinary edge coloring offers every job the same collection of slots. List edge coloring lets each job have its own availability restrictions and asks for a compatible schedule.

For two edges sharing one endpoint, ordinary edge coloring needs two colors. Lists {red,blue} and {blue,green} still each have size two, although their union has size three; choosing red for the first edge and blue for the second is valid. The conjecture compares the number of choices available to each edge, not the total number of distinct color names used across all lists.

Identical lists are permitted, so χ′_ℓ(G) is always at least χ′(G). The question is whether arbitrary overlaps among different lists can ever create an additional obstruction. An ordinary coloring alone does not answer this, since a color assigned to an edge may be absent from that edge’s list.

The reference quantity is the chromatic index, rather than just maximum degree. A triangle has maximum degree two but needs three edge colors. If each of its three edges is doubled, the multigraph has maximum degree four, yet all six edges are pairwise adjacent and need six colors. Allowing parallel edges therefore matters to the target.

Galvin proves the conjecture for every bipartite multigraph, whose vertices split into two parts with all edges crossing between them. In that class both indices equal maximum degree. The theorem permits arbitrary lists and parallel edges; restricting lists to one shared palette would miss its main content.

Kahn’s theorem settles the general multigraph question asymptotically. In particular, for every ε>0, all multigraphs of sufficiently large maximum degree satisfy χ′_ℓ(G)≤(1+ε)χ′(G). This leaves the exact question intact: a relative gap tending to zero can still allow an extra color.

The August 2026 preprint of Jafari claims exact equality for the complete graphs K_(p−1) and K_(2p) whenever p is an odd prime; K_r denotes the simple graph with every pair of its r vertices adjacent. The respective claimed values are p−2 and 2p−1. These are specific families, and the paper itself leaves the general even-order complete-graph case open. Its proofs have not been independently verified in this review.

It holds for bipartite multigraphs, and a general asymptotic theorem leaves only a vanishing relative gap.

cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let OPT(X) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree T₀ and every X, $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)$? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.

context_blocks.text: A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost Θ(n), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by O((OPT(X)+n) log log n · log² log log n). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

cards.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
cards.definitions: Keys are [n]={1,…,n}, n≥1, ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence X∈[n]*, cost_splay(X;T₀) is the sum of these costs starting from T₀. A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. OPT(X) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.

progress.text: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree.
Tango trees give an online BST with an $O(\log\log n)$ competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying.
The preprint proves $O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)$ total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.

cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer k≥2 and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions F_n on an n-word database and a k⌈log₂ n⌉-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity t*F(n), with word size ⌈4log₂ n⌉ bits and n⌈log₂ n⌉² memory cells, satisfies t*F(n)/log₂ n→∞ as n→∞?
cards.definitions: For each integer n≥2 put w=⌈4log₂ n⌉ and s=n⌈log₂ n⌉². A database is D∈({0,1}^w)^n, a query is q∈{0,1}^{k⌈log₂ n⌉}, and F_n(D,q)∈{0,1}. Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes F_n(D,q), given (1^n,D,q), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map E_n into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output F_n(D,q) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through E_n(D). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define t*F(n) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real B>0 there is N such that t*F(n)>B log₂ n for every n≥N. Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite B>0 such that t*F(n)≤B log₂ n for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an O(log n) bound for all sufficiently large n.
cards.why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.

cards.status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least n² possible queries, while the stored representation has only O(n log³ n) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is O(log n), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to Θ(log n)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is Ω(min{log(m/s), n/log s}) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most O(log n). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further Ω((log n/log log n)²) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further Ω((log n/log log n)²) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time static dictionaries
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer d≥1 there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs A_d,Q_d and a constant C_d≥1 such that, for every n≥2, every word length ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉≤w≤d⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, A_d builds a static dictionary in at most C_d n operations and C_d n words of total space, and Q_d answers every membership-and-value query in at most C_d operations.
cards.why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. cards.definitions: The universe is U_w={0,…,2ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs (x_i,v_i)∈U_w×U_w with pairwise distinct x_i and arbitrary v_i; the input order is unrestricted. On query q∈U_w the output is (1,v_i) if q=x_i and (0,0) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved w=Θ(log n) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.

context_blocks.text: A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records (12,5), (47,9) and (103,2) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of n² possible keys occupies n² cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic O(n log n) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general O(m(log log m)²) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to Θ(log m). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.

cards.title: Deque conjecture
cards.formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing $n$ ordered keys, and perform $m$ legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always $O(n+m)$, with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
cards.why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
cards.definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.

progress.text: Pettie proves $O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))$ total cost, where $\alpha^*$ counts how many iterations of the inverse-Ackermann function reduce the argument to a constant.
Levy and Tarjan connect the deque conjecture to a subsequence property sufficient for dynamic optimality. This provides a structural route to a proof, not the required linear bound itself.
The new analysis of splay competitiveness still describes the deque guarantee as nearly constant per operation. Its general search bound does not supply constant amortized deque cost.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 splay result. The conjecture asks for linear total cost under insertions and deletions at either end.

context_blocks.text: A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.

cards.title: Optimal decrease-key in pure pairing heaps
cards.formal: For the pure pairing heap defined below, is there a universal constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations starting with empty heaps costs at most $C[M+D(1+\log N)+K(1+\log\log(N+2))]$? Here D counts delete-min operations, K counts decrease-key operations, and $N\ge2$ is the maximum of 2 and the total number of live items across all heaps at any moment. The allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld, decrease-key, and delete-min. Count comparisons and pointer-machine steps; keys are distinct opaque values in a totally ordered set, compared at unit cost. Handles to the affected items and heaps are supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this total-cost bound for the specified algorithm, or construct legal operation sequences for which its ratio to the displayed budget is unbounded. Changing the heap algorithm or obtaining the bound only for a different self-adjusting heap does not establish a positive answer.
cards.definitions: A heap is one rooted heap-ordered tree whose child lists are ordered from left to right. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger root the leftmost child of the smaller; cut removes a node with its subtree from its parent in constant time. Store O(1) pointers per item, with doubly linked child lists. Make-heap creates an empty tree; find-min returns its root; insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the roots and destroys the old heap handles. Decrease-key changes the supplied key and, if its node is not the root, cuts that node and links its subtree with the remaining root. Delete-min removes the root and scans its children left to right, linking disjoint adjacent pairs; an unpaired last child remains. Winners keep their positions in the root list. Identify its minimum-key remaining root v, remove v from that list, and prepend all other remaining roots in their existing order to the child list of v. The resulting tree is the heap. Use the ordinary constant-time list splice, rather than doing an additional recursive linking pass. All loops, comparisons, pointer accesses, and writes are charged. Logarithms have base two.
cards.why: This is a precise opportunity to separate an analysis gap from a structural limitation of a simple data structure. Priority-queue costs propagate into graph algorithms, and the problem tests how little explicit balancing information is sufficient for optimal amortized behavior.

progress.text: Iacono and Özkan prove an Omega(log log n) decrease-key lower bound in the pure heap model under logarithmic extract-min bounds. The model name refers to a class, not specifically the 2026 data structure.

Sinnamon and Tarjan establish optimal logarithmic-logarithmic decrease-key bounds for slim and smooth heaps, with a further log log log n factor for multipass pairing heaps. The journal version appeared in 2025.

Tarjan and Xu introduce pure pairing heaps and bound decrease-key by O(log log n times log log log n), retaining O(log n) delete-min and O(1) insert/meld amortized bounds. Section 10 explicitly leaves the remaining factor open.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 primary preprint. The displayed bound uses the maximum live population, while the source also develops finer bounds that omit items never deleted. This card fixes one algorithm and one total-cost target.

context_blocks.text: A decrease-key call changes an item that is already present. It may execute only a few pointer operations immediately, yet the structural disorder it creates can make later deletions more expensive. Its amortized cost measures this delayed effect. Counting only the instructions inside the decrease-key procedure would miss the question entirely.

The pure pairing heap simplifies deletion by pairing neighboring roots once and then attaching all survivors beneath the smallest survivor. It does not maintain a rank or balance invariant. The desired estimate asks whether this sparse restructuring still prevents expensive configurations from being recreated too often.

The operation budgets must be considered together. A sorting sequence already forces substantial comparison work when many minima are deleted, so the logarithmic delete-min allowance is intentional. The unresolved issue is how much additional work to attribute to key decreases while keeping insertions and melds cheap. Using the maximum live population N makes that accounting explicit for a whole finite sequence.

Other self-adjusting heaps already attain the desired decrease-key order. This makes the remaining gap an informative algorithm-analysis problem: is the simpler rule equally efficient, or does its exact restructuring lose something asymptotically? A bound for slim or smooth heaps does not answer this question about pure pairing heaps.

cards.title: Randomized complexity of ordered integer partitioning
cards.formal: The source asks whether randomization can further accelerate ordered partitioning of word-sized integer keys and thereby improve approximate heap operations. It studies n keys, word length w and target bucket size Δ, with a deterministic upper bound O(n·max{1,log₂(log₂n/log₂(wΔ))}) in the nontrivial range, interpreting the expression as linear time whenever the ratio inside the outer logarithm is at most a constant. The intended new randomized bound and parameter regime are not stated. Since Δ=1 is exact sorting and the source already cites randomized sorting speedups, the bare assertion “randomization improves this deterministic bound for some parameters” is not certified as a new open question.
cards.why: Ordered partitioning captures how much order information is needed for approximate priority queues, potentially allowing improvements that are invisible when one insists on fully sorting every item. Its meaningful randomized tradeoff must go beyond already-known sorting speedups.

cards.definitions: In the source’s word-RAM model, a memory cell holds w bits and a key fits in one word, with w≥⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ so item positions can be addressed. Standard arithmetic, comparisons, bitwise operations, shifts and indexed memory access on a constant number of words cost one operation; arbitrary-precision integers do not have unit cost. An ordered partition of a collection A of n keyed items is a list of disjoint buckets A₁,…,A_b whose union is A and such that every key in A_i is at most every key in A_j for i<j. Items need not be ordered inside a bucket, and repeated keys cause no difficulty in this non-strict ordering convention. The balanced Δ-partition version has b=Θ(n/Δ) and buckets of size Θ(Δ), allowing boundary rounding, for 1≤Δ≤n. At Δ=1 this means sorting, up to constant-size buckets that can be sorted in linear additional time. A second version takes sorted splitters s₁<⋯<s_b and assigns each item to its interval between consecutive splitters; interval buckets may be highly unbalanced. The source relates these static problems for its asymptotic equivalences but they are not identical output requirements. An approximate Δ-min query returns one of the Δ smallest stored items. An approximate heap supports insertion, deletion and Δ-min; its parameter is an additive rank tolerance, not multiplicative key error. A general approximate select query instead receives a target rank and returns an item whose rank differs by less than Δ. The source establishes different bounds for those operations. A soft heap uses yet another convention, allowing a bounded fraction of keys to be increased, and its equivalence is to exact sorting at a smaller size. The source’s data structures use linear space; reported amortized bounds can be made worst-case by cited methods. For a new randomized target, Las Vegas correctness (always correct, expected time) and Monte Carlo correctness (bounded error with a time bound), as well as worst-case versus expected time, must be distinguished. None is chosen for the broad concluding question.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a source-supported unresolved randomized ordered-partition target, including the exact input/output version, n,w,Δ regime, randomness/error convention, space and requested time improvement over all applicable known bounds. Then establish that improvement or matching lower bounds at the required precision. Merely quoting the existing randomized sorting algorithm, the linear square-root-bucket partition theorem, or a result for approximate select instead of approximate min does not complete the intended new tradeoff. The remaining target is not yet fully specified.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal: Does there exist a single deterministic data structure and fixed constants C,c,d>0 such that, for every n≥2, an initially empty undirected simple graph on vertex set [n] can be maintained under any online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, using at most C n^d words of memory and at most C(log₂ n)^c time for each individual operation? Initialization may take at most C n^d time and depends only on n. All connectivity answers must be exact in the word-RAM model specified below.
cards.definitions: An insertion insert(u,v) adds a previously absent unordered edge {u,v}, where u≠v; a deletion delete(u,v) removes an existing edge. A query connected(u,v) returns whether the current graph contains a path from u to v, with connected(u,u)=true. Updates are valid, arrive one at a time and must finish before the next operation is revealed. No future operations or advance description of the sequence is supplied. The data structure must work for every finite sequence, including sequences chosen in response to its previous behavior. The word RAM has word size w=⌈a log₂ n⌉ for a fixed constant a large enough to address its polynomial space. Unit-cost instructions are indirect reads/writes, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient/remainder, comparisons, Boolean bit operations and shifts; arithmetic results stored in one word are reduced modulo 2ʷ where appropriate. Arbitrary-precision computation costs its constituent word operations. All maintenance, rebuilding and query work is charged to the operation performing it. The exponent c is independent of n and of the length or contents of the operation sequence. The graph is unrestricted apart from being undirected and simple; no planarity, bounded-degree or expansion promise is given.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic unresolved guarantee for dynamic graph data structures. Connectivity is both a natural maintenance problem and a source of techniques used throughout graph algorithms; combining determinism, exactness and fast individual updates would close a longstanding gap.

importance.reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The SODA 2026 connectivity paper explicitly retains deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case updates as open. Its unconditional new bound is randomized and expected; its deterministic polylogarithmic conclusion depends on the stated static low-congestion sparsifier construction. Deterministic subpolynomial worst-case bounds and polylogarithmic amortized bounds are already known.

context_blocks.text: The difficulty is deleting an edge that belongs to a maintained spanning forest. Removing it splits one tree into two parts, but the graph might still connect those parts through an edge outside the forest. The data structure must find such a replacement quickly or correctly certify that none exists. A single deletion can expose a large cut, so simply scanning all candidate edges gives no small bound on the time of that update.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give deterministic O(log² n) amortized operation bounds for connectivity, using a hierarchy of forests and edge levels. Their result establishes that long update sequences can be processed efficiently. The accounting permits an individual deletion to spend work paid for by other operations. Guaranteeing low latency after every deletion requires more than redistributing the same amortized accounting on paper.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy obtain polylogarithmic worst-case update time with randomization and a small error probability. Their cutset sampling technique tries to isolate a remaining edge across a cut, which can then be recovered from a compact sketch. Failure to recover an edge may mean either that the cut is empty or that the random samples missed it. Eliminating this uncertainty while keeping every update fast is part of the deterministic challenge.

Chuzhoy and coauthors use deterministic balanced-cut machinery to achieve n^{o(1)} worst-case update time, removing the earlier polynomial barrier. This is a major improvement but still leaves the present target open. For example, exp(√log n) is smaller than every fixed positive power of n and larger than every fixed power of log n. Thus a subpolynomial theorem does not imply the polylogarithmic bound merely by choosing a small exponent.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 algorithm is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest and achieves polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time, even against an adaptive adversary with access to its state. It alternates vertex and edge sparsification in a hierarchy. Each graph update changes the output forest by at most two edges, so maintaining the explicit answer itself does not cause large update costs. The expectation remains a distinction from the deterministic target.

The same paper gives a concrete sufficient condition for derandomization. If a deterministic algorithm constructs a near-linear-edge subgraph together with paths routing the original edges through it in m·polylog(m) time, with congestion at most (m/n)·polylog(m), the framework yields deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity. Congestion counts how many routed paths use the busiest retained edge. Finding any spanning forest is insufficient: its tree edges may carry far too many such paths.

A companion SODA 2026 result by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Saranurak controls both the time and the number of vertices removed when pruning an expander after one edge deletion. This avoids a large burst of changes propagating through a hierarchy. It is an ingredient in the recent randomized progress; it does not by itself supply the deterministic sparsifier construction needed for the full conclusion.

Known lower bounds do not rule out the target. Pătraşcu and Demaine prove logarithmic amortized cell-probe lower bounds, including for connectivity on disjoint paths. Those results show that dynamic connectivity already has a real information-transfer cost in very simple graphs, but a logarithmic barrier is compatible with polylogarithmic upper bounds. The open issue is whether exact connectivity, deterministic computation and a bound on every operation can be achieved simultaneously.

cards.context:
The difficulty is deleting an edge that belongs to a maintained spanning forest. Removing it splits one tree into two parts, but the graph might still connect those parts through an edge outside the forest. The data structure must find such a replacement quickly or correctly certify that none exists. A single deletion can expose a large cut, so simply scanning all candidate edges gives no small bound on the time of that update.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give deterministic O(log² n) amortized operation bounds for connectivity, using a hierarchy of forests and edge levels. Their result establishes that long update sequences can be processed efficiently. The accounting permits an individual deletion to spend work paid for by other operations. Guaranteeing low latency after every deletion requires more than redistributing the same amortized accounting on paper.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy obtain polylogarithmic worst-case update time with randomization and a small error probability. Their cutset sampling technique tries to isolate a remaining edge across a cut, which can then be recovered from a compact sketch. Failure to recover an edge may mean either that the cut is empty or that the random samples missed it. Eliminating this uncertainty while keeping every update fast is part of the deterministic challenge.

Chuzhoy and coauthors use deterministic balanced-cut machinery to achieve n^{o(1)} worst-case update time, removing the earlier polynomial barrier. This is a major improvement but still leaves the present target open. For example, exp(√log n) is smaller than every fixed positive power of n and larger than every fixed power of log n. Thus a subpolynomial theorem does not imply the polylogarithmic bound merely by choosing a small exponent.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 algorithm is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest and achieves polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time, even against an adaptive adversary with access to its state. It alternates vertex and edge sparsification in a hierarchy. Each graph update changes the output forest by at most two edges, so maintaining the explicit answer itself does not cause large update costs. The expectation remains a distinction from the deterministic target.

The same paper gives a concrete sufficient condition for derandomization. If a deterministic algorithm constructs a near-linear-edge subgraph together with paths routing the original edges through it in m·polylog(m) time, with congestion at most (m/n)·polylog(m), the framework yields deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity. Congestion counts how many routed paths use the busiest retained edge. Finding any spanning forest is insufficient: its tree edges may carry far too many such paths.

cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |M|≥ν(G)/(1+ε) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
cards.definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set [n], n≥2; ν(G) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed ε and constant a≥1, require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm A_{ε,a} such that every sequence of T≤n^a updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most K[n+T(log₂(n+2))^d]. Words have B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least 1−n^{−3}, after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes O(1) time; enumerating all matching edges costs O(n) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on ε and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε, adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to ν(G) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to n^{1/2+o(1)} amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a 2−√2−η fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed η>0. The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

The dependence is roughly n^{o(1)} times the ordered-RS count for matchings of linear size, with accuracy-dependent parameters. A strong enough combinatorial upper bound would yield subpolynomial update time. This does not currently establish polylogarithmic time: n^{o(1)} can grow faster than every fixed power of log n, and the required extremal bounds are themselves unresolved. This connection is not an unconditional lower bound.

Pratt’s SOSA 2026 note relates the ordered and ordinary RS notions at the level of polynomial exponents. Dense ordered examples would imply nearly comparably dense ordinary examples. It resolves a structural question about the reduction’s graph families, but does not determine the density needed for a polylogarithmic dynamic algorithm.

Liu’s 2024 work gives a different advance for bipartite graphs: amortized update time n/2^{Ω(√log n)} times a polynomial in 1/ε. It also relates stronger update bounds to online matrix-vector problems. The dependence on accuracy is essential in those statements. In particular, the ordinary-OMv equivalence stated for approximate vertex cover should not be silently transferred to matching, and a barrier using inverse-polynomial accuracy does not settle this card’s fixed-ε question.

The adversary convention leaves useful flexibility. An oblivious sequence may be carefully chosen to be difficult, but it cannot react to random decisions or the current matching. The algorithm nevertheless receives updates one at a time; knowing that the sequence was fixed does not give access to future deletions. Similarly, amortization permits occasional expensive repairs as long as their expected total cost satisfies the bound.

The inherited Max Planck report explicitly identifies near-optimal fully dynamic matching with polylogarithmic updates as a long-term target. Its page 123 also distinguishes maintaining matching edges from estimating their number, and describes faster progress in the insertion-only setting. Allowing deletion of a vertex, which removes all its incident edges together, does not automatically supply an algorithm for arbitrary individual edge deletions.

The fundamental issue is whether a changing combinatorial optimum can be tracked almost as cheaply as the graph itself is updated. A positive result would close a major gap between coarse approximation and near-optimal explicit solutions. It would also clarify how much global matching structure must be recomputed when each input change is local.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic worst-case updates for exact dynamic minimum spanning forests
cards.formal: Can an exact minimum spanning forest of a fully dynamic n-vertex graph with polynomially bounded integer weights be maintained with polylogarithmic worst-case time per edge update, polynomial preprocessing and space, and high-probability correctness against an oblivious adversary?
cards.definitions: The graph is simple and undirected on the fixed labelled vertex set [n], n≥2, and starts empty. An update inserts one currently absent edge with integer weight in {1,…,n⁴}, or deletes one present edge. Edge weights remain fixed until deletion. A minimum spanning forest consists of one minimum-total-weight spanning tree for each connected component. Break equal-weight ties by the fixed lexicographic order (weight, smaller endpoint, larger endpoint), so the target is the unique forest selected by Kruskal’s algorithm in that order. After each update the data structure must report the edges removed from and added to the maintained forest; on a correct execution at most one edge of each kind changes. These reports specify the entire current forest starting from the empty one. Use a uniform randomized classical word RAM with Θ(log n)-bit words, standard word operations and random-word generation; all input processing and memory accesses count. For every fixed pair of integers a,b≥1, the target permits a separately tuned uniform data structure and constants K,C≥1 whose preprocessing and space are n^{O(1)}, and for which every update takes at most K(log₂(n+2))^C steps on every execution. For every valid update sequence of length at most n^a fixed before its random choices, all reported forests must be correct simultaneously with probability at least 1−n^{−b}. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on a,b, but not on n or the sequence. This is a Monte Carlo worst-case-time formulation; an always-correct deterministic solution would also suffice. The integer range n⁴ is an explicit specialization, and weights occupy O(1) words. There is no advance access to future updates.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct data structures satisfying the stated bounds for every fixed a,b, or prove the proposition false. Amortized polylogarithmic updates, merely subpolynomial worst-case updates, or maintaining an approximate minimum forest are insufficient. A lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone does not rule out the allowed randomization. A data structure that only stores the graph and postpones finding the forest to an expensive query does not meet the required per-update reporting guarantee.
cards.why: A basic dynamic optimization problem with very small changes to its answer but potentially expensive global replacement searches. It tests whether amortized efficiency can be made reliable for every update.

importance.reason: One of the main unresolved worst-case update barriers in dynamic graph algorithms, closely connecting connectivity, weighted optimization, sparsification and expander maintenance.

progress.text: Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup establish deterministic O(log⁴ n) amortized minimum-spanning-forest updates.

Nanongkai–Saranurak–Wulff-Nilsen give Las Vegas subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability.
Chuzhoy and coauthors obtain deterministic n^{o(1)} worst-case updates via deterministic expander decomposition.
Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s SODA paper gives expected polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity maintenance; its weighted extension is (1+ε)-approximate with inverse-ε overhead.

context_blocks.text: One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all n−1 tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic O(log⁴ n) amortized update bound. Amortization allows occasional expensive operations as long as their cost can be charged across a sequence. The present target limits the time of each individual update, so long rebuilds and large replacement-edge searches must be spread out while keeping the current answer ready.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains O(log⁴ n/log log n) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain Las Vegas maintenance with subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability. Their approach combines expander maintenance with a reduction to graphs having few edges beyond a forest. Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently derandomize the needed expander-decomposition component and obtain deterministic n^{o(1)} worst-case updates.

Subpolynomial is still weaker than polylogarithmic. For example, exp(√log n) grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of n but faster than every fixed power of log n. Thus a statement of n^{o(1)} update time does not automatically meet this card’s bound. The 2020 deterministic theorem resolves an earlier polynomial-exponent barrier while leaving the sharper target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a (1+ε)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to log(U)/ε for weights in [1,U]. The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

For integer weights, one could force an approximation guarantee to become exact by taking ε smaller than the reciprocal of a polynomial upper bound on the optimum cost. But the displayed 1/ε overhead would then become polynomial in n. The straightforward reduction therefore does not preserve polylogarithmic update time for exact optimization. It identifies a concrete gap between maintaining connectivity at a few approximate weight thresholds and identifying the exact cheapest replacement edge.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.

But the displayed 1/ε overhead would then become polynomial in n. The straightforward reduction therefore does not preserve polylogarithmic update time for exact optimization. It identifies a concrete gap between maintaining connectivity at a few approximate weight thresholds and identifying the exact cheapest replacement edge.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
cards.formal: Can a fully dynamic simple, unweighted, undirected n-vertex graph maintain its exact global minimum-cut value with expected polylog(n) amortized update time, worst-case polylog(n) query time and polynomial space, with high probability over every polynomial-length oblivious operation sequence?
cards.definitions: Fix vertices [n], n≥2. Start from the empty graph. A legal update inserts one absent unordered edge or deletes one present edge; there are no loops, parallel edges, weights or vertex updates. A query returns the integer λ(G)=min{ |{uv∈E:u∈S,v∉S}| : ∅≠S⊊[n] }. In particular λ(G)=0 for a disconnected graph; no distinguished terminals are supplied. Only the value is required, not a list of vertices or edges realizing the cut. Use a uniform randomized word-RAM with Θ(log(n+2))-bit words, ordinary arithmetic, bit operations and random access, and count all maintenance and query work. Precisely, ask for fixed exponents b,c and an algorithm accepting any fixed constant a≥1 as a confidence parameter. For every legal sequence with U updates and Q queries, U+Q≤n^a, fixed independently of its random bits, it uses O_a(n^b) words on every execution; expected total initialization and update work is O_a(n^b+U log^c(n+2)); each query takes O_a(log^c(n+2)) worst-case time; and all query answers are simultaneously correct with probability at least 1−n^(−3). Initial preprocessing may take O_a(n^b) time, accounting for the additive term. Each operation must finish before the next is revealed. The exponents are independent of λ(G), n and a. This fixes an expected-amortized Monte Carlo convention explicitly; it does not demand correctness against updates chosen from the random internal state.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a data structure satisfying the complete specification for unrestricted cut values, or prove that no such data structure exists in the stated model. Conditional lower bounds must state their assumptions. Algorithms for insertion-only sequences, approximate cut values, bounded connectivity or subpolynomial but superpolylogarithmic update time are partial progress. Hardness for weighted cuts or fixed-terminal s–t cuts alone is not a negative resolution.
cards.why: A central exact dynamic graph problem asking whether a global measure of edge connectivity can be updated as efficiently as basic connectivity, across the full range of cut values.

importance.reason: A fundamental data-structure question with a persistent gap between incremental, approximate and exact fully dynamic algorithms; common terminal-cut lower bounds do not settle it.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No exact fully dynamic algorithm meeting the polylogarithmic bounds at unrestricted connectivity was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 exact n^{o(1)} result has a cut-size restriction, and the unrestricted 2026 tree-packing bound remains polynomial rather than polylogarithmic.

context_blocks.text: The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes λ=0 from λ≥1; the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to n−1.

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. This simple stability is useful, but it does not tell an algorithm whether the answer actually changed. Certifying that no alternative cut is smaller is the difficult global part of an update.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention λ=0 for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

The update model is also decisive. Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup obtained deterministic polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. In that setting edges are only inserted. Deletions can invalidate the compressed structural information retained during a monotone growth process, so this theorem does not settle fully dynamic maintenance.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors obtained exact fully dynamic algorithms with roughly linear-in-n randomized worst-case update time and sublinear-in-m deterministic amortized update time. Their 2024 revision corrects a runtime in the expander-decomposition analysis. This establishes substantial reuse across updates without reaching a polylogarithmic bound.

De Vos and Christiansen improve the deterministic amortized bound to Õ(m^(11/12)); their final 2026 theorem gives the more detailed minimum of m^(11/12), m^(11/13)n^(1/13), and n^(3/2), up to logarithmic factors. Their analysis uses greedy tree packings: either a packed tree crosses a minimum cut only once, or a suitable contraction exposes a minimum cut around one vertex. Both structural outcomes help reduce the candidate cuts that must be maintained.

The inherited SODA 2026 paper of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li reaches n^{o(1)} deterministic amortized update time for exact cuts of size up to 2^{Θ((log n)^(3/4−η))}, for fixed 0<η<3/4 in the stated parameter regime. This greatly expands the previous small-cut range. It still restricts the minimum-cut value, and n^{o(1)} does not itself mean a fixed power of log n.

The same paper explains the accuracy barrier behind this restriction. Its recursive procedure controls a very small multiplicative approximation error, allowing exact recovery while the integral cut value stays below the inverse error. Making that error much smaller increases the work propagated between recursive levels. Thus simply substituting a large cut value into the theorem does not preserve its running time.

Approximation has progressed separately. El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm maintains a (1+o(1))-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. For an integer optimum λ, rounding a multiplicative estimate to an exact answer generally needs additive error below one, hence relative error on the order of 1/λ. A fixed approximation guarantee cannot supply this for arbitrary connectivity.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.

cards.title: Dynamic APSP with edge-linear updates
cards.formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants a,d >= 1 such that the following holds for all n >= 2 and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in {1,...,n^c}, under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
cards.definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for s=t, and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with Theta(log n)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
cards.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

importance.reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.

progress.text: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs.

Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise.
Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-O(n^(5/2)) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee.

Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.

cards.status_note: The edge-sensitive target is open in the 2021 source. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate an exact algorithm with the stated sparse update and query bounds. This is a deterministic bounded-integer-weight specialization; approximate and worst-case vertex-update results are recorded with their different guarantees.

context_blocks.text: Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the n^(5/2) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.

cards.definitions: The domain D is a fixed finite set throughout a run; updates do not create or delete vertices. An element y is covered when at least one red predecessor x has an arc x→y. A covered vertex is counted once, regardless of how many red predecessors it has, and it need not itself be red. E is a binary relation, so loops are allowed; R is unary. The four update types are ins_E(u,v), del_E(u,v), ins_R(u), and del_R(u). Insertions of present tuples and deletions of absent tuples leave the input relation unchanged and are also allowed. A program chooses finitely many auxiliary relation symbols S, each of a fixed finite arity, including a distinguished zero-ary answer bit Ans. For each S and update type δ it supplies a first-order formula φ_{S,δ}(p̄;z̄), where p̄ are the changed tuple’s parameters and z̄ has the arity of S. The formula may use equality, the current input and auxiliary relations, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual domain elements. It has no parity/counting quantifier, quantification over sets, function symbol or built-in numeric relation. After update δ(ā), each auxiliary relation becomes {b̄:(I,A)⊨φ_{S,δ}(ā;b̄)}, evaluated on the old input I and old auxiliary state A. All auxiliary updates occur simultaneously, alongside the specified input change. Empty initialization makes Ans false, correctly answering the empty covered set. The program’s formulas and arities are independent of |D| and of the update history. The number and arities of auxiliary relations are unrestricted finite constants chosen by the program; thus it may use polynomially many auxiliary bits, with its own fixed polynomial exponent. DynFO measures expressibility of these updates, rather than sequential constant-time execution of a formula on a Turing machine.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer is a finite collection of first-order update formulas and a proof of correctness from empty initialization for every finite domain and every finite update sequence. A negative answer must show that every such program, allowing arbitrary fixed auxiliary arities, fails on some domain and sequence. A lower bound only for quantifier-free formulas or a fixed arity, a program requiring unrestricted initial advice, or an algorithm for a bounded-degree variant does not settle the stated DynFO question.
