cards.status_note: The Nisan–Ronen proof, now published in JACM in February 2026, resolves only deterministic truthful mechanisms. Its randomized discussion records 2−1/m and (m+5)/2 bounds. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no matching unrestricted randomized bounds; results for task-independent mechanisms, fractional objectives, Bayesian types or no-payment models do not resolve this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A machine has a reason to exaggerate how long jobs take: receiving fewer jobs reduces its work. Payments are intended to counteract that incentive while keeping the overall schedule short. The private information is a whole vector, since a machine may be fast on one job and slow on another. A single speed parameter would describe a different and substantially more structured scheduling model.

The optimization objective creates the difficulty. Minimizing total processing cost can be implemented truthfully by a VCG mechanism, which assigns each job to a cheapest machine. But total cost and makespan differ. The largest load is at most the total cost, while the total cost of an optimal makespan schedule is at most m times its makespan. Thus this familiar truthful rule gives an m-approximation. Without incentive constraints and with unlimited computation, one could simply choose an optimal assignment.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that the factor m is unavoidable for deterministic truthful mechanisms, resolving the Nisan–Ronen conjecture. Their result appeared as a 2023 preprint and in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It is an unconditional incentive restriction, independent of computational hardness. The paper’s related-work discussion expressly separates the unresolved randomized setting from this deterministic conclusion.

There are two different ways to randomize truthfully. A universally truthful mechanism draws a deterministic truthful mechanism before seeing the reports. Truthfulness in expectation only asks that honest reporting maximize expected utility; individual random outcomes need not implement truthful rules on their own. Universal truthfulness implies the latter condition, but the definition in this card permits the larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira nevertheless prove a lower bound of 2−1/m even for that larger class.

Randomization already helps when there are two machines. Lu and Yu’s STACS 2008 mechanism is universally truthful and beats the deterministic factor two. Their later WINE 2008 paper gives a truthful-in-expectation mechanism with ratio (m+5)/2 for general m, using a fractional allocation and a suitable rounding procedure. The improvement is substantial in its leading constant, but the guarantee still grows linearly with the number of machines.

The WINE paper also proves a lower bound (m+1)/2 for its task-independent class. A mechanism in the full question may use all reported jobs together and correlate their assignments. Consequently, a lower bound that treats each job separately does not close the gap between the general constant lower bound and linear upper bound. Whether such global dependence can change the asymptotic answer is part of what makes this question interesting.

Expected makespan must be distinguished from the largest expected machine load. Consider m identical machines and m unit jobs. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly random machine gives expected load one on every machine, yet the makespan is always m. Assigning one job per machine has makespan one. Thus the same marginal load target can conceal a factor-m difference in the objective. A truthful fractional solution, or an argument that controls only marginal probabilities, needs a valid rounding analysis before it yields a guarantee for this card.

Fine numerical results for small cases illuminate mechanisms without settling the asymptotic problem. Kuryatnikova and Vera obtain almost matching bounds near 1.505996 for two machines and two jobs within a class of randomized monotone scale-free algorithms. Their paper does not identify the optimal ratio over every truthful-in-expectation mechanism, every job count and a growing number of machines. Both the input restriction and mechanism restriction matter when interpreting the result.

The final question is whether allowing random outcomes fundamentally reduces the price of truthful multidimensional cost reporting. A constant answer would permit useful load balancing despite unrestricted private processing times. A growing lower bound would show that even risk-neutral incentives and unrestricted payments cannot recover the efficiency available to a scheduler who knows the true costs. Matching bounds would quantify that loss as a function of system size.

cards.title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Do absolute constants C,d>0 and a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol exist that, for every n and every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations, use at most Cn^d queries to produce a complete exactly envy-free allocation, allowing disconnected pieces?
cards.definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Agent i has an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure μ_i: values are nonnegative, countably additive, μ_i([0,1])=1 and μ_i({x})=0 for every point x. No density formula, bounded-density promise or random valuation model is supplied. The protocol learns valuations only through exact queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μ_i([x,y]); Cut(i,x,α), with 0≤α≤μ_i([x,1]), returns a point y≥x for which μ_i([x,y])=α. Endpoints used by the protocol are 0, 1 and previously returned cut marks; interval values can be combined by additivity. If several cut points satisfy a query, the protocol must remain correct for any valid response. Count each evaluation or cut query as one; finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-complexity bound. Output a partition (A₁,…,A_n) of the entire cake into finite unions of intervals with endpoints among the known marks. Assign cut endpoints arbitrarily, since every agent values them at zero. Require μ_i(A_i)≥μ_i(A_j) for every ordered pair i,j. There is no unallocated residue, approximation error, randomization, or connected-piece requirement. The bound Cn^d is uniform over all valuation profiles and valid query responses.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic protocol with the stated worst-case polynomial query bound, or prove that every such protocol has superpolynomial worst-case query complexity as n grows. A lower bound on the number of queries used by one known protocol is not a general impossibility result. A finite bound depending arbitrarily on n, an average-case polynomial bound, or a polynomial protocol permitting positive envy or discarded cake leaves this question open.
cards.why: A central information-complexity question in fair division: how many exact preference queries are necessary to allocate an entire divisible resource without envy?

importance.reason: The main worst-case complexity gap for exact envy-free cake cutting; recent single-exponential and average-case results sharpen the boundary without settling polynomial query complexity.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Polynomial worst-case query complexity remains open. The latest checked general upper bound is the n^{O(1)}2^n protocol reported in the Ye–Bai preprint of 4 September 2026; Chèze’s polynomial result is over random valuation profiles.

context_blocks.text: Envy-freeness asks each person to compare the allocated pieces using their own valuation. It does not require different people to agree on values or to receive pieces of equal geometric length. For two agents, cut-and-choose works: one divides the cake into two equally valued parts and the other selects a preferred part. Extending this idea while controlling every pairwise comparison becomes much harder as the number of agents grows.

Completeness prevents a trivial answer. If the protocol could discard everything, giving everyone an empty piece would create no envy. Allocating the full cake also makes envy-freeness imply proportionality: for each agent, the value of their own piece is at least the average value of the n allocated pieces, namely 1/n. The converse fails because receiving a fair share does not prevent preferring someone else’s larger-valued share.

Disconnected pieces are essential to the computational question being asked. Exact envy-free allocations with connected pieces cannot, in general, be obtained by finite Robertson–Webb protocols once there are at least three agents. That obstruction does not apply when an agent may receive several intervals. Likewise, a bound on the number of final cut locations alone is not a bound on the number of valuation questions needed to discover suitable locations.

Nonatomicity gives the cut oracle its power: an interval can be cut to achieve any intermediate value. It does not impose a simple shape on preferences. A valuation may put almost all its mass in a very small region or have intervals of zero value. Exact comparisons must remain valid on these profiles, so a fixed numerical mesh or a small positive tolerance cannot silently substitute for an exact protocol.

Procaccia’s general lower bound is Ω(n²) Robertson–Webb queries. This already separates envy-free division from the Θ(n log n) query complexity of proportional division, but it remains compatible with a polynomial protocol. A quadratic lower bound cannot justify describing the target as impossible or necessarily exponential.

Aziz–Mackenzie’s FOCS 2016 breakthrough establishes a bound depending only on n for every profile, resolving the earlier question of whether any bounded protocol exists. Their displayed upper bound is a tower of six copies of n. This is stronger than merely terminating on each profile: earlier finite procedures could require arbitrarily many queries while n stayed fixed. The existence of a bounded protocol leaves the growth rate of that bound open.

Sokolov’s June 2023 preprint revises parts of the protocol and sharpens the analysis to n^{8n²(1+o(1))}. That is a major quantitative reduction, equal to 2^{(8+o(1))n² log₂n}, although it remains far above polynomial. The inherited 2025/2026 average-case article still quotes the older tower benchmark; the progress account here therefore also checks subsequent and separately posted algorithmic work.

A very recent advance is Ye–Bai’s September 4, 2026 preprint. Its Theorem 1.1 states a deterministic protocol using n^{O(1)}2^n queries for complete envy-free allocation with arbitrary nonnegative additive nonatomic valuations. The proof replaces a very large family of partial allocations by a polynomial-sized collection and controls how their pieces can be reassigned without conflicts. This is the latest reported general upper bound found in the review, and is identified as a preprint.

The same paper distinguishes query complexity from local computation. A helper construction uses exhaustive search after the relevant values have been elicited; Appendix C explains its deterministic choices and implementation through ordinary Robertson–Webb queries. Expensive transcript processing is allowed in the present question. Thus the reported single-exponential query bound should not be advertised as an equally fast bit-time algorithm, and it still does not give polynomially many queries.

Chèze’s inherited article studies a probability distribution on valuation profiles, following a full-independence framework. Under its uniform model, the probability of needing at least n^{12} queries tends to zero. This probability concerns the sampled preferences, rather than random bits used by a protocol facing an arbitrary fixed profile. Rare or specially chosen valuations remain relevant to the worst-case question. The article appeared online in September 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume.

Approximate envy-freeness creates another distinct regime. Bounds polynomial in n and inverse tolerance can produce small positive envy, including versions with connected pieces. Sending the tolerance to zero does not yield a finite exact protocol if the query count diverges. Exactness, completeness, access through queries and unrestricted disconnected allocations are therefore all part of this card’s answer criterion.

The fundamental issue is the amount of preference information needed for an exact global fairness guarantee. A polynomial protocol would show that the enormous historical bounds reflect limitations of the constructions rather than an intrinsic elicitation barrier. A superpolynomial lower bound would reveal a sharp information cost of exact envy-freeness even when computational work between queries is unrestricted.

cards.formal: Determine the infimum D* of the universal worst-case metric distortion achievable by any randomized ordinal voting rule, when the rule sees every voter’s full ranking and minimizes expected total distance to voters. The infimum ranges over all rules for all finite positive numbers of voters and candidates, with the model and zero-cost convention below.

cards.definitions: An election E consists of disjoint finite labeled sets V of n≥1 voters and C of m≥1 candidates, and a strict total order ≻_v on C for each v∈V. A consistent distance d is a pseudometric on V∪C: d(x,x)=0, d(x,y)=d(y,x)≥0, and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z) for all points, with a≻_v b implying d(v,a)≤d(v,b). Distinct named points may be colocated. Equal distances may be broken in any order in the reported ranking; the guarantee must hold for every consistent pair (E,d). The social cost SC_d(a)=Σ_v∈V d(v,a), and OPT_d=min_a∈C SC_d(a). A randomized ordinal rule f assigns each election E a lottery p=f(E), where p_a≥0 and Σ_a p_a=1. Its expected cost is Σ_a p_a SC_d(a). The lottery depends only on n,m and the full rankings, not on d or additional distance queries. It may use arbitrary real probabilities and unbounded computation. No anonymity, neutrality, incentive-compatibility or tournament-only restriction is imposed. Define Dist(f)=inf{D≥1: for every E and every consistent d, Σ_a f(E)_a SC_d(a)≤D·OPT_d}, taking inf∅=+∞. This inequality requires zero expected cost if OPT_d=0 and avoids dividing by zero. Set D*=inf_f Dist(f), over single rule families defined on all finite elections. The expectation is over the selected candidate, while elections and consistent metrics are worst-case choices. Replacing total cost by average cost divides both sides by n and gives the same distortion.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |a−D*|≤1/100. The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds ℓ≤u of width at most 1/50 qualify by taking a=(ℓ+u)/2. An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The 1/100 tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Rankings hide the size of a preference
context_blocks.text: Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

context_blocks.title: What randomization changes
context_blocks.text: If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively 3−2p and 1+2p. At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

context_blocks.title: The old value-2 conjecture is false
context_blocks.text: Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

context_blocks.title: Recent upper bounds leave a smaller gap
context_blocks.text: Frank’s August 2026 preprint gives an upper bound of 2.5. Shah’s revision of 6 September improves this to 2.1441; its first version had the weaker value 2.3282. The 8 September preprint of Cai and coauthors states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a gap of less than 0.025 above the reported general lower bound. These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

context_blocks.title: Restricted rules answer different questions
context_blocks.text: A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

context_blocks.title: Why this constant matters
context_blocks.text: D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.

cards.definitions: There are exactly three agents, indexed 1,2,3, and m≥0 goods indexed by [m]={1,…,m}. The input gives m and each value v_i,g=p_i,g/q_i,g with integers p_i,g≥0 and q_i,g>0 encoded in binary. N is the total bit length of this explicit table and its delimiters. For any bundle S⊆[m], v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g. A complete allocation is an ordered partition (A₁,A₂,A₃) of [m]; bundles may be empty. The output assigns each good one owner in {1,2,3}. It is EFX if v_i(A_i)≥v_i(A_j∖{g}) for every i,j∈{1,2,3} and every g∈A_j, including goods with v_i,g=0. The removed good is evaluated by agent i. An empty A_j gives no inequality; a singleton leaves the empty bundle of value zero. Removal is hypothetical and does not discard a good from the output. Values may have arbitrary magnitudes and denominators. The algorithm is uniform, deterministic and always correct, with ordinary bit-operation cost and no oracle, payments or divisible goods. Its running time must be polynomial in N, not in the numeric values.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives an algorithm and proves completeness, every EFX inequality, and a worst-case polynomial bit bound on all inputs. A negative answer proves that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists. Existence alone is already established for this three-agent additive model; a particular unfair allocation, pseudopolynomial runtime or a relaxed fairness guarantee does not answer the computational question.

context_blocks.title: Every possible removed good matters
context_blocks.text: Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods in another bundle at 5 and 1. Removing the good worth 5 would remove her envy, but removing the one worth 1 would leave value 5, still above 4. This pair passes the weaker “some good” test of EF1 and fails EFX. The test always uses the envious agent’s values, since the agents may disagree about an item’s worth.

context_blocks.title: Existence has already been proved
context_blocks.text: Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn establish complete EFX allocations for three additive agents. Their definition tests all goods, and their perturbation lemma handles zero values and ties. Thus this card asks how efficiently such an allocation can be found. The general existence card TCS-0011 concerns more agents and uses its explicitly stated positive-good convention.

context_blocks.title: Why pseudopolynomial time is insufficient
context_blocks.text: A value as large as 2^L needs only L+1 binary digits. An algorithm whose time grows polynomially in that value may therefore take exponentially many steps in its encoding length. The inherited question requires a bound polynomial in the complete valuation table’s bit length, including denominators. It does not require the stronger guarantee that the number of arithmetic operations be independent of value bit lengths.

context_blocks.title: Nearby guarantees do not give exact EFX
context_blocks.text: Ashuri, Gkatzelis and Sgouritsa’s 2025 result computes EF2X for three agents in polynomial time: envy disappears after removing any two goods, a weaker requirement. Their paper explicitly leaves exact EFX at the pseudopolynomial frontier. The May 2026 preprint reports improved multiplicative approximations, including 2/3-EFX for up to eight agents; this also permits remaining envy and does not settle exact EFX for three.

cards.definitions: An instance has n≥1 agents, m≥0 goods and an explicit table of values v_i,g=p_i,g/q_i,g, with integers p_i,g≥0 and q_i,g>0 in binary. Its bit length N includes n, m and the table. For S⊆[m], v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g. An allocation (A₁,…,A_n) partitions [m] into labeled bundles, possibly empty; its output lists one owner for each good. It is α-EFX if v_i(A_i)≥α·v_i(A_j∖{g}) for every pair i,j and every g∈A_j, including goods worth zero to i. All comparisons use i’s values. Empty A_j imposes no inequality; a singleton leaves value zero. Each fixed α in the set must have one finite, always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,k with runtime at most C(N+1)^k on every instance. The machine, C and k may depend on α, but not on n, m or the valuations. α is a fixed guarantee, not an input; no polynomial dependence on an accuracy parameter is required. The supremum is the least upper bound of these achievable factors; attainment at the endpoint is not assumed. The set is nonempty since α=0 is trivial, and is bounded by 1 by definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |a−α_alg|≤1/100. The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds ℓ≤u of width at most 1/50 qualify by taking a=(ℓ+u)/2. An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The 1/100 tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any additional complexity assumption must remain explicit and yields only a conditional bound.

context_blocks.title: How to read the approximation factor
context_blocks.text: Higher α means a stronger guarantee, with α=1 giving exact EFX. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods of another bundle at 5 and 1. For this pair, the restrictive removal leaves value 5, so the inequality holds exactly when α≤4/5. This illustrates one pair’s test, not a lower bound for every allocation of an instance.

context_blocks.title: The known general guarantee
context_blocks.text: Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos give a polynomial-time algorithm with factor (√5−1)/2≈0.618. Their definition covers every good, even zero-valued ones. Thus the checked bounds are (√5−1)/2≤α_alg≤1; the upper endpoint here comes from the definition, not from an impossibility theorem.

context_blocks.title: Why the number of agents matters
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint reports a 2/3-EFX algorithm for up to eight agents. This improves the guarantee on that restricted domain, while the present question requires a single algorithm for arbitrarily many agents. Its stronger-looking factors for EF2X and other k-good relaxations allow more removals and therefore do not give the same EFX guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Existence, computation and a supremum
context_blocks.text: TCS-1116 asks about universal existence without an efficiency requirement; this card additionally requires polynomial bit complexity. The 2023 survey treats the existence frontier and explains the known algorithmic guarantees. Even α_alg=1 would not by itself provide an exact EFX algorithm: different algorithms might approach 1 without any attaining it. The word supremum deliberately preserves this distinction.

cards.definitions: An instance has n≥1 agents, m≥0 indivisible chores, and finite real costs c_i,g≥0. Agent i assigns a bundle S⊆[m] the additive cost c_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}c_i,g; lower cost is better. Let Π_n([m]) be the finite set of ordered partitions of [m] into n disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. Define μ_i=min_{(P₁,…,P_n)∈Π_n([m])} max_{1≤j≤n} c_i(P_j). All bundles in this minimum are evaluated using the same agent i’s costs. A complete allocation belongs to Π_n([m]): each chore has exactly one owner, with no splitting, disposal or payments. The allocation must satisfy all agents’ inequalities simultaneously, although their benchmark partitions can differ. The inequalities also apply when μ_i=0, without dividing by zero; in that case every chore has zero cost to i. There is no computation-time requirement or fixed bound on n or m. The smallest universal factor exists: for each finite instance its feasible factors form a closed upper interval, and the known universal upper bound makes the intersection of these intervals nonempty.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |a−α*|≤1/100. The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds ℓ≤u of width at most 1/50 qualify by taking a=(ℓ+u)/2. An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The 1/100 tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The burden an agent can guarantee herself
context_blocks.text: Imagine partitioning all chores into n bundles before receiving the most costly bundle. The minimax share is the smallest worst burden that the agent can arrange. With two bundles and chore costs 4, 3 and 3, this benchmark is 6, achieved by {4} and {3,3}; the proportional cost is only 5. Indivisibility is why the two benchmarks differ.

context_blocks.title: Exact fairness can fail
context_blocks.text: Different agents can disagree about which chores are difficult, so their individually optimal partitions need not fit together. Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-chore example in which every agent’s minimax share is 43 but every complete allocation gives someone cost at least 44. Thus α*≥44/43>1.

context_blocks.title: The universal gap
context_blocks.text: Huang and Segal-Halevi prove that factor 13/11 always suffices. Together with the negative example, the checked bounds are 44/43≤α*≤13/11, approximately 1.0233 to 1.1818. The upper bound is an existence statement at the exact factor; finding such an allocation within a specified running time is an additional question.

context_blocks.title: What newer guarantees cover
context_blocks.text: The 2025 bin-packing paper gives a 15/13 multiplicative guarantee for personalized bivalued costs and improves a different, ordinal MMS benchmark in general. These do not replace the general multiplicative bound here. The September 2026 comparison-query preprint still uses 13/11 as the general frontier and studies how little preference information an algorithm needs.

context_blocks.title: Why this optimum matters
context_blocks.text: The factor measures the unavoidable loss caused by allocating whole burdens while respecting everyone’s own costs. A factor closer to 1 means that every agent can be kept closer to her personal benchmark. The easy/difficult-chores source gives exact fairness in special cost models, illustrating why those models must be distinguished from unrestricted additive costs.

cards.definitions: The goods are M=[m]. For i∈{1,2}, finite real numbers v_i,g>0 define v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g for every S⊆M. Different bundles may have equal value. Budgets b₁,b₂ are arbitrary positive real numbers. A price vector assigns each good a real price p_g≥0, with p(S)=∑_{g∈S}p_g. A competitive equilibrium consists of p and a partition (A₁,A₂) of M, allowing an empty bundle, such that p(A_i)≤b_i and v_i(A_i)≥v_i(S) for every S⊆M with p(S)≤b_i, for both agents simultaneously. All goods must be allocated once. Agents value only their goods: unspent budget has no utility and need not be exhausted. Ties among best affordable bundles are permitted. For each fixed valuation pair, its exceptional set lies in (0,∞)² and must have Lebesgue measure zero, meaning it can be covered by countably many rectangles whose total area is smaller than any prescribed ε>0. The exceptional set may depend on the valuations. The allocation and prices may depend on the valuations and budgets. This is an exact existence statement with no running-time or finite-encoding requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exceptional budget set has measure zero for every finite positive additive two-agent instance, or give one such instance and prove that its nonexistence set has positive two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Failure at a single budget pair, including equal budgets, is insufficient for a negative answer; approximate clearing or a result confined to near-equal budgets is insufficient for a positive answer.

context_blocks.title: Why equal budgets can fail
context_blocks.text: Suppose both agents value one good positively and each has budget 1. At any price at most 1 both can afford and prefer the good, but only one can receive it; at a price above 1 neither can buy it. If the budgets become 1 and 1.01, a price of 1.005 gives a competitive equilibrium: only the richer agent can afford the good. This simple example explains why an exceptional line of budget pairs may be allowed.

context_blocks.title: What almost all means
context_blocks.text: The question covers budgets with arbitrarily unequal purchasing power as well as nearly equal ones. It permits a set of failures with zero area, rather than requiring existence at every pair or merely at many sampled pairs. A positive answer would mean that a budget pair drawn from any continuous density avoids the exceptional set with probability one.

context_blocks.title: The gap beyond known cases
context_blocks.text: Babaioff, Nisan and Talgam-Cohen establish existence for two additive agents with sufficiently close unequal budgets, and generic existence for identical preferences under their stated preference conventions. Segal-Halevi’s account gives almost-all existence with at most four goods and leaves the arbitrary additive case with five or more goods open. Failure examples for more general monotone preferences do not automatically give additive counterexamples.

context_blocks.title: Prices as allocation rules
context_blocks.text: Budgets represent purchasing entitlements and prices coordinate which bundles are simultaneously affordable. The target retains exact allocation of every good and exact optimality for each agent. Adding utility for cash, allowing unsold goods or replacing each whole good by fractions produces a different market.

cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite set G of m≥0 indivisible goods and n agents. Each number vᵢg is a nonnegative real, and vᵢ(S)=∑g∈S vᵢg for S⊆G. Let Πd(G) denote all labeled partitions (P₁,…,Pd) of G into d pairwise disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. The 1-out-of-d maximin share of agent i is μᵢ(d)=maxP∈Πd(G) min1≤j≤d vᵢ(Pⱼ). The maximum is attained because the set of partitions is finite. A complete allocation A belongs to Πₙ(G): every good goes to exactly one agent, with no copies, payments, disposal or fractional goods. Define Dₙ as the set of positive integers d such that for every m and every valuation table there exists such an A with all n inequalities. Then d*(n)=min Dₙ. Increasing d weakens each benchmark. Known universal upper bounds make Dₙ nonempty, so this minimum is attained. The quantifiers are ∀n, choose d*(n), then ∀instances, ∃allocation; d may not depend on the number or values of the goods. This is an existence extremum, with no computation-time or preference-query restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |g(n)−(d*(n) : ℝ)|≤1/100 for every integer n≥1, using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions ℓ(n)≤d*(n)≤u(n) with u(n)−ℓ(n)≤1/50 also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for d*(n) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.title: Relax the number of benchmark bundles
context_blocks.text: An agent imagines dividing all goods and then receiving her least valuable bundle. Ordinary MMS uses n bundles, one per real agent. Using a larger imaginary number d lowers the required share, while the actual allocation still has n recipients. The question is how little this benchmark must be weakened to make it universally achievable.

context_blocks.title: A small example
context_blocks.text: If an agent values each of six goods at 1, her 1-out-of-2 share is 3 and her 1-out-of-3 share is 2. Those numbers describe her personal benchmarks, not how many agents must actually receive goods. Different agents can value the same goods differently, so their best benchmark partitions need not coincide.

context_blocks.title: What ordinal means here
context_blocks.text: The fairness comparison is determined by each agent’s ranking of complete bundles. It is preserved if that ranking stays the same. Knowing only an ordering of individual goods does not generally determine the ordering of their sums. Thus this question does not assume an algorithm receives only individual-item rankings.

context_blocks.title: The known denominator bounds
context_blocks.text: For n≥2 the checked results give d*(n)≤min{2n−2, ⌊3n/2⌋, 4⌈n/3⌉}; retaining the minimum handles rounding for small n. The last bound comes from the 2024 result. Trivially d*(1)=1 and d*(n)≥n: with only d<n goods valued at 1 by everyone, a 1-out-of-d guarantee would require a good for every agent. The exact universal denominator remains undetermined.

context_blocks.title: Why the exact threshold matters
context_blocks.text: An exact answer would identify how much competition an indivisible-resource fairness benchmark must tolerate before everyone can be protected. Recent work combines ordinal shares with envy guarantees in restricted preference classes. Those additional guarantees are useful, but they do not settle the unrestricted denominator function asked for here.

cards.title: Bounded protocols for connected envy-free proportional cake cutting
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For every fixed integer n≥4, does there exist a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol Pₙ and a finite integer Bₙ such that, for every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations and all valid query answers, Pₙ uses at most Bₙ queries and returns disjoint connected bundles A₁,…,Aₙ satisfying μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for all i,j and μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for all i, while permitting unallocated cake?

cards.definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure μᵢ: values are nonnegative and countably additive, μᵢ([0,1])=1, and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μᵢ([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a), for 0≤a≤μᵢ([x,1]), returns y≥x with μᵢ([x,y])=a. Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. In this question each Aᵢ must be one interval, up to ownership of its endpoints. The intervals may have gaps between them, and the residue [0,1]∖⋃ᵢAᵢ may be discarded. Envy is compared with other agents’ assigned intervals, not with the residue. Count every Eval and Cut call as one query. The bound Bₙ depends only on the fixed n and its protocol, never on the valuation profile or oracle responses. The statement permits a separate finite protocol for each n; it does not require Bₙ to be polynomial, and does not add an algorithm that generates all Pₙ.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a bounded protocol for every fixed n≥4, or prove that for at least one fixed n≥4 no deterministic protocol and finite bound satisfy the stated guarantees. Existence of a suitable division alone, a procedure that merely converges to one, approximate proportionality, or allowing an agent several intervals does not meet this target.

context_blocks.title: Fairness with one usable piece
context_blocks.text: A connected share is a single interval, as in a continuous appointment slot or one tract of land. Envy-freeness says each person prefers her own assigned interval to anyone else’s. Proportionality additionally protects the amount she receives: at least one n-th of her value for the whole resource.

context_blocks.title: Why disposal changes the question
context_blocks.text: With disposal, giving everyone nothing is envy-free. For example, agents with identical uniform values can each receive an interval of length 1/(2n), leaving half the cake unused; none envies another, but all receive less than their proportional share. The exact 1/n requirement excludes such wasteful outcomes.

context_blocks.title: The connected impossibility has a specific scope
context_blocks.text: Stromquist proves that no finite protocol can always allocate the entire cake envy-freely with one interval per agent once n≥3. This assumes complete allocation. Allowing residue is the change studied here, so that theorem does not refute this question.

context_blocks.title: Known partial-allocation guarantees
context_blocks.text: Waste Makes Haste gives a bounded connected envy-free proportional protocol for three agents in its density model. For four agents its connected guarantee is 1/7 instead of the required 1/4. Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded connected partial allocation with a 1/(3n) value guarantee in general. These results motivate the question but do not supply exact proportionality for all n≥4.

context_blocks.title: Later progress allows fragmented shares
context_blocks.text: The September 2026 Ye–Bai preprint reports a single-exponential query bound for complete envy-free allocation. Complete envy-freeness implies proportionality, but the output may contain multiple intervals per agent. It therefore does not answer this connected-piece question.

cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer k≥1 such that, for every n≥1, every finite set G of goods, and every table of nonnegative additive valuations vᵢ, there is a complete allocation (A₁,…,Aₙ) for which vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥vᵢ(Aⱼ∖S) for all agents i,j and every S⊆Aⱼ with |S|=min{k,|Aⱼ|}?
cards.why: Asks whether a bounded additive relaxation suffices for fairness independently of the number of agents.

cards.definitions: For agent i, each good g has a nonnegative real value vᵢg and every bundle B⊆G has value vᵢ(B)=∑g∈B vᵢg; the empty bundle has value zero. A complete allocation partitions all goods into n labeled, disjoint bundles, possibly empty. Each good goes to exactly one agent. The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to any k goods, abbreviated EFkX: each comparison uses the potentially envious agent i’s values on both sides. The removed set S is hypothetical and is chosen universally, not chosen by the allocation algorithm to make the inequality easier. Actual goods are not removed or discarded. If |Aⱼ|≤k, the comparison is automatically satisfied because its right side is zero; this agrees with treating the source’s k-item condition as vacuous for shorter bundles. Zero-valued goods count as goods and may belong to S. The constant k is chosen before the instance and is independent of n, the number of goods and all values. This is exact existence; it imposes no efficiency requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that at least one universal constant k satisfies the stated existence claim, or prove its negation: for every integer k≥1 there is a finite additive goods instance such that every complete allocation violates at least one of its required inequalities. A counterexample for one k, or an allocation with a multiplicative factor below 1, does not resolve this quantifier structure.

context_blocks.title: How much envy can indivisibility explain?
context_blocks.text: One indivisible valuable item can prevent exact envy-freeness. EFkX allows a bounded number of items in the envied bundle to account for that discrepancy. It requires envy to disappear even after deleting the least helpful k items from the envious agent’s perspective. The question is whether some fixed allowance works for arbitrarily many agents.

context_blocks.title: Any removal versus a favorable removal
context_blocks.text: Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 5 and another bundle’s three goods at 6, 1 and 1. Removing its 6-valued good eliminates her envy, but removing either 1-valued good leaves value 7, so the pair fails EF1X. It also fails EF2X: removing the two 1-valued goods leaves value 6. This illustrates why an existential choice of removed goods is a different, weaker condition.

context_blocks.title: The connection to EFX
context_blocks.text: For k=1 this is the usual any-item EFX condition, including zero-valued items. A universal EFX existence theorem would answer this question positively. This card permits any fixed k, so it asks for a weaker universal guarantee. Choosing k separately for each instance, for example as its total number of goods, would make the property vacuous and is excluded.

context_blocks.title: Exact results for a fixed number of agents
context_blocks.text: The AAAI 2025 result establishes EF2X for four agents, in a valuation class that includes additive goods. That is a concrete exact existence theorem. It fixes the number of agents and therefore does not supply the universal constant-k guarantee for unrestricted n.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 approximation result
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint gives (k+1)/(k+2)-EFkX allocations for every fixed k≥2 and any number of agents. This relaxes the inequality to vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥αvᵢ(Aⱼ∖S), where α<1. Although α approaches 1 as k grows, no finite k in that theorem attains exact fairness. Its negative graph-orientation results additionally restrict who may receive a good.

cards.definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure μᵢ: values are nonnegative and countably additive, μᵢ([0,1])=1, and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μᵢ([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a), for 0≤a≤μᵢ([x,1]), returns y≥x with μᵢ([x,y])=a. Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. Here A₁,…,Aₙ must be pairwise disjoint but need not cover [0,1]; the residue may be discarded. No bound is imposed on the number of intervals per agent except finiteness. Envy is compared only with assigned bundles. Both Eval and Cut calls cost one query, including marks that do not appear in the final allocation. For each n, let Q(n) be the minimum integer B for which a deterministic finite protocol for n agents always returns such an allocation within B queries, for every valuation profile and all valid answers. Known bounded complete-allocation protocols imply that this set of B is nonempty; its least integer is attained. The requested complexity is the asymptotic order of Q(n), with exact fairness on every input and no average-case, error or expected-cost convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a function f(n), constants 0<c≤C and n₀ such that c f(n)≤Q(n)≤C f(n) for every n≥n₀. The upper bound must be realized by valid protocols and the lower bound must apply to every valid deterministic protocol in the stated model. Logarithmic or polynomial-factor gaps do not count as matching constant-factor bounds. This card uses the usual asymptotic interpretation of optimal query complexity, rather than asking for an exact integer query count at every n.

context_blocks.title: Two protections for each recipient
context_blocks.text: An agent should prefer her own bundle to every other assigned bundle, and should value it at least as much as one n-th of the original cake. These are separate conditions when some cake can remain unallocated. For identical uniform valuations, equal bundles of length 1/(2n) are envy-free but fail proportionality.

context_blocks.title: Why count questions?
context_blocks.text: A value measure can be arbitrarily complicated, so the protocol cannot read it as a finite table. Evaluation queries reveal interval values and cut queries reveal where a prescribed value ends. The cost measures how much exact interaction is necessary; it does not charge the local arithmetic or require the resulting bundles to be connected.

context_blocks.title: An established finite upper bound
context_blocks.text: Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded partial-allocation protocol meeting both envy-freeness and exact proportionality, with an exponential query bound. This already ensures Q(n) is finite. Their separate connected-piece result guarantees only a 1/(3n) share and addresses a different output requirement.

context_blocks.title: Recent complete-allocation progress also applies
context_blocks.text: The September 2026 Ye–Bai preprint reports n^{O(1)}2^n queries for a complete envy-free allocation. Such an allocation is also a permitted output here, since disposal is optional and completeness implies proportionality under nonnegative additive valuations. The reported bound is an upper bound for this problem, not a matching optimality result.

context_blocks.title: The value of allowing residue
context_blocks.text: Discarding some cake may make fairness easier to achieve, but the 1/n guarantee prevents an empty or arbitrarily small allocation. A tight query bound would show whether this freedom substantially reduces the information needed for exact fairness. A lower bound proved only for protocols that allocate everything would need a further argument to cover the more permissive target here.

cards.definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure μᵢ: values are nonnegative and countably additive, μᵢ([0,1])=1, and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μᵢ([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a), for 0≤a≤μᵢ([x,1]), returns y≥x with μᵢ([x,y])=a. Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. The output is a complete partition of the cake into bundles A₁,…,Aₙ. A final cut is an internal endpoint between two positive-length intervals assigned to different agents, after adjacent intervals with the same recipient have been merged. Thus an output with r such successive intervals uses r−1 final cuts; 0 and 1 do not count. Isolated endpoint ownership has no cost or fairness effect. Following the cited Stromquist paper, a point merely queried or marked during the protocol is not a final cut unless it is used as an allocation boundary. A protocol is finite if it terminates after finitely many queries on every profile and every valid sequence of answers. That query count may depend on the valuations and need not be bounded by a function of n; local computation must also terminate. In contrast, the number of final cuts must have the uniform bound c*(n). More formally, c*(n) is the minimum over nonnegative integers c for which such a finite protocol for n agents exists. Bounded complete-allocation protocols show this set is nonempty, so the integer minimum is attained. This question charges output cuts, not evaluation queries, queried marks, or total running time.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |g(n)−(c*(n) : ℝ)|≤1/100 for every integer n≥1, using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions ℓ(n)≤c*(n)≤u(n) with u(n)−ℓ(n)≤1/50 also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for c*(n) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.title: Questions and physical fragmentation are different costs
context_blocks.text: A protocol can ask an agent to mark many candidate boundaries and then use only a few in the final division. This card follows the source’s explicit convention that cuts are the boundaries actually used. It asks how fragmented a division must become when it also has to be findable through finitely many queries.

context_blocks.title: A simple counting example
context_blocks.text: Suppose four successive intervals go to agents A, B, A and C. There are three final cuts, and A receives a disconnected bundle. If the first two intervals both went to A, their common boundary would disappear when those intervals were merged. Counting marks made during the search would be a different objective.

context_blocks.title: Existence does not imply a finite protocol
context_blocks.text: A complete connected envy-free division exists, using n−1 final cuts. Stromquist shows that no finite protocol can always find one for n≥3. Since every recipient in a complete envy-free division has positive value, an n−1-cut division would give exactly one interval per agent. Thus c*(n)≥n for n≥3, despite the existential n−1 bound.

context_blocks.title: The extremum is finite
context_blocks.text: For n=1 no cut is needed, and for n=2 the standard cut-and-choose protocol uses one final cut. General bounded protocols of Aziz and Mackenzie guarantee a finite number of cuts for every n. The September 2026 single-exponential query claim gives another reported upper bound, but its purpose is query complexity and it does not establish the least final-cut count.

context_blocks.title: A recent exact cut theorem has different requirements
context_blocks.text: The MFCS 2026 equal-length result determines an existential cut bound for proportional division with a prescribed physical length per agent. This question imposes exact envy-freeness and finite oracle computation, with no equal-length requirement. Those distinctions prevent transferring the numerical answer directly.

sentences: The whole cake must be allocated so that every agent prefers her own bundle to anyone else’s.
A finite query protocol may give an agent several intervals and may mark more candidate boundaries than it ultimately uses.
The objective is the smallest worst-case number of final allocation cuts for each n.
Connected envy-free divisions exist, but for n≥3 no finite protocol can always find one.

cards.context:
A protocol can ask an agent to mark many candidate boundaries and then use only a few in the final division. This card follows the source’s explicit convention that cuts are the boundaries actually used. It asks how fragmented a division must become when it also has to be findable through finitely many queries.

Suppose four successive intervals go to agents A, B, A and C. There are three final cuts, and A receives a disconnected bundle. If the first two intervals both went to A, their common boundary would disappear when those intervals were merged. Counting marks made during the search would be a different objective.

A complete connected envy-free division exists, using n−1 final cuts. Stromquist shows that no finite protocol can always find one for n≥3. Since every recipient in a complete envy-free division has positive value, an n−1-cut division would give exactly one interval per agent. Thus c*(n)≥n for n≥3, despite the existential n−1 bound.

For n=1 no cut is needed, and for n=2 the standard cut-and-choose protocol uses one final cut. General bounded protocols of Aziz and Mackenzie guarantee a finite number of cuts for every n. The September 2026 single-exponential query claim gives another reported upper bound, but its purpose is query complexity and it does not establish the least final-cut count.

The MFCS 2026 equal-length result determines an existential cut bound for proportional division with a prescribed physical length per agent. This question imposes exact envy-freeness and finite oracle computation, with no equal-length requirement. Those distinctions prevent transferring the numerical answer directly.

cards.definitions: The n agents are indexed by {1,…,n}. Each utility is an arbitrary real-valued function on all subsets of the finite set M, normalized only at the empty set; no additivity, monotonicity, submodularity, common ranking or identical-utilities assumption is imposed. A complete allocation is an ordered partition of M into n pairwise disjoint bundles, with empty bundles allowed. An agent i envies j when uᵢ(Aᵢ)<uᵢ(Aⱼ). The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) for mixed items. If there is no envy, X=∅ works. Otherwise one may hypothetically remove one item from i’s bundle or one item from j’s bundle, and compare both remaining bundles using i’s utility. Removing one item from both bundles simultaneously is not permitted. The choice of X may depend on i,j and the whole allocation. These removals only define the fairness comparison; no item is discarded or transferred from the complete allocation. Items have no required permanent designation as goods or chores, since an item’s marginal utility may depend on the surrounding bundle. The question concerns existence and imposes no input encoding, value-query bound or running-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove EF1 existence for every n≥3 and every normalized arbitrary utility profile on a finite item set, or give a finite profile and prove that every complete allocation violates the displayed inequality for some ordered pair, for every allowed one-item removal. An impossibility result for a stronger fairness notion does not refute EF1, and an existence theorem permitting two removed items does not establish it.

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent
cards.formal: Determine the matrix multiplication exponent ω=inf{τ∈ℝ: ∃C>0 ∀n≥2, s(n)≤C n^τ}, where s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates computing every entry of the product of two arbitrary n×n complex matrices exactly, in the circuit model below.
cards.definitions: The inputs are 2n² independent complex variables a_ij,b_ij. The required n² output polynomials are c_ij=sum_{k=1}^n a_ik b_kj. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with binary addition, subtraction, and multiplication gates; any complex constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate values are allowed. Size counts arithmetic gates, including operations involving constants. Input nodes, constant nodes, and output designations are not gates. No division, order comparisons, branching, approximation, or randomization is permitted. A different circuit may be chosen for every n: this is the standard nonuniform arithmetic-complexity formulation over C. The cost of encoding a complex number in bits is outside this model. The elementary lower bound s(n)>=n² for n>=2 follows because the n² distinct non-input output polynomials require distinct gates. The infimum defines a real number between 2 and 3. It need not be attained: determining ω does not require an O(n^ω) circuit bound. An exact candidate w must have upper bounds s(n)=O_ε(n^{w+ε}) for every ε>0 and no bound s(n)=O(n^τ) for any τ<w.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |a−ω|≤1/100. The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds ℓ≤u of width at most 1/50 qualify by taking a=(ℓ+u)/2. An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The 1/100 tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
cards.why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.

importance.reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

progress.text: Strassen gives O(n^(log₂7)) arithmetic operations, establishing that cubic multiplication is not optimal.

Alman proves that the universal method applied to any Coppersmith–Winograd tensor cannot yield an exponent below 2.16805. This is a limitation of that tensor-based route, not a proof that omega exceeds two.
The SODA paper More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication gives omega<2.371339 by extending the combination-loss analysis. The original preprint appeared in April 2024.

Dupont and coauthors report omega<2.371177. Section 4 describes rounding the optimized parameters to rationals and verifying directed bounds for logarithms; it says the verification repository is being prepared. This catalogue has not independently replayed that certificate.
Version 3 of More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication incorporates the new optimization bound. The remaining gap to two persists.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes n² inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent log₂7.

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar ω=2 conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because ω is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

There are also lower bounds on what specific tensor methods can achieve. For example, Alman’s universal-method barrier for Coppersmith–Winograd tensors prevents that route from reaching exponent two. It is not a lower bound on all arithmetic circuits for matrix multiplication. The distinction leaves room for different starting tensors or mathematical constructions.

cards.title: Permanent versus determinant
cards.formal: Over the complex numbers, is the sequence dc_C(permₙ) unbounded by every polynomial in n? Explicitly, for every C>0 and integer k≥1, must there be n≥1 such that dc_C(permₙ)>C(n+1)^k?
cards.definitions: The polynomial permₙ(X)=Σ_{σ∈Sₙ}∏_{i=1}ⁿx_{i,σ(i)} has n² algebraically independent commuting variables and degree n; Sₙ is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. Its determinantal complexity dc_C(permₙ) is the smallest positive integer m for which there exist constant complex m×m matrices A₀ and Aᵢⱼ satisfying the exact polynomial identity permₙ(X)=det(A₀+Σ_{i,j=1}ⁿxᵢⱼAᵢⱼ). Thus every matrix entry is an arbitrary affine-linear form in all input variables. The representation may depend on n and use arbitrary complex constants without a bit-length or constructibility restriction. The resource is matrix dimension m. No symmetry, sparsity, multilinearity of intermediate expressions, regularity, or read-once restriction is imposed. Equality is in C[X], for every complex substitution, not only on 0/1 inputs. Border complexity, which permits a limit of representations, is a separate measure. Characteristic two is excluded by fixing C: in that characteristic the permanent equals the determinant. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central concrete target in algebraic complexity: determine whether one canonical efficiently computable polynomial can simulate a canonical algebraic counting polynomial at polynomial cost. Its formulation invites tools from algebraic geometry and representation theory while retaining a precise computational meaning.

importance.reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.

progress.text: Valiant establishes the foundational algebraic simulation framework: formulas and branching programs have small determinantal representations, and the permanent is complete for VNP.
Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2 using Hessian ranks at zeros. This remains a polynomial lower bound.

Grenet gives a 2ⁿ−1-dimensional representation; Landsberg and Ressayre prove exponential optimality when specified symmetries must be respected. Their unrestricted-versus-equivariant comparison is left open.
Kumar and Volk survey the permanent bounds and develop a new singular-locus method for a different explicit polynomial, a diagonal power sum. That theorem does not raise the permanent lower bound.
The algebraic cost of Boolean summation distinguishes permanent and determinant under a local fixed-additive-size simulation requirement, leaving general polynomial-size representations open.
Bogart and Valero’s journal paper studies generalized permanents and continues to state the superpolynomial ordinary-permanent problem as open.

context_blocks.text: The permanent and determinant sum the same products indexed by permutations; the determinant attaches a permutation sign. Those signs enable cancellations behind efficient determinant computation. A determinantal representation asks whether a larger matrix with carefully chosen affine entries can reproduce the unsigned sum exactly. Merely showing that changing signs in the original n×n matrix fails leaves almost all permitted representations untouched.

The model is nonuniform and algebraic. It asks about the existence of a family of polynomial-size representations even if finding their complex coefficients is computationally difficult. Determinants characterize polynomial-size algebraic branching programs up to polynomial overhead, whereas unrestricted arithmetic circuits define the potentially larger class VP. The requested lower bound separates the permanent from the branching-program model; it should not be identified without qualification with a separation from all of VP.

The unrestricted complex-field lower bound is still quadratic in the original matrix dimension: Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2. Their argument compares the rank of the matrix of second partial derivatives, the Hessian, at carefully chosen zeros of the two polynomials. Because the permanent has n² input variables, this is only linear in its number of variables, despite being quadratic in n.

There is also an explicit exponential upper bound, dc_C(permₙ)≤2ⁿ−1, due to Grenet. Landsberg and Ressayre prove that this construction is optimal under particular equivariance requirements involving permutations and diagonal rescaling. Removing those requirements is essential: the question allows a representation to break every visible symmetry of the polynomial. Whether symmetry can be imposed with only polynomial overhead is itself another open problem.

Progress can reveal structural differences without giving an unrestricted lower bound. Orzel, Srinivasan, Tavenas, and Yehudayoff show that a local Boolean-summation operation can be absorbed into a permanent by a fixed additive increase in dimension, whereas the analogous uniform fixed-additive-cost property fails for determinants. Their FSTTCS 2025 result explains a step in the VNP-completeness construction; it does not exclude a different, global polynomial-size determinant representation.

Bogart and Valero extend upper- and lower-bound techniques to two generalized permanent families. Their 2026 journal version still identifies the Mignon–Ressayre estimate as the best known characteristic-zero bound for the ordinary permanent for n≥5. This provides a recent status check while illustrating how sensitive the geometric lower-bound method is to the polynomial being studied.

cards.title: Shub–Smale τ-conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant C≥1 such that, for every nonzero polynomial f∈Z[x], the number z_Z(f) of distinct integer roots satisfies z_Z(f)≤(1+τ(f))^C, where τ(f) is its minimum number of addition, subtraction, and multiplication operations starting only from 1 and x?
cards.definitions: A straight-line program begins with registers containing 1 and the indeterminate x. Each subsequent register contains u+v, u−v, or u·v for two previously available registers; the two operands may be equal. Previously computed registers may be reused without restriction. A designated register must equal f as a formal polynomial over the integers. The cost is the number of arithmetic operations, and τ(f) is the minimum over all such programs. A zero-operation program may output 1 or x. No arbitrary integer constants are supplied: for example 2 must be built as 1+1, and all operations constructing other constants count. Division, comparisons, branching, and exponentiation as a primitive are forbidden. Multiplication counts even when both operands are constants; no bound is placed on intermediate degree or coefficient bit length. This is arithmetic operation count, not bit running time or formula size. Define z_Z(f)=|{a∈Z:f(a)=0}|; repeated roots are counted once. The zero polynomial is excluded. The same universal C must work for all f, regardless of degree, coefficients, or root magnitudes.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial bound with one absolute exponent C, or prove that no such exponent exists. A negative answer must yield polynomials violating every candidate polynomial exponent—for example, a family whose integer-root counts grow faster than every fixed power of their exhibited program lengths. One polynomial violating a proposed small exponent, or exponentially many real or complex roots, is insufficient. No uniform efficient procedure for finding the roots is requested.
cards.why: A precise number-theoretic route to major arithmetic circuit and algebraic machine lower bounds. It probes whether sharing intermediate computations can create many independent integer zeros cheaply, linking computational compression with arithmetic geometry and proof complexity.

importance.reason: A central arithmetic complexity conjecture with a very elementary statement and strong consequences for algebraic P versus NP and constant-free circuit lower bounds.

progress.text: Shub and Smale relate integer-root complexity to the intractability of complex polynomial feasibility and the separation P_C≠NP_C.

Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch, and Tzameret publish conditional Ideal Proof System lower bounds from the τ-conjecture for a binary-value variant over rational functions.

Santibañez-Leal’s version 0.03 reports an exact census through eight operations in a convention with free −1,0,1. This finite computational claim is not independently reproduced here and gives no asymptotic resolution.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The universal integer-root bound remains unresolved in the sources reviewed. The August 2026 census is explicitly a finite computational claim, not a resolution. Full operation count, distinct integer roots, and the exclusion of the zero polynomial are fixed.

context_blocks.text: A short arithmetic program can represent an enormous polynomial. After s squarings, x^(2^s) has exponential degree although its computation has only s operations. Degree therefore gives only the elementary bound z_Z(f)≤2^τ(f). The conjecture says that distinct integer roots are much harder to pack into such a compressed representation than degree alone suggests. Multiplicity cannot replace distinctness: the same repeated-squaring example already has a root of exponential multiplicity.

The restriction to integer roots is substantive. Iterating q_0(x)=x and q_(j+1)(x)=q_j(x)^2−2 uses only a constant number of new operations per stage and gives 2^j distinct real roots for j≥1. Indeed q_j(2 cos θ)=2 cos(2^j θ), so the roots can be written down through distinct cosine values. Thus the unrestricted statement with real roots in place of integer roots is false. Conjectures about real roots of particular sparse sums of products impose additional circuit restrictions.

Shub and Smale connect a polynomial integer-root bound to P_C≠NP_C in the Blum–Shub–Smale model, where exact complex arithmetic has unit cost and branching tests equality. This explains why an apparently elementary univariate question belongs among fundamental complexity problems. The conclusion concerns computation over complex numbers; it must not be silently identified with a proof of Boolean P≠NP.

Rojas develops a p-adic approach, including a reduction showing that a polynomial bound only for integer roots congruent to 1 modulo one fixed prime would already imply the full conjecture. He also bounds rational roots by exp(O(s log(s+1))) in terms of additive complexity s, which charges additions and subtractions while allowing powers and multiplicative structure more freely. This is useful when additive complexity is small; it is not a polynomial bound in the full operation count τ.

The conjecture has consequences beyond the original machine model. Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch, and Tzameret recall its implication for separating the constant-free algebraic classes VP^0 and VNP^0, and use it to obtain conditional lower bounds for a variant of the binary value principle in the Ideal Proof System over rational functions. These implications do not establish the conjecture, and their non-Boolean instances do not directly yield Frege lower bounds.

An August 2026 preprint reports exhaustive enumeration through eight operations, using the convention that −1, 0, and 1 are all free. Such a fixed change of constants can be simulated with constant extra cost in the model here, but exact small-length records depend on the convention. The computation is finite experimental evidence and has not been reproduced for this card; it cannot settle the existence of a universal exponent.

cards.title: VP versus VBP over the complex numbers
cards.formal: Is VP_ℂ=VBP_ℂ? Explicitly, for every family (f_n)_{n≥1} of commutative polynomials over ℂ with a polynomially bounded number of variables and total degree, if f_n has an arithmetic circuit of size n^O(1), must f_n also have an algebraic branching program of size n^O(1)? The polynomial bounds may depend on the family but not on n; all equalities are exact polynomial identities.
cards.definitions: An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output, input gates labelled by variables or arbitrary complex constants, and binary addition or multiplication gates; subtraction is expressible using the constant −1. Intermediate results may be reused without restriction. Size counts gates and wires, with each field constant of unit cost; no division gates are allowed. An algebraic branching program (ABP) is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source s and sink t, whose edges are labelled by affine linear forms α₀+∑_j α_j x_j over ℂ. Its output is the sum over all directed s-to-t paths of the product of their edge labels. Its size counts vertices, edges and the nonzero coefficients and variable occurrences used in those labels. Layering can be imposed with polynomial overhead but is not required here. There is no width, variable-order, read-once, multilinearity, homogeneity, monotonicity or symmetry restriction. Both circuit and ABP families are nonuniform: no efficient algorithm producing them is required, and complex constants need not have bounded bit descriptions. VP_ℂ consists of the stated polynomial-degree families with polynomial circuit size; VBP_ℂ consists of families with polynomial ABP size and polynomially many variables. Polynomial ABP size already bounds the degree.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every family in VP_ℂ admits polynomial-size ABPs, or exhibit a family in VP_ℂ whose minimum ABP size is not polynomially bounded: for every constant c, infinitely many n require more than n^c size. A negative answer must retain small general circuits for the separating family and allow arbitrary complex constants in the competing ABPs. Lower bounds only for multilinear, symmetric, noncommutative, monotone or read-once ABPs do not suffice. Approximation in coefficient space, called border complexity, is a different question.
cards.why: One of the central unresolved separations inside algebraic complexity: it asks whether determinant-like path-sum computation captures every efficiently computed polynomial of polynomial degree.

importance.reason: A basic class equality linking general arithmetic circuits, algebraic branching programs and determinant universality; current symmetry and multilinearity results remain model-specific.

progress.text: Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction yields quasipolynomial simulations; the polynomial-size equality remains stronger. The ITCS 2024 paper reviews this consequence.
Sinhababu–Thierauf establish polynomial-size factor closure for ABPs in characteristic zero, first in CCC 2020 and then in Computational Complexity.
Fabris–Limaye–Srinivasan–Yehudayoff study the power of min-partition rank for multilinear ABPs through combinatorial set systems.
Dwivedi–Pago–Seppelt publish symmetric-model separations and new completeness results at STOC 2026; these do not separate unrestricted VP and VBP.
The revised Bhargav–Dwivedi–Saxena survey retains VF⊆VBP⊆VP with no strict containment known, in Remark 7.3.
