cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The June 2026 survey explicitly leaves the VP–VBP inclusion unresolved. STOC 2026 symmetry separations, multilinear lower-bound methods and min-plus-semiring results use different models. This card fixes characteristic zero over ℂ, unrestricted commutative ABPs and exact nonuniform computation.

context_blocks.text: A circuit can multiply two complicated intermediate results and reuse each of them elsewhere. An ABP has a more linear form of reuse: the polynomial reaching a vertex is obtained by adding predecessor polynomials multiplied by affine edge labels. This is equivalent, with polynomial overhead, to skew circuits, where each multiplication has an input operand that is a variable or constant. The problem asks whether general multiplication and reuse can always be reorganized into this form at only polynomial cost.

The degree restriction rules out an immediate artificial separation. Repeated squaring computes x^{2ⁿ} with n multiplication gates. An ABP with affine labels needs a path of length at least 2ⁿ to produce that degree. This family is excluded from VP because its degree is exponential. The open problem persists when the output degree is polynomial, so a solution must address the structure of efficient computations rather than this simple degree obstruction.

The determinant provides a useful equivalent perspective. Polynomial-size ABPs can be represented by determinants of polynomial-size matrices of affine forms, and the symbolic determinant itself has polynomial-size ABPs. Thus equality would make the determinant universal for all polynomial-degree, polynomial-size circuit computations under polynomial-size affine projections. This differs from the determinant-versus-permanent problem: the permanent is not known to belong to VP, whereas a separation here must already have an efficient circuit on the easy side.

Classical depth reduction supplies a quasipolynomial simulation. If quasipolynomial size is allowed throughout, formulas, ABPs and general circuits compute the same polynomial-degree families. Dutta and coauthors recall this consequence of the Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction in their ITCS 2024 work. What remains unknown is whether the overhead can always be reduced to a fixed polynomial, or whether some efficient circuit computations necessarily resist it.

ABPs also support more algebra than their restricted multiplication rule might suggest. Sinhababu and Thierauf prove that factors of an ABP-computed polynomial have polynomial-size ABPs in characteristic zero. This establishes a closure property that was previously known for general circuits. Sharing factor closure does not establish equality of the models; the June 2026 factoring survey explicitly retains the unresolved chain VF⊆VBP⊆VP.

Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt’s STOC 2026 work separates symmetric analogues of formulas, skew circuits and general circuits and connects them to graph homomorphism polynomials. These analogues require symmetries of the variables to extend to the computation and measure the largest orbit of gates, rather than simply imposing the ordinary total-size bound. Their separations therefore do not establish VP≠VBP. The work also supplies natural complete polynomial families, potentially useful targets for future unrestricted lower bounds.

A January 2026 paper by Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff investigates the min-partition rank method for multilinear ABPs through a combinatorial set-system problem. It recovers a separation between multilinear formulas and multilinear ABPs and studies the potential of the method for stronger lower bounds. The general ABPs in this card can reuse variables along paths and can cancel nonmultilinear terms. A lower bound that forbids those behaviors does not constrain every allowed representation.

A positive answer would show that general efficient algebraic computation can be expressed through path sums and determinants with only polynomial overhead. A negative answer would prove a basic hierarchy inside efficient computation itself. Either result would clarify how much computational power comes from multiplying and reusing rich intermediate expressions, independently of the larger question of whether permanent computation is efficient.

cards.title: VP versus VNP
cards.formal: Over the field $\mathbb C$, do there exist constants C,k such that, for every integer n≥1, the polynomial $\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}$ can be computed by an arithmetic circuit with at most C(n+1)^k gates? Equivalently, is $\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}$? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
cards.definitions: X has n² independent indeterminates and S_n is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes labeled by variables or arbitrary complex constants, binary +, −, × operation gates, and one output. Its size counts operation gates; intermediate results can feed any number of later gates. Division, comparisons, oracle gates, approximation, and limits of circuits are absent. The output must equal the permanent as a formal polynomial. Circuits may depend on n without a uniform construction algorithm; constants have unit arithmetic cost, with no bit-encoding restriction. VP consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded numbers of variables and total degrees, computed by polynomial-size circuits. VNP consists of polynomial families f_n(x)=Σ_{y∈{0,1}^{p(n)}} g_n(x,y), for some polynomial p and some such polynomial-size, polynomial-degree circuit family g. The witness sum is over Boolean strings even though the coefficients lie in C.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated circuit family, or prove that the minimum circuit size of the permanent is not bounded by any polynomial in n. A lower bound for every polynomial-size general circuit family suffices. Lower bounds only for formulas, monotone circuits, bounded-depth circuits, or determinantal representations do not by themselves settle this formulation.
cards.why: This is the central separation question for arithmetic computation. It tests whether summing exponentially many efficiently describable algebraic contributions inherently requires more computation than evaluating one polynomial-size circuit, and organizes lower-bound research across algebra, geometry, and pseudorandomness.

importance.reason: A foundational separation for general arithmetic circuits, with a complete concrete target in the permanent and consequences across algebraic complexity and explicit lower-bound constructions.

progress.text: Ryser’s inclusion-exclusion expression gives an exponential-size formula, for example O(n²2^n) arithmetic operations. This substantially improves direct enumeration of n! permutations but remains far above a polynomial bound.
Valiant establishes algebraic completeness of the permanent over fields of characteristic different from two. Over C this yields the equivalence between polynomial-size permanent circuits and VP=VNP.

Limaye, Srinivasan, and Tavenas prove superpolynomial lower bounds against arithmetic circuits of every constant depth in characteristic zero. Those circuits may have unbounded fan-in, with size accounting for their description; the fixed depth is an essential restriction. The result does not separate general VP and VNP.

Narayanan relates elusive polynomial maps to expansion of iterated sumsets and obtains improved superlinear bounds in certain sublogarithmic-depth regimes. An explicit elusive-curve construction has exponential degree; the paper explains that its parameters do not yet imply VP≠VNP.

context_blocks.text: The permanent sums one product for every perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph. Substituting a zero-one adjacency matrix counts perfect matchings. This card asks for an exact symbolic arithmetic computation valid on all complex matrices. The model permits cancellations and unrestricted reuse of intermediate results, so it captures substantially more than enumerating matchings.

The permanent and determinant have the same permutation products, but the determinant attaches a sign to each one. Determinants have polynomial-size division-free circuits despite their factorially many displayed terms. Thus counting the monomials in the permanent is not a circuit lower bound: the question is whether an equally effective algebraic compression exists for its unsigned sum.

Valiant makes this example universal. Every family in VNP reduces to a polynomially larger permanent by substitutions of variables and constants. A polynomial circuit for the permanent would therefore compress every efficient Boolean-witness sum in the definition of VNP. Conversely, separating these classes forces the permanent to escape polynomial circuit size.

Important partial results restrict how computations are organized. A formula cannot reuse an intermediate result; a constant-depth circuit permits only a fixed number of operation layers. Even proving that the permanent has no small determinant representation would rule out only that representation model. None of these restrictions is part of the circuit model in this card.

Recent lower bounds illustrate both the progress and the gap. Superpolynomial bounds are known at every fixed depth, and new work constructs polynomial maps that evade low-complexity parametrizations. The latter can yield stronger circuit lower bounds if its degree and dimension parameters improve sufficiently. The constructions currently cited do not give the required unrestricted superpolynomial bound.

cards.title: Polynomial-size arithmetic formulas for the determinant
cards.formal: Do there exist constants K,C≥1 such that for every n≥1 the symbolic determinant Det_n(X)=Σ_{π∈S_n}sgn(π)∏_{i=1}^n x_{i,π(i)} has an arithmetic formula over the complex numbers with at most K n^C nodes?
cards.definitions: The n² entries x_{ij} of X are distinct commuting indeterminates. S_n is the set of permutations of [n], and sgn(π) is +1 or −1 according to the parity of π. An arithmetic formula is a rooted binary tree. Leaves are labelled by input variables or arbitrary constants from ℂ; internal nodes apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. The output must equal Det_n as a formal polynomial in ℂ[x_{11},…,x_{nn}]. Size counts every node, including each repeated occurrence of a variable, constant or copied subformula. Intermediate results cannot be shared between different parents. Constants are charged unit size, without a bound on their bit description; this is nonuniform algebraic complexity, so no algorithm generating the family is required. Division, comparisons, branching and input-dependent constants are not allowed. Intermediate polynomials may contain higher powers of individual variables and cancellations of those powers; only the final polynomial is required to be the determinant. There is no multilinearity, homogeneity, fixed-depth, monotonicity or bounded-coefficient restriction on intermediate computation. The fixed field ℂ is an explicit characteristic-zero specialization of the inherited question.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit polynomial-size formulas with one fixed size exponent for all n, or prove that the minimum formula-size function is not bounded by any polynomial: for every K,C≥1 there is an n for which every allowed formula has more than K n^C nodes. A fixed-power lower bound such as Ω(n³) is insufficient to refute polynomial size. A lower bound restricted to multilinear formulas, noncommuting variables, or bounded depth does not settle this unrestricted commutative formula question.
cards.why: The canonical test of whether reusing intermediate expressions gives a superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic expression trees, even for an efficiently computable polynomial.

importance.reason: A fundamental separation inside algebraic computation, equivalent to the formula-versus-branching-program question through determinant completeness and linked to many explicit polynomial families.

progress.text: Berkowitz gives division-free polynomial-size, O(log² n)-depth determinant circuits; unfolding yields quasipolynomial-size formulas.
Kalorkoti proves an unrestricted Ω(n³) formula lower bound for an n by n determinant, also allowing division.
Raz establishes n^{Ω(log n)} lower bounds for formulas that remain multilinear at every gate; the original ECCC report precedes the journal publication.
Chaugule and coauthors relate formula complexity of Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to the generic determinant.
Boyapati–Chillara–Vempati’s sparse-determinant preprint retains the strong multilinear lower bound with Θ(n log⁶ n) nonzero entries; it appears at CCC 2026.
The updated factoring primer explicitly records that polynomial-size symbolic determinant formulas are still unknown, despite new formula-factoring results.

cards.status_note: The June 2026 primary survey explicitly retains the question. Sparse and dense multilinear lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted intermediate computations, and recent factoring progress does not furnish determinant formulas. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The determinant is computationally easy when an algorithm may save intermediate work and reuse it. A formula imposes a stricter discipline: each computed quantity has only one consumer. To use the same expression twice, the expression must be copied. This can turn a compact computation graph into a much larger tree. The problem asks whether the determinant has an alternative expression that avoids this potential blow-up.

The familiar permutation expansion has n! terms, but this does not prove that every formula is that large. Algebraic identities can compress a sum dramatically, just as a product of short sums can represent many expanded monomials. Conversely, Gaussian elimination is not itself a small formula: its usual presentation reuses entries, performs divisions and selects pivots. Its numerical running time therefore cannot answer the stated symbolic question.

Berkowitz’s division-free construction gives polynomial-size arithmetic circuits of depth O(log² n). Unfolding a bounded-fan-in circuit of that depth into a tree gives a formula of size 2^{O(log² n)}=n^{O(log n)}. This is quasipolynomial, already far below the permutation expansion, but still larger than a fixed power of n. A polynomial-size formula would close this remaining gap.

The determinant is also a complete problem for polynomial-size algebraic branching programs, whose outputs are sums of products of edge labels along directed source-to-sink paths. Consequently, polynomial-size determinant formulas would imply VF=VBP: every polynomial family having polynomial-size branching programs would have polynomial-size formulas. The larger class VP allows general arithmetic circuits. The June 2026 factoring primer still lists VF⊆VBP⊆VP without a known strict containment and explicitly leaves small determinant formulas unresolved.

An unrestricted lower bound is known, but it is only a fixed power. Kalorkoti proves Ω(n³) formula size for the n by n determinant, even in a model allowing division. Here n is the matrix dimension; there are n² independent variables. Thus the bound is cubic in dimension and only a power 3/2 in the number of variables. It must not be described as a cubic lower bound in the input-variable count.

Raz proves a much stronger n^{Ω(log n)} lower bound when every intermediate polynomial is multilinear. This restriction is substantive even though the final determinant is multilinear. For a simple illustration, (x+y)²−x²−y² equals 2xy, a multilinear output obtained through nonmultilinear intermediate terms. The example does not establish a size advantage, but it shows why output multilinearity alone cannot justify applying a theorem that assumes multilinearity throughout a computation.

Recent progress tests which determinant features are needed for that restricted lower bound. Boyapati, Chillara and Vempati prove the existence of sparse n by n symbolic matrices with only Θ(n log⁶ n) nonzero entries whose determinants still require n^{Ω(log n)} multilinear formulas. This shows that the dense n²-variable presentation is not essential to Raz’s obstruction. It leaves the permission to use nonmultilinear intermediate computations untouched.

The question also organizes complexity outside generic matrices. Chaugule and coauthors connect small formulas for Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to small formulas for the general determinant. Such reductions make the determinant a useful benchmark for whether apparently special algebraic expressions really admit efficient tree computations. A separation would reveal a basic cost of forbidding reuse, already within problems that possess efficient arithmetic circuits.

cards.title: Word problem for one-relation monoids
cards.formal: Is there a single algorithm that, given a finite alphabet A and four finite words u,v,s,t∈A*, always halts and decides whether s and t represent the same element of the monoid presented by ⟨A | u=v⟩?
cards.definitions: A* consists of all finite strings over A, including the empty word ε, with concatenation as multiplication and ε as identity. The presentation ⟨A | u=v⟩ denotes A*/≡, where ≡ is the least equivalence relation containing u≡v that is compatible with concatenation on both sides. Equivalently, s≡t exactly when some finite sequence s=w_0,w_1,…,w_k=t exists in which each adjacent pair is xu y,xv y in either order for some x,y∈A*. The fixed words u and v are literal strings, not variables that can be substituted by arbitrary words. Empty sides are permitted: replacing ε means inserting the other side at a gap in the current string. The alphabet and all four words form a finite explicit input; one may encode A as {1,…,a} and its letters as integers. The requested algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine for all presentations and all word pairs, with no oracle and no unbounded advice. There is no polynomial-time or other prescribed resource bound, but termination is required on both equal and unequal pairs. This is an ordinary monoid presentation. No inverse operation, cancellation law, group axiom or commutativity assumption is present. The presentation itself varies with the input: the card asks for uniform decidability, not merely a separate non-effectively selected procedure for each fixed presentation.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an always-terminating uniform decision procedure with a correctness proof, or prove that the language of positive presentation-and-word-pair instances is undecidable. One explicit fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem would suffice for a negative answer, but is stronger than is logically required to refute uniform decidability. Enumeration that halts only on equal words, or a procedure whose termination on unequal words is unproved, is insufficient. An exponential derivation-length lower bound is compatible with decidability.
cards.why: A foundational decidability boundary for rewriting: can reachability under one literal reversible string rule already escape every terminating uniform algorithm?

importance.reason: One of the central minimal-presentation decision problems, connecting string rewriting, algebraic normal forms, computability and reductions between monoids, inverse monoids and groups.

progress.text: Magnus solves the one-relator group word problem; later work solves major ordinary-monoid special cases, without providing a general procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda surveys the unresolved problem, reduction methods, special cases and gaps in earlier claimed arguments.
The survey’s corrigendum fixes historical attributions and technical wording, including nontermination versus literal looping of Adian’s procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda gives monadic one-relation monoids with exponential Dehn functions but decidable word problems, separating short derivations from decidability.
Gray–Reilly prove undecidability for certain two-generator one-relator inverse monoids; their introduction explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open.

cards.status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the ordinary one-relation-monoid word problem as open. Its inverse-monoid undecidability theorem does not resolve this ordinary presentation problem. Checked through 11 September 2026. The inherited input includes the presentation, so the card explicitly targets uniform decidability and distinguishes it from the per-presentation quantifier.

context_blocks.text: This is a minimal string-transformation problem. There is only one reversible replacement rule, and it can be applied inside any surrounding context. Starting with a word, repeated replacements can generate many others. Equality asks whether the target lies in this reachability set. The alphabet symbols themselves have no hidden arithmetic meaning; any complicated computation would have to emerge from overlaps and repeated applications of this one rule.

Positive answers are always semidecidable. Enumerate all finite replacement sequences from s and stop if t appears. Every individual stage has finitely many choices, even when one side of the relation is empty. The missing ingredient is an effective stopping argument for negative instances. Seeing no derivation within a long search does not establish inequality when intermediate words may continue to grow.

Length-preserving relations illustrate an easy case. If |u|=|v|, every reachable word has length |s|, so exhaustive search takes place in a finite graph. Unequal input lengths immediately imply inequality. When the relation changes length, that finite-state argument disappears. The question permits enormous running times, so even an impractical computable bound on the needed search would be a meaningful resolution.

Simply orienting a rule toward shorter words need not produce unique normal forms. For the relation baba=aba, the word bababa can shorten through ababa to aaba, or directly to baaba. Neither aaba nor baaba contains baba, so both are irreducible under the shortening rule, although they are equal in the presented monoid. This example shows why termination of one chosen reduction strategy is different from a complete equality test.

The surrounding algebra offers major positive results. Magnus proved decidability for one-relator groups in 1932. For ordinary monoids, classical work handles important cases such as a single relation equating a word to the identity, and presentations satisfying appropriate cycle-free conditions. Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family ⟨a,b | baa(ba)^N=a⟩ for N≥2 with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

The inverse-monoid connection is still useful: positive decidability results for the appropriate intermediate class would imply positive results for ordinary one-relation monoids. A negative result in a broader intermediate class need not transfer backwards through that implication. The fundamental goal remains an exact boundary for algorithmic equality under extremely small presentations, with consequences for rewriting systems, normal forms and the ways finite algebraic syntax can encode unbounded computation.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time factorization over finite fields
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing algorithm that, for every explicitly represented finite field F_q and every nonzero dense univariate f∈F_q[x] of degree n≥1, outputs its complete irreducible factorization using (n+log₂q)^{O(1)} bit operations, with one absolute polynomial bound?
cards.definitions: The field is supplied as F_q=F_p[t]/(h(t)), where p is a binary-encoded prime, h∈F_p[t] is a supplied monic irreducible polynomial of degree e≥1, and q=p^e. These field promises are part of the input specification; no algorithm for constructing h is required. An element is represented by its e coefficients of degree below e, each in {0,…,p−1}. The polynomial f is given by all n+1 coefficients in this representation. Output a unit u∈F_q\{0}, pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials g₁,…,g_r∈F_q[x], and positive integer multiplicities m₁,…,m_r with f=u∏_i g_i^{m_i}. Output order is irrelevant. Arithmetic, conversions, preprocessing and writing the factors all count in bit time. Repeated factors and characteristic-p inseparability are allowed. The running-time exponent must be independent of n,p,e and f. No randomness, number-theoretic hypothesis, factorization oracle or precomputed field-specific advice is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives a correct complete-factorization algorithm with the stated uniform worst-case polynomial bit bound for every valid input. A negative answer proves no such algorithm exists in this model; failure of a particular deterministic strategy is insufficient. Polynomial dependence on q or p instead of log q, average-case bounds, fixed-degree results, or conditional algorithms do not resolve the claim.
cards.why: A canonical exact derandomization problem in computer algebra, with broad consequences wherever finite-field factorization is used as a subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem in algebraic computation: randomized polynomial-time search is known, while uniform deterministic polynomial bit complexity remains unresolved even for basic root-finding cases.

progress.text: Berlekamp and subsequent randomized splitting algorithms establish the classical framework for finite-field factorization.
Shoup reduces the characteristic dependence of general deterministic methods to roughly a square root, as reviewed in the later sources.
Evdokimov obtains deterministic quasipolynomial degree dependence under GRH, not a general polynomial bound.
Guo’s P-scheme framework supplies GRH-based polynomial algorithms for additional Galois-group classes and a common treatment of earlier results.
Altman gives unconditional amortized factorization over many primes, with dependence on splitting-field degree.
Umans–Wang propose a number-theoretic route to better degree exponents in fast factorization; general deterministic finite-field factoring is not resolved.
Chuyoon–Shpilka’s sparse multivariate results explicitly retain the univariate-factorization cost and a polynomial dependence on p for the finite-field subroutine.

context_blocks.text: Finite-field polynomial factorization is a setting where randomization already gives efficient exact algorithms. The desired output has a short representation and is unique up to ordering after normalizing the factors. The open issue is therefore whether random choices are essential for guaranteed efficiency, rather than whether factorization is possible or whether its answer is too large to write down.

The logarithm of the field size is the relevant parameter because one coefficient occupies about log₂q bits. Enumerating all q field elements may be reasonable for a tiny field, but is exponential in the coefficient length when q grows. This distinction is already visible for quadratics over a prime field: the general problem includes finding roots of x²−a modulo an arbitrary large odd prime when a is a quadratic residue.

The field presentation makes a potentially hidden prerequisite explicit. Supplying an irreducible h gives a concrete way to add, multiply and invert extension-field elements using polynomial arithmetic modulo h. The algorithm is not being asked to discover a field representation. At the same time, arithmetic operations are not free: the requested complexity includes their bit cost and must remain polynomial as the extension degree and characteristic vary.

Classical algorithms organize the work into squarefree factorization, separation by irreducible-factor degree, and splitting products whose factors have equal degree. The first two stages have deterministic polynomial-time methods. Randomized equal-degree splitting then completes the factorization efficiently. This organization, surveyed by von zur Gathen–Panario, isolates a concrete source of the derandomization difficulty.

A proposed answer can be checked efficiently without solving the search problem from scratch. Multiplying the claimed factors verifies their product, and finite-field irreducibility tests use modular powering and gcd computations. For a monic polynomial g of degree d, one checks divisibility by x^{q^d}−x and excludes common factors with x^{q^{d/ℓ}}−x for prime divisors ℓ of d. The huge exponents are handled by repeated powering modulo g, not by writing enormous polynomials.

Unconditional deterministic methods do work in time polynomial in n, log q and the characteristic p. Consequently fixed characteristic is already a tractable regime even when the extension field is large. The general obstacle is a large characteristic encoded in only log p bits. Guo’s account records a p^{1/2} dependence up to factors polynomial in n and log q for the best general deterministic methods discussed there.

GRH does not currently remove every obstacle. Evdokimov’s algorithm gives quasipolynomial degree dependence under GRH, and Galois-theoretic methods obtain polynomial time for certain supplied lifts with controlled groups. Guo’s P-scheme framework extends those special cases and unifies earlier methods. Neither its polynomial-time subclass theorem nor the general quasipolynomial bound is a general deterministic polynomial-time factorization theorem.

The inherited September 2025 paper by Altman changes the averaging question. Starting from one integer polynomial f, it factors its reductions for every prime below a bound N. The average cost per prime is polynomial in the input parameters and the degree m of the splitting field over Q. This gives a strong amortized result when m is polynomially bounded, but m can be as large as n!, and processing all primes below N does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for one arbitrary prime supplied in binary.

Altman also distinguishes averaging over primes from older averaging over input polynomials. A deterministic procedure can run quickly on most randomly selected polynomials and still have hard individual inputs. The present question requires a worst-case bound for every f over every supplied field. Neither kind of averaging can silently replace that quantifier.

Recent multivariate factorization results sometimes suppress the underlying univariate cost in their headline bounds. Chuyoon–Shpilka’s March 2026 paper explicitly restores this dependence in Remark 1.7 and §2.2. Its finite-field subroutine runs in time polynomial in p, log q and the degree; its multivariate theorem includes a factor T for univariate factorization. Specializing the number of variables does not erase that cost.

Umans–Wang’s November 2025 work pursues a different improvement: a number-theoretic conjecture could reduce the degree exponent in fast polynomial-factorization algorithms below the familiar three-halves bound. It also has a separate consequence for deterministic integer factoring. Those are valuable quantitative directions, but the abstract’s deterministic integer result must not be misread as a general derandomization theorem for finite-field polynomials.

The problem is fundamental because polynomial factorization is repeatedly used as a subroutine in symbolic computation and computational number theory. A deterministic solution would make many algorithms independent of randomized splitting choices. A proof that no such solution exists would instead establish a striking separation for an exact algebraic search problem whose answers are efficiently verifiable.

cards.title: Conjugacy problem for one-relator groups
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, on input a finite one-relator group presentation G=⟨x₁,…,x_k | r=1⟩ and two words u,v, decides whether some word w satisfies w⁻¹uw=v in G?
cards.definitions: The input consists of an integer k≥1 and three explicitly written finite words r,u,v over the letters x₁,…,x_k and their formal inverses. The group is the quotient of the free group F(x₁,…,x_k) by the normal subgroup generated by r. The relator may be empty, in which case G is free. Equality in the displayed equation is equality in this quotient, rather than literal equality of strings. A conjugating word w may have any finite length. The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine that must halt with the correct yes/no answer for every valid input; the presentation is part of the input. No polynomial-time or other specified resource bound is imposed. This is the uniform decision formulation; a separate algorithm for each fixed group, without an effective way to obtain it from a presentation, is not by itself sufficient.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such presentations and pairs of words, or prove that this input language is undecidable. A one-relator group with an undecidable fixed-group conjugacy problem would suffice for a negative answer. A result only for torsion groups, a decision procedure for word equality, or undecidability of a different equation or membership problem does not settle this question.
cards.why: A central decision problem at the boundary between decidable symbolic equality and existential reasoning in finitely presented algebraic structures.

importance.reason: One of Dehn’s classical algorithmic problems, still unresolved in a basic class defined by a single relation; it tests how far decidability survives beyond word equality.

Linton–Nyberg-Brodda’s comprehensive survey records the general conjugacy problem as open and describes why the word-problem induction does not automatically extend.
Gray–Levine obtain undecidability results for related Diophantine problems, including subgroup-constrained equations; these do not settle unrestricted conjugacy.
Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of unrestricted Diophantine problems in one-relator groups while explicitly retaining conjugacy as an open question.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general conjugacy problem remains open in the checked primary literature. This card fixes the uniform presentation-input formulation. The 2026 undecidability results cited concern different equation, membership or inverse-monoid problems.

context_blocks.text: A finite presentation describes a group through generators and identities. Here there is just one defining identity, but it can be reused inside arbitrarily long products. The conjugacy question asks whether two elements become equal after a change of reference element: u and v are equivalent when v=w⁻¹uw. It is one of Dehn’s classical decision problems. The 2025 survey explicitly identifies the general one-relator conjugacy problem as unresolved.

Conjugacy is already different from equality in a free group. The words ab and ba are conjugate, since a⁻¹(ab)a=ba, although they represent different free-group elements. At the opposite extreme, the identity element is conjugate only to itself. Consequently, a conjugacy algorithm also decides whether an input word represents the identity, by setting v to the empty word. The reverse implication is the difficult part.

Magnus’s 1932 theorem supplies a uniform algorithm for word equality in one-relator groups. Its inductive approach, clarified through the Magnus–Moldavanskii hierarchy, decomposes presentations into simpler group constructions. The corresponding transfer of conjugacy algorithms is much more delicate: the survey gives examples of HNN extensions and amalgams with undecidable conjugacy even though the relevant word problems are decidable. These examples explain a barrier to extending the proof; they are not one-relator counterexamples.

The known word algorithm does at least give a positive semidecision procedure for the present question. Enumerate all finite words w and test whether w⁻¹uwv⁻¹ represents the identity. If u and v are conjugate, a witness eventually appears. If they are not, this search continues forever. A complete decision procedure must also provide a way to terminate on every negative input.

Equivalently, one could give a computable uniform bound on the length of a shortest necessary conjugator as a function of the input length. Such a bound permits a finite search. Conversely, a decision procedure permits computing a bound: enumerate the finitely many inputs of bounded encoding length, identify the positive ones, and search for one witness for each. This observation concerns computability, without claiming that a useful or small bound follows.

The torsion case has been solved for decades. Newman’s 1968 thesis proves decidability of conjugacy for one-relator groups with torsion, including an extended conjugacy problem relative to specified subgroups. Standard presentations for this class have relator R^m with m≥2 and R not a proper power. The spelling theorem controls the possible cancellations strongly enough to support effective arguments. A solution for this class leaves the general torsion-free case to address.

A later structural theorem gives another source of negative certificates in the torsion case. Minasyan–Zalesskii prove that one-relator groups with torsion are hereditarily conjugacy separable: nonconjugate elements in every finite-index subgroup remain nonconjugate in some finite quotient of that subgroup. In particular, for the original group, a finite quotient can witness a negative conjugacy answer.

To see the algorithmic significance, enumerate finite multiplication tables and assignments of the presentation’s generators that satisfy its relator. Each assignment defines a homomorphism to a finite group, where conjugacy can be checked exhaustively. In a conjugacy-separable group, this search eventually finds a separating image for every nonconjugate pair. Run it alongside the search for a conjugator. The argument requires the separation property; finite images alone are not a general-purpose certificate system.

Recent developments illustrate why the exact decision problem matters. Gray–Levine prove undecidability of Diophantine problems in several classes close to one-relator groups, and also obtain undecidability with a fixed subgroup constraint in a one-relator group. General systems of equations, or restrictions on where variables may range, are more expressive than the single unrestricted conjugacy equation on this card. Undecidability for those tasks does not imply undecidability here.

Nyberg-Brodda’s August 3, 2026 preprint goes further: it proves that the unrestricted Diophantine problem is undecidable in certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. Its introduction still explicitly identifies general one-relator conjugacy as open. Undecidability for arbitrary systems of equations therefore cannot be substituted for undecidability of the special single conjugacy equation.

Gray–Reilly’s August 2026 preprint constructs two-generator one-relator inverse monoids with undecidable word problem. It also constructs a two-generator one-relator group with an undecidable prefix membership problem. Inverse monoids are a different algebraic structure, while prefix membership asks about a particular submonoid of the group. Neither result contradicts Magnus’s word algorithm or supplies a conjugacy counterexample.

The significance is a sharp computability boundary inside an extremely economical symbolic formalism. One defining group relation is sufficient to create complicated infinite behavior, yet ordinary equality remains decidable. Settling conjugacy would determine whether this additional existential search can always be controlled. A very slow total algorithm would answer the card; an efficient algorithm for a broad but restricted subclass would be progress without completing it.

cards.title: Isomorphism problem for one-relator groups
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given any two finite one-relator group presentations G=⟨x₁,…,x_k | r=1⟩ and H=⟨y₁,…,y_ℓ | s=1⟩, decides whether G and H are isomorphic as abstract groups?
cards.definitions: The input consists of integers k,ℓ≥1 and explicitly written finite words r and s in the respective generators and formal inverses. The groups are the free groups on these generators modulo the normal closures of r and s. An empty relator is permitted and presents a free group. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism of the resulting abstract groups; it need not carry a listed generator to a listed generator, preserve the spelling of a relator, or come from an automorphism of a free group on the given generators. The numbers of displayed generators may differ. The sought procedure is one deterministic Turing machine which halts and answers correctly on every valid pair of presentations. No polynomial-time, elementary-time or other quantitative runtime bound is imposed. There is no promise of torsion, hyperbolicity, nontrivial center, genericity or a supplied geometric decomposition.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such pairs, or prove that the isomorphism language on these one-relator presentations is undecidable. A procedure that halts only for isomorphic pairs, or one correct only on a specified subclass or almost all random presentations, is insufficient. Undecidability for arbitrary finite presentations, systems of equations or other algebraic structures must be connected to this exact input class by a valid reduction to count as a negative solution.
cards.why: One of the central decision problems for finitely presented groups, testing whether a single defining relation permits effective recognition of abstract algebraic structure.

importance.reason: A classical unresolved computability boundary with deep connections to geometric group theory, effective classification and the limitations of presentation-based invariants.

progress.text: Counterexamples to the Magnus conjecture show that free-group equivalence of relators cannot characterize all isomorphisms; torsion and center subclasses admit positive results.
Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain obtain strong generic rigidity and fast isomorphism algorithms for random one-relator groups.
Dahmani–Guirardel solve isomorphism for all hyperbolic groups, covering one-relator groups with torsion.
Linton–Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the unrestricted one-relator isomorphism problem as open.
Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability for the separate Diophantine problem in one-relator groups.
Kapovich’s preprint extends generic small-cancellation stability and isomorphism rigidity to fixed generator and relator counts.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform algorithm or undecidability theorem for isomorphism of arbitrary one-relator group presentations was found in the checked sources. The 2026 generic algorithms and Diophantine undecidability result do not settle this all-input isomorphism question.

context_blocks.text: A group presentation is a finite description of an often infinite algebraic object. The same group can have quite different descriptions: for example, ⟨a,b | b=a²⟩ and ⟨x | empty relator⟩ both describe an infinite cyclic group. The question is whether one defining relation leaves enough structure to recognize abstract equality of group types algorithmically, even when the supplied generators and words look unrelated.

This is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality compares elements within one fixed presentation; conjugacy asks for a particular kind of equivalence between elements; isomorphism compares the entire groups. Linton and Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the general one-relator isomorphism problem as open, despite broad positive results for subclasses.

The known uniform word algorithm gives a useful positive semidecision procedure. Enumerate possible word images u₁,…,u_k for the generators of G in H and v₁,…,v_ℓ for the generators of H in G. Check that the images satisfy each defining relation and that the two compositions fix every generator. Every check is a finite collection of word-equality tests. If mutual inverse homomorphisms exist, their finite descriptions eventually appear.

The missing part is termination on nonisomorphic inputs. Searching longer for generator images cannot certify that none exist. Equivalently, an effective bound on the lengths of some pair of mutually inverse generator-image tuples, depending only on the input length, would permit a finite search. Conversely, a total isomorphism algorithm would allow such a computable bound to be assembled by checking the finitely many inputs of bounded length and finding witnesses for the positive cases.

Easily computable invariants can reject some pairs. Abelianization, for example, takes the exponent sums of the relator and gives a finitely generated abelian quotient whose isomorphism type can be computed by integer linear algebra. But it is incomplete: the free group on two generators and ℤ² have the same abelianization, whereas one is nonabelian and the other is abelian. The free group is represented here using the allowed empty relator, and ℤ² by the commutator relation.

Another tempting simplification is to ask whether an automorphism of the free group carries one relator to the other, allowing inversion. Whitehead’s algorithm handles the corresponding orbit question. The survey explains that this sufficient condition is not necessary for isomorphism of the quotient groups: the Magnus conjecture asserting such a converse was disproved, and some groups have infinitely many inequivalent one-relator descriptions.

Hyperbolic groups form a large positive case. Dahmani and Guirardel solve isomorphism uniformly for all hyperbolic groups, including those with torsion. Their result also handles peripheral structures and automorphism computations, reflecting how geometric decompositions can organize otherwise unbounded searches. It is a decision theorem, not merely a heuristic for finding likely isomorphisms.

All one-relator groups with torsion are hyperbolic, so this theorem covers that entire subclass. The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center and other structured families. General torsion-free one-relator groups remain beyond these combined results. Even elementary examples such as ℤ² show that the one-relator condition does not imply hyperbolicity.

Generic-case results explain why many randomly generated instances may nevertheless be tractable. Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain establish rigidity for large classes of random one-relator presentations: isomorphism can be forced by simple transformations of the displayed generators and relator. The exceptional inputs are small in a specified distributional sense, but an undecidable set of inputs could still lie among such exceptions.

Kapovich’s August 18, 2026 preprint extends a generic rigidity program to fixed numbers of generators and relators. It gives an algorithmically recognizable generic family and a quadratic-time generic isomorphism algorithm, using small-cancellation stability and rigidity under free-group automorphisms. Its one-relator specialization is relevant progress, while its guarantee remains a generic one rather than a terminating decision procedure for every input.

A different August 2026 result by Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of the Diophantine problem for certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. That task asks whether arbitrary systems of equations with coefficients have solutions. It demonstrates that one relation does not ensure decidability of every natural algebraic question. However, it supplies no automatic reduction to isomorphism between two one-relator presentations, so the present problem remains distinct.

A resolution would clarify whether this very economical presentation format has an effective classification in principle. The positive answer could be extremely slow and still be decisive. The negative answer would require encoding undecidable information into abstract group type while retaining a single defining relator—a much more specific construction than demonstrating difficult equations inside one fixed group.

sentences: Two group presentations can describe the same abstract group despite using different generators and relations.
The reviewed question asks to decide isomorphism between arbitrary finite one-relator presentations.
Candidate mutually inverse homomorphisms can be enumerated and checked using the known word algorithm.
The missing ingredient is an effective way to stop when no such isomorphism exists.
A solution would distinguish complete algebraic types within this concise presentation class, extending beyond equality and conjugacy questions about elements of one already fixed group.

cards.context:
A group presentation is a finite description of an often infinite algebraic object. The same group can have quite different descriptions: for example, ⟨a,b | b=a²⟩ and ⟨x | empty relator⟩ both describe an infinite cyclic group. The question is whether one defining relation leaves enough structure to recognize abstract equality of group types algorithmically, even when the supplied generators and words look unrelated.

This is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality compares elements within one fixed presentation; conjugacy asks for a particular kind of equivalence between elements; isomorphism compares the entire groups. Linton and Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the general one-relator isomorphism problem as open, despite broad positive results for subclasses.

The known uniform word algorithm gives a useful positive semidecision procedure. Enumerate possible word images u₁,…,u_k for the generators of G in H and v₁,…,v_ℓ for the generators of H in G. Check that the images satisfy each defining relation and that the two compositions fix every generator. Every check is a finite collection of word-equality tests. If mutual inverse homomorphisms exist, their finite descriptions eventually appear.

The missing part is termination on nonisomorphic inputs. Searching longer for generator images cannot certify that none exist. Equivalently, an effective bound on the lengths of some pair of mutually inverse generator-image tuples, depending only on the input length, would permit a finite search. Conversely, a total isomorphism algorithm would allow such a computable bound to be assembled by checking the finitely many inputs of bounded length and finding witnesses for the positive cases.

Easily computable invariants can reject some pairs. Abelianization, for example, takes the exponent sums of the relator and gives a finitely generated abelian quotient whose isomorphism type can be computed by integer linear algebra. But it is incomplete: the free group on two generators and ℤ² have the same abelianization, whereas one is nonabelian and the other is abelian. The free group is represented here using the allowed empty relator, and ℤ² by the commutator relation.

Another tempting simplification is to ask whether an automorphism of the free group carries one relator to the other, allowing inversion. Whitehead’s algorithm handles the corresponding orbit question. The survey explains that this sufficient condition is not necessary for isomorphism of the quotient groups: the Magnus conjecture asserting such a converse was disproved, and some groups have infinitely many inequivalent one-relator descriptions.

Hyperbolic groups form a large positive case. Dahmani and Guirardel solve isomorphism uniformly for all hyperbolic groups, including those with torsion. Their result also handles peripheral structures and automorphism computations, reflecting how geometric decompositions can organize otherwise unbounded searches. It is a decision theorem, not merely a heuristic for finding likely isomorphisms.

All one-relator groups with torsion are hyperbolic, so this theorem covers that entire subclass. The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center and other structured families. General torsion-free one-relator groups remain beyond these combined results. Even elementary examples such as ℤ² show that the one-relator condition does not imply hyperbolicity.

Generic-case results explain why many randomly generated instances may nevertheless be tractable. Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain establish rigidity for large classes of random one-relator presentations: isomorphism can be forced by simple transformations of the displayed generators and relator. The exceptional inputs are small in a specified distributional sense, but an undecidable set of inputs could still lie among such exceptions.

Kapovich’s August 18, 2026 preprint extends a generic rigidity program to fixed numbers of generators and relators. It gives an algorithmically recognizable generic family and a quadratic-time generic isomorphism algorithm, using small-cancellation stability and rigidity under free-group automorphisms. Its one-relator specialization is relevant progress, while its guarantee remains a generic one rather than a terminating decision procedure for every input.

A different August 2026 result by Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of the Diophantine problem for certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. That task asks whether arbitrary systems of equations with coefficients have solutions. It demonstrates that one relation does not ensure decidability of every natural algebraic question. However, it supplies no automatic reduction to isomorphism between two one-relator presentations, so the present problem remains distinct.

A resolution would clarify whether this very economical presentation format has an effective classification in principle. The positive answer could be extremely slow and still be decisive. The negative answer would require encoding undecidable information into abstract group type while retaining a single defining relator—a much more specific construction than demonstrating difficult equations inside one fixed group.

cards.definitions: For every integer n≥1 the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with 0≤a,b<2^n; leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let t_M(n) be its maximum running time over the 2^(2n) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A matching rate g(n)>0 means some correct M has t_M(n)=O(g(n)), while every correct M has t_M(n)=Ω(g(n)); constants and thresholds may depend on M. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only O(n).
cards.answer_criterion: Give an asymptotic rate g(n) and prove both the existence of a single correct deterministic multitape machine running in O(g(n)) worst-case time and an Ω(g(n)) worst-case lower bound for every correct machine. This asks for matching bounds up to multiplicative constants, not necessarily the particular rate n log n. An upper bound without a matching universal lower bound, or a lower bound for a restricted computational model, is a partial result.

context_blocks.title: A familiar operation with an unknown limit
context_blocks.text: For example, 11₂ multiplied by 11₂ is 1001₂: the input integers are 3 and 3, and the exact product is 9. The question asks how the cost grows when each input contains millions or many more bits. The school multiplication procedure performs quadratically many elementary digit operations. That describes one procedure, not a lower bound on every possible algorithm.

context_blocks.title: Bits and data movement are charged
context_blocks.text: A machine instruction that multiplies two arbitrarily large integers in one step would make the question trivial by placing the entire task inside the instruction set. Here each tape head accesses one cell at a time. Arithmetic on long numbers and rearranging their bits therefore take time. The explicit output alone gives a linear lower bound. It does not establish the additional logarithmic factor in the best known upper bound.

context_blocks.title: What the O(n log n) theorem settles
context_blocks.text: Harvey and van der Hoeven proved that binary integer multiplication takes O(n log n) time in this multitape model. Their 2021 theorem settles the upper-bound conjecture associated with Schönhage and Strassen. It does not prove that all algorithms require this much time. The 2025 paper by the same authors states that even a superlinear lower bound remains unknown in the unrestricted multitape model. The gap is between a linear lower bound and an n log n upper bound.

context_blocks.title: The matrix-transposition connection
context_blocks.text: A 2025 theorem relates multiplication to moving data: transposing an s×s binary matrix written row by row. Even a 2×2 matrix with entries a,b,c,d changes its row-order encoding from abcd to acbd. If every multitape machine needs Ω(s² log s) time for the general transposition task, their theorem implies Ω(n log n) time for multiplication. The transposition premise is itself unproved, so this is a conditional relationship between lower bounds, not an unconditional proof of multiplication’s optimality.

context_blocks.title: Which later results concern this question
context_blocks.text: Qin’s August 2026 result bounds the width of ordered binary decision diagrams computing a middle product bit on restricted inputs. Width in that model does not bound the running time of every multitape machine. Likewise, arithmetic-operation counts and performance on typical or small inputs answer other questions. This card concerns exact products, the worst input at each length, and one fixed algorithm working at all lengths.

cards.title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
cards.formal: For every n≥1 and every tensor T∈ℂ^n⊗ℂ^n⊗ℂ^n whose three flattenings all have rank n, is lim_{k→∞} R(T^⊗k)^(1/k)=n?
cards.definitions: R(T) is the least r such that T=Σ_{i=1}^r a_i⊗b_i⊗c_i with a_i,b_i,c_i∈ℂ^n. Each flattening views the tensor as a linear map from the dual of one factor into the tensor product of the other two. In T^⊗k the first, second and third tensor factors are respectively grouped, producing a tensor with three factors ℂ^(n^k). Submultiplicativity of rank makes the displayed limit equal to inf_{k≥1} R(T^⊗k)^(1/k). This is exact rank over ℂ, not border rank, and there is no explicitness or computational requirement on T.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank has a simple algebraic characterization, whereas tensor rank changes substantially when many independent copies are considered jointly. Strassen’s conjecture says that in the asymptotic setting the three flattening dimensions already determine the answer.

The cubic concise formulation is the target proposed in the personal list. It includes matrix-multiplication tensors, so a positive resolution would imply matrix multiplication exponent two; the reverse implication is not claimed. The 2024–2026 source studies structural properties of asymptotic rank without proving this equality.

cards.definitions: For n≥1 set ω_n=exp(−2πi/n), and define DFT_n(x)_j=Σ_{k=0}^{n−1}ω_n^{jk}x_k for j=0,…,n−1 and x∈ℂ^n. This is the unnormalized cyclic DFT. A straight-line program is a finite acyclic list of scalar instructions. Each instruction either adds, subtracts or multiplies two previously available values, or multiplies one value by a fixed complex scalar. Input coordinates and any fixed complex constants are available initially. Values may be reused without limit, and all n required output coordinates must occur among the computed values. Size is the number of instructions; each complex scalar operation costs one, regardless of operand magnitude. The sequence and all constants may depend on n but not on x. Constants need not be efficiently generated or have a bounded bit representation. There is no restriction on circuit depth, reuse, storage, intermediate magnitudes or numerical conditioning. Operations are exact and must compute the required polynomial identities for every complex input. This is the standard division-free arithmetic-circuit formulation used to make the imported model precise; subtraction and multiplication by any reciprocal constant are allowed. No comparison, branching, floor, bit extraction, approximation or quantum operation is present. For this linear output map, allowing products of input-dependent intermediate values changes minimum size by at most a constant factor compared with linear circuits using only addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, as stated in the cited circuit reference. Counting a two-input linear combination as one instruction instead of at most three also changes cost only by a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform lower bound for every sufficiently large power-of-two length and every program in the stated model, or refute it. Precisely, a refutation must show that for every c>0 and every threshold N there is a power of two n≥N and a program of size less than c n log₂n. A family using o(n log n) operations would suffice, but the full logical negation does not require a uniformly generated family or such a bound at every length. A lower bound requiring bounded coefficients, unitary gates, limited storage or numerical stability does not establish the target.

context_blocks.title: A fast transform reuses intermediate values
context_blocks.text: For four inputs, form a=x₀+x₂, b=x₁+x₃, c=x₀−x₂ and d=x₁−x₃. The four Fourier outputs are a+b, c−id, a−b and c+id. Shared sums let the same work serve several output coordinates. The classical FFT extends this reuse to obtain O(n log n) operations; the question is whether a different unrestricted program can do asymptotically better.

context_blocks.title: Normalization should not decide this question
context_blocks.text: Dividing all outputs by √n gives the normalized DFT. In the unbounded-scalar model, converting either normalization to the other costs at most n extra operations, so the conjectured asymptotic lower bound is equivalent for the two. A lower-bound argument tied to one normalization may nevertheless fail for the other when its coefficients are restricted.

context_blocks.title: What the classical lower bound assumes
context_blocks.text: Morgenstern’s lower bound, recalled in both full sources, gives order n log n for the unnormalized transform when scalar magnitudes have a fixed bound. The determinant magnitude of that transform is n^{n/2}, whereas the normalized matrix has determinant magnitude one. Arbitrarily large scalars invalidate the bounded per-operation growth used by that result. Thus the known theorem does not already settle this card.

Subsequent results relate possible speedup to numerical ill-conditioning. These are meaningful restrictions on computations; the present model permits general arithmetic, arbitrary reuse and large intermediate values, so those lower bounds have a narrower scope.

It does not give an unrestricted DFT operation lower bound. Counting only multiplications, approximating Fourier outputs at fixed precision, or applying a quantum Fourier transform to state amplitudes also asks a different question from computing this entire classical complex output vector.

cards.title: Cubic min-plus circuit lower bounds for shortest paths
cards.formal: For n >= 2, assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight x_{ij} to every unordered edge {i,j} of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates x_{ij} and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates min(a,b) or a+b, unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute f_n exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let s(n) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is s(n)=Omega(n^3)? Equivalently, do there exist constants c>0 and n0 such that every such circuit has at least c n^3 gates for every n>=n0?
cards.definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences x_{ij} and x_{ji} denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every c>0 and every n0 there is an n>=n0 with a correct circuit using fewer than c n^3 gates. An o(n^3)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.
cards.why: This is a basic unconditional lower-bound question for dynamic programming. A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.

importance.reason: A central explicit lower-bound problem for tropical circuits, linking shortest paths, pure dynamic programming, and provenance computation. The gap concerns a basic polynomial-time task rather than a specialized graph family.

context_blocks.text: The numerical task is elementary to state: return one shortest-path distance. The difficulty is understanding what can be done by a fixed network of minimum and addition operations. An algorithm that chooses which vertex to process next using comparisons may use information to control its future computation. This circuit model cannot turn the identity of a minimum into arbitrary control flow. Consequently, a fast implementation of a graph-search algorithm does not automatically supply a circuit of comparable size.

A concrete upper bound comes from repeated relaxation. Initialize d_0(1)=0 and d_0(v)=infinity otherwise, and compute d_k(v)=min(d_{k-1}(v), min over u distinct from v of d_{k-1}(u)+x_{uv}). After n-1 layers, output d_{n-1}(n). Each layer uses O(n^2) gates. Nonnegative weights ensure that deleting cycles cannot increase a walk’s cost, so these layers suffice for the simple-path optimum. This gives O(n^3) gates.

Every edge can influence the answer: choose a simple source-to-target path through that edge, make its other edges cheap, and all edges outside the path expensive. Thus dependence on the quadratic number of inputs gives a quadratic lower bound, but does not charge separately for repeated reuse of intermediate computations. The missing factor n is the substantive issue.

For all-pairs shortest paths, a cubic lower bound is known in the same general min-plus framework. Its many required outputs are essential to the usual argument; requesting only the distance from 1 to n leaves room for different sharing. The database formulation places the question in absorptive semirings, where adding an unnecessary detour is absorbed. This card fixes the nonnegative tropical instance so that its allowed operations and output are unambiguous.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for integer multiplication
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and n₀≥1 such that, for every integer n≥n₀, a Boolean circuit of at most Cn gates maps every pair of n-bit unsigned integers to all 2n bits of their exact product?
cards.definitions: The circuit has input bits a₀,…,a_{n−1},b₀,…,b_{n−1}, representing a=Σᵢaᵢ2ⁱ and b=Σᵢbᵢ2ⁱ, and output bits c₀,…,c_{2n−1} satisfying Σⱼcⱼ2ʲ=ab. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; constants 0 and 1 are allowed. Size counts gates, excluding input nodes and output wires. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. There is one circuit for each n, with no uniformity requirement on how these circuits are generated. Every input must be answered exactly, with no randomness. Leading zeros are permitted. Let M(n) be the minimum gate count in this model; the proposition is M(n)=O(n). Changing to any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes size by only a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified linear-size upper bound, or prove its negation: for every C and every n₀ there is n≥n₀ with M(n)>Cn. A lower bound c·n with fixed c, a lower bound for bounded depth or restricted wiring, or a limitation of a particular multiplication algorithm does not give the required negative answer. A uniform linear-bit-time algorithm would imply the upper bound, but is a stronger demand than the existence of these nonuniform circuits.

context_blocks.text: Addition admits circuits whose gate count grows linearly with the input width. Multiplication is another elementary arithmetic operation, but the corresponding linear-size bound remains unknown. Goldreich singles it out immediately after the general challenge of proving a superlinear Boolean-circuit lower bound for an explicit function.

The circuit computes every output bit, including carries and the most significant half of the product. Treating a multiplication instruction on a whole machine word as one operation would hide the work being measured. The target concerns exact Boolean computation at individual-bit granularity.

Viola’s author manuscript, carrying a 2023–2026 revision notice, explicitly retains the linear-size multiplication question in Section 4.2. It also proves that multiplication and squaring are equivalent for this linear-size threshold: multiplication gives squaring immediately, and the converse uses squares together with linear-size addition and subtraction.

A negative answer would give a superlinear lower bound for a particularly concrete, efficiently computable family of multi-output Boolean functions. It would apply even to circuits tailored separately to each input length. A positive answer would show that the familiar logarithmic overhead of fast multiplication constructions is not necessary in this circuit model.

The existing TCS-7174 asks for optimal time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine. This card asks only about nonuniform gate count. The archived Karatsuba entry TCS-5168 concerns a reversible pebbling tradeoff, and TCS-6494 asks for a particular reduction from matrix transposition; neither is this unrestricted linear-size question.

cards.title: Exponential multilinear-formula lower bounds for the permanent
cards.formal: Does there exist c>0 such that, for every sufficiently large n, every multilinear arithmetic formula over ℂ computing perm_n has at least 2^(cn) gates?
cards.definitions: The permanent is perm_n(X)=Σ_{π∈S_n}∏_{i=1}^n x_{i,π(i)}. An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted tree with variable or complex-constant leaves and binary addition or multiplication gates, evaluated as a commutative polynomial. Every gate must compute a multilinear polynomial: every variable has degree at most one in every monomial after cancellation. The formula must agree identically with perm_n on ℂ^(n²), not merely on Boolean inputs. Size counts all gates, including leaves. No restriction on the numerical complexity of complex constants is imposed.

context_blocks.text: Multilinear formulas give a restricted but important setting in which superpolynomial lower bounds are known for an explicit central polynomial. The exponential target asks how far that separation can be taken even after substantial algebraic structure is imposed.

Raz’s lower bound grows as n^{Ω(log n)}, which is superpolynomial but not exponential in n. The broader permanent circuit problem permits sharing subcomputations and intermediate nonmultilinear polynomials, so these are not interchangeable targets. The survey records the unresolved exponential strengthening.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, given any integer-coefficient polynomial f(X₁,…,Xₘ), always halts and correctly decides whether $\exists (q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m:f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0$? The number of variables and polynomial degree are unrestricted parts of the finite input.
cards.definitions: Encode m≥1 and a finite list of monomials, each with a signed binary integer coefficient and an m-tuple of nonnegative binary exponents. Repeated monomials may be combined effectively; zero polynomials are allowed. A rational solution consists of exact fractions qᵢ=aᵢ/bᵢ, where aᵢ∈ℤ and bᵢ is a positive integer, with no prescribed bound on numerators or denominators. The required algorithm is one finite deterministic program, independent of m, degree, and coefficients. It must return yes exactly when a rational zero exists and no otherwise; it may use any finite amount of time and space on each input. Malformed encodings are rejected. The task supplies no oracle, height inequalities, integrality constraints on the unknowns, or promise of a solution. Rational coefficients would give an equivalent problem by clearing coefficient denominators. A finite system f₁=⋯=fᵣ=0 is equivalent over ℚ to the single equation f₁²+⋯+fᵣ²=0.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is a fundamental boundary between algorithmic arithmetic and undecidability. It asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver, connecting computation, logical definability, and the arithmetic geometry of rational points.

importance.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively. The rational-solution analogue remains distinct.
Koenigsmann gives a universal first-order definition of ℤ in ℚ and related low-quantifier undecidability results. This does not supply an existential definition.
Anscombe and coauthors survey local-global methods and explicitly identify Hilbert’s tenth problem over number fields, including ℚ, as open.
Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove undecidability after adjoining finitely many height-comparison conditions. Those extra conditions are not part of ordinary rational solvability.

Rank-stability advances imply undecidability over rings of integers of all number fields. Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the proof and gives an alternative Diophantine-definability argument; the domains remain rings of integers.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be enumerated by increasing bounds on their numerators and denominators, and substitution into an integer polynomial is exact and computable. Thus yes-instances can already be recognized eventually. The difficulty is knowing when to stop searching and certify that no rational point exists. The question asks about computability itself, before any requirement of efficiency.

Hilbert’s original problem required integer solutions. Matiyasevich’s completion of the Davis–Putnam–Robinson program proves that version undecidable. Permitting fractions changes the problem: a polynomial can have a rational zero and no integer zero, so applying a rational solver directly to the same equation would not decide the integer problem. A reduction must encode the missing integrality restriction using only the allowed rational polynomial equations.

An existential definition of ℤ inside ℚ would provide such an encoding and imply undecidability. Koenigsmann instead gives a universal definition of the integers, which is a major advance in definability but uses a different quantifier form. The full first-order theory of ℚ is already undecidable; the unresolved target concerns its existential fragment.

Recent results settle the analogous problem over the ring of integers of every number field. A ring of integers restricts denominators; it is not the whole number field. In particular the ring of integers of ℚ is ℤ, so this breakthrough does not decide the question on this card. Poonen’s July 2026 account explains how rank stability of abelian varieties yields the required Diophantine definitions for those rings.

Other nearby formulations add conditions comparing heights of rational coordinates. Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove an undecidability result with finitely many such conditions. Their formulation includes predicates absent here, and their paper explicitly retains ordinary Hilbert’s tenth problem over ℚ as open. This distinction matters when interpreting a result whose title refers to undecidable effectivity for rational points.
