cards.title: Capacity of the binary deletion channel
cards.formal: Determine the capacity function C(δ) of the binary independent deletion channel for every fixed δ∈[0,1], in bits per input bit.
cards.definitions: For input x=x₁⋯x_n∈{0,1}^n, retain each bit independently with probability 1−δ and output the retained subsequence in its original order. The receiver sees the subsequence and its length, but neither terminal sees the deletion locations; there are no erasure markers, substitutions, insertions, feedback or side channels. Both terminals know n and δ. A block code consists of deterministic maps Enc_n:[M_n]→{0,1}^n and Dec_n:⋃_{k=0}^n{0,1}^k→[M_n]. Its average error is Pr[Dec_n(Y)≠M], where M is uniform on [M_n] and Y is the channel output on Enc_n(M). A rate R is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with liminf_{n→∞}(log₂ M_n)/n≥R and average error tending to zero. Define C(δ) as the supremum of achievable nonnegative rates. Encoding and decoding have no computational or storage restrictions. The parameter δ is fixed as n grows. Equivalently, Dobrushin’s coding theorem gives C(δ)=lim_{n→∞} C_n(δ), where C_n(δ)=(1/n) max_{P_X on {0,1}^n} I(X;Y), with base-two mutual information. These C_n are normalized per input bit; the random output length is not the normalization. The endpoints are C(0)=1 and C(1)=0.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real δ∈[0,1], and prove in Lean that |g−C(δ)|≤1/100 pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.
cards.why: The simplest channel with hidden synchronization errors still lacks an exact nontrivial capacity formula. Resolving it would establish how much information is fundamentally lost through missing alignment.

context_blocks.text: A deletion removes a bit and also hides where it belonged. For example, receiving 00 after sending three bits is compatible with several input strings and deletion patterns. The output length reveals how many symbols survived, but it does not reveal their positions. This uncertainty couples the interpretation of consecutive output symbols even though the deletion decisions themselves are independent.

If the receiver were additionally given the deletion locations, the channel would become the binary erasure channel with capacity 1−δ. Revealing information cannot make decoding harder, so C(δ)≤1−δ is an immediate upper bound. The challenge is to quantify the further loss caused by missing alignment. Counting surviving bits alone therefore does not determine the answer.

The basic coding theorem is known. Optimizing mutual information over distributions on n-bit inputs and letting n grow gives the operational capacity. Moreover, C_n(δ)−log₂(n+1)/n≤C(δ)≤C_n(δ). Thus the issue is not the absence of a definition or an approximation scheme in principle. The finite optimization has 2^n possible inputs, and its rapidly growing size obstructs useful evaluation at large block lengths.

The input bits should not automatically be assumed independent. Correlations can make runs of equal symbols easier to identify after deletions. Run-based constructions choose a distribution on run lengths and analyze how deleted runs disappear and neighboring surviving runs merge. Rubinstein and Con optimize such distributions to prove C(δ)>0.1221(1−δ) for every 0<δ<1. This establishes a positive constant fraction of the surviving-bit rate throughout the parameter range.

Near the noiseless endpoint, a much sharper asymptotic description is available. Kanoria and Montanari prove C(δ)=1+δ log₂ δ−A₁δ+A₂δ²+O(δ^{3−ε}) for every fixed ε>0 as δ tends to zero, with explicit constants A₁≈1.15416377 and A₂≈1.67814594. They also identify input distributions achieving this order. This determines several leading terms, but its remainder does not vanish identically at a fixed nonzero deletion probability.

Numerical converse bounds use finite channels in which the input and output lengths are bounded and the transition matrix is explicit. Blahut–Arimoto optimization can bound their capacities, which in turn upper-bound the unsegmented deletion channel. Pinto and Ribeiro’s 2026 implementation handles larger instances, including selected input lengths of 31, and reports C(δ)≤0.3578(1−δ) for δ≥0.64. These are computer-assisted bounds reported by the authors; this review has not rerun their large computations.

The half-deletion point illustrates the remaining gap. Rubinstein and Con report an achievable rate above 0.104075, while the 2026 upper-bound table gives 0.1896. A universal lower bound proportional to 1−δ is useful for the whole curve, but it can be weaker than a pointwise run-length optimization. These different types of statements should therefore not be collapsed into one purported best numerical bound for every parameter.

An August 2026 preprint by Chen claims a further half-deletion lower bound above 0.11032415, using joint information from several output runs and a rational certificate. Its asserted slightly sharper upper number is conditional on a precision assumption about a previously published table. This card records the new lower bound as a preprint claim whose certificate has not been independently reproduced here, and does not present the conditional upper number as a separately established converse. Even if the new lower bound is confirmed, a substantial gap remains.

This is a transmission problem: the sender may select a codebook designed for the channel. Trace reconstruction instead starts with an arbitrary unknown string and observes repeated independently deleted copies of that same string. Adversarial deletion codes also use a different error model. Progress in either neighboring subject can be informative without giving the capacity curve with the certified accuracy required here.

cards.title: Binary codes beyond the Gilbert–Varshamov bound
cards.formal: Do constants δ∈(0,1/2) and η>0 and binary codes C_n⊆{0,1}^n for arbitrarily large n exist with minimum Hamming distance at least δn and log₂|C_n|/n≥1−H₂(δ)+η?
cards.definitions: A code is any nonempty subset of the binary strings of length n; linearity, explicit construction and efficient decoding are not required. Hamming distance is the number of unequal coordinates, and minimum distance is the minimum over distinct codewords. H₂(t)=−t log₂t−(1−t)log₂(1−t). The constants δ and η must be chosen before n and remain fixed along an unbounded sequence of block lengths. Finite-length improvements vanishing in normalized rate do not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: The Gilbert–Varshamov bound describes a rate-distance tradeoff achievable by random binary codes. Whether an asymptotically better tradeoff exists is a fundamental question about the information lost to adversarial errors.

This is a nonconstructive existence question, independent of whether codes meeting the bound can be efficiently written down. A polynomial improvement in the number of codewords at fixed length need not yield a positive constant improvement in rate. The coding-course materials distinguish these two open challenges.

cards.title: Decidability of unconditional Shannon information inequalities
cards.formal: Does a Turing algorithm exist that, given n≥1 and rational coefficients (a_S) for nonempty subsets S⊆{1,…,n}, always halts and decides whether Σ_{∅≠S⊆[n]}a_S H(X_S)≥0 holds for every joint distribution of n finite-valued discrete random variables?
cards.definitions: The finite input lists n and all nonzero coefficients, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator, with its subset S encoded explicitly; omitted coefficients are zero. X_S is the tuple (X_i)_{i∈S}. Its Shannon entropy in bits is H(X_S)=−Σ_x p_S(x)log₂ p_S(x), with 0log₂0=0. Each variable has a finite alphabet, but alphabet sizes are unrestricted and are not supplied as bounds in the input. Joint probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers in [0,1] summing to one. No independence, conditional-independence, functional-dependence, fixed-marginal or support-size promise is imposed. The inequality is a single homogeneous linear inequality, with non-strict ≥0 and no affine constant, premise, disjunction or nonlinear entropy term. cards.status_note: Open for a single unconditional homogeneous rational linear inequality over all finite-valued distributions, based on primary sources and a later-result check through 11 September 2026. Invalidity is semidecidable. Conditional undecidability, restricted set-function domains and inequality-generation algorithms do not establish undecidability or decidability of this exact problem.

context_blocks.text: For a given distribution, each subset of variables has an entropy. Collecting these numbers produces one point in a space with 2^n−1 coordinates. The question asks whether an input linear halfspace contains every such point, across all finite alphabets and distributions. It is therefore a question about all possible information structures, rather than about estimating entropies from a dataset.

Familiar examples are easy to express in this format. Subadditivity is H(X₁)+H(X₂)−H(X₁,X₂)≥0. Conditional mutual information is H(X₁,X₃)+H(X₂,X₃)−H(X₃)−H(X₁,X₂,X₃)≥0. Both hold without a premise. A negative coefficient is perfectly legitimate; it is the full linear combination, rather than each individual summand, whose sign is being decided.

The standard Shannon inequalities give a finite linear-programming proof method for each n. They express nonnegative conditional entropies and conditional mutual informations, or equivalently normalized monotone submodular set functions. If a candidate follows from them, it is universally valid. But the first non-Shannon inequality of Zhang–Yeung showed in 1998 that this proof method is incomplete. Rejecting an attempted Shannon derivation therefore cannot be used as a negative answer about entropy validity.

The unrestricted alphabet quantifier is a major part of the difficulty. A computation on binary variables explores only a small portion of the permitted distributions. Increasing a guessed alphabet bound may discover new counterexamples, but an unsuccessful search at every bound examined so far provides no effective stopping criterion. A solution cannot quietly replace all finite alphabets by one fixed support limit depending on a heuristic.

There is a rigorous semidecision procedure for invalidity. If an inequality is false, it is strictly negative at some distribution with finite alphabets. Entropy is continuous on that finite probability simplex, so a sufficiently close rational distribution still violates it. Enumerate alphabet sizes and rational distributions, and compute certified entropy approximations of increasing precision. Eventually the negative value is certified. The arithmetical-hierarchy study of Abo Khamis–Kolaitis–Ngo–Suciu places validity in co-r.e.

This explains precisely what a positive solution would add: a way to halt on every valid inequality as well. A complete effective enumeration of proofs of all valid inequalities, coupled with the counterexample search, would suffice. Existing automated methods can produce many correct certificates, but no completeness theorem for all rational unconditional inequalities is supplied by the inspected sources.

Taking the topological closure of the entropic region does not change this particular validity problem. A continuous linear form nonnegative on every entropic point is nonnegative on every limit point, and the reverse implication is immediate. Thus the same unconditional linear inequalities hold for entropic and almost-entropic vectors. This observation depends on the exact logical form; it does not authorize replacing the domain inside arbitrary conditional statements.

Cheuk Ting Li’s 2023 theorem establishes undecidability for conditional information inequalities and conditional-independence implication. Those inputs include premises that must hold exactly. Merely deleting a premise changes the statement. The theorem therefore does not by itself establish undecidability of a single unconditional inequality.

Adding a fixed penalty for violating a premise need not capture its limiting behavior. Kaced–Romashchenko explicitly show essentially conditional inequalities that do not extend to unconditional linear inequalities in the proposed manner. Their results explain why this seemingly direct route from conditional to unconditional validity needs additional justification.

Hannula’s 2024 work studies useful decidable simplifications: different classes of set functions and syntactic forms connected to database bounds. Its coNP-completeness result is for normal polymatroids, a restricted semantic domain, while another polynomial-time result uses monotone functions. These are precise complexity results for different domains, not a classification of validity over all entropy vectors.

The connection to databases gives the question an algorithmic role beyond coding theory. Entropy inequalities constrain how large a relational join can be under information about its inputs and degrees. Related logical forms occur in query containment and dependency implication. Understanding which constraints admit complete reasoning procedures helps explain why some query bounds can be computed effectively while broader formulations encounter undecidability.

The 2025 exploration by László Csirmaz compares the Copy Lemma, maximum-entropy constructions and the Ahlswede–Körner method, and leaves their completeness unresolved. Előd P. Csirmaz and László Csirmaz’s 2026 paper derives two infinite collections of five-variable inequalities and computes consequences through nine generations of its construction. Its enumeration concerns that method’s extremal inequalities; even the proposed characterization of the method is not a characterization of the entire entropy region.

cards.title: Capacity of the general two-user interference channel
cards.formal: Determine F_IC(W,λ)=sup_{(R₁,R₂)∈C_IC(W)}[λR₁+(1−λ)R₂] for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-user interference channel W and every real λ∈[0,1], with independent private messages and no feedback, in the model below.
cards.context:
Two sender–receiver pairs share a channel, but each sender initially knows only its own independent message. This separates interference from broadcasting, where one encoder knows both messages. The full rate tradeoff matters because improving one receiver’s rate can reduce the other’s.

The weighted capacity function describes all supporting directions of the capacity region. The fixed numerical tolerance makes the desired approximation explicit without imposing a one-letter formula or restricting the coding scheme. The original Han–Kobayashi reference supplies a fundamental inner bound, not a general matching converse. Gaussian interference is a separately significant continuous-alphabet model, and discretizing it requires its own approximation argument.

cards.definitions: A channel consists of nonempty finite alphabets X₁,X₂,Y₁,Y₂ and real probabilities W(y₁,y₂|x₁,x₂)≥0 summing to one over (y₁,y₂) for each input pair. Conditional on the input sequences, n uses have product law ∏_{t=1}^n W(y₁,t,y₂,t|x₁,t,x₂,t). Messages Mᵢ are independent and uniform on {1,…,Kᵢ,n}. Encoder i is a deterministic map from its own message to Xᵢ^n; receiver i uses a deterministic decoder Yᵢ^n→{1,…,Kᵢ,n}. Error is the probability that at least one receiver estimates its message incorrectly, averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A nonnegative pair (R₁,R₂) is achievable when codes on block lengths n_j→∞ have error tending to zero and liminf_j (log₂Kᵢ,n_j)/n_j≥Rᵢ for i=1,2. C_IC(W) is the closure of achievable pairs. Both codebooks and W are known at all terminals. There is no common message, output feedback, transmitter or receiver cooperation, input cost or computational restriction. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The region is compact, convex and downward closed; its nonnegative supporting values for λ∈[0,1] determine it exactly. F_IC is measured in bits per joint channel use. The task quantifies over arbitrary real channel laws as mathematical objects; no finite-precision input or algorithmic evaluation model is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on every channel W defined below and every real λ∈[0,1], and prove in Lean that |g−F_IC(W,λ)|≤1/100 pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.

cards.title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
cards.formal: Do there exist constants r∈(0,1], δ∈(0,1/2) and A>0 such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with k≤n≤k/r, an encoding C:{0,1}^k→{0,1}^n, and randomized local decoders Dec_i for i∈{1,…,k}, satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word z∈{0,1}^n differing from C(x) in fewer than δn positions, and every requested index i, Dec_i with oracle access to z outputs x_i with probability at least 2/3 while making at most ⌈A log₂(n+1)⌉ bit queries on every execution.
cards.why: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.

cards.definitions: Here k counts message bits and n counts stored codeword bits; rate is k/n and Hamming distance counts unequal coordinates. “Arbitrarily large” means that every threshold K is exceeded by an admissible k; the constants r, δ and A must be fixed before K. The encoding is deterministic and injective. A decoder knows C, k, n and the requested index, but learns the received word only by querying named coordinates, each returning one bit. Queries may be adaptive. A randomized decoder can be represented as a probability distribution over finite binary decision trees with the stated depth bound, whose leaves output 0 or 1. Computation, description length and encoding time are unrestricted: this is the source’s existence question, without an additional requirement of efficient uniform construction. The success guarantee is separate for each triple (x,z,i); it does not require one random seed to recover all bits simultaneously. The adversary may choose corruptions knowing x and C, but z is fixed before the decoder’s private randomness. There is no secret key, channel-computation bound or input-dependent auxiliary information. The decoder must return the requested bit, rather than an erasure or a list of candidates.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family with all the stated fixed constants and guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A negative result must exclude every choice of positive constant rate, positive constant error tolerance and logarithmic-query constant for unbounded message lengths. A construction over a growing alphabet or a decoder that may fail on some requested positions under the allowed corruption guarantee does not establish the proposition.

context_blocks.title: Recover one item without reading everything
context_blocks.text: A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

context_blocks.title: Why simple repetition does not suffice
context_blocks.text: Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

context_blocks.title: The remaining query gap
context_blocks.text: The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses 2^{O(√(log n·log log n))} queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

context_blocks.title: Related decoding guarantees
context_blocks.text: The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.

cards.title: Rate–distortion tradeoff for distributed lossy source coding
cards.formal: Determine F_RD(P,d₁,d₂,D₁,D₂,λ)=inf_{(R₁,R₂)∈R(P,d₁,d₂,D₁,D₂)}[λR₁+(1−λ)R₂] for every finite-alphabet memoryless source pair, finite per-symbol distortion tables, feasible distortion targets and λ∈[0,1], where R is the separate-encoder joint-decoder rate–distortion region defined below.
cards.context:
Separate encoders cannot coordinate their descriptions by inspecting one another’s source blocks, even though the decoder can use both descriptions together. Correlation can therefore save rate while creating a tradeoff between the two encoders. Allowing a controlled reconstruction loss gives a different problem from exact recovery.

This card represents the lower boundary of the rate region by its minimum weighted rate. Distortion targets below the minimum attainable expected per-symbol distortion are excluded explicitly, so the target stays finite. The numerical tolerance is in compression-rate units, with the distortion constraints themselves kept exact. The known lossless and single-sided side-information cases do not determine the general two-source lossy tradeoff.

cards.definitions: The source alphabets X₁,X₂ and reproduction alphabets X̂₁,X̂₂ are nonempty finite sets. P is an arbitrary real joint probability table on X₁×X₂, and the pairs (X₁,t,X₂,t) are independent draws from P over time. Each dᵢ:Xᵢ×X̂ᵢ→ℝ≥0 is a finite-valued distortion table. Let Pᵢ be the marginal law and Dᵢ,min=∑_{x∈Xᵢ}Pᵢ(x) min_{z∈X̂ᵢ}dᵢ(x,z). The domain has finite Dᵢ≥Dᵢ,min and real λ∈[0,1]. An n-block code has two deterministic maps fᵢ:Xᵢ^n→{1,…,Mᵢ,n} and one deterministic decoder mapping the two indices to (X̂₁^n,X̂₂^n). Encoder i observes only its own source block; the encoders cannot communicate or see the other block. Define average distortion Δᵢ,n=(1/n)∑_{t=1}^n E[dᵢ(Xᵢ,t,X̂ᵢ,t)], with expectation over the iid source pair. cards.formal: Determine Θ(C₇)=sup_{t≥1} α(C₇^{⊠t})^{1/t}, the zero-error Shannon capacity of the seven-cycle, where the graph power and independence number are defined below.
cards.context:
Shannon capacity measures how many mutually distinguishable messages can be encoded across repeated uses of a confusability graph. cards.definitions: C₇ has vertex set {0,…,6}, with distinct vertices adjacent when their difference modulo 7 is 1 or 6. For an integer t≥1, the strong power has vertex set {0,…,6}^t. Two distinct tuples are adjacent when, in every coordinate, their entries are equal or adjacent in C₇. An independent set contains no adjacent distinct pair, and α is its maximum cardinality. The capacity is measured in distinguishable symbols per channel use, rather than its logarithm in bits. It lies between 3 and 7; the supremum need not occur at a finite power. There is no computational restriction on independent sets or their construction.

cards.definitions: W is a table of arbitrary real conditional probabilities W(y₁,y₂|x₁,x₂) on nonempty finite alphabets X₁,X₂,Y₁,Y₂, with nonnegative entries summing to one over outputs for each input pair. Given these inputs and the entire prior history, the output pair is drawn according to W. Node 1 estimates M₂ from (M₁,Y₁^n), and node 2 estimates M₁ from (M₂,Y₂^n), using deterministic decoders. cards.definitions: Encode G with vertices {1,…,n}, n≥0, by n and its symmetric zero-diagonal n×n binary adjacency matrix; encode k, a and b as signed or unsigned binary integers as appropriate. For m≥1, the strong power G^⊠m has vertex set {1,…,n}^m. Distinct tuples x,y are adjacent exactly when, for every coordinate j, either x_j=y_j or {x_j,y_j} is an edge of G. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; α(H) is its maximum cardinality, with α of the graph with no vertices equal to zero. Define Θ(G)=sup_{m≥1} α(G^⊠m)^(1/m). For nonempty G the supremum equals the limit as m→∞, and 1≤Θ(G)≤n; set Θ(G)=0 when n=0. The desired output approximates Θ itself, not its logarithm. The same machine must work for all graphs and precision requests, with no oracle or graph-dependent advice. It may use arbitrarily much finite time and memory on each input.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a single algorithm and proves termination and the stated absolute-error bound for every valid graph and precision. A negative answer proves that no such uniform algorithm exists. Hardness of exact independent-set computation, failure of a particular approximation scheme, or failure of any finite power to attain the limit does not by itself answer this computability question.

context_blocks.title: Zero-error communication as a graph
context_blocks.text: Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

context_blocks.title: Why longer blocks matter
context_blocks.text: A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity √5. For nonempty graphs, log₂Θ(G) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

context_blocks.title: A limit needs an effective error guarantee
context_blocks.text: Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

context_blocks.title: Recent progress and the scope of the question
context_blocks.text: The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of C₇ is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given a finite family F of finite simple graphs, decides whether induced-F-freeness admits a one-sided dense-model tester sampling at most C·ε^{−c} vertices, for some constants C,c depending only on F?
cards.definitions: The input to the classification algorithm is a finite list of adjacency matrices; the empty list is allowed. Let P_F contain exactly the finite simple graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of F. For an n-vertex graph G, define dist(G,P_F) as the minimum number of edge additions or deletions needed to obtain a graph in P_F on the same vertex set, divided by n²; define the distance as +∞ when no such graph exists. For an integer s, the canonical tester chooses a uniformly random subset S of min{n,s} distinct vertices, queries all adjacencies in S, and rejects exactly when G[S] contains an induced member of F. Say that F is polynomially testable if there are integers C,c≥1 such that for every rational ε∈(0,1), every n≥1 and every G with dist(G,P_F)>ε, this tester with s=⌈Cε^{−c}⌉ rejects with probability at least 2/3. It automatically accepts every graph in P_F. The requested deterministic classification algorithm must halt on every finite F and answer YES exactly for these families. No runtime bound on that classification algorithm is imposed, and it need not output the constants C,c. Graph order n and accuracy ε are universally quantified in the property being classified; they are not additional inputs to the classification algorithm.

cards.why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

context_blocks.text: The source survey asks for a characterization of finite forbidden-induced-subgraph families whose canonical sample complexity is polynomial in inverse accuracy. To make the requested output unambiguous, this card fixes an effective classification question: can that class of finite inputs be decided at all? This additional effectiveness requirement is an editorial specification, rather than wording attributed to the survey. It distinguishes the target from an equivalent reformulation involving another unresolved infinite condition.

There are two separate computational tasks. Given a fixed family F and a particular finite graph, exact membership in P_F can be checked by searching for its finitely many forbidden patterns. The question here concerns a statement about every possible host graph and arbitrarily small ε. Finite decidability of each individual membership test does not by itself provide a decision procedure for the existence of uniform polynomial sampling bounds.

The dense-model normalization matters. Being ε-far means that a positive ε fraction of all possible vertex pairs must be changed, up to the fixed normalization factor. It does not mean that an ε fraction of the edges currently present must be removed. A sparse graph can therefore be close to a property even when many of its own edges would need modification. No bounded-degree or sparse-input model is implicit.

One-sided error gives rejection a concrete witness: the sampled vertices contain a forbidden induced graph. For an induced copy, both edges and nonedges must agree with the pattern. Thus a four-clique contains an ordinary four-cycle as a subgraph, but no induced four-cycle. Replacing induced copies with arbitrary copies changes the classification problem substantially.

The general hereditary testing theorem guarantees some sample bound depending only on ε, but that bound can be much larger than every polynomial. For finite F, inspecting all pairs in a sample squares its size, which preserves the distinction between polynomial and nonpolynomial dependence. Since F is fixed during testing, exhaustive checking inside the sample also has a fixed polynomial exponent, although that exponent need not be uniform across families.

Gishboliner–Shapira prove a useful sufficient condition: a finite family containing a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph is polynomially testable. Here co-bipartite means a union of two cliques, and split means a partition into a clique and an independent set; the three roles may be played by the same graph. Their necessary condition requires a bipartite and a co-bipartite member, but this is not sufficient.

The gap between these conditions is real. There are finite families containing a bipartite and a co-bipartite graph that are not polynomially testable. Conversely, split graphs themselves form a polynomially testable class, described by forbidding C₄, its complement and C₅, although none of those forbidden graphs is split. Thus simply promoting either known condition to an equivalence would give wrong answers on known examples.
Even a singleton family remains instructive. Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability for cographs, which are precisely graphs with no induced four-vertex path.
Induced C₄-freeness and its complement remain the exceptional cases identified in the 2025 survey.
Gishboliner–Shapira obtain a single-exponential sample bound for induced C₄-freeness; that improves substantially on regularity-based bounds but is not polynomial in 1/ε.

An August 2026 preprint by Carenini–Seth–Yoshida gives a new quantitative characterization using ordered containers. Roughly, property-satisfying induced subgraphs inside a graph far from the property must fit into smaller vertex sets determined by short fingerprints. Theorem 1.4 translates between tester bounds and these container parameters by explicit polynomial transformations. This is relevant new progress beyond the survey.

Its effectiveness has a specific meaning: given suitable quantitative bounds on one side, the theorem supplies bounds on the other. The container premise still ranges over all sufficiently large host graphs and all accuracy parameters. The inspected theorem does not give a terminating procedure that takes only F and decides whether polynomial container parameters exist. It therefore does not establish the effective finite-family classification asked here.

The distinction is useful independently of how the eventual classification looks. An affirmative answer would provide a finite method for recognizing when global violations must have abundant small witnesses. An undecidability theorem would show that no universal terminating rule can perform this recognition from arbitrary finite forbidden lists, even though each list defines a straightforward graph-membership problem. Either outcome would identify a fundamental limit of turning qualitative testing theorems into systematic algorithm design.

cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: For every isomorphism-invariant property P of finite simple graphs with P_n nonempty for every n≥1, does existence of a uniform randomized tester using polynomially many queries in 1/ε, independently of n, imply existence of such an additive-ε distance estimator, in the dense model defined below?
cards.definitions: P_n is a nonempty subset of graphs on [n], invariant under vertex permutations. For n≥2, dist(G,P)=min_{H∈P_n}|E(G)△E(H)|/binom(n,2); for n=1 it is zero. An algorithm receives n and an integer t≥2, with ε=1/t, and accesses G only by adaptive queries asking whether a specified unordered pair is an edge. A tester returns a bit, accepts each G∈P_n with probability ≥2/3 and rejects each G with dist(G,P)≥ε with probability ≥2/3; no condition is imposed between those cases. Polynomial testability means there exist one probabilistic Turing oracle machine and constants C,a≥1 with at most Ct^a adjacency queries on every input and every execution. An estimator is another such uniform machine and constants C′,b≥1, using at most C′t^b queries and returning a binary-encoded rational q with Pr[|q−dist(G,P)|≤1/t]≥2/3 for every G. Computation between queries and total output length have no prescribed bound, but every execution terminates. Coins are independent fair bits; programs and constants may depend on P and cannot depend on n,t or G. Neither algorithm receives a description of P or graph-dependent advice. This asks only the polynomial-testability implication named in the title. The stronger quantitative q_P(poly(ε)) conversion in source Problem 5.4 is not asserted equivalent to it.

cards.why: Separates recognizing a robust violation from measuring its magnitude and asks whether polynomially efficient dense-graph testing automatically provides polynomial distance estimation.

importance.reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.

cards.review_note: The former short index record is upgraded to the precise Problem 5.4 formulation from the 2025 survey. The exponent c is a normalization of q_P(poly(ε)); the dense-model distance and query quantifiers are explicit.

context_blocks.text: Testing asks only for a robust decision: accept graphs in the property and reject graphs that are ε-far from it. Estimation asks for the actual distance to the property, so it must distinguish every pair of nearby distance scales rather than only the two extremes used by a tester.

In the dense graph model the input has Θ(n²) possible adjacency queries, yet many properties can be tested with a number of samples depending only on ε. The central quantitative issue is whether this efficiency survives when the algorithm must estimate distance rather than detect a large violation.

Known reductions convert a tester into an estimator with very large overhead. The 2025 survey of polynomial property testing records an explicit open problem asking whether q_P(ε) can be replaced by q_P(poly(ε)); for polynomial testers this would yield a polynomial estimator. Existing results establish the implication only with exponential or otherwise much larger transformations in general.

Some important classes already have polynomial estimators, including selected hereditary partition properties and several induced-subgraph examples. Such positive cases show that the gap is not caused by a universal information-theoretic obstruction, but they do not give the transformation for every graph property.

The question is about query complexity in the dense model. A result in the bounded-degree model, a computational-time bound after reading the full graph, or a tester that estimates only whether the distance is above one fixed threshold addresses a different problem.

references.title: Sublinear.info
references.locator: Problem 41

cards.definitions: The graph is a finite loopless directed graph with vertex set {1,…,n}; opposite arcs are allowed, but parallel copies of an arc are not. An oracle query specifies a vertex v, a direction IN or OUT, and an index i∈{1,…,d}; it returns the ith neighbor in that direction or a null symbol if the slot is empty. Lists are consistent with one fixed graph and have arbitrary fixed order, so correctness must hold for every permitted ordering. Vertex labels, n,d and ε are given to the tester; it may choose any vertex label, use independent fair random bits, and adapt future queries to previous answers. Internal computation is not charged to query complexity. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices v₁,…,v_k, k≥2, with arcs v_i→v_(i+1) and v_k→v₁; acyclic means no such cycle exists. Let τ(G) be the minimum number of arcs whose deletion makes G acyclic. An input is ε-far if τ(G)>εdn. Additions cannot remove cycles, so this agrees with the minimum-edge-edit convention for this property. The tester must accept each acyclic graph with probability at least 2/3 and reject each ε-far graph with probability at least 2/3. There is no guarantee for graphs between these cases. Q is the least integer query bound attainable on all n-vertex inputs and all random branches by a randomized query procedure with these guarantees. An upper-bound family must be generated by a uniform algorithm from n,d and the binary encoding of rational ε; there is no running-time requirement beyond termination. The requested Θ bounds concern growth in n, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed d and ε. One-sided error, which must always accept acyclic inputs, is a separate restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic bound F(n,d,ε), a uniform tester using O(F) queries, and a matching Ω(F) lower bound for the same adaptive two-sided, bidirectional model, for each fixed d,ε in the stated range. Hidden constants may depend on d,ε, but no factor growing with n may be left unmatched. The source’s broad best-algorithm question is made precise here as optimal query complexity; total runtime is not the cost being classified.

context_blocks.title: A local test of a global obstruction

context_blocks.title: One cycle is not necessarily far from acyclic
context_blocks.text: A directed cycle on n vertices becomes acyclic after deleting one arc. Its normalized distance is 1/(dn), so for fixed positive ε and large n it is outside the promised far case. Property testing asks for reliable rejection only when many arc deletions are unavoidable.

cards.title: A dimension-free directed L¹ Poincaré inequality
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant C<∞ such that, for every integer n≥1 and every Lipschitz function f:[0,1]ⁿ→ℝ, d₁^mono(f) ≤ C ∫_[0,1]ⁿ (Σ_{i=1}^n max{−∂ᵢf(x),0}²)^{1/2} dx? Here d₁^mono(f) is the L¹ distance to the coordinatewise nondecreasing functions. The same C must work for every dimension and every finite Lipschitz constant.
cards.why: Would connect local directional decreases to global distance from monotonicity with a universal constant, extending a central isoperimetric principle to real-valued functions on continuous cubes.

references.title: Directed Poincaré Inequalities and L¹ Monotonicity Testing of Lipschitz Functions
references.locator: Conjecture 1.8; PDF page 7

cards.definitions: Lebesgue measure on [0,1]ⁿ has total mass one. A function g:[0,1]ⁿ→ℝ is coordinatewise nondecreasing if g(x)≤g(y) whenever xᵢ≤yᵢ for all i. Define d₁^mono(f)=inf_g ∫|f(x)−g(x)|dx, over measurable integrable coordinatewise nondecreasing g; g need not have the same Lipschitz constant as f. A function f is Lipschitz if there is a finite L with |f(x)−f(y)|≤L‖x−y‖₂ for all x,y in the cube. Its gradient exists almost everywhere; its values on the exceptional null set may be set to zero without changing any integral. The negative gradient is ∇⁻f(x)=(max{−∂₁f(x),0},…,max{−∂ₙf(x),0}). The right-hand side is C·E[‖∇⁻f(X)‖₂] for a uniform point X in the cube. It is not C·(E[‖∇⁻f(X)‖₂²])^{1/2}. No boundary condition, mean-zero assumption or fixed bound on the range of f is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed inequality with one universal finite C, or refute the existence of such a C by showing that the ratio d₁^mono(f)/E‖∇⁻f‖₂ is unbounded across the stated functions and dimensions (including a function with positive distance and zero denominator, if one existed). A bound whose constant grows with n, or a bound using the L² norm of the gradient over the cube, is insufficient.

cards.title: Sample complexity of uniformity testing with less than one stored sample
cards.formal: Determine the minimum sample count q*(n,ε,m) for one-pass uniformity testing with m bits of persistent memory, including when this count is infinite, in the scarce-memory regime m=o(max{log₂ n,log₂(1/ε)}). Here n≥2 is an integer, 0<ε<1, and m≥1 is an integer. The tester receives independent samples from an unknown distribution P on [n], must accept P=Uₙ with probability at least 3/4, and must reject every P with ‖P−Uₙ‖₁≥ε with probability at least 3/4. The central case in the source is fixed ε and m=o(log n); the displayed wider regime is its explicit extension for small ε. Determine matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds up to universal constant factors in sample count throughout the stated regime.
cards.why: Would locate the statistical power of streaming computation below the memory needed to retain one observation and determine whether extra samples can compensate for this severe storage restriction.
cards.status_note: Checked the complete 2019, 2021 and 2022 papers, including the later paper’s explicit distinction between time-varying and time-invariant updates. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated time-varying scarce-memory sample tradeoff; this is not an exhaustive current-status certification.

progress.text: The original streaming work poses the existence of uniformity testers using o(log n) bits.

cards.definitions: Write [n]={1,…,n}, Uₙ(j)=1/n, and ‖P−Uₙ‖₁=Σⱼ₌₁ⁿ|P(j)−1/n|. A tester with horizon q is a layered randomized streaming machine: after t samples its state M_t lies in a set of at most 2^m possibilities. An initial state or initial state distribution is fixed independently of P. At step t its new state is chosen using only M_{t−1}, the current sample X_t and fresh independent randomness. The transition kernel may depend on t,n,ε,m,q, but not on P. After exactly q samples it outputs a Boolean decision from M_q, possibly with fresh randomness. Every item of retained information, including retained random bits, belongs to the state; past samples cannot be revisited. The current input symbol is available for the transition without first being copied into persistent memory. Transition tables, the layer index and computation between arrivals are not charged as extra memory; no uniform construction-time or running-time bound is imposed. This is the time-varying information-theoretic streaming convention, not a single fixed transition rule forced to store its own clock. Probability is over the independent sample stream and all tester randomness. q* is the least nonnegative integer q admitting such a tester, and is ∞ if no finite q works. The source’s little-o regime means parameter sequences with n→∞ and m/max{log₂ n,log₂(1/ε)}→0; constants in the requested sample bounds do not depend on those parameters. No correctness promise is imposed at intermediate distances 0<‖P−Uₙ‖₁<ε.
cards.answer_criterion: Characterize exactly which parameter sequences in the stated scarce-memory regime permit finite-sample testing and give a sample bound with a matching lower bound up to constant factors there. cards.definitions: Let n≥1, 1≤k≤n and ε∈(0,1). A function f:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} is a k-junta if some J⊆[n], |J|≤k, and g:{0,1}ᴶ→{0,1} satisfy f(x)=g(x_J) for every x. Let J_{n,k} be the class of all such functions. For a distribution D on {0,1}ⁿ, dist_D(f,J_{n,k})=min_{g∈J_{n,k}}Pr_{X∼D}[f(X)≠g(X)]. The target function and D are fixed before the randomized test. The source supplies a membership oracle returning f(x) on any chosen x and a sample oracle returning a fresh independent X∼D. The tester is given n,k,ε but no explicit description of D. It must accept if f∈J_{n,k}, reject if dist_D(f,J_{n,k})≥ε, and may behave arbitrarily between these cases. Probability is over its random bits and sample-oracle draws. Two-sided error is allowed; the separate one-sided question is not imposed here. In a batch of membership queries, all queried strings are chosen before any values from that batch are revealed; later batches may depend on earlier answers. A constant-round bound requires some fixed integer r independent of n,k,ε,f,D, and poly(k/ε) requires fixed C,b with worst-case charged cost at most C(k/ε)ᵇ. Which calls are charged and whether an initial labeled-sample phase counts toward r must still be fixed. Obtaining a label from the source’s unlabeled oracle requires a membership query. In contrast, the 2018 oracle returns (X,f(X)) directly, charges that sample and permits a nonadaptive membership batch to depend on all initial labeled samples. These conventions are explicitly distinguished; the card does not identify them without a resource-preserving argument. There is no requested bit-operation running-time bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Recover a consistent sample-cost and adaptation-round convention from the source question and its underlying testing model. A uniform-distribution tester or a tester with a number of rounds growing with k does not answer the intended distribution-free constant-round question.

cards.title: Quadratic advantage of MA over AM proofs of proximity
cards.formal: Does there exist a family Π of finite-input properties admitting a Merlin–Arthur proof of proximity (MAP) of complexity O(√n) at every fixed positive proximity parameter, but for which every Arthur–Merlin proof of proximity (AMP) has complexity Ω(n) at some fixed positive proximity parameter ε₀? Here n is the full input-table length in bits and complexity is proof length plus input bits read. More precisely, ask for Π, a rational constant ε₀∈(0,1/2), and one MAP verifier V such that for every fixed rational ε∈(0,1) there are Cε,Nε with p_V(n)+q_V(n,ε)≤Cε√n for all admissible n≥Nε. For every AMP verifier W for Π there must be c_W>0,N_W such that p_W(n,ε₀)+q_W(n,ε₀)≥c_W n for every admissible n≥N_W. Neither bound hides factors growing with n. The same family and the same distance notion are used on both sides.
cards.why: Would determine whether keeping verifier randomness private achieves the largest possible advantage in minimally interactive verification of large inputs. The comparison isolates the information revealed to a prover while keeping proof length, input access and error requirements comparable.

cards.definitions:
To cover the source’s function properties, a candidate specifies an infinite decidable set I of admissible bit lengths, and, uniformly from n∈I, positive integers m(n),b(n) with m(n)b(n)=n and a finite alphabet Σ_n⊆{0,1}^{b(n)} of at least two symbols. An input is a table x∈Σ_n^{m(n)}, equivalently a function [m(n)]→Σ_n, and Π_n is a nonempty subset of these tables. The family and its finite alphabet descriptions must be mathematically specified; no polynomial-time membership test for Π is required. Boolean strings are the case b=1,m=n. Distance is Δ(x,Π_n)=min_{y∈Π_n}|{j:x_j≠y_j}|/m(n), the fraction of differing table entries, not the fraction of differing bits inside their symbols. A NO input has Δ>ε; members are YES inputs; no verdict is required for nonmembers with Δ≤ε. A query chooses j and reads x_j, charging b(n) bits. Queries may depend on the proof and on earlier answers. This is ordinary oracle access, not independent sampling, proof-oblivious access or a distribution-testing model. All n-asymptotics range over I.

A verifier is one finite, uniform oracle algorithm for the whole family, given n and rational ε∈(0,1) explicitly. It halts on every input, proof and random tape; it uses a finite computably bounded number of independent fair bits for each n,ε. Local computation and random bits are not charged and have no polynomial-time restriction. The prover knows the entire input and is computationally unrestricted. Proofs are binary strings of the specified length; shorter proofs may be padded, and oversized strings can be rejected without querying the input. Cost counts the whole permitted proof length, even if the verifier reads fewer proof bits. Query bounds hold for all inputs, proofs and randomness, not only in expectation.

For an MAP, the prover sends w before the verifier uses private randomness r. Completeness requires, for every n and x∈Π_n, a single w of length p(n), independent of ε and r, such that Pr_r[V^x(n,ε,w;r)=1]≥2/3 for every rational ε∈(0,1). Soundness requires Pr_r[V^x(n,ε,w;r)=1]≤1/3 for every allowed w when Δ(x,Π_n)>ε. For an AMP the verifier first reveals its entire random tape r, independently of the input; the prover then sends w=w(x,n,ε,r) of length p(n,ε). The verifier has no private or subsequently hidden coins and is deterministic given r. Completeness is Pr_r[∃w:W^x(n,ε,w;r)=1]≥2/3 for every member; soundness is Pr_r[∃w:W^x(n,ε,w;r)=1]≤1/3 for every ε-far input. cards.title: Private PAC sample complexity from VC and Littlestone dimensions
cards.formal: Is there a universal polynomial p such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class C on a finite nonempty domain X admits a realizable, possibly improper PAC learner using some number $m\le p(1+\mathrm{VC}(C),1+\log^*\mathrm{LD}(C))$ of independent labeled examples, with error at most 1/10 and confidence at least 9/10, while satisfying $(1,1/(100m^2))$-differential privacy? The learning guarantee must hold for every distribution on the domain and every target concept in C. Computation time is unrestricted. Take both dimensions to be at least one; constant classes can be handled separately.
cards.why: The problem seeks a privacy analogue of a foundational characterization theorem in learning theory.

context_blocks.text: VC dimension characterizes nonprivate learning. Finite Littlestone dimension $\mathrm{LD}$ characterizes the existence of private learning but does not determine its optimal quantitative cost.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. Two classes can have the same ordinary capacity measure while differing in how difficult it is to hide the influence of an individual training example.

The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. The proposed relation asks whether the extra price of privacy can be controlled by ordinary statistical complexity together with a very slowly growing function of online-learning complexity.

cards.definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to {0,1}. VC(C) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. LD(C) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record. Here X is finite, distributions on X are arbitrary probability vectors, and a learner is a probability kernel from length-m labeled samples to the finite set {0,1}^X of hypotheses. The sample size m is a positive integer chosen for C before the target and distribution. For every target h∈C and distribution D on X, with probability at least 9/10 over m independent draws x_i from D and learner randomness, the returned hypothesis has D-probability of disagreement with h at most 1/10. Privacy holds for all labeled samples, including unrealizable ones, and all subsets E of the hypothesis set. The same kernel and m work for all D,h. This finite-domain convention retains the finite-class target: points in an arbitrary domain with the same label vector (h(x))_{h∈C} can be identified, giving at most 2^|C| cells and preserving both dimensions. A learner on those cells lifts to the original domain. No running-time or computable-representation requirement is imposed.

cards.definitions: For an integer T≥2, a mechanism is a family of Borel probability distributions M_x on ℝ^T, one for each binary stream x∈{0,1}^T. Its output Y_t is released immediately after observing x_t. Causality means that whenever x and x′ have the same first t bits, the marginal distributions of (Y₁,…,Y_t) under M_x and M_x′ are equal. The horizon T is known before the first output. Streams are fixed inputs, not adaptively chosen in response to outputs. Neighbors differ in exactly one bit, and pure privacy requires M_x(S)≤exp(1/2)M_x′(S) for every pair of neighbors and every Borel S⊆ℝ^T. This protects the entire joint transcript, with no additive failure allowance. There is no restriction on computation, memory, real precision, output integrality or monotonicity; internal randomness may be correlated across times. A different family of probability distributions may be chosen for each T. The maximum over streams is outside the expectation; the maximum over time is inside it. The infimum is used without assuming attainment. E(T) is finite, for example because a data-independent all-zero transcript has error at most T. All logarithms in asymptotic comparisons may use any fixed base greater than one.

context_blocks.text: Continual counting publishes a running total as events arrive. For the stream (1,0,1,1), the exact outputs are (1,1,2,3). Changing its second bit gives (1,1,1,1) and exact outputs (1,2,3,4): one protected event changes several releases. Privacy must therefore hold for the whole visible transcript. Separate guarantees for isolated timestamps do not establish the stated joint guarantee.

The causal requirement forbids using future events to improve earlier releases. It also concerns their joint distribution, not merely the marginal law of each single output; otherwise correlations among old outputs could reveal future data. The offline query-release problem may inspect the complete database before producing any answer and consequently asks for a different capability.

The order of maximum and expectation is central. Imagine an error vector that equals one at a single uniformly random timestamp and zero elsewhere. Its expected maximum is one, but the largest expected absolute error at any predetermined timestamp is only 1/T. This example concerns error criteria, not a proposed private mechanism. Squared-error bounds and average-over-time bounds also cannot be substituted without checking the conversion.

For the fixed privacy budget here, the July 2026 Bairaktari–Larsen result gives the lower benchmark Ω(log^{3/2}T), while the best upper bound summarized in their Table 1 is O(log²T). The binary-tree mechanism aggregates intervals and reuses their noisy counts across prefixes. The paper closes the dependence on T for approximate privacy at fixed parameters, but its pure-privacy row retains the square-root-of-logarithm gap.

Arkhipov and Kalinin improve constants for mean and maximum per-coordinate squared error using matrix mechanisms. Those criteria take expectations before choosing the worst coordinate, or average squared errors. Improving them is useful, but does not by itself determine the expected largest absolute error of the entire transcript.

Bhowmik and Hasan’s August revision claims tight squared-error order for arbitrary real factorizations within Laplace matrix mechanisms. It explicitly excludes expected maxima and unrestricted non-matrix mechanisms. Thus even accepting its claimed theorem would not settle this card’s minimax quantity.

Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff independently give a near-optimal lower bound for a prefix-matrix factorization cost. Its quantification is over factorizations, while this card allows every causal private output distribution. The distinction remains essential when reading a result advertised as optimal for a class of mechanisms.

A matching order for E(T) would identify the unavoidable worst-time accuracy cost of a basic continually released statistic under pure privacy. The target is a minimax information bound: it does not additionally ask for an efficient implementation or restrict the form of a candidate mechanism.

cards.answer_criterion: Determine an asymptotic rate g(T) and prove constants c,C>0 and T₀ such that c g(T)≤E(T)≤C g(T) for every T≥T₀. The upper guarantee must be achievable by permitted causal pure-private mechanisms, and the lower guarantee must cover all such mechanisms. Constants may not depend on T. The expected maximum absolute-error criterion must be the same on both sides.

cards.title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer C≥1, a function α:N_{≥2}→[0,1] with lim_{d→∞}α(d)=0, a uniform randomized mechanism M and a uniform deterministic evaluator E, such that for every d≥2 and every database D∈({0,1}^d)^n with n=d^C, M runs in time polynomial in n,d, satisfies (1,1/(100n²))-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite synopsis S for which, with probability at least 2/3, E(S,q) approximates q(D) within α(d) simultaneously for every marginal query q?
cards.definitions: A marginal query is a pair (J,a), where J⊆{1,…,d} and a∈{0,1}^J, and q_{J,a}(D)=|{i∈{1,…,n}:D_{ij}=a_j for all j∈J}|/n. The empty J query has value one. Queries of every order up to d are included. The database is an explicitly stored ordered n-by-d bit matrix; neighbouring databases have the same dimensions and differ in exactly one row. Differential privacy means that for every ordered pair of neighbours D,D′ and every set O of output strings, Pr[M(D)∈O]≤e·Pr[M(D′)∈O]+1/(100n²). M uses independent fair random bits and has one worst-case polynomial bound p(n+d) on bit operations, output length and random bits. Its output is a finite binary string S. E receives d,S,J,a, has a worst-case bound given by one polynomial in d+|S| and outputs a binary-encoded rational number. E has no access to D, private state of M or an additional oracle. Both algorithms are ordinary classical Turing machines, with no nonuniform advice. The accuracy event is simultaneous over all queries and its probability is over M’s randomness alone, separately for every D. Low-order marginals describe small groups of attributes, while all marginals permit every such pattern. The family contains exponentially many queries even though one query has a short description. A synopsis is therefore an efficiently evaluable representation, rather than a literal list of exponentially many answers.

Privacy and accuracy quantify different objects. The privacy guarantee compares the complete output distributions after changing one person’s row. Accuracy concerns all queries simultaneously on each fixed database. Once a successful synopsis has been released, its deterministic evaluation reveals no additional access to the original records. An algorithm answering only a prespecified small batch is not automatically an algorithm for this target.

Vadhan’s Open Problem 7.8 asks about polynomial-time private estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error using only polynomially many rows in the dimension. Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give subexponential-time private algorithms for marginal queries on small databases. Their result illustrates useful progress between exponential and polynomial cost. The constant-accuracy, per-query statement in that paper does not provide the polynomial-time, vanishing-error synopsis required here.

Requiring synthetic records would impose an extra restriction. The benchmark permits any binary synopsis with an efficient evaluator, because hardness of synthetic-data generation need not rule out other ways of answering queries. The existing TCS-0506 concerns private PAC sample complexity, while TCS-6040 asks about strong approximation of coverage functions. Neither asks this computational query-release question.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every pair of fixed finite relational structures A,B of the same finite signature, with a homomorphism A→B, is the decision promise problem of distinguishing I→A from I↛B either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions?
cards.definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols R with fixed positive arities a_R. A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and, for each R, a relation R^A⊆A^{a_R}. A homomorphism h:I→A is a map on domains such that (v₁,…,v_a)∈R^I implies (h(v₁),…,h(v_a))∈R^A for every R and tuple. The templates A,B and their relations are fixed for each computational problem. Only I varies; its domain and relation tuples are explicitly listed in binary, of total length L. The algorithm must accept all I admitting a homomorphism to A and reject all I admitting no homomorphism to B. On I→B but I↛A, either answer is allowed. A→B makes the yes and no sets disjoint. Polynomial time means one deterministic algorithm for the fixed pair, halting on every input in O(L^c), with c and hidden constants allowed to depend on A,B. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time map from 3-SAT formulas φ to structures I_φ such that satisfiable φ yield I_φ→A and unsatisfiable φ yield I_φ↛B. The question is about deciding the promise, not producing a B-valued assignment. No uniform algorithm for classifying templates is required. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

references.authors: Demian Banakh; Alexey Barsukov; Tamio-Vesa Nakajima

cards.status_note: Open classification question in the cited survey, with relevant partial results checked through 10 September 2026. The card asks for an unconditional decision dichotomy over all fixed finite template pairs; it does not assume decision/search equivalence or a complete algebraic classification.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary constraint satisfaction asks whether a collection of local requirements can all hold simultaneously. Promise CSPs keep two versions of each requirement: the input is guaranteed to admit a solution satisfying the stronger version, while the relaxed task uses the weaker one. For graph colouring, A=Kₖ and B=K_c with k≤c produces the decision task of distinguishing k-colourable graphs from graphs that are not c-colourable. Graphs in between impose no decision requirement.

When A=B, the promise disappears. Bulatov and Zhuk independently proved in 2017 that every finite-template CSP is either in P or NP-complete. The present question asks whether a comparable exclusion of intermediate complexity survives arbitrary finite promises. It does not follow merely by applying the classical theorem to A and B separately: the relaxed task can be easier than either endpoint CSP.

A concrete tractable example promises that each listed triple of Boolean variables can have exactly one 1 and asks only for a not-all-equal assignment. Solve the equations x+y+z=1 over the integers, then map positive values to 1 and nonpositive values to 0. No such triple can become all zero or all one. Barto proves that this tractability cannot be explained by sandwiching the pair through a tractable finite-domain CSP, unless P=NP. Finite templates can therefore need an infinite intermediate domain in this natural algorithmic framework.

The algebraic approach studies operations that combine several A-solutions coordinatewise into one B-solution. These polymorphisms capture useful structure for algorithms and reductions, but their input and output domains can differ, preventing the direct use of all the composition arguments available in ordinary CSP. The survey emphasizes that a full dichotomy was not yet backed by enough evidence to be asserted as a settled consensus conjecture; this card poses it as a precise open question.

Important subclasses are classified. Brakensiek and Guruswami obtain a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise CSPs allowing negations, with tractable cases going beyond a direct reuse of Schaefer’s classical Boolean CSP classification. That theorem does not classify all Boolean templates or all finite domains.

The 2026 work of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima expands the logical viewpoint by relating Promise MMSNP to finite-domain PCSPs. It also classifies a family defined by forbidden monochromatic cliques under the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture. Both the restricted family and the additional assumption matter: this is not an unconditional classification of every finite template pair.

cards.title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
cards.formal: For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous structure A over a finite relational signature, and every finite-signature first-order reduct B of A, is CSP(B) either decidable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed finite arities. A is homogeneous if every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of A. It is finitely bounded if there is a finite set F of finite structures in its signature such that a finite structure embeds into A exactly when none of the structures in F embeds into it; embeddings preserve both relations and their complements. Countable allows finite or countably infinite domains. B has the same domain as A, with finitely many relations each definable by a first-order formula over A without parameters; it may forget original relations and introduce definable ones. For each fixed B, an input to CSP(B) is an explicitly encoded finite structure I in B’s signature. Accept exactly when there is a map h from the domain of I to that of B preserving every relation tuple. Equivalently, a finite conjunction of atomic B-constraints must have a satisfying assignment. h need not be injective. A, B and their defining formulas are fixed, not part of the input; running times are measured in the finite instance’s bit length. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

context_blocks.text: The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers (ℚ;<) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare P/NP-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.

cards.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
cards.formal: Is there a fixed integer C≥3 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph G promised to be 3-colourable, outputs a proper vertex colouring using at most C colours with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly given graph G=([n],E), n≥1, with no loops or parallel edges, encoded by its adjacency matrix. A proper k-colouring is a map c:[n]→[k] such that c(u)≠c(v) for every {u,v}∈E. The promise is existence of a proper 3-colouring; such a colouring is not supplied. There must be one C, one randomized Turing machine A, and fixed constants K,d such that A uses at most K(n+1)^d bit operations on every graph and every random tape. On each promised input, the probability, over independent unbiased internal random bits, of outputting a proper C-colouring is at least 2/3. Invalid outputs can be replaced by a failure symbol after checking all edges. No correctness requirement is imposed on non-3-colourable inputs, but the time bound still applies. The algorithm may colour such an input whenever it can; it need not recognize the promise. C is independent of n, degree, density and the input graph. No planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition promise is available. Randomization is explicitly permitted in this version of the inherited question; a deterministic algorithm would be a stronger positive result. The algorithm must colour every vertex and avoid every monochromatic edge on a successful run.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm for at least one fixed C, or prove that no such C and randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist. A growing colour bound, a partial colouring of most vertices, or a guarantee only on a restricted graph family is insufficient. NP-hardness of the 3-versus-C promise for every fixed C would establish the usual complexity-theoretic obstruction; excluding randomized algorithms from that obstruction additionally uses NP≠RP. Hardness for C=5 alone leaves all larger constants unresolved. Conditional hardness results must keep their assumptions explicit.
